“He saved six or seven people and he is still blaming himself, saying, ‘I couldn’t save my daughter’.”

The second victim was a 54-year-old woman.

News.title: The embarrassing before and after photos that left me feeling violated – and it could happen to anyone
News.content:
THE before and after photographs of Nicola Dexter’s weight loss journey are inspiring for anyone keen to lose a few pounds.

But there’s a sinister truth behind the images: Nicola has never been bigger than a slim size 10 and the ‘before’ picture has actually been doctored by scammers.





Scammers had crafted fake “before” shots of her as a plus-size model and coupled them with her real photographs, claiming she’d shed the pounds by taking their product, Pinkies.

Nicola said the convincing TikTok posts attracted scores of comments from people asking where they could buy the supposed treatment.

She said: “I was in shock that someone could take my image and make me look a certain way in order to make money.

“They’d made me look very overweight and blown up. What the hell?”





She added: “Some of the customers were asking – is this you? Did you used to look like that?

“I felt embarrassed. It’s my identity they’d stolen, and it’s not nice.

“I felt violated; like people were laughing at me.”

Her daughter, Antonia Dexter, 27, said: “It was so stressful. No matter how many times we reported it, it seemed like TikTok didn’t care.

“We were worried that they were promoting a drug that could have been anything.

“Her face was all over the internet.”



Nicola and Antonia run Style By Eleven, a mother-and-daughter clothing boutique based in Ossett, West Yorks.

They established the business around the covid pandemic and have since built-up a loyal following in their shop and online.

Nicola models the outfits while Antonia takes the photographs and manages the company’s online platform.

The pair had no idea theit images were being misused until a concerned customer sent them screenshots.

Antonia said: “We weren’t aware of the account. One of our customers reached out to us. They told us that they were using my mum’s pictures to promote this drug. We were shocked.

“Each post had loads of comments asking where they could buy the weight loss drug. We were really worried for the people who were interested in buying it.

“We didn’t want people to think that we were promoting it.”

Antonia believes the stolen photographs were manipulated using AI to enlarge her mum’s body.

The account then paired them with the original pictures and falsely claimed Nicola’s apparent transformation had been achieved using the weight-loss product.

It also linked to an external website where capsules and “food noise patches” could be purchased.



Antonia said: “We think they’ve taken the pictures from our Facebook page and have used AI to make her look overweight.

“Then they post an unedited picture of my mum saying that she’s used this weight loss drug with a caption saying it’s solved all her problems.

“It’s not a nice thing to see. She has thick skin and doesn’t take many things to heart, but when someone steals your images and changes what you look like to sell a product you’ve never heard of, it’s quite distressing.”

The family warned customers about the fake account and urged them to report it – but were told the posts did not breach TikTok’s guidelines.

Antonia spent five weeks filing reports and even submitted a ‘cease-and-desist’ form in a desperate attempt to remove the material.

They tried placing a watermark behind Nicola when taking new photographs, but the scammers cropped it out.

Antonia fears the scam could have damaged the family business if customers mistakenly believed it was promoting the products.

She said: “We still have no idea who was behind it. It could have damaged the business if customers genuinely thought it was us.

“I think there should be a law that comes in to protect people’s images against AI. These people have got away with what they did. There are no consequences for it.

“TikTok need to take action – because these images did look believable. It feels like TikTok are allowing people to scam others.”



It would appear Nicola was not the first victim of the bogus firm, with a number of other influencers sharing similar experiences and warning users about the company’s fake products.

TikTok has now removed the account. A spokesperson said: “We have banned this account for breaching our community guidelines.”

The Sun found no trace of the company on any platform.

The social media company said its rules prohibit users from infringing other people’s copyrights, trademarks and intellectual property rights.

It added that it does not permit content promoting risky weight-loss methods or harmful body comparisons, or the sale and promotion of regulated, prohibited or high-risk goods.

News.title: Lucy Letby inquiry - latest: Nurse's 'boyfriend' doctor 'put her before patients'
News.content:
Serial killer Letby, now 36, was convicted of killing seven babies - a scathing report has criticised the hospital where she worked and her 'boyfriend' doctor

An inquiry into the crimes of Lucy Letby, who was convicted of killing seven babies and attempting to murder seven more, has found three deaths could have been avoided if hospital staff had acted differently - and criticised her doctor "boyfriend".

A scathing report said there was a "complete failure to protect babies" at the Countess of Chester Hospital, where Letby, now 36, worked between 2015 and 2016.

The report found safeguarding action should have been taken after a doctor, named in the report as Dr ZA, disregarded an insulin test result for Baby F in August 2015. Had action been taken, the death of Baby I, a two-month-old girl who died in October 2015, would have been prevented.

It also found that, if Letby been moved off the ward following Baby I's death, the deaths of two of three triplet brothers who suffered unexplained collapses in June 2016 - Baby O and Baby P - would have been prevented. It would also have prevented attacks on babies G, H, J, K, L, M and N.

The inquiry found that Letby's doctor "boyfriend", consultant paediatrician Dr Mark Deakin, a colleague of the killer nurse at the hospital, had "blurred boundaries" and put his desire to help her above his duties to his patients.

Other findings included that senior nurses never accepted concerns from consultants about Letby were - or might be - justified, and there was a delay in senior management calling the police. Lady Justice Thirlwall, who chaired the inquiry, said the "lack of consideration shown to parents" by hospital management was "reprehensible".

Letby was found to have killed and harmed babies by injecting air into their blood, poisoning them with insulin and overfeeding them with milk.

News.title: Immigration shake-up will scupper Andy Burnham's national care service goal, nursing chiefs warn
News.content:
Immigration shake-up will scupper Andy Burnham's national care service goal, nursing chiefs warn

EXCLUSIVE: The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) has claimed plans to change indefinite leave to remain (ILR) rules amount to a 'betrayal' of migrant care workers, with the UK already one of the most restrictive places to move to

View 3 Images Shabana Mahmood is set to announce a final decision later this year (Image: Dan Kitwood/PA Wire)

Shabana Mahmood's sweeping immigration shake-up will scupper Andy Burnham's plans for a new National Care Service, nursing chiefs have warned.

‌



In a scathing report, the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) says proposals being weighed up by ministers amount to a "betrayal" of migrant nursing staff. Analysis carried out for the RCN found the UK already has one of the most restrictive sets of rules for settling nurses in the world - and this would get worse if the Home Secretary's reforms are passed.

‌



Ms Mahmood is weighing up measures that would see care workers from overseas forced to wait 15 years before qualifying for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) - up from its current level of five.

‌



This change would be applied retrospectively - meaning thousands of people already in the UK would be affected. Ms Mahmood, who argues settlement must be earned, told MPs on Tuesday that a final decision will come later this year.

Face scanning phone apps can now be used for age checks in pubs and clubs READ MORE :

View 3 Images Professor Nicola Ranger has called for the planned changes to be torn up (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

Professor Nicola Ranger, the RCN's general secretary, told The Mirror: "The Home Secretary must scrap these proposals and recognise they are entirely incompatible with building a thriving and stable National Care Service.

‌



"If she doesn't, our brilliant migrant colleagues will choose to leave for where they feel more welcome and supported. At a time when domestic nursing workforce growth has stalled, these proposals would be a disaster for any hope to successfully reform social care”.

Shortly after becoming PM, Andy Burnham pledged to finally fix the social care system after decades of failure. But the RCN has warned tens of thousands of care workers and nurses in the care sector will leave if settlement rules change.

New analysis carried out for the RCN found the UK would be an outlier if the settlement delay is brought in for care workers. In the US and Australia, skilled professionals like registered nurses are offered immediate permanent residency.

‌



In Canada, care workers can settle after 16 months, while New Zealand and Ireland have a two year wait. The UK is also the most expensive place to apply for permanent residency, with a cost of £3,029 per person.

The RCN has called on migrant health and social workers to be offered immediate ILR - with the processing cost reduced to £523. Prof Ranger said: "Migrant nursing staff hold our health and care system together and have built lives in our country and become part of our communities. The Home Secretary's proposals would amount to a betrayal by reneging on our commitment to them because it’s politically convenient and would make the UK a significant outlier internationally.

"The Home Secretary must scrap these proposals and recognise they are entirely incompatible with building a thriving and stable National Care Service. If she doesn't, our brilliant migrant colleagues will choose to leave for where they feel more welcome and supported. At a time when domestic nursing workforce growth has stalled, these proposals would be a disaster for any hope to successfully reform social care."

‌



View 3 Images Andy Burnham has pledged to finally fix Britain's broken social care system (Image: DOMINIQUE JACOVIDES-POOL/SIPA/Shutterstock)

It is estimated by Skills for Care that 38% of care workers and senior care workers, and 43% of registered nurses in adult social care are not British nationals.

Earlier this year an RCN survey found 60% of migrant care workers who do not have ILR said it is very likely extending the qualifying period would affect their decision to remain in the UK. This could mean up to 46,000 nursing staff are at risk of leaving, it said.

‌



Under current rules, those in the UK on health and care worker visas have no recourse to public funds - meaning they cannot claim benefits or council housing. Ms Mahmood said the changes are necessary because of years of high net migration, with 1.6million people forecast to qualify for ILR by 2030.

Other nations allow migrant nurses to claim benefits sooner - including Canada, which permits them to claim benefits immediately after being granted permanent residence. New Zealand and Ireland allow full access after two years, while in Australia this wait is between two and four years.

In the US access to means-tested benefits is permitted after five years. The RCN report said: "Nursing staff working on a visa in the UK already face an increased risk of financial distress due to their inability to access public funds. In cases of long-term sick leave, these staff may have no income at all as they have no recourse to means-tested ill-health benefits."

‌



It continues: "Whilst many comparable countries are moving to simplify and accelerate pathways to settlement for health and care workers, the UK is moving in the opposite direction. Instead of recognising their long-term contribution and valuing internationally educated nurses, the UK government’s proposals create additional barriers to staying in the UK, increase cost and uncertainty, and risk positioning the UK as an international outlier."

The Home Secretary faces calls to tear up plans to apply changes retrospectively, including for care workers. Earlier this year Angela Rayner - who returned to the Cabinet when Andy Burnham became PM - branded the move "un-British".

Addressing the cross-party Home Affairs Committee on Tuesday, Ms Mahmood said: "We're trying to do a proper piece of work where we have the right arrangement that strikes the right balance between our responsibilities to people who have come here to work, our recognition of the failures that we inherited as a government and also our need to do right by the people who are already here who pay for the systems we already rely on."

Article continues below

She said it is a long-standing principle that the rules migrants would have to abide by would be those in place when they apply for ILR. The Home Secretary stated: "The rules that apply to you are the rules that are in force at the point of your application, not when you arrived in the country."

A Home Office spokesman said: "Last November, we set out reforms to double the standard qualifying period for settlement to 10 years for most migrants, with shorter routes for those who contribute the most to the UK.

“Under the proposals, key public service workers, including doctors and nurses, may settle after five years. A consultation on elements of those reforms has now closed, and we will set out our response in due course."

News.title: Families 'will never know for sure' how many babies could have been saved if Lucy Letby had been stopped sooner
News.content:
Families 'will never know for sure' how many babies could have been saved if Lucy Letby had been stopped sooner

Publishing her Thirlwall Inquiry today at Liverpool town hall, Lady Justice Thirlwall said there was a "complete failure" to protect babies at the Countess of Chester Hospital where Lucy Letby worked

View 7 Images Families "will never know for sure" how many Lucy Letby victims could have lived (Image: Cheshire Constabulary/AFP via Ge)

Grieving families affected by killer nurse Lucy Letby "will never know for sure" how many babies could have been saved if the hospital acted sooner, an inquiry has found today.

‌



The Thirlwell Inquiry into the murders said: “It is clear that some babies would have been saved and some attacks would have been prevented if action was taken earlier.”

‌



Delivering her report at Liverpool town hall, Lady Justice Thirlwall found there was a "complete failure" to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. In a series of devastating findings, the inquiry suggested it was possible three babies may have lived if action against Letby had been taken sooner.

‌



Families say government must fully implement findings of inquiry into killer nurse Lucy Letby READ MORE :

View 7 Images Lady Justice Thirlwall published her report into the Lucy Letby murders (Image: Getty Images)

'No apology or action can undo what happened'

Newborn twins may not have died and five others harmed if she had been removed from the unit in October 2015 after the death of a baby, when corridor conversations about Letby began.

A third baby who died, a two-month-old girl, and two others who suffered unexplained collapses may also have been protected if a doctor had detected an earlier insulin poisoning in August that year, the report said.

‌



During the inquiry, Dr ZA said she “deeply regretted not recognising or flagging signs of deliberate harm saying it felt “so fantastical and unlikely”.

The Trust said today: “No apology or action can undo what happened at our hospital.”

View 7 Images Lucy Letby being quizzed by cops (Image: Cheshire Police)

‌



Jane Tomkinson, chief executive of the Countess Trust, said: “We are however truly sorry for the events that occurred in 2015 and 2016.

“We acknowledge the findings of the Thirlwall Report and will approach its recommendations with openness and a firm commitment to build on the progress we have already made in improving our hospital's governance, safety and culture since that time.”

She said they were a “different organisation” today but acknowledged there is “more to be done” adding: “What took place at the Countess of Chester Hospital NHS Foundation Trust in 2015 and 2016 and the impact it had on so many people will not be forgotten. We will always remember.”

‌



Letby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms after being convicted of the murder of seven babies and attempted murder of seven other newborns at the hospital in 2015-2016.

View 7 Images Thirlwall Inquiry report into Lucy Letby's crimes released at Liverpool Town Hall (Image: Eleanor Barlow/PA Wire)

‌



Yvette Cooper says government must act

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper described the report was thorough and devastating and said it was now the government’s responsibility to act.

She said: “At the heart of this inquiry have been 13 families who lost their newborn babies, or who saw them experience serious collapse or injury at the hospital 10 and 11 years ago.

She could not fathom the grief and pain of the parents and families and pointed to shocking failures at the hospital.

‌



Cooper added: “Worst of all, the trust repeatedly failed the parent. It failed to keep their beloved babies safe. For parents to be kept in the dark for years about what was happening is, as Lady Justice Thirlwall has said, reprehensible”

Addressing the families directly, she added: “On behalf of the government and the health service, I am profoundly sorry for the failures set out so clearly in this report, for the harm, distress and unthinkable loss for their families and for the failures to keep their babies safe.”

She said she had asked officials to urgently develop plans for cot cams, one of the key recommendations of the inquiry.

‌



View 7 Images Carla Duprey, solicitor for some of the families of several victims in the Lucy Letby case (Image: Getty Images)

'This cannot be allowed to happen again'

Lawyers for the families called for what they called “meaningful and lasting change”. Carla Duprey, from Bond Turner, said: “What matters now is that the findings are properly understood, that the recommendations receive the attention they deserve and that they lead to meaningful and lasting change.

‌



“For the families involved, the consequences have been life-changing and continue to this day.”

Richard Scorer, from Slater and Gordon, who acts for three families said: “The families I represent were looking for a clear analysis of what went wrong and strong recommendations to prevent this happening again. The report delivers both. Lady Thirlwall is clear that the police should have been informed in August 2015, not 18 months later, and that hospital managers misled the families and the trust failed in its duty of candour.”

He said the families welcomed the 17 recommendations made by the report, adding: “The challenge now is to ensure that recommendations are implemented without delay. Far too often public inquiry recommendations are left to gather dust. This cannot be allowed to happen again."

‌



View 7 Images Lucy Letby is arrested in connection to hospital murders (Image: Cheshire Police)

'This cannot be the end of the matter'

Tamlin Bolton, from Irwin Mitchell, representing the families of seven children, said: “Today will be an emotional day for many families, many of whom continue to live with the consequences of what happened.

“Lady Thirlwall’s report paints a damning picture of what happens when concerns over patient safety are not listened to and acted on. In her own words a dispiriting and at times shocking account of multiple and repeated failings by organisations and individuals.

‌



“Failing to escalate concerns, failing to appreciate the seriousness of the risk, failures in safeguarding, failures in governance and oversight, failures in the HR and whistleblowing process, failures in the interactions with external bodies.”

She added: “At the Countess of Chester, patient safety should have come first. It did not. The families recognise that no system can guarantee that deliberate criminal acts will never occur. But when concerns are raised about patient safety, they must be listened to, investigated properly and acted on without delay.

“The report today and the criticisms and failings highlighted in it cannot be the end of the matter. The families deserve more than expressions of regret and promises of change.”

‌



Management at the hospital was described as “dysfunctional” with behaviour that was “high-handed… and foolhardy” the report said.

Director of nursing, Alison Kelly, medical director, Ian Harvey and chief executive Tony Chambers, who were all named in the report, released a joint statement saying: “We are carefully reviewing the Thirlwall report and its recommendations. Given that there are a number of investigations under way, and that the work of the Criminal Cases Review Commission has not yet completed, it would be inappropriate for us to offer any further comment at this time. Our thoughts remain with the families affected by the tragic events that took place at the Countess of Chester Hospital.”

View 7 Images Lucy Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms (Image: Chester Standard / SWNS.com)

‌



The Care Quality Commission admitted it failed to be “sufficiently investigative and inquiring” when it came to the Countess.

Dr Toli Onon, the chief inspector of hospitals, said the regulator was "truly sorry" and will play its part in implementing the recommendations.

She said: “Our 2016 inspection of Countess of Chester Hospital did not identify an increase in neonatal mortality. Crucial information was not shared by the hospital - however, what is also very clear is that we as the regulator did not take an approach which was sufficiently investigative and inquiring.”

‌



Cheshire Police said they would review the contents in light of their ongoing investigations.

The force has launched an investigation into the Countess of Chester Hospital focusing on the senior leadership and decision-making to determine whether any criminality has taken place concerning the response to the increased levels of fatalities.

Three members of the senior leadership team arrested on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter were bailed pending further enquiries.An individual was arrested and bailed on suspicion of perverting the course of justice

‌



A force spokesman said: “Our thoughts remain with the families of the babies – who have always been at the heart of this case.”

Letby’s case is currently being reviewed by the Criminal Cases Review Commission. Her barrister Mark McDonald said: “The reality of the Thirlwall Inquiry is that it has been conducted on the premise that an innocent woman is guilty of crimes she has not committed.

"Millions of pounds of taxpayers’ money have been spent on the inquiry, which would have been far better spent on addressing the UK’s broken neonatal system and providing equipment and support to wards across the country.

Article continues below

"Reports from over 30 world-leading experts now sit with the CCRC, and it is paramount that Ms. Letby’s case is referred to the Court of Appeal as a matter of extreme urgency.”

While the inquiry report was being published a small group gathered outside the town hall to protest in support of Letby.

News.title: Reform leader in Wales quits after being arrested
News.content:
Reform leader in Wales quits after being arrested

Politicians returned to Cardiff Bay today after the summer recess, but Dan Thomas failed to show up for the session, and has now announced his resignation as leader

View 2 Images Dan Thomas has stood down as leader after his arrest (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

Reform’s leader in Wales has stepped down after he was arrested on suspicion of controlling or coercive behaviour.

Dan Thomas was only named Welsh leader in February and led Reform to become the second largest party in the Senedd at an election in May, but has now quit in a fresh blow to Nigel Farage.

Politicians returned to Cardiff Bay today after the summer recess, but Mr Thomas failed to show up for the session, and has now announced his resignation.

In a statement, he said: “It has been the honour of my life to have been the leader of Reform Wales and see this party go from zero to 34 elected members and become the largest opposition group in Welsh history.

“With deep regret, I am now standing down from this position due to personal reasons. Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge.

Crypto billionaires hand Reform more than 10 times what Labour gets from unions READ MORE :

View 2 Images Dan Thomas has quit as leader (Image: PA)

“I stress that I have done nothing wrong, but I do not want the coming headlines to be a distraction from the fantastic work our Senedd team is doing in holding this government to account. I will continue to serve my constituents in Casnewydd Islwyn and will fully back whoever the group selects as its next leader.”

Welsh-born former London council leader Mr Thomas, who grew up in Wales, was the Conservative leader of Barnet Council from 2019 to 2022 and joined Reform UK last year. In December he quit as a councillor for Finchley Church End after returning to Wales with his family.

In a statement, Gwent Police said: “On Sunday 13 September a 45-year-old man, from the Aberbargoed area, was arrested on suspicion of assault and engaging in controlling/coercive behaviour. He has been bailed pending further enquiries.”

Meanwhile, in a fresh blow to Reform, Plaid Cymru said Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, who was elected as a Reform Member of the Senedd in May, had defected to join the governing party.

She said: “Reform has no interest in the work I came here to do. They are not serious about governing Wales. They are far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions."

The departure is yet another blow for Reform UK, who last week saw Mr Farage's popularity reach a new low, with nearly seven in 10 Brits having a negative view of the under-fire Reform UK chief.

News.title: UK's virus experts address concerns AI can create disease to wipe out humanity
News.content:
UK's virus experts address concerns AI can create disease to wipe out humanity

AI fears have been addressed by Covid-19 pandemic modeller Professor Neil Ferguson and Britain’s other leading experts following warnings about the risk of human extinction

View 4 Images AI can now modify viruses to kill bacteria (Image: Getty Images/Science Photo Library RF)

Virus experts have warned we should be vigilant against AI using germ warfare against the human race.

‌



Pandemic modeller Prof Neil Ferguson said it is “unlikely” super intelligent machines would design a virus to wipe out humanity - but said he couldn’t rule it out. He joined a panel of experts convened to discuss Britain’s defences against biosecurity threats in the week that AI leaders warned the danger of rapidly developing artificial intelligence causing human extinction was now “over 10%”.

‌



Prof Ferguson was joined by top virologist Professor Wendy Barclay who told how scientists have used AI to develop a virus which can kill harmful bacteria — warning this could be a “duel-edged sword” if rogue AI used the tech against us.

‌



View 4 Images Prof Ferguson appearing before the Covid-19 Inquiry (Image: PA)

Prof Ferguson, of Imperial College London, whose modelling unit shaped the UK’s response to Covid-19, was asked at a media briefing about dangers of the race to develop super intelligent AI.

The academic said: “This is an important philosophical question and we can’t necessarily stop it, we can at best, regulate it.” He continued there was a risk of human understanding "being outstripped", adding: "I think we need to be aware of that and avoid that happening because that does lead us down an avenue where we are not in control any more."

‌



Last week, a top safety researcher at AI developer Anthropic warned its model is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade. The whistleblower’s statement has triggered widespread agreement among the leaders of major AI firms that such a risk existed.

View 4 Images Anthropic is one of the firms leading the way developing deep learning AI (Image: SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

It came in the same week US firm Anthropic, which makes the AI tool Claude, said it had disrupted attempts to use its tech to develop biological weapons.

‌



Prof Barclay is one of Britain’s leading experts in how viruses evolve and is involved in advising the UK government about biosecurity threats. She told the briefing: “The recent revelations from Anthropic describing ways in which bad actors have been trying to use AI are concerning.

“We should remember that we have been genetically engineering viruses in laboratories for some decades now. The problem that we've got is that the same knowledge base is needed in our efforts to counter these viruses, to make new drugs and vaccines against them and detect them.

"So we have now a dual edged sword. Some people could use this new knowledge for good, others for bad.”

‌



View 4 Images Professor Barclay holds the prestigious title of Regius Professor of Infectious Disease at Imperial (Image: Imperial College London)

It comes after scientists at Stanford University used AI to develop a virus to kill the E. coli bacteria. They say such technology could potentially create viruses to tackle diseases like TB as well as drug-resistant hospital superbugs.

Prof Ferguson said: “We’ve had terrible pandemics over human history… which wiped out a significant fraction of humanity. But actually wiping out an entire species like ours… capable of using technology to respond, I think is highly unlikely.

‌



“That doesn’t mean I think there is zero threat. We wouldn’t be here today [doing this briefing] if we thought there was zero threat from AI-assisted organisms.”

Experts fear that the race between tech giants in the US and China to develop AI programmes that solve humanity’s problems could end up with the models proliferating and seeking their own goals.

Professor Tom Ellis, a synthetic biologist at Imperial who is part of a global collaboration to engineer DNA, said: “Super intelligence through AI is worth developing but we need to make sure the interests of the AI is very aligned with the interests of being a human on Earth. It’s that alignment issue, which is not necessarily anything to do with biosecurity… that’s really the crux of the issue.”

Article continues below

He added: “In terms of biosecurity though, we shouldn't just assume that there are no issues so it's wise that we are considering how AI is going to impact and generate biosecurity threats in the future, whether that be man made threats or maybe the designs of misaligned AIs themselves.”

News.title: Toddler, 2, dies after ‘choking on sausage’ at Hertfordshire nursery as prosecution launched
News.content:
Toddler, 2, dies after ‘choking on sausage’ at Hertfordshire nursery as prosecution launched

Two-year-old Sadie Salt is thought to have choked while eating lunch at Mini Learners in Radlett, Hertfordshire - the toddler sadly died in hospital two days later

View 2 Images Sadie Salt, two, died after choking on food at nursery (Image: Leigh Day / SWNS)

A health and safety prosecution has been launched after a two-year-old girl choked to death on a sausage at nursery.

‌



Sadie Salt is thought to have choked while eating lunch with 25 other young children at Mini Learners in Radlett, Hertfordshire, on November 12, 2020. The toddler tragically died in hospital two days later.

‌



Hertsmere Borough Council said that after "a full and thorough investigation," it had today authorised a prosecution under health and safety laws.

‌



Sadie's parents Zoe and Adam said they were grateful for the council's investigation, adding that it was important the legal process is able to run its course.

In a statement through their solicitor, they said: "Nearly six years have passed since Sadie's death, and throughout that time we have continued to suffer grief and heartbreak every day.

View 2 Images Sadie with parents Zoe and Adam Salt (Image: Leigh Day / SWNS)

‌



"Nothing can make up for the devastating loss of our daughter, and the impact of her death remains with us in every aspect of our lives.

"We are grateful to Hertsmere Borough Council for its thorough investigation of Sadie's case and to everyone who has worked to help bring matters to this point.

"As formal charges have been brought, it is important that this legal process is allowed to run its course.

‌



"In due course we will be looking to the inquest into Sadie's death to give us answers we have been waiting so long to know."

An inquest into Sadie's death was opened and adjourned in 2022.

Since her passing, her parents have campaigned to stop nurseries feeding higher risk foods such as sausages and grapes to under fives.

Article continues below

Jill Paterson from legal firm Leigh Day said: "Today's announcement is an important milestone for Sadie's family, who have shown remarkable strength and resilience since her death.

"We will continue to support them as they seek and await answers about what happened to their daughter at Mini Learners nursery in Hertfordshire in November 2020."

News.title: Ex-Grenfell housing chief Laura Johnson given new £157,000-a-year council role
News.content:
Ex-Grenfell housing chief Laura Johnson given new £157,000-a-year council role

Laura Johnson, former housing director, who oversaw renovations at Grenfell tower before the fire which killed 72 people has landed a new job managing social properties

View 3 Images 72 people died in the Grenfell fire in June 2017 (Image: Getty Images)

A former housing chief who oversaw cost-cutting measures at Grenfell Tower before the deadly fire has landed a new £157,000-a-year role in a London council.

‌



Laura Johnson was the director of housing at the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea (RBKC) when the 2017 blaze killed 72 people, in the West London tower. She has now been hired as the permanent director of development and property at the Barnet Group - which manages the borough's 13,000 council homes.

‌



This move has been slammed by the bereaved families of Grenfell victims, with one person calling her appointment a "slap in the face".

‌



View 3 Images Laura Johnson has landed a £157,000-a-year job with Barnet Council

The Grenfell inquiry found that Johnson had used "decisive influence" to replace the original contractor that meant to carry out renovations on the tower. Evidence heard at the inquiry said the housing chief had lost patience with contractors Leadbitter after they said the plans would cost £1.2m more than the budget.

At the time, the Tory-run council had delegated the responsibility for this decision to Kensington and Chelsea Tenant Management Organisation (TMO) but Johnson "overruled" their decision. The TMO later appointed Rydon to carry out the works at a cheaper price - it company swapped metal cladding for combustible plastic-filled panels which led to the spread of the fire in June 2017.

‌



The inquiry also heard that Johnson changed the main priority of the Grenfell project from keeping a for the works schedule to "value for money".

It was also heard the then-housing boss had slowed self-closing mechanisms being installed on fire doors at Grenfell for "financial and practical reasons.

View 3 Images 72 people were killed in the 2017 fire (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Grenfell survivor Ed Daffarn, who escaped from the 16th floor of the tower, said Johnson's new job was "an absolutely outrageous decision", according to The Guardian.

He said: "The fact that we, as bereaved survivors, haven't received any justice nine years after the fire, and yet the people that were involved in senior decision-making are able to carry on working in the social housing sector, have responsibility for health and safety, and receive massive salaries – it feels so disrespectful. If I was a resident in a Barnet council home, I’d be absolutely petrified."

Johnson had been given the role on an interim basis but was handed it permanently with a £157,078-a-year salary, the Barnet Post reported. Grenfell United, the group of families and survivors from the tower fire, called the move by Barnet Council a "slap in the face".

‌



In a post on X, the group wrote: "This appointment shows a complete disregard for the findings of the Grenfell Inquiry. Yet another slap in the face for bereaved and survivors whilst we continue to wait for justice. We know culture in social housing must change. But decisions like this give us little confidence that lessons are being learned."

A spokesperson for The Barnet Group told the Mirror: "The role of group director of development and property at The Barnet Group was publicly advertised and attracted a competitive field of candidates.

"We were aware of the Grenfell Inquiry findings and considered them carefully during the recruitment process. We also took into account Ms Johnson's professional experience, subsequent performance, references, qualifications, and overall suitability for the role. Following a robust and publicly advertised recruitment process, we concluded that she was the strongest candidate and legally eligible to hold the position.

Article continues below

"Barnet Homes and Barnet Council will not discuss matters relating to members of staff which took place during previous employment."

News.title: Louise Haigh vows to fight those who think 'democracy is up for sale' over Reform £72million row
News.content:
Louise Haigh vows to fight those who think 'democracy is up for sale' over Reform £72million row

Andy Burnham's second-in command also blasted Nigel Farage for accepting a £5million gift from a crypto billionaire - and later speaking openly about stripping away workers' rights

View 2 Images Louise Haigh, Andy Burnham's second-in command, blasted Nigel Farage in a speech to the Trades Union Congress (Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire)

Louise Haigh has promised to fight those who think Britain's democracy is up for sale amid a major row over Reform's £72million donations mega-haul.

‌



Andy Burnham's second-in command also blasted Nigel Farage for accepting a £5million gift from a crypto billionaire - and later speaking openly about stripping away workers' rights.

‌



Her intervention at the Trades Union Congress (TUC) conference comes after two separate donations to Reform of £36million from crypto tycoons Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo electrified the debate over money in British politics.

‌



Addressing delegates in Brighton, Ms Haigh said: "But every single day, in government we are campaigning against the vested interests, the forces trying to stop progress. Against the unaccountable crypto billionaires - living thousands of miles away - who think our democracy is up for sale.

"Against the politicians who pretend to be on the side of workers but pocket millions in undeclared donations and speak openly about their plans to strip working people of the very protections they rely on."

Crypto billionaires hand Reform more than 10 times what Labour gets from unions READ MORE :

View 2 Images Louise Haigh blasts Nigel Farage plan to strip away workers' rights (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Ms Haigh, who was standing in at the TUC for the Prime Minister following the death of his father, said Mr Burnham was sorry he could not address the conference for the first time as Labour leader.

She said: "It’s at times like these that you want to be surrounded by the people closest to you. And that’s one of the reasons why I know Andy is so sorry he couldn’t be here today, with his, with our, Labour family. Because the Prime Minister understands that the strength of our movement is drawn from our roots in the trade unions."

Earlier union general secretaries met behind-the-scenes at the TUC conference to thrash out an emergency statement on Reform's record donations.

‌



They did not go as far as a demand for a cap on individual donors, but the statement said: "We will continue to work with policymakers to clean up our politics and strengthen public trust in our democratic system. We expect our Government to protect our democracy from being captured by the super-rich."

It added: "We cannot afford to see the Americanisation of our politics, with out of control political spending, funded by stratospheric sums of crypto and corporate cash. These donations show clearly whose side Reform are on, with crypto billionaires, foreign and powerful corporate interests lining up to pour in eye-watering sums of money to advance their agendas.

"Trade union funding is the cleanest money in politics. Union donations are made up of the collective subscriptions of care workers, teaching assistants, shop workers and millions of trade union members, democratically controlled and heavily regulated. Working people deserve - and need - a meaningful stake in how Britain is run."

‌



Their statement followed a threat from Nigel Farage, who said he would retaliate by cutting off Labour's union funding if Reform ever wins power.

In article for The Telegraph, he said: " I would just warn the Labour Party here and now: if you try and ban our donors, we in government would certainly ban funding from the trade unions.

"I don't want to go down that route. But it is something we would be prepared to do."

‌



It also emerged today that Reform crypto-billionaire backers could face tougher checks to demonstrate their continued presence in the UK.

Ministers have already taken steps to introduce a £100,000 ceiling on the sum of money that can be donated to political parties by anyone living abroad, which would also be enforced for the first 12 months after British expats come back to the UK.

‌



The changes would be backdated to March, prompting questions about whether Reform can retain the twin £36million contributions from Mr Delo, who was living in Hong Kong until recently, and Mr Harborne, who was living in Thailand.

The government is now looking at strengthening proposed legislation by introducing an "enhanced" residency test requiring donors to demonstrate they have lived in the UK for a certain period, with details to be set out shortly.

Downing Street denied the proposed checks were a bid to prevent Reform UK specifically from using the £72million it received. Asked on Tuesday if it was, the Prime Minister's official spokesman said: "No, I completely reject that."

Article continues below

No 10 insisted the plans were to ensure people who contribute vast sums to political parties have a stake in the UK. "There are multiple precedents under successive administrations, particularly to address the risk of people taking action immediately to avoid the new rules," the spokesman said.

News.title: Baby 'cot cams' plan after inquiry finds Lucy Letby crimes could have been prevented
News.content:
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has said officials will "urgently develop plans" to introduce live-streaming cameras on England's baby wards after an inquiry into Lucy Letby's murders and attempted murders.

Inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall called for a series of urgent reforms to neonatal units, including CCTV for all cots and incubators, and restricting access to insulin.

Thirlwall said some of the babies Letby killed could have been saved if managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital had taken action earlier.

Her report criticises a "complete failure to protect babies" and a "profound failure of management, governance and safeguarding" at the hospital.

Thirlwall said this was because "no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt."

She said it would never be possible to know exactly how many lives could have been saved if safeguarding procedures had been properly followed.

News.title: The key findings and recommendations from the Lucy Letby inquiry
News.content:
A report into how serial killer Lucy Letby was able to murder seven babies at the Countess of Chester Hospital has found that some deaths could have been prevented.

Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more.

She was convicted in 2023 and has twice been denied permission to appeal against her convictions.

Responding to the report, the hospital says it is "sorry for the events that occurred in 2015 and 2016", and it's a "different organisation today with new leadership, stronger governance and safety processes". Letby maintains her innocence.

Protesters supporting Letby could be seen and heard near Liverpool Town Hall as the report was published.

BBC correspondent Judy Moritz reports from Liverpool.

More on this story.

News.title: Dan Thomas resigns as Reform Wales leader after arrest on suspicion of assault
News.content:
Reform UK's Dan Thomas has quit as the party's Welsh leader, after he was arrested on Sunday of suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Gwent Police confirmed that a 45-year-old man from Aberbargoed, in Caerphilly, was bailed pending further enquiries.

In a statement issued by his party, the Member of the Senedd for Casnewydd Islwyn said he was "standing down" from his position due to personal reasons.

He said he had been "released without charge" and had "done nothing wrong".

Thomas was appointed Welsh party leader by Nigel Farage in February.

Plaid Cymru, which runs the Welsh government, said: "Reform UK is descending into chaos."

Thomas did not take part in First Minister's Questions earlier today.

He was first elected to the Senedd in the elections in May, where his party went from having two politicians in Cardiff Bay to 34.

Reform came second behind Plaid Cymru in the vote, with Thomas becoming leader of the opposition in the Senedd.

Thomas said: "It has been the honour of my life to have been the leader of Reform Wales and see this party go from zero to 34 elected members and become the largest opposition group in Welsh history.

"With deep regret, I am now standing down from this position due to personal reasons.

"Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge."

He added: "I will continue to serve my constituents in Casnewydd Islwyn and will fully back whoever the group selects as its next leader."

The news came on the same day that Reform MS Sarah Cooper-Lesadd defected to Plaid Cymru.

News.title: Former England footballer Raheem Sterling admits dangerous driving on motorway before crash
News.content:
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before he crashed a Lamborghini in May.

The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.

Sterling, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of 28 May.

Sterling has 82 England caps, the last of which was won at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

News.title: State pension likely to top £13,000 a year as UK wage growth slows to 3.9%
News.content:
The state pension is expected to top Â£13,000 a year, reigniting the debate about its long-term affordability and generational fairness.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to rise by Â£488 a year in April, based on the latest official earnings figure released on Tuesday.

The so-called triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.

Labour made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock until 2029, however economists have warned about the cost of the policy ahead of the Budget although pensioner groups say many people still face poverty in old age.

News.title: Trump criticises Supreme Court after justices block mail-in ballot restrictions
News.content:
The US Supreme Court has rejected President Donald Trump's plan to restrict voting by mail before November's midterm elections, in a setback for the White House.

The justices upheld a federal judge's order that temporarily blocked the US Postal Service (USPS) from moving forwards with new requirements for postal ballots.

Trump called the decision a blow to his political party. "Republicans just got another bad decision from the United States Supreme Court," the president wrote on Truth Social.

One legal group said in response that the decision would prevent the USPS from "sowing chaos in our elections".

The ruling is unlikely to be the final word on the matter. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a conservative, agreed with the ruling, but indicated he might later rule in Trump's favour as litigation in the case continues.

Trump, who argued the rules would combat electoral fraud, signed an executive order in March that directed the USPS to deliver ballots only to voters on lists of citizens.

Legal challenges argued that the move violated states' constitutional rights to run elections.

Election officials from 24 Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia also warned that the proposed changes were not ready for implementation and could prevent ballots from reaching voters.

Meanwhile some Republican-led states, including Florida, Louisiana, and Montana, supported the president in court filings.

Justice Kavanaugh wrote in the opinion that there was "at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority". But he argued that "applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious".

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, also conservatives, dissented. They wrote that the challenge to Trump's order was a "Hail Mary pass" that was unlikely to be successful ultimately.

In a Truth Social post, Trump criticised the top court's Monday decision, as well as other key rulings against him such as striking down his executive order to limit birthright citizenship, and also a key element of his tariff policies.

"The Supreme Court has really let our Country down!" he wrote, alleging some justices were "totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America".

"These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," the president wrote.

News.title: Two dead after car hits group of pedestrians
News.content:
Two people have died and four have been seriously injured after a car crashed into a group of people in Doncaster.

South Yorkshire Police said officers were called to White Rose Way when a black Mitsubishi L200 hit a group of pedestrians at 11:00 BST on Sunday, before hitting a black Audi and silver BMW on the opposite carriageway.

The force said two of the pedestrians had died at the scene while four other people were taken to hospital with serious injuries.

The driver of the Mitsubishi, a 30-year-old man, was arrested on suspicion of two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, two counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and driving while unfit and later released on bail.

News.title: Harry and Meghan change children's school over security concerns due to traffic
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have changed their children's school only days after they first started over security concerns about traffic during the school run.

The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.

It's understood that the security for the children meant travelling with another car, and that driving in convoy proved difficult in the busy school run traffic.

The checks on the route are believed to have initially taken place before term time, but with the school traffic it was deemed not safe enough.

A source close to the couple said: "The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family's security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements."

They added: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

It has also emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

News.title: Political donors could face tougher residency rules
News.content:
MPs have supported the government's proposals by approving amendments to the Representation of the People Bill. The bill is currently being scrutinised in the House of Lords.

Speaking as the bill was debated by peers, Communities Minister Baroness Taylor of Stevenage said: "We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring that the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy."

Baroness Taylor said this was "in addition to introducing a robust regime that ensures that donors contributing above the Â£100,000 annual cap must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection" to the UK.

Tax is one area that already has residency requirements. The criteria includes someone being declared resident for tax purposes if they have lived in the UK for at least 183 days in the tax year.

Challenged on whether the government was targeting Reform donors, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said policy on donations is "never about one political party or one particular set of issues".

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "Fundamentally we need to make sure that people who want to influence British politics, who want a say in British politics have a stake in Britain.

"That should apply to everyone and will apply to everyone, so I wouldn't make it about any particular donations or anything that's been in the public domain."

When the government set out its plans to cap foreign donations in March and July, it did not mention the idea of an enhanced residency test for political donors.

Asked repeatedly by reporters whether the idea of tightening residency rules had only been discussed after Delo and Harborne's most recent donations to Reform, the prime minister's official spokesman would not give a timeframe.

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart accused the government of "playing whack-a-mole", as she said Labour's residency requirements "aren't good enough".

She said: "We must urgently go further and introduce a universal donation cap to stop Trump's America becoming Farage's Britain."

On Monday, Farage criticised the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal.

He told the BBC: "If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way.

"We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'."

Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost Â£43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

News.title: Fall in small boat Channel crossings down to law enforcement, agency says
News.content:
Law enforcement activity has been a "key factor" in reducing the number of small boat Channel crossings, the National Crime Agency (NCA) says.

The number of people arriving in the UK in the first half of 2026 was down 41% on the year before, government figures show.

The NCA said the drop followed a "significant increase in arrests and seizures", although added "fluctuating demand" for crossings, and the French authorities preventing boat launches had also played a role.

However, Mihnea Cuibus, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, says it is "impossible" to disentangle the effects of government policy and other factors on small boat arrivals.

While recent policy changes appear to have led smugglers and migrants to alter their behaviour, Cuibus says fewer unauthorised arrivals into the EU and developments in key origin countries - such as improved security in Syria - may be partially behind the decline.

"It is hard to know how much restrictive measures contributed to reducing [arrivals] in 2026," he continues.

He said limitations on refugee family reunion and a reduction in the asylum grant rate could also have had an impact.

The Conservatives have previously said the weather played a huge role in the fluctuating numbers of crossings from France and Belgium.

NCA director general of operations Rob Jones said the agency was "devoting more resources to tackling organised immigration crime than ever before".

"That is bringing results.

"However, we are not complacent, and the job is by no means done," he continued.

"We must continue to keep up the pressure on these criminal gangs, as they continue to put lives at risk in the Channel."

News.title: AI poses huge risks to national security without guardrails, minister says
News.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) poses "huge risks" to the UK's national security and society without the right protections, a senior minister has warned.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh - Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy - told the TUC congress on Tuesday that the government needed to "heed the warnings" of those "at the forefront" of developing the technology.

She added the government was "ready to work with international partners" to prioritise public safety and national security.

Fears about the potential dangers of AI have ramped up in recent days after executives and current and former staff in the field warned the tech could endanger humanity.

On Monday, a spokesman for UK Prime Minister Burnham welcomed the open discussion among those developing the technology of the risks and rewards.

Speaking at the TUC congress on Tuesday afternoon, Haigh acknowledged the "enormous potential" of AI for public services, businesses and science.

While she said the UK needed to make the most of this, she added: "There are clearly huge risks to our national security and society if the right guardrails are not put in place...

"We have a solemn duty to mitigate the risks and ensure that it is for the benefit - not the detriment - of our society."

In an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier on Tuesday, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said people should not be complacent about the risks of AI - but also not "hyperbolic".

It comes as MPs in the UK are seeking new laws on AI after a report found the technology was responsible for numerous abuses of human rights.

"Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose," Labour MP and committee chair Alex Sobel said.

News.title: Number of people claiming key disability benefit hits record high
News.content:
The number of people claiming Personal Independence Payments (Pip) in England and Wales has hit a record high, according to new government figures.

As of July, just over four million people were entitled to claim the benefit, compared to 3.83 million the previous year, an increase of 7%, data from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) showed.

Pip is designed to support people with the extra costs of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions, and eligibility is not affected by a person's income or savings.

In July, Sir Stephen Timms, who is leading a review on Pip, said in his interim report that the system was "not fit for purpose".

Of the 4.1 million claimants, those aged 50 and above accounted for more than half.

Just under three in ten were aged 30 to 49, while 17% of claimants were aged 16 to 29.

Pip seeks to offset the extra costs that can occur for those living with certain long-term health conditions.

According to the charity Scope, the extra cost of being disabled â known as the disability price tag â has reached more than Â£1,100 a month.

The DWP said the increase in the Pip caseload had actually "slowed", falling from a rise of 400,000 in the 12 months to July 2024, to 260,000 in the 12 months to July 2026.

But they agreed the system was "no longer fit for purpose", adding that the Timms review's recommendations would "lay the foundation for sustainable reform".

But Helen Whatly, shadow work and pensions secretary, said Labour was "too quick to write people off and too slow to help them into work" - adding that it was "costing us a fortune".

Pip has been in the spotlight since the summer of 2025 when the government, led by former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer, proposed reforming and tightening eligibility criteria for the benefit as the cost of running the system increased.

Spending on Pip stood at Â£16.3bn in 2019-20, when adjusted for inflation to today's prices, and had increased to Â£27.3bn by 2024-25, government figures showed.

It is currently forecast to rise to Â£41.5bn by 2030-31.

News.title: Government to end ban on Catholic and Jewish PMs' involvement in Church appointments
News.content:
The government has introduced a bill to end antiquated laws preventing Roman Catholic or Jewish prime ministers from being involved in the process of making Church of England appointments.

It was among the first pieces of legislation to be introduced to Parliament under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, himself a Catholic, who has called the current laws "unacceptable".

When appointing bishops and archbishops, the Church presents a candidate to the prime minister who then advises the monarch on who to install in the role.

Although the involvement of the prime minister in this process has become more of a formality in recent years, legislation still exists that specifically bars Roman Catholics and Jews from exercising this responsibility.

That is why earlier this month Burnham, the first Catholic prime minister, transferred the responsibility of advising the King on Church appointments to the Lord Chancellor.

But the prime minster said it was "unacceptable for there to be a legislative bar against people of any faith performing all the functions of my office".

The Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829 and the Jews Relief Act 1858 are the existing laws in question.

When those laws were introduced, they actually eased some of the restrictions on Catholics' and Jews' participation in public life.

This included what was, in effect, a prohibition on them becoming MPs.

But the law still stipulated that prime ministers of those faiths could not be involved - "directly or indirectly" - in advising during the process of making Church appointments.

News.title: Lost oyster beds rediscovered thanks to Gaelic and Scots language
News.content:
Ecology and wildlife experts hope to use the discoveries to help rebuild oyster populations in suitable coastal locations.

The recent findings marked the culmination of several years worth of hard work, titled Project Eisirean.

It is a collaboration between ecology and environment researchers, Gaelic and education experts at the University of Glasgow and local community organisations on the west coast of Scotland.

Dr Anna McGregor, an expert in coastal ecology and a lecturer at the University of Glasgow , had the original idea of locating oysters through traditional place-names, then applying scientific techniques to confirm oyster presence within them.

She explained: "This is a really exciting outcome, for a project that started off looking for the historic distribution of oysters along the West Coast.

"We thought that as native oysters are now really rare throughout Europe, is there a way to look where they used to be, using people's memory and understanding - that can come through place names.

"We found two areas with oyster in the name, both on Mull, and after about two years we found another one on Lewis. Then we broadened the search to look for habitat related names, like sand banks."

The group then examined those locations for factors like the sea bed and the level of the water flow.

News.title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules
News.content:
Trade unions are putting pressure on the government to soften proposed changes to immigration rules, which would make it harder for foreign workers to secure permanent residency in the UK.

If the plans are approved, most migrants would have to wait 10 years to qualify for permanent residence, rather than five years, while foreign workers on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait.

The proposals were announced last year by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, who has kept the same role under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Delegates at the Trades Union Congress (TUC) backed a motion calling for any changes affecting workers already in the UK to be withdrawn.

A government spokesperson said ministers had received 200,000 responses to a consultation on the proposals, which was launched under Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, and they were carefully considering them.

Giving evidence to MPs on the Commons Home Affairs Committee on Tuesday, Mahmood said technical details for her new migration system were now being worked on and she expected to announce policy later this year.

"We're trying to strike the right balance between our responsibilities to people who have come here to work, our recognition of the failures we inherited as a government, and also our need to do right by the people who are already here, who pay for the systems that we all rely on," she said.

Under the government's proposals the standard wait to qualify for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain, would increase to 10 years.

People who arrived on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait, while those who relied on benefits for more than 12 months would have to wait 20 years.

Indefinite leave to remain gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

The changes would not apply to people who have already obtained settlement but would cover people already living in the UK, including those who had been expecting to get permanent residence in the coming months.

Some Labour MPs have also criticised plans for the changes to apply to migrants already in the UK.

Earlier this year, when she was a backbench MP and not a government minister, Angela Rayner, herself a former care worker, labelled the proposals "un-British".

Rayner, who has since been appointed housing secretary by Burnham, warned that "moving the goalposts undermines our sense of fair play".

At the time, Burnham, who was still Greater Manchester mayor, said he understood where Rayner was "coming from" and that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say".

News.title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age
News.content:
Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.

Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff.

Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list.

The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would.

The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work.

It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document.

The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it.

Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app.

The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age.

This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult.

Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'".

Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step".

He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector.

This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said.

News.content:

The Tampa Bay Times reported the death of an elderly woman on Sept. 8, 2026. Her family says local doctors attributed her death to dengue fever, although the Florida Department of Health has not yet confirmed that.

This death was likely part of a larger dengue outbreak in Hillsborough County, where there have been 95 documented cases of dengue since July 2026. In August, the Hillsborough County Health Department issued a mosquito-borne illness alert due to reports of multiple locally acquired cases.

This cluster of locally spread cases is a stark reminder that a disease which most Americans associate with faraway tropical vacations is increasingly being caught at home.

Dengue is often called “breakbone fever,” and the nickname is earned. People who get sick typically develop a sudden high fever along with a pounding headache, pain behind the eyes and deep aches in the muscles, joints and bones. Many also feel nauseated, throw up or break out in a blotchy rash a few days in.

The cycle is simple and hard to break: A mosquito bites an infected person, then bites someone else days later, giving them the virus ( Getty/iStock )

As an infectious diseases physician and tropical medicine specialist who directs a travel clinic, I see how easily dengue slips past both patients and doctors. In parts of the U.S. where the disease is still uncommon, it is easily mistaken for the flu or COVID-19, and that delay can be dangerous.

How it spreads

Dengue is not passed from person to person like a cold. It spreads through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, mainly Aedes aegypti, a species commonly found in Florida. These mosquitoes thrive in warm cities and can breed in as little as a bottle capful of standing water. These mosquitoes bite during the day, not just at dusk.

The cycle is simple and hard to break: A mosquito bites an infected person, then bites someone else days later, giving them the virus.

Dengue is especially tricky because most infections cause no symptoms at all. Roughly 3 in 4 people who catch the virus never feel sick. For the 25% who are symptomatic, those symptoms don’t appear until four to 10 days after being bitten.

In addition, there are four different strains of the dengue virus, and surviving one gives you lasting protection against only that one. A second infection with a different type actually raises the odds of severe disease.

A life-threatening turn

Most people suffer with dengue for a miserable week and then recover on their own. But about 1 in 20 patients progress to severe dengue, a life-threatening turn that tends to strike just as the fever breaks – often around days three to seven, when patients and their families may wrongly assume the worst is over.

In severe dengue, tiny blood vessels throughout the body start leaking fluid, blood pressure can crash and dangerous bleeding or organ damage can follow. Warning signs that someone is sliding into this phase include severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the gums or nose, extreme drowsiness or restlessness, and blood in vomit or stool.

About the author Andrés Henao is a Professor of Medicine and Infectious Disease, University of Colorado Anschutz. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article .

Some groups face higher risk, including infants, pregnant women, adults over 65 and people with conditions like diabetes, obesity or kidney disease. Left untreated, severe dengue can kill up to 10% of patients. With prompt hospital care, that number drops below 1 in 100 – which is why recognizing it early matters so much.

A dengue vaccine exists, but it is not recommended for the average American traveler. The available shots are used only in select cases, such as children who live in high-transmission areas and have already had dengue once. So prevention still rests mostly on avoiding mosquito bites.

How dengue is treated

There is no antiviral drug that cures dengue. Care is all about supporting the body while it fights the virus. For people well enough to stay home, that means rest, plenty of fluids and acetaminophen, commonly known in the U.S. by the brand name Tylenol, for fever and pain.

Patients who may have dengue must avoid aspirin, ibuprofen and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. These drugs raise the risk of bleeding, which is already a danger with dengue.

Patients who develop more severe symptoms need to be admitted to the hospital, where doctors give carefully measured intravenous fluids and watch closely. Too little fluid and the patient can go into shock; too much and the lungs can flood.

A worsening global problem

Dengue is surging worldwide. The World Health Organization recorded more than 14 million cases in 2024, its worst year on record, across some 100 countries. That’s a 2,600% increase from the more than 505,000 cases reported in 2000.

Warmer temperatures, rapid urban growth and global travel are all helping the mosquitoes – and the virus – expand into places where it has never been a problem before. South Asia, Southeast Asia and Latin America carry the heaviest burden, but the map is spreading north.

Why the U.S. should pay attention

Most U.S. dengue cases are still picked up abroad. Travelers return home sick. In 2023 alone, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly 1,900 such travel-related cases.

But every infected traveler is a spark, and in warm states the tinder is already there.

In the U.S. territories, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands see the most cases by far. Florida has the highest risk among the 50 states, with Miami-Dade County recording more than 300 locally acquired dengue infections between 2010 and 2024. Local cases have also turned up in Texas, California, Arizona and Hawaii.

What to do if you think you have dengue

If you develop a sudden fever after traveling to a dengue-prone area, or after mosquito exposure in South Florida, see a doctor and mention where you’ve been. Rest, drink fluids and use acetaminophen – not ibuprofen or aspirin.

Most importantly, watch for the warning signs. Severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding or sudden drowsiness means get to an emergency room right away.

And to protect yourself and your neighbors: Use insect repellent, wear long sleeves and dump out any standing water in your yard where mosquitoes breed.

News.content:

Labour has pledged to make it harder for employers to block staff doing their job from home, in a bid to hand more power to workers.

Speaking to the annual Trade Unions Congress (TUC) in Brighton, Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, said businesses would have to show they had “properly” considered a worker’s request before rejecting it.

“That is what putting power back into the hands of working people looks like,” she told delegates.

She added that “life isn’t always as neat as employers would like it to be”.

“There’s kids to pick up. Parents to look after. Families who rely on us at short notice. And sometimes, a little bit of flexibility can make all the difference,” she said.

Ms Haigh added that while “not every job can be done from home and not every request can be agreed”, each request “can be taken seriously”.

She said: “If an employer wants to turn down a request, they will have to sit down with their employee, properly consider and explain why.”

open image in gallery A recent survey found that almost half of all UK businesses want staff to return on a full-time basis ( Getty/iStock )

She also praised the unions for their work campaigning for the Employment Rights Act, which she said was “the biggest uplift” in workers’ rights in a generation.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the TUC, said flexible working was not “just a perk – it’s a lifeline”.

He added: “That’s why this move is a welcome step forward. It makes it harder for employers to turn down requests while giving workers a stronger voice in the process.

“Improving access to flexible working benefits workers, businesses and the economy – whether it’s through increasing staff productivity or higher retention.”

Research last year suggested almost half of all businesses across the UK now want staff back in the office on a full time basis, in a push to pre-pandemic levels.

The survey by the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), of more than 500 businesses, also found one in ten businesses reported that staff had quit over a lack of flexible working.

While work from home is not a new phenomenon, its popularity soared after it became a necessity during the Covid pandemic.

Since then, some workers have preferred not to return to the office full-time, even as senior leaders call for their return and some say productivity and innovation increases when all employees are together.

Ms Haigh also used her speech to warn artificial intelligence (AI) poses “huge risks” to national security unless the proper safeguards can be put in place.

News.content:
