Red card. Happy to confirm? Confirming the red card for Manchester City 47. A kick to the midriff with two feet.

Just roll through to check that Bruno does nothing. I'm absolutely certain he doesn't. No, he kicks the ball; it's fine.

Assistant VAR: No, the other one [Bruno's first kick]. That's not what they're talking about. That is the one they're talking about.

Webb: Foden decision was correct but Fernandes avoids 'petulant' yellow

Pro Ref chief operating officer Howard Webb:

"I agree with the red card for Phil Foden for violent conduct. He kicks out with force into the upper body of Bruno Fernandes. We saw a player sent off for Aston Villa, Joao Gomes, for a similar thing.

"That is seen by the referee on the field and that is the on-field decision.

"When you look at the footage, there is the petulant kick from Fernandes into the back side of Foden. It is more petulant than violent. To be violent conduct, it has to have excessive force or brutality.

"When you look at that at full speed, it does not have that element. It would be a yellow card and VAR cannot step in to give a yellow.

"If all of it was missed and nothing was given against Foden, then VAR could step in and see Foden's actions for a possible red card and capture Fernandes' yellow card action. Because the referee gave the red card, that option is not open for VAR."

Analysis: Fernandes deserved equal treatment to Foden

Sky Sports' Laura Hunter:

The review of this incident is all over the place. But the most alarming element is the reading of Bruno Fernandes's part.

Lead VAR official Matt Donohue is distracted by a previous incident in real time.

His VAR assistant leads with "possible kick out" by Foden. The immediacy of the on-field decision from Michael Oliver to send Foden off is the determining factor here. Oliver acts fast which suggests he is sure, and so VAR allows the call to stand.

The bar for intervention by VAR has been deliberately lifted higher for subjective decisions, remember, to avoid re-refereeing of games. This remains a grey area but less VAR interference is a good thing in my book.

Most can accept that Oliver's decision to dismiss Foden is not a "clear and obvious error" given where he makes contact with Fernandes. Whether it meets the threshold for "violent conduct" is of course open to interpretation.

What the VAR room failed to spot, however, is the trigger for Foden's reaction. Why is that not scrutinised in more detail?

"I'm absolutely certain he doesn't [do anything]," Donohue says of Fernandes's involvement. In reality, the Man Utd captain is the first offender and Foden's kick was retaliation for the kick he received after being fouled.

The decision not to punish Fernandes for the exact same action Foden is red-carded for is surely a huge oversight. Both deserved equal treatment in my opinion, especially important as Oliver clearly missed the first part from his position on the pitch. There is never any mention of it.

VAR's job is to alert him. Isn't that what the pitchside monitor is there for?

Denzel Bentley, the WBO world champion at 160lbs, is open to fighting Benn.

Benn twice boxed his family rival, Chris Eubank Jr, at middleweight before boiling back down to welterweight to challenge Ryan Garcia for the WBC title.

"Although the public might not think he deserves another world title shot in my eyes I feel like his profile is big enough for him to skip the queue," Bentley told Sky Sports.

"It's unfair but that's the sport we're in. Obviously it's beneficial for me, especially financially, so 100 per cent that's the fight I would take. I've never had any beef with Conor, we've always been cool.

"Firstly he needs to get himself right, well and fit. I think he should take a lot of time off and recover. I don't think there's any rush for him to get back into a boxing ring or even a gym. That weight cut was a fight in itself for him I think. Probably took a lot out of himself.

"Once he's well and fit, if he decides to move up to 160lbs and he does want the challenge, I think that's probably a conversation we can probably have ourselves: 'If you want to do this, let's push for it.'"

Bentley though had a warning for him. "I think I'm dangerous for anyone. I'm a lot bigger than him and I can punch."

But he added: "I think he will be a lot better with the extra weight.

"I think at 160lbs he'll be a lot more fuelled. But, listen, I punch as well and there were a lot of flaws in his game that night that I could exploit."

Sports.title: Sterling admits driving Lamborghini dangerously ahead of motorway crash
Sports.content:
Raheem Sterling, 31, was charged with dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen, over an incident on May 28; Sterling pleaded guilty at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Tuesday

England footballer Raheem Sterling has admitted dangerously driving a Lamborghini on the motorway.

Sterling pleaded guilty at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Tuesday to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road before he crashed on May 28.

The 31-year-old admitted possession of six nitrous oxide cannisters for wrongful inhalation, a class C drug, and failing to provide a specimen.

Sterling attended the Hampshire court wearing a black suit jacket, black trousers, black shoes and a dark top.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary previously said the charges followed a single-vehicle collision on the M3 southbound, near Minley interchange, on May 28.

The force said that no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.

Sterling scored 20 goals in 82 appearances for England, helping Gareth Southgate's side reach the 2018 World Cup semi-finals and the final of Euro 2020.

He came through the academy at QPR before joining Liverpool, where he made his senior debut.

Sterling, who was born in Kingston, Jamaica, moved to Manchester City in 2015 and won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and the 2019 FA Cup.

He left for Chelsea in 2022 but, after falling out of favour, spent the 2024-25 campaign on loan at Arsenal.

Sterling joined Dutch club Feyenoord on a short-term deal until the end of last season, and is currently without a club.

In the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours, Sterling was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport after fronting anti-racism and discrimination campaigns and speaking out strongly against racism on and off the pitch for several years.

Sports.title: Raheem Sterling could face prison for reckless driving while using nitrous oxide
Sports.content:
Raheem Sterling pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and could be sent to prison after driving his Lamborghini for more than an hour on motorways during rush hour while inhaling nitrous oxide.

The former Chelsea and Manchester City forward stood in the dock to accept three charges before Basingstoke magistrates court heard how he embarked on a prolonged period of reckless driving on the M25 and M3, inhaling nitrous oxide balloons, before crashing his £270,000 car. Sterling was disqualified from driving and bailed until 25 November, when his sentence will either be determined or referred to the crown court.

Sterling also admitted possession of nitrous oxide and refusing to provide a specimen.

The maximum term for Sterling would be two years in prison, although a sentence of 12 to 18 months is considered more likely and, with mitigation, that could be suspended.

Prosecutor Simon Jones told the court one witness had “genuine concerns the driver might kill someone” and described Sterling’s driving as “absolutely horrendous”.

“As she moved past the vehicle she thought the airbag had been deployed, it was a large white deflated balloon,” Jones said. “She had no idea if the driver could see ahead.”

View image in fullscreen Raheem Sterling (centre) arriving at Basingstoke magistrates court on Tuesday. Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PA

Between 7.45am and 8.52am on 28 May, police received multiple calls reporting dangerous driving – shortly after Sterling had returned to England after a loan at Feyenoord, where he had attempted to revive his career.

Dashcam footage provided to police by one witness showed Sterling’s car swerving between lanes and almost colliding with the central reservation. Witnesses reported seeing the driver inhaling balloons while driving.

After leaving the M3, the Lamborghini veered off the carriageway on the A327 near the Minley interchange in Hampshire. All four tyres blew out and there was damage to the bodywork. Body-worn footage from officers attending the scene, played in court, showed Sterling, 31, sitting in the passenger seat with two canisters on his lap before confirming he had been driving.

Jones said Sterling appeared keen to move a deflated balloon from beside him on to the back seat. His saliva was tested and no presence of cannabis or cocaine was found, but he later refused to provide a blood sample to test for other substances.

Quick Guide How do I 

Another witness told police they had seen the Lamborghini driving erratically at 1.10am. They reported it entering the drive-through at “alarming speed”, Jones said, and saw the driver holding an inflated balloon.

After his arrest, Sterling was taken to Basingstoke investigation centre. “During the process he had disclosed to staff that he had a problem with nitrous oxide,” Jones said.

Sterling failed a series of impairment tests, including walking in a straight line without swaying and placing his fingertip on the end of his nose. He was also asked to judge 30 seconds with his eyes closed but recorded 52.

Jones said Sterling “appeared to be quiet, withdrawn and lethargic and actively fidgeting” during the tests. “His eyelids were drooping, consistent with fatigue or drug impairment. He said he was feeling very cold, despite this being in the middle of a heatwave with 33-degree temperatures.”

The former England international, who won 82 caps between 2012 and 2022 and played in five major tournaments, was taken to a medical room where he refused to provide a blood sample without providing a reasonable excuse and despite repeated and clear warnings.

At 5.13pm, Sterling was interviewed with a legal representative present. A signed, prepared statement was read out in which he said he had not slept all night and was tired and confused. He then answered “no comment” to officers’ questions.

Defence barrister Jason Bartfield KC did not dispute this was a top-category case, given the prolonged driving and clear serious impairment. Bartfield cautioned, however, that there would have been “short periods” of “serious impairment”, compared with consuming cannabis or alcohol.

View image in fullscreen Raheem Sterling after being stopped by police in May. Photograph: Crown Prosecution Service/PA

Bartfield did not accept the car damage was serious, describing it as “relatively superficial” and “minor scratching” alongside the blown tyres. He also argued that the fact there were two canisters in Sterling’s lap when police arrived showed “this was very much not a case of trying to conceal anything from them”.

The court was not told the full mitigating circumstances, but Bartfield said: “Clearly there is extensive personal mitigation. Voluntary steps have been taken to address them I hope this has weight with the court.”

District judge Kirsty Allman ordered a pre-sentence report and adjourned the hearing. She said she had not decided whether to retain jurisdiction or commit sentencing to the crown court. A magistrates court cannot impose a sentence of more than 12 months.

“I’m going to release you on unconditional bail,” she said. “If you don’t attend, a warrant will be issued for your arrest. I’m going to disqualify you from driving as of today. You must not drive a motor vehicle on the road as of today. I will determine the period if I sentence you, otherwise it will be for the crown court. You must not drive while disqualified – if you drive while disqualified you will be committing a prisonable offence.”

Sports.title: Manchester United shocked as talented youngster JJ Gabriel asks to leave
Sports.content:
Manchester United have been left confused and shocked by the news that the talented 15-year-old player JJ Gabriel has asked to leave the club, a day before he was to be included in the first-team squad to face Brighton.

Gabriel could have become United’s youngest player in the Carabao Cup third-round tie at Old Trafford on Wednesday. But the Guardian understands he has asked for his registration to be cancelled.

United are unsure what has prompted this decision and believe they have done everything they can to show Gabriel and his family there is a pathway to the first team. Those efforts have included meetings with Ruben Amorim, when the Portuguese was head coach, and Sir Alex Ferguson.

United believe the situation, first reported by the Telegraph, is rectifiable given the time remaining on Gabriel’s contract. Club officials say the player has a deal to the end of the season and cannot be deregistered despite his request. The north London-born Gabriel cannot sign a professional contract until he turns 17 in October next year, but can sign a scholarship agreement when he turns 16.

Gabriel, who has been with United since the age of 11, has emerged as one of the most exciting prospects at Carrington in years, scoring a hatful of goals for the youth teams, most recently a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut against Sabah last week. He regularly plays for older age groups at United, scoring 26 goals in 29 games last season, and has made two appearances for England Under-17s. Gabriel is also the most recent, and youngest, winner of United’s prestigious Jimmy Murphy young player of the year award. He has regularly trained with the first team.

Quick Guide Carrick say VAR blunder will fuel United Show Michael Carrick believes Manchester United will have an edge against Brighton in the Carabao Cup owing to the wrong video assistant referee decision that allowed Erling Haaland’s winner in Sunday’s defeat by Manchester City. United host Fabian Hürzeler’s side on Wednesday aiming to bounce back after Haaland’s 60th-minute strike was judged to be legal by the VAR, who ruled that Enzo Fernández was not interfering with play in the buildup. Pro Ref admitted the goal should not have been allowed and that Matt Donohue, the VAR, had made the wrong decision. He has been stood down for this weekend's Premier League action. Carrick, speaking before Pro Ref’s statement, was asked whether his players would have an edge against Brighton owing to their annoyance at ruling. “It does give you something, when something like that happens, to use moving forward," the manager said. "The players have got an edge. They've shown that to me since I've been here. We've had setbacks, and they've bounced back particularly well and had some really good performances and good results." United have taken four points from their first four games. “We've got to move on [from City loss]; we've got to win games,” said Carrick. “We have done – we've won a lot of games, and we need to continue to do that. I understand it's a new season, and the points tally right now is not what we want it to be. I'm not hiding from that, but it's more of about getting back to winning games, that feeling, getting the habit. It's easier said than done, but we're capable of it.” Luke Shaw may be available after a knock. Jamie Jackson Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Speaking after that 5-0 win against Sabah, Adam Lawrence, United’s lead under-21 coach, said: “JJ is surrounded by people that really, really believe in him from the top of the club right the way through. He’s been at the club for so long. He’s got real good relationships with the players, with the staff, so I think over the course of time obviously that helps as well.

“At the moment, just in terms of his game, his games programme, his training programme, it’s about making sure that he’s getting the right exposure across different levels. We’re obviously not perfect but it’s definitely something we put a lot of thought into.”

Sports.title: Howard Webb says accidental handball law ‘a nonsense’ and calls for reform
Sports.content:
Howard Webb has described the law around accidental handball as “a bit of a nonsense” and called for its reform to stop referees being drawn into “ridiculous situations”.

The chief refereeing officer for English football made his remarks on Tuesday, when he also fronted up over the error that allowed Manchester City to win Sunday’s Manchester derby. Webb said he was “really disappointed” with the video assistant referee call that failed to spot Enzo Fernández interfering with play from an offside position before Erling Haaland scored the only goal.

Speaking on Match Officials Mic’d Up, Webb reviewed a number of controversial incidents from the Premier League season. He said the buildup to an Ipswich own goal at Manchester United, where the ball hit Harry Maguire’s hand before he took a shot that deflected off Jacob Greaves and into the net, highlighted problems with the handball law.

“It’s a bit of a nonsense, isn’t it?” Webb said. “If [Maguire] strikes the ball beautifully into the top corner, then the goal gets disallowed. [But] he skews his shot, it becomes an own goal, and it’s awarded.”

The handball law says it is an offence “if a player scores in the opponent’s goal directly from their hand/arm [or] immediately after the ball has touched their hand/arm, even if accidental”. If another player touches the ball before it goes in, however, only a deliberate handball would lead to play being brought back. Webb said he believed this was the wrong approach.

“The law should change away from that idea,” he said. “We’re in this ridiculous situation whereby the goal is allowed to stand because it’s an own goal. You also get officials having to work out: was the shot on target, was it not on target? The worst-case scenario for us is that the officials decide that the ball is going wide and it’s an own goal, but then later on the goal is attributed to the player that scored, whose arm it hit. So, I think we ought to look at this and just allow the officials to determine whether it’s a normal handball offence. Did he make himself bigger? Did he deliberately handle the ball? And I don’t think [Maguire] does those things in this situation.”

Webb, who has promised greater transparency from Pro Ref, is increasingly expected to give a public verdict on controversial decisions and it was not a surprise to find Match Officials Mic’d Up scheduled for TV 48 hours after the farrago in the Manchester derby.

The VAR Matt Donohue and his assistant Blake Antrobus were stood down from their duties on Monday, after Pro Ref acknowledged “an error of judgment’ in assessing City’s winning goal. Donohue was called on to check the decision to disallow Haaland’s 60th-minute strike for offside. Using semi-automated offside technology, Donohue was able to establish that the striker was onside and he overturned ­Oliver’s call. But he failed to spot Fernández had influenced play from an offside position, an ­infringement which Pro Ref said should have led him to recommend an on-field review.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Erling Haaland celebrates after his goal in the derby was cleared to stand. Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty Images

Webb said it was “important” this error had been acknowledged. “I was really disappointed with this outcome, we all are, none more so than the officials themselves,” he said. “They take a lot of personal pride in what they do and they’re obviously hurting now, having fallen short in this situation. They’ll not be officiating again until after the international break.”

Webb said that Donohue had got “tunnel vision” while assessing the lead-up to the goal, concentrating on Haaland and not Fernández, because the on-field decision was against Haaland. “Donohue doesn’t truly evaluate the full impact of Fernández’s position,” Webb said. “He has a look to see if he touches the ball, because then that relates to potentially knocking it to Haaland, who goes on to score. He doesn’t touch the ball, but he doesn’t truly evaluate other elements of offside. In that moment, he gets tunnel vision. He gets focused on Haaland, and it’s down to the rest of his team to pull him out of that tunnel, and unfortunately, that didn’t happen.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Have laudable Leeds left the chaos behind them?
Sports.content:
THE DAMN FINE UNITED?

It’s been quite the stomach-churning white-knuckle ride for Leeds United over the past decade. Their fans have been forced to endure more highs, lows, loops, corkscrews and rolls than a thrill-seeking visitor on Nemesis Reborn at Alton Towers. There have been b@nter eras, multiple owners, near-misses, promotions, relegations and managerial churn. The Marcelo Bielsa years will always be remembered as fondly as the Thomas Christiansen months have been erased from collective memory. Under Jesse Marsch, Leeds secured dramatic final-day Premier League survival at Brentford, before dropping through the trapdoor the following season despite the best efforts of the High Performance American and Lower Performance Javi Gracia and Big Sam Allardyce.

Three years ago, they were taken over by 49ers Enterprises, a USA USA USA-based organisation pursuing the endearingly romantic notion of extending their “brand into sports, entertainment and technology, leveraging team capabilities in marketing and operations”. Ever since, Leeds have been on an upward trajectory and on Monday night they secured a statement 4-1 victory that suggested for the first time in over 10 years, a period of long overdue stability – if not total serenity, admittedly – may be about to reign over Elland Road for a couple of weeks at least.

Under what the media are now obliged to describe as the [insert pertinent day of the week here] night lights of Elland Road, Leeds didn’t so much beat Newcastle as give them a horse-whipping. Stronger, faster, hungrier and quicker to every ball, there was one sustained period of dominance after they’d already gone 2-0 up when they left their visitors quite literally chasing shadows around the floodlit pitch. Watching his team concede another two goals before nabbing a late consolation, Matthias Jaissle looked shellshocked by their poor performance in the face of such an onslaught. “We couldn’t match the intensity and you see how difficult it can be to win a game in the Premier League,” sighed the German, whose promising start as Eddie Howe’s successor could scarcely have come to a more abrupt halt.

Despite admitting he prefers to celebrate a win by enjoying a hot beverage and cake on his sofa, such was the dominance of Leeds over Newcastle that Daniel Farke might have been tempted to unleash the inner “fire beast” to which he has previously alluded and swing from the chandeliers. “It’s important we stay humble, down to earth and can’t allow ourselves to be too big-time or too carried away,” he parped, suggesting a quiet night in with a mug of tea and a couple of accompanying fat rascals lay in store. Having seen their team leapfrog fellow title contenders Hull City to go third in the table, one suspects the post-match celebrations of many fans will not have been as abstemious. A tough bunch to please and often with good reason, they are happily marching on together. Onwards, upwards and in the direction of Arsenal’s Emirates Stadium in just two matches’ time.

View image in fullscreen Daniel Farke delivering his trademark nice touch. Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty Images

My goalkeeper received threats against his life, his wife and his mother – he was told that if he didn’t pay a specific sum or concede three goals, they would be killed” – Guabirá head coach Leonardo Egüez claims that Juan Manuel Ferrel received death threats before their 6-0 defeat by Club Always Ready in the Bolivian top flight. “Football must not be tainted,” said Club Always Ready’s legal adviser Marcelo Ortiz. “We will ask the public prosecutor’s office to investigate so that the sport’s integrity is preserved.”

So can we not just say everyone in the penalty area is active, no matter what they’re doing, and judge offsides accordingly?” – Hugh Fordham.

Sports.title: Craig Bellamy rejected Burnley manager’s job to stay in ‘right place’ with Wales
Sports.content:
Craig Bellamy said he rejected the chance to take charge of Burnley in the summer after deciding the Wales job is “the right place for me”. The 47-year-old was among the managers targeted by the Championship club, who appointed Nicky Hayen.

Bellamy is preparing to lead Wales in the Nations League, with the trip to Portugal on Thursday next week the first of four matches across the extended international break. Bellamy spent two years on the staff at Burnley, working as an assistant to Vincent Kompany and taking caretaker charge after Kompany left for Bayern Munich. Burnley were granted permission to hold talks with him after a triggering release clause in his Wales contract.

“This is the first time I’m talking about it and I made the decision to stay because this is the right place for me,” Bellamy said. “There’s only one person you have to prove [something] to, and that’s to yourself, your morals, what you live by. I’ve never moved for money, I’ve never done anything for money and I ain’t going to change now.

“I’m comfortable with myself, I’m comfortable with the decision I’ve made and I have always been committed in everything I do, that hasn’t changed. I said: ‘No, it’s not for me.’ There was no walking away from discussions. It wasn’t for me. It was that simple.”

Bellamy revealed, when addressing a question about his decision to remain silent in recent months, that he spent a week in intensive care last summer after rupturing his appendix before Wales won in Kazakhstan last September.

“I try to stay quiet, mostly,” he said. “I feel like I’ve got nothing worth saying when I’m not working … l lead a very boring life. I’m sorry if it looks that way [that I have been quiet]. I’ve really enjoyed this summer and got a hang of it. I’ve enjoyed my time with the family and my time working as well.”

Sports.title: From Segura to Maltby: six breakout stars from the Women’s Under-20 World Cup
Sports.content:
The 2026 Under-20 Women’s World Cup is entering the knockout stage in Poland and, after an intriguing group stage, we pick some of the young stars who have stood out.

Celia Segura (Spain and Barcelona)

Segura is no stranger to knockout football having helped Spain to silver at the Under-17 World Cup two years ago and finishing with the Bronze Ball and Bronze Boot. She has picked up the mantleagain as La Roja eased through their group. Her four goals against New Caledonia were an illustration of her pure scoring instinct and she has also played a key role with her high technical skills and instinctive ability to both make space for and find her teammates. Her back-heel assist to set up Pau Comendador against China was a memorable one. A product of the Barcelona academy, the 19-year-old forward made her debut for the senior side back in February and will return to Atlético Madrid for a season-long loan at the conclusion of this tournament.

Annika Paz (Argentina and Inter)

Paz has taken this tournament by storm with performances that have shown a maturity beyond her 17 years. She is one of a few stars in Poland who have already made their debut for their senior national team – she marked her first cap with a goal against Uruguay in 2025, becoming Argentina’s youngest ever goalscorer. Paz netted four goals against Benin here in Poland before also scoring the opener in Argentina’s dramatic 3-2 win over Mexico to send them through. Her pace, movement off the ball and finishing are exceptional, alongside her composure in front of goal. Having progressed from the River Plate pathway to the senior team, Paz made her move to Europe back in January to join Inter.

Rachel Maltby (England and Aston Villa)

After a breakthrough campaign with Aston Villa last season and now a second youth World Cup with England, it has been a memorable year for Maltby. With her four goals and an assist, the 19-year-old has played a crucial role here in England’s progress to the last 16. As she did at the under-17 edition of the tournament back in 2024, the 19-year-old has caught the eye with her assured, attacking performances down England’s left. Full of energy, composure and with an instinctive ability to time her runs into the box, she has displayed her versatility in switching between her more established full-back role and left wing with ease. Her three penalties, which she can take with either foot, are further examples of how mature she has become over the past 12 months.

Annabelle Chukwu (Canada and Notre Dame Fighting Irish)

There is plenty of excitement in Canada around this young forward. Chukwu changed the game from the bench with the opening goal in their 1-1 draw with England and then added two more in their 6-0 routing of Tanzania to send her side through to the knockout stage. Pacy and clinical, her direct transitional threat is second-to-none. Currently at university, the 19-year-old has excelled playing for the Notre Dame Fighting Irish and through the national youth pathways. Earning her name as a prolific goalscorer – she broke the record for most goals scored for Canada’s youth teams with 28 in 34 appearances – she received her first senior debut back in June and surely has her focus set on being part of Casey Stoney’s side at next summer’s World Cup in Brazil.

View image in fullscreen Annabelle Chukwu of Canada. Photograph: Mateusz Słodkowski/FIFA/Getty Images

Huang Jiaxin (China and Shanghai Shengli WFC)

The centre-back has been one of China’s clear standouts in Poland – not just for her efforts at the heart of the defence but also for her goalscoring ability. Her acceleration up the field and 12-minute hat-trick against New Caledonia illustrated not only her willingness to support her side further up the pitch but also her qualities as an instinctive finisher in front of goal. Her manager, Wang Jun, emphasised this versatility in an interview with Fifa. “She has own characteristics,” he said. “In the future, I hope that she can play in Europe and bring her skills to the senior national team.” At 20, that prospect is not far away, particularly with a World Cup for China on the horizon.

Evelin (Brazil and Santos)

Given Brazil’s performances so far in this tournament and with a home senior World Cup to come, it would have been a terrible decision not to include a Brazilian in this list. While there have been quite a few to choose from, 18-year-old Evelin has particularly impressed. She might be small in stature but there is nothing little about her game with her innate natural ability, energy and eye for a finish. She kicked off the tournament with two almost identical finishes against Tanzania and has also registered two assists to help her team cruise through to the last 16. Domestically, she came up through the ranks at Santos where she has progressed into the senior setup. She was part of the Brazil team that finished fourth at last year’s Under-17 World Cup and made her senior debut in April 2026.

Sports.title: How Promise David emerged from Maltese shadows into the Premier League
Sports.content:
Promise David had a five‑year plan. He would score bags of goals, earn a transfer to a top European league and play for Canada at the 2026 World Cup. There was just one problem: apart from his parents, teammates and coaches, no one in soccer seemed to know his name.

It was 2023, and the striker was scrapping for minutes in Estonia’s Meistriliiga – a league small enough that streaming services didn’t bother with its matches. He was 22 and already a football nomad. He had been cut from his hometown club’s academy. Passed over by NCAA college programs. Relegated to the reserve squad of almost every club for which he played.

Even to an optimist, the prospect of playing at a World Cup – let alone a move to the Premier League – was about as distant as Brighton’s shores from David’s home town of Brampton, Ontario. But then, David has never minded the road less travelled.

“He’s worked a lot to get where he is,” says Kaido Koppel, David’s former head coach at Estonia’s Nomme Kalju. “It’s not by accident.”

That perseverance has paid off: David’s loan from Royale Union Saint-Gilloise to Brighton, if made permanent, may yet become the second-most expensive Canadian soccer player transfer in history, after the $34m move of Jonathan David (no relation) from Gent to Lille in 2020. This past summer, Promise David became the fifth Canadian to score at a men’s World Cup. Another appearance in 2030 seems likely.

Even to those who have known the wandering striker since the beginning, his rapid ascent has defied expectations. And now the biggest question is what comes next.

View image in fullscreen Promise David turned heads with impressive performances for Royale Union Saint-Gilloise in Belgium. Photograph: Luc Claessen/BELGA/AFP/Getty Images

‘He’s not missing’

David, born Promise Oluwatobi Emmanuel David Akinpelu, is used to being overlooked. He was cut from Toronto FC’s academy at age 15. He was a riddle for coaches: smart and preternaturally gifted but, like many a teenager, unfocused.

He was “never on time for anything”, says Jorden Feliciano, who coached a teenaged David at Vaughan SC, where he played after getting cut by Toronto. Still, Feliciano says, “the kid could turn it on when he wanted”.

Vaughan, a semi-pro soccer club north of Toronto, has a reputation as one of Canada’s best incubators for men’s and women’s talent, having produced players such as Celtic’s Alistair Johnston and Chelsea’s Kadeisha Buchanan.

“On the field, you never really knew what you were getting from him,” says Stefan Copetti, David’s teammate at Vaughan. “Either he was going to come off the bench and score two goals, or kind of just coast around.” Still, Copetti says, “When he’s in front of goal, he’s not missing.”

View image in fullscreen Promise David, back row, center, pictured with Vaughan SC in 2019. Photograph: Courtesy Jorden Feliciano

A footballing odyssey

Most of David’s teammates at Vaughan earned full-ride scholarships to US college soccer programs. He received one offer: a partial scholarship to Appalachian State University. At the suggestion of a trainer, he took a shot at a Toronto-area talent showcase hosted by NK Hrvatski Dragovoljac, a second-tier Croatian club. He impressed the scouts and club president Niko Tokic Kartelo enough to earn an invite to their youth academy in Zagreb. But as soon as David landed in Croatia, Kartelo was ousted from his role. The club offer fell through. The former president took David into his home. “I could not simply abandon [him] in a foreign country,” Kartelo says. He tried to find David another playing opportunity in Croatia, but met closed doors. “No club wanted him.”

David landed in Croatia’s third division, but left after getting little playing time. His journey continued, first to FC Tulsa in the USL Championship and then, in 2022, to Valletta in the Maltese Premier League. He arrived as a 21-year-old with dwindling hopes of a pro career, and wasted no time making an impression. He scored a 90th-minute equalizer in his third match for the club, then followed up with another goal in his next game. In 14 appearances, he notched four goals and assists apiece, including the goal that sent Valletta to the Maltese FA Trophy final.

“Lots of clubs try to get these tall, physical strikers,” says the Valletta forward Andrea Zammit, a former teammate, “but how ‘Tobi’ was built – 6ft 5in, physical, a good finisher – it’s quite rare to find someone like that.”
