World.title: Air pollution spiked after the Trump administration stopped embassy monitoring
World.content:
Air pollution spiked after the Trump administration stopped embassy monitoring

toggle caption Photo by Melvin James Urubio/NurPhoto/via Getty Images

Growing up in Shanghai in the early 1990s, Eric Zou remembers the air.

"I lived a couple of miles next to a chemical plant and it was just really bad, really foggy," he says. "It's the middle of the day, but you can't see the sun."

Intensive industrial activity blanketed many cities in China during the 1990s and 2000s with extremely hazardous air. But Zou, now an environmental economist at the University of Michigan, says that many people didn't really understand this smog as air pollution, or something that could harm them.

"When you have a big smog event, people often talk about that as fog, they think it was just like bad weather," says Zou. One big key to changing that sentiment, he says, was information initially provided by the United States.

Sponsor Message

In 2008, U.S. officials installed an air quality monitor on the embassy in Beijing and began making the information public. Over time, that helped spur demand for cleaner air, says Zou. "Once you have pollution information, it tends to be that it actually helps people to realize, 'Oh, I actually value air quality.' "

Since 2008, the State Department's monitoring initiative has expanded to more than 80 embassies and consulates. Research suggests that monitoring contributed to measurable improvements in air quality, especially across many low- and middle-income countries with limited monitoring systems of their own.

But in March 2025, the Trump administration shuttered that program, citing monetary costs. Research out this week suggests the move had health costs for the people living in those countries. Over the several months following the shutdown, air pollution levels measured via satellite increased by 24-33%, researchers reported Monday in the journal PNAS.

The State Department declined to comment on the study itself. In a statement to NPR, it did say the State Department is in the process of restoring public reporting of air quality monitoring data, but did not give a timeframe for when it would resume.

"It's a great study, high quality. And it's a real pity," says Andrea La Nauze, an environmental economist at Deakin University in Australia who has researched the benefits of the program but wasn't involved in this study. The program "led to sustained improvements in air quality that were continuing to increase after 10 years," she says.

Sponsor Message

She says this new research suggests those improvements aren't guaranteed if monitoring stops.

Measuring the consequences of not measuring

When Zoey Yiyuan Zhou first heard the news that the Trump administration was shuttering the embassy air quality monitoring, it struck her as a research opportunity.

"It's such a rare case to study this drawback," says the Columbia University climate researcher. While there's ample evidence of the benefits of increased monitoring, she says there aren't many examples of a sudden falloff of surveillance.

Zhou and her colleagues decided to compare air pollution levels before and after monitoring ceased across 46 cities. Since they didn't have on-the-ground measures of air quality for the latter part of that comparison, they used satellite data for both.

The team found no significant trends in air pollution over the 300 days preceding the end of U.S. reporting. But about three to four months after reporting ended, pollution had gone up, on average by about 30%. Satellite data isn't a perfect substitute for monitors that can measure on-the-ground pollution. The researchers estimate their satellite measurements translate to about a 4% increase in PM2.5 — the small suspended particles that can enter the lungs and bloodstream and cause health problems.

"That magnitude is certainly concerning," says La Nauze. "Particulate matter is a serious and dangerous thing, and being exposed to it is not good."

The increase was highest in Southeast Asian cities, including Manila in the Philippines, Rangoon in Myanmar and Vientiane in Laos, says Zhou. Pollution also spiked more in cities with fewer monitoring alternatives.

The study can't say why pollution increased after monitoring stopped.

For countries with nonexistent or nascent monitoring programs, U.S. data may have prompted more regulatory action, says Zou. "Maybe the U.S. Embassy was a really strong force in terms of a third-party auditing mechanism, and once that's removed, people are like 'Now I can just pollute, right?'"

Sponsor Message

In many industries, it costs money to cut down on pollution, says Zhou. When monitoring stops, companies may see it as an opportunity to cut those costs.

But the researchers did find some potentially hopeful news. Pollution levels seemed to go back down somewhat after peaking about three or four months after monitoring stopped.

It's difficult to say why this decrease happened, Zhou says, or whether the trend will continue. She suspects that it may reflect other forms of monitoring, by individuals or local governments, coming online in the wake of the U.S. withdrawal.

But not all areas may have the ability to readily make up for what's been lost, she says, especially in regions where air quality monitoring is new.

"Data is just so important," says Zhou. "Having access to information is necessary to make sure that these previous gains can continue. Public information creates accountability."

World.title: NATO jets shoot down a drone in Lithuanian airspace
World.content:
NATO jets shoot down a drone in Lithuanian airspace

toggle caption AP

VILNIUS, Lithuania — NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight, officials said Tuesday, the day after the head of NATO said strikes close to its territory would only increase its support for Ukraine in its war against Russia's full-scale invasion.

Military officials in Lithuania, a NATO member, said the incident marked the first time that a drone had been shot down in its airspace. Authorities didn't comment on the drone's origin or purpose, saying the incident needed further investigation.

The drone in Lithuania was downed near the village of Pratkūnai, about 60 miles (100 kilometers) west of the capital, Vilnius, and near the Kaunas Reservoir, Lithuania's National Crisis Management Center said Tuesday.

Officials in NATO countries including Germany, Denmark, the United Kingdom, and Poland have in recent weeks accused Russia of involvement in acts such as drone incursions, sabotage, arson, surveillance of defense facilities and planning to use a drone carrying explosives to attack an airport.

Sponsor Message

Rutte on Monday said strikes "close to NATO territory" showed Russian President Vladimir Putin's "desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror."

"Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine," Rutte said. He also pledged to bolster the 32-nation alliance's own defenses along its long eastern border with Russia and with Belarus, a Russian ally.

Drone "likely" to be carrying explosives

The menace of drones has repeatedly loomed over the skies of Lithuania, which shares borders with Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. In May, residents of Vilnius were told to take shelter and the president and prime minister were taken to safe locations amid an alarm over drone activity near the border with Belarus.

Stray Ukrainian drones have also previously crossed the border into Baltic airspace, including in May when a NATO fighter jet shot down a Ukrainian drone over southern Estonia.

Antanas Matutis, commander of the Lithuanian air force, said that the wreckage had been found, and the drone was "likely" carrying explosives.

Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the crisis center, told Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT that the drone most likely entered from Belarus. It remained in Lithuanian airspace for about 30 minutes and flew along the outskirts of populated areas before being intercepted, he said.

Sponsor Message

In a separate encounter Tuesday, Denmark's Foreign Ministry said that a Danish air force helicopter had been fired upon with flares in connection with "routine photographic coverage" of a Russian frigate in waters off the port of Gedser in the Baltic Sea.

"This is completely unacceptable," the ministry wrote on X, saying that the Russian ambassador was summoned over the incident.

Meanwhile, Russia's ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, addressed the incident by saying it was "not the first time" that Danish Air Force helicopters had "carried out dangerous maneuvers near Russian warships."

He also said that the Danish helicopter had carried out "provocative actions against the Russian frigate."

The Kremlin declined to comment Tuesday, with presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov saying that he did not have details of the event.

Kyiv says it's "ready to support de-escalation"

Meanwhile, Russian drone strikes continued across Ukraine following a social media post from U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure.

Trump didn't offer further details on the purported agreement. Previous efforts to broker even a partial ceasefire have repeatedly fallen apart within hours, with both sides accusing each other of violations.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said late Monday that Kyiv was "ready to support de-escalation" if the United States could ensure "Russia is genuinely ready to stop this war."

But Zelenskyy said in a statement on Tuesday that Moscow had continued to attack Ukraine's energy sector, logistics and critical infrastructure, and that Kyiv had responded by striking an oil refinery in Syzran, a city in western Russia.

"There is no alternative to ending this war. And all forms of pressure on Russia must create the right diplomatic conditions," Zelenskyy said.

The Kremlin said Tuesday that it considered Trump's proposal for a ceasefire on energy infrastructure to be "a good idea."

Sponsor Message

However, it stressed that strikes on Russian oil refineries were not the root cause of global supply issues for gas or diesel.

"The core problem lies in the export of petroleum products to global markets," said Peskov. He said that countries instead needed to guarantee safe navigation for oil tankers and lift global sanctions on Russian oil.

Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Tuesday that Russian strikes on Kyiv had killed one person and wounded seven other people since the start of the day, with attacks carried out on the capital's gas stations.

Another two people were killed in separate Russian strikes in the Ukrainian cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.

Elsewhere, Russian forces shot down 222 Ukrainian drones overnight, Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.

A "massive" Ukrainian drone attack sparked several fires in the Russian city of Taganrog, regional Gov. Yuri Slyusar said. He said on Telegram that two apartment buildings and three private homes had been damaged, as well as an educational institution, agricultural warehouses and a site belonging to Russian e-retailer Ozon.

Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Kyiv's forces had targeted a drone production facility in the city.

Ukrainian parliament votes to dismiss prosecutor general

Ukraine's parliament voted to dismiss Ruslan Kravchenko from the post of prosecutor general Tuesday, as a series of graft investigations pushed tensions in Kyiv to a new high.

Kravchenko submitted his resignation on Sept. 7 amid a National Anti-Corruption Bureau investigation into corruption in his office, though no notice of suspicion was issued against him. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had suspended Kravchenko from the post the day before. Kravchenko had served as prosecutor general since June 21, 2025.

Various corruption scandals have hurt Zelenskyy's approval ratings at a time when Ukraine is still fighting for survival against Russia's 4 1/2-year full-scale invasion.

World.title: For thousands of Haitians in the U.S., end of protected status brings fear, grief and defiance
World.content:
For thousands of Haitians in the U.S., end of protected status brings fear, grief and defiance

toggle caption Eva Marie Uzcategui for NPR

MIAMI — Herlain, a registered nurse who was born in Haiti, barely leaves her house these days.

The few times she has, she was terrified. She instructed her family members about how to record on their phones in case she gets detained by federal immigration authorities.

"You would think I was on the run," she told NPR. "Who am I on the run from? This is crazy!"

Even at home she fears strangers and refused to open the door to a salesman who requested water on a humid Florida day during a recent heatwave.

"That's not me. I'm a nurse, I help people," she recounted through tears.

Sponsor Message

Herlain, along with nearly 350,000 other Haitian migrants, lost her temporary protected status, or TPS, in July. She asked NPR to only use her first name because of her immigration status.

For 16 years, many Haitians living in the U.S. have been shielded from deportation due to TPS. The designation allowed Haitians to live and work here legally, safe from the violence, instability and earthquakes that have torn apart their home country.

But now, Haitian TPS holders are facing deportation after the Trump Administration revoked their protected status this summer.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson defended the decision, in an emailed statement to NPR stating "Temporary Protected Status is exactly that — temporary."

"For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent," the agency wrote.

Deportation to a deteriorating country

toggle caption Eva Marie Uzcategui for NPR

Father Reginald Jean-Mary, a reverend at Notre Dame d'Haiti Catholic Church in Miami, called what the government is doing to Haitians "psychological warfare."

"The government knows deep down that they cannot deport 350,000 people!" said the reverend, who goes by Father Reggie.

Father Reggie said depression and anxiety are rampant among his parishioners, who fear going back to Haiti where conditions have worsened.

Sponsor Message

Heavily armed gangs have taken over the capital and are rapidly expanding.

Recently dozens of people were massacred, including women and children sheltering in a church, according to the UN .

toggle caption Eva Marie Uzcategui for NPR

"We look like the forsaken people," Father Reggie said, adding that all of this has tested his faith.

"You ask yourself, 'When, God? When is it going to stop?'" he said. "When you look at what's going on in Haiti you ask yourself, 'Where, God? Where are you?'"

The death of 20-year-old Pierre Damas Bel in Springfield, Ohio has also shaken this South Florida community to its core. The Haitian man apparently died by suicide after losing his TPS and being outfitted with an ankle monitor.

Father Reggie said prayer service attendance has plummeted, including at the church's adult learning school, which started the year with 231 students and is now down to 17.

He knows of 14 parishioners who have been detained by immigration officers.

"This is a community being deconstructed completely," Father Reggie said.

Ghost town

toggle caption Eva Marie Uzcategui for NPR

Little Haiti, the heart of the Haitian community in South Florida, is usually bustling. But since the Trump Administration began posting about the deportation flights of Haitians on social media, few people spend time along the main business corridor, and most shops have their metal shutters down.

A popular restaurant in the area had most of its staff picked up by ICE. A nearby barbershop closed after the owner got detained.

At Libreri Mapou, the Haitian Creole bookstore, owner Jan Mapou explained the emptiness of his store and others.

toggle caption Jose A. Iglesias/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images

"Everybody is in hiding," Mapou said. "Everybody is afraid, traumatized."

People are so afraid to go out that a food bank has opened inside a local church.

But Farah Larreux is not hiding.

The former TV and radio broadcaster came to the U.S. from Haiti after being openly critical about political corruption in her home country.

After losing TPS, she says she doesn't have any other option but to continue speaking out this time against politicians in the U.S. who are demonizing Haitian immigrants who were invited into the country years ago.

"I don't want to give up," Larreux said. "I want to look at Trump in his eyes and tell him how evil he is."

Sponsor Message

She says going back to Haiti now would be a "death sentence" for her, because of how vocal she has been.

Larreux said people are focusing too much on the 'temporary' aspect of TPS. Instead, she said, people should focus on the 'protective' aspect of the program.

She points out the hypocrisy of the Trump Administration, whose State Department has told U.S. citizens not to travel to Haiti because it's too dangerous, and yet is deporting Haitians there.

toggle caption Eva Marie Uzcategui for NPR

"So, is the message that my life has no value?" Larreux asked. "Or my life is less valued than the life of an American citizen?"

She wants another legal pathway for immigrants like her who've fled violence and instability. But under Trump, few legal options now remain for Haitians who want to continue to build a life in the U.S.

Still, many Haitians say they are clinging to their faith. It's the only way many can navigate the risks of being in the country illegally.

Father Reggie said he's been reminding his parishioners to hold on to each other.

"We will not give up because I believe Satan has his hour," he said. "But God has his day."

World.title: NASA rushed engineers out of their labs. They say it risks future space missions
World.content:
NASA rushed engineers out of their labs. They say it risks future space missions

toggle caption Jolearra Tshiteya/NASA via AP

When NASA launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida late last month, engineers were anxious.

Expectations were high. The telescope is supposed to collect more information than any other has before about how the universe is expanding and how many previously hidden planets might be in the galaxy. Fifteen years of preparation and $4 billion had led to this moment.

But with spacecraft, the smallest of mistakes can derail everything. And at NASA's premier space flight complex, the Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., engineers knew that teams working on the telescope had been operating under tenuous conditions. NASA's management had forced scientists to quickly move out of their labs at Goddard multiple times since last November — and as recently as a month before Roman's launch, engineers said.

Sponsor Message

That affected work on the telescope. Propulsion engineers had to run tests on Roman's fuel using less sensitive gear, two engineers told NPR, because some of their tools — which they say were higher quality and more precise — had been lost in a move months before. NASA asked staff at a radio communication lab to test an antenna for Roman before launch, but they'd lost almost all their equipment.

"We can't do the work because we don't have our $6 million antenna chamber anymore," an engineer said.

NPR spoke with seven current and former NASA scientists and engineers at Goddard who said the moves that have continued over the past 10 months have resulted in the loss of specialized workspaces, employees and expensive machines that were critical to making Roman and other spacecraft. Current employees requested that NPR not use their names because they fear retribution for speaking to the media.

NASA's management said that moving scientists out of buildings last year was aimed at reducing costs and eliminating "waste and redundancies," according to internal NASA documents reviewed by NPR. Moving scientists out of more than 80 facilities aligned with a previously published master plan for changes to Goddard's campus and would allow the center to avoid paying tens of millions of dollars in deferred maintenance, NASA has said.

Sponsor Message

But the relocations are hurting NASA's mission, workers said. For decades, NASA helped the U.S. lead the world in the race to space, and Goddard built the spacecraft vital to that mission. Goddard's diminished capacity has been delaying projects and hindering the agency's ability to produce spacecraft in the future, scientists said.

toggle caption Michael S. Williamson/The Washington Post via Getty Images

"That only adds a whole lot of risk to an already risky endeavor," said Jack Kiraly, chief of advocacy at the Planetary Society, a nonprofit that champions space science and exploration. "These are potentially billions of dollars' worth of taxpayer investment. We don't do ourselves any favors by putting the people that make this happen in precarious situations."

One engineer said they had to launch a satellite before it was ready — something they had never done in their more than a decade of working at Goddard. The project, called GRITSS, was launched in July to help other satellites accurately track changes to Earth's water levels and landmasses from space.

But scientists interviewed by NPR say they don't know whether the satellite will be able to do that, because they weren't able to test its ability to radio communications back to Earth before it launched.

"We are half-blind in terms of trying to troubleshoot it," said a scientist who worked on the GRITSS satellite. "The project had to eat the risk."

NASA's management moved a radio communications lab out of its previous space at Goddard in November while employees were home during the government shutdown, engineers told NPR. The engineers lost almost all their equipment and their one-of-a-kind radio communication testing facility, they said, and they were not allowed to try to stop their machines from being taken away.

"We were actively prevented from going to recover material," said another engineer who worked with the lab. "This was ripped away from the hands of NASA employees that would have been most capable of utilizing the equipment."

Sponsor Message

An engineer on a different team said their work on a spacecraft being built to explore Venus, called DAVINCI, was delayed in August because they didn't have a place at Goddard to do their part of the job. Their team's lab and a specialized "clean room" for working on large spacecraft were all moved out of another building at Goddard in November.

"We do not have a replacement lab," the engineer said. "I did not have anywhere to start laying out the components and figure out what we have, what we need and all of that."

Meanwhile, as of August, the lab space they were rushed out of at Goddard remains vacant, the engineer said.

"They clearly don't have a long-term plan," the engineer said, "which was not really how we feel you should be treating world-class engineering labs."

toggle caption Patrick Semansky/AP

The statements from scientists largely contradict a report issued in June from the NASA Office of Inspector General that said moving teams out of labs at Goddard had not hurt ongoing projects and would "not impact NASA's anticipated missions."

NASA didn't respond to NPR's questions about the impacts of the relocations.

NASA officials acknowledged in that report that there was "an increased risk that property may not have been properly accounted for during this process," though the agency said it didn't violate policy.

Internal emails, interviews with scientists and data reviewed by NPR indicate that this wasn't always true. NPR tracked down equipment and found that some of it was auctioned, donated or thrown in the trash, and that NASA's rules for disposing of supplies were not always followed during the moves.

Barbara Thompson, a physicist and founder of NASA's Center for HelioAnalytics, said it disturbed her to see dumpsters filled with equipment and thousands of books that scientists weren't able to keep as they were rushed out of their old labs.

"These items were purchased with taxpayer dollars," Thompson said, "so it felt unethical to me."

More than 300 items from NASA Goddard were also posted on the U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) auction site over the past six months, NPR found.

Sponsor Message

The original cost to NASA for the materials, which included dozens of pieces of specialized lab gear and pieces of telescopes, was around $5.4 million. Although some of the items were categorized as salvage or scrap, employees said those descriptions weren't always accurate, since the items were sometimes labeled by people who weren't engineers and didn't understand the equipment.

Bidders tried to get incredible deals. An aspheric test blank, a piece of unpolished material that can be used to test imaging systems for telescopes, was originally purchased by NASA for more than $250,000. The last bid on it, before the sale closed in May, was for $300.

The government restricts who can buy its spacecraft hardware. About a third of the NASA items auctioned by GSA, including that test blank, were classified as items whose sale was supposed to be restricted because of their importance to missile technology, national security, anti-terrorism or regional stability, according to an NPR analysis of GSA's catalog data.

toggle caption U.S. General Services Administration

People who buy those sorts of items are typically subject to heightened restrictions, like U.S. citizenship requirements and a statement that outlines how bidders plan to use the materials, GSA confirmed to NPR.

NPR asked NASA whether the agency was aware the items were restricted when they were put up for auction, but the agency did not answer the question. A GSA representative said all bidders on the restricted items signed online statements that certified they were allowed to buy them.

Kiraly said it was deeply unusual that so many restricted items and pieces of advanced technology from NASA were put up for auction.

"Say it does fall into the hands of another country's military or civil space program," Kiraly said. "It's the fact that they have access to it — that is the big concern."

NASA also gave away other equipment to educational institutions, a practice that is permitted if scientists no longer need the materials. But NASA donated hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of radio communications equipment to Capitol Technology University without the knowledge of the scientists who used it, NPR found.

When those scientists discovered their equipment had been given away, they asked a supervisor whether they could have it back, internal emails show, but were told that reclaiming it was unlikely.

Sponsor Message

Jeffrey Volosin, the professor at Capitol Technology University who received the donation, said he didn't ask for the equipment. As soon as he learned that NASA scientists were looking for their machines, he said he invited them to borrow the gear and initially offered to return some of it. But the equipment belongs to the university now, Volosin confirmed in August, and is being installed in a campus lab for primarily student use.

"The fact that scientists are not being consulted about what their instruments are going to be used for, what their hardware is going to be used for, is really outside of the norm," said Kiraly. "That center leadership can just give away materials without that buy-in is beyond the pale."

NASA didn't respond to NPR's questions about the donation.

The government's actions come on the heels of a significant federal workforce reduction. Goddard lost about a third of its employees in 2025, which left the center's staffing out of balance with the work the agency had to do, a government watchdog group concluded in a report published in July. Even more scientists are leaving now. Thompson, the physicist, worked for NASA for 30 years. But she lost trust in NASA's leadership after her lab was moved and decided to quit in June.

toggle caption Laura Betz/NASA via AP

She isn't alone. Almost 60% of Goddard engineers surveyed by NASA this year said they plan to leave soon, according to internal survey results reviewed by NPR. More cuts could be on the horizon. The White House budget request proposes $5.6 billion less for NASA in 2027, a 23% decrease from the agency's budget in 2026.

Some scientists say the agency won't be able to perform at nearly the standard it did before.

"When we were packing up our labs," said an engineer who helped work on Roman, "we were pretty much point-blank told to 'pack as if you are never going to build another propulsion system again.'"

Sponsor Message

NPR would like to hear from more people who work with federal agencies and have information to share. You can email the reporter of this article, Chiara Eisner, at ceisner@npr.org or contact her on Signal here, username ceis.78.

World.title: This  bill could reshape crypto in America -- and it's sparking a major battle
World.content:
This bill could reshape crypto in America — and it's sparking a major battle

toggle caption Karen Bleier/AFP via Getty Images

It could be a game changer for the cryptocurrency industry. That is, if it can survive fierce opposition and actually become law.

On Tuesday, the Senate will hold a key procedural vote on the Clarity Act — officially called the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act — which has been at the top of the crypto sector's wish list for years.

The massive bill — which stretches over 600 pages — would establish the first regulations for the crypto sector in U.S. history.

But opponents see this as the industry's attempt to encode into law a set of rules that are far too lenient on the industry, without enough safeguards.

Sponsor Message

A version of the bill already passed the House last year, but it has faced a long and torturous road in the Senate as opponents have fought tooth and nail.

Here's 5 key things to know about the Clarity Act — and why opponents are fighting so hard to prevent it from ever being passed.

What's in it?

Just like with most things dealing with crypto, the details are complicated and a bit geeky. But it effectively establishes a clear legislative framework for the crypto sector for the first time in U.S. history.

That would mark a sea change from today, where crypto regulation can change depending on who controls the White House. Under President Biden, for example, the Securities and Exchange Commission took an aggressive approach against the crypto sector. But that changed radically under President Trump with the agency now led by Paul Atkins, a former adviser to the industry.

"Tens of millions of Americans are investing in products that don't have clear regulatory oversight," said Ryan VanGrack, vice chair of Coinbase, a major crypto firm. "That's an abomination."

"Whether you love crypto or you hate crypto, you should want it regulated," he added. "And this is the best opportunity we have ever had to do just that."

Sponsor Message

The crypto sector has also grown beyond Bitcoin to include all kinds of cryptocurrencies – such as meme coins. Meanwhile, the technology underpinning Bitcoin and some other cryptocurrencies are also starting to be adopted by the broader financial sector.

The Clarity Act would formally split oversight of the crypto sector between the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. But — controversially— it would give the CFTC, a far smaller regulator, the majority of control.

Critics say handing the CFTC the bulk of the reins is the crypto sector's way to avoid heavy regulatory scrutiny. Crypto industry executives deny that's the case, and Trump administration regulators have defended their oversight of the industry.

toggle caption Alex Wong/Getty Images North America

What's at stake for Tuesday's vote?

It's effectively a vote to decide if the bill gets to move forward at all. The Senate would need 60 "yes" votes to clear that hurdle — meaning all 53 Republicans would have to back it, along with seven Democrats or Independents.

That's far from guaranteed. The bill still faces significant opposition, and Tuesday's procedural vote is its most critical test to date. If it does advance, the Senate can move ahead with debate, and, eventually, a final vote.

Even if the bill passes the Senate, though, it would not go straight to President Trump. Because senators have changed the bill since it passed the House last year, both chambers would still have to agree on a final version.

But it's unclear how soon that might happen, with a busy agenda in Congress — and midterm elections coming up fast in early November.

The crypto sector had been hoping to pass the Clarity Act much sooner — and have amassed tens of millions to spend on the upcoming elections. But money hasn't been enough to erase the disagreements that have dogged the bill for months.

Why are Democrats pushing back?

For Democrats, a key sticking point is an ethics clause intended to prevent presidents and other elected officials from profiting from the crypto industry while in office. Democrats, including Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have argued the clause doesn't do enough to prevent conflicts of interest.

Sponsor Message

Notably, the Department of Justice would be tasked with enforcing the ethics clause, which Democrats strongly object to since they don't believe the agency would provide a meaningful check on a sitting president. The DOJ is currently led by Todd Blanche, who used to be Trump's attorney.

Those concerns intensified after President Trump disclosed he and his family had earned $1.4 billion last year from his crypto ventures — an unprecedented sum for a sitting president.

Republicans are now trying to break the impasse.

Under the new language unveiled by Republicans, federally elected officials and their spouses would not be allowed to issue their own cryptocurrencies. That could effectively prevent Trump from continuing $TRUMP, a meme coin he launched early last year— a point Trump agreed to abide by.

Officials would also have to divest "significant" financial stakes in the crypto sector, a provision that could affect some of Trump's crypto business interests — though critics say the language is loose enough to allow the president to avoid it altogether.

The new language would also give state attorney generals more ability to bring lawsuits if they suspect a breach of ethics rules.

toggle caption Alex Wong/Getty Images North America

Are others opposing the Clarity Act?

Yes. Many people in the banking sector— especially community bank leaders — are against it.

One of the main disputes involves a segment of the crypto market called stablecoins. The bill would offer financial rewards such as interest payments to customers who place their money with these crypto companies.

Banks argue those incentives allow crypto companies to compete for customers' money without being subject to the same regulations as traditional banks.

Crypto companies have disputed that characterization and argue these incentives are similar to what many credit card companies offer, such as cash backs or points.

Community bankers have been especially vocal. They say allowing crypto companies to offer these types of incentives would pose a direct threat to their business and lead them to lose customers.

Rebeca Romero Rainey, president and CEO of the Independent Community Bankers of America, says keeping their customers' money with local banks is critical because it allows them to provide small business and agricultural loans to members of their communities.

Sponsor Message

"If community banks aren't there, and those local deposits aren't there to fund it, who's going to fund those small businesses and ranchers and farmers?" she said. "I don't think it's going to be the crypto industry."

So what are the odds of passage?

It's impossible to say whether Republicans have the votes to survive Tuesday's hurdle — or whether they would need to try again at a later date.

The vote is a priority for Trump, who has strongly supported the crypto industry. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) set up Tuesday's vote before the Senate took a break for recess even though the outcome remained uncertain.

But the Clarity Act has faced so many twists and turns that even if it survives beyond Tuesday, the path ahead remains uncertain.

World.title: Alberta referendum pitches more control over immigration. Here's what you need to know
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Albertans will head to the polls on Oct. 19 to cast their votes on 10 questions put forward by the provincial government.

You’ve probably heard of the one related to separation . The other nine have received far less attention.

Five of the questions in the referendum will address immigration policies and could lead to major changes for newcomers to the province.

But both the questions and the process citizens face on voting day are unprecedented in Alberta and, it’s been argued, are also unfamiliar and complex.

CBC News is breaking down the referendum questions and providing some important context so you feel better prepared to vote.

The first immigration-related ballot voters will see is: “Do you support the government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?”

Let’s delve deeper into what the question is asking, how we got here, and what the full picture looks like when it comes to immigration to Alberta.

Breaking down the question

If you come away from reading the 34-word question confused, you’re not alone . There are several aspects to that one sentence, so let’s break it down, bit by bit.

First, there’s the heart of the UCP government’s proposition: It’s asking you, the voter, whether the Government of Alberta should take increased control over immigration.

Immigration is a shared jurisdiction of the federal and provincial governments with federal paramountcy, so what’s implied here is that the province would have more say when it comes to newcomers entering Alberta.

Then, there’s this next bit: "for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels."

So, it seems the province wants to see fewer newcomers move to Alberta. But what exactly are the “sustainable levels” of immigration it’s trying to achieve?

When asked to define the phrase, Sam Blackett, the premier’s director of media relations, said: “Alberta supports balanced and sustainable immigration levels that maintain a strong focus on economic immigration to address skilled-labour shortages. Immigration levels should be responsive to our province’s current and future economic needs.”

The province hasn’t provided exact immigration targets it would consider “sustainable,” and experts tell us it’s a hard term to define. More on that later.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks during a news conference on the October referendum in Calgary on May 22, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Let’s move on to the next point in the referendum question: “prioritizing economic migration.”

When the province says it wants to prioritize economic migration, it means it wants to attract skilled workers who already have the training and abilities to fill the specific needs of Alberta’s economy.

Those immigrants would take on skilled positions that are not being filled by Albertans or Canadians, the province clarifies in the FAQ section of its official referendum website .

Lastly, the referendum question suggests Alberta wants more control over immigration for the purpose of giving “Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities.”

The critical question here is: who is an "Albertan"?

The definition of "Canadian” is straightforward enough, because having citizenship determines whether someone is legally Canadian.

But the definition of "Albertan" is trickier to spell out. Canadians and permanent residents can move to Alberta from another province at any time and establish residency for health care and driving purposes after living in the province for 90 days.

When asked, the province did not define who it views as the “Albertans” who would be given priority for new employment opportunities, should the question receive a majority.

So, the first referendum question on immigration is a hefty one that comes with a complex history. Let’s get into that next.

How we got here

Over the past decade, Alberta has experienced a period of rapid growth. Its population increased by roughly 600,000 in the five-year period from July 2021 to July 2026, according to Statistics Canada.

Last year, the province crossed a total population of five million .

Two-thirds of that increased population comes from international migration (408,000) and 20 per cent from people coming to Alberta from other provinces (122,000), according to the federal agency.

Compared to the other major provinces (Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia), Alberta reached the highest growth rate over that period, which was in line with a national increase as the country welcomed more immigrants.

Alberta is still growing the fastest among the major provinces, though population growth has slowed down significantly.

In the five-year period of rapid growth, Alberta made efforts to bring more people into the province.

In 2022, the Government of Alberta under former premier Jason Kenney launched its “Alberta is Calling” campaign, initially aimed at attracting skilled workers from Toronto and Vancouver. In March 2023, it rolled out a second round of the ad campaign, this time targeting skilled workers from Ontario and Atlantic Canada.

And then there’s the provincial nominee program that allows the province to nominate people for permanent residence, including skilled workers, entrepreneurs and others, based on economic priorities. Nominees may also include temporary foreign workers who already work in Alberta, as a way to transition them to permanent residency.

Each year, the allocation target is different. In 2026, it was 6,600 people.

In 2024, the allotment was closer to 10,000. In a letter that year, Smith called on former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government to double the number of Alberta's federal immigration allotments to 20,000 and add 10,000 on top of that for Ukraine evacuees.

The province now says the current immigration level isn’t sustainable. And as with so many things, there's a mix of politics and policy at play.

The UCP government blames Trudeau’s “open border” immigration policy for bumping the number of newcomers, including “millions of individuals without the skills needed to fill our nation's and province's specific economic needs,” it says on its referendum website.

In 2024, Canada admitted 483,600 immigrants as permanent residents — the highest annual number recorded by Statistics Canada since 1972. The preliminary number of non-permanent residents living in Canada peaked at 3,149,000 on Oct. 1, 2024, according to the agency, which will update the number in September.

It wasn’t just Alberta pointing the finger. Trudeau-era policies have been widely criticized for an immigration increase , especially in the number of temporary foreign workers and international students (who largely make up the non-permanent resident pool) admitted to Canada.

But to say Trudeau had an "open border" policy isn’t accurate in the literal sense. That term typically refers to the free movement of people across international boundaries with minimal restriction — something the Liberal government of the day did not allow.

Another claim Alberta is making is that some employers have relied "far too heavily on temporary foreign workers to fill employment positions without giving Albertans and other Canadians adequate opportunity to secure those jobs first," according to the province's referendum FAQ online.

It’s important to remember here that in order for a Canadian employer to hire a temporary foreign worker to fill a position, they have to fill out a labour market impact assessment first to prove there are no Canadians available to take on that job.

WATCH | Alberta's referendum website prompts complaints: Alberta's referendum website prompts complaints | Duration 2:04 An Alberta government website laying out questions — about immigration and the constitution — for upcoming referendums is being criticized by some who say it provides one-sided information.

All in all, the province says Ottawa’s “unsustainable” immigration policies have had a negative impact on Alberta’s ability to fund and deliver social services like health care and education, "directly impacting Albertans' access to these services and costing taxpayers billions of dollars."

For many Albertans grappling with the growing pains of a rising population, that message resonates.

Polls commissioned by CBC News in 2025 found over 60 per cent of Edmontonians and Calgarians felt their city was growing too fast.

Some have pinned the blame more directly on immigrants. At one of the province’s Alberta Next Panel events last year, the Lloydminster crowd cheered at the idea of mass deportations .

A recent poll commissioned by CBC News also found more than half of Albertans want the province to take a more active role in setting the rules for immigration.

Christopher Worswick, a labour economist and professor at Carleton University whose work explores the economics of immigration, said the policies that allowed the surge in temporary residents and immigrants to Canada have turned public sentiment against welcoming newcomers.

“I think that there was a sense that came out of that that the housing implications in particular, but also the health-care implications of providing services to this rapidly growing segment of the population under the immigration/temporary migration categories, sort of led people to think that this was too much,” he said.

“And so you started to see public opinion shifting away from … unconditional support for immigration.”

Immigration levels already on the decline

Data shows immigration is already on the decline, due in large part to the federal government.

That’s the first thing people need to know before answering the first question on the October ballot, according to Ethel Tungohan, an associate professor of politics at York University in Toronto.

“[Canada has] gone down from an expected 500,000 [permanent resident] admissions in 2025 to 395,000 admissions to now in 2026: 380,000 admissions. So already we are cutting back on immigration,” said Tungohan, the Canada Research Chair in Canadian migration policy, impacts and activism.

While Alberta is still growing the fastest amongst the major provinces, fewer immigrants are moving to Alberta . The number of immigrants who moved to the province in the first quarter of 2026 (11,100) fell by about 18 per cent from the same time last year, according to Statistics Canada.

Temporary resident targets reduced

Preliminary Statistics Canada data shows more temporary residents left the province than arrived over the past year, contributing to Alberta’s population growth slowdown.

Temporary residents are non-permanent residents, including international students and temporary foreign workers.

This past year, the province saw its lowest increase in population since 2021, at 0.94 per cent, according to Statistics Canada.

As of June, Alberta has about 260,000 temporary residents. Of those, 66 per cent were work permit holders (including some who also have a study permit). A little more than 14 per cent of Alberta’s non-permanent residents only hold a study permit, down from 27 per cent about five years ago.

Ottawa’s 2026-28 Immigration Levels Plan reduces the temporary resident target by almost half , from 673,650 in 2025 to 385,000 in 2026, and 370,000 in 2027 and 2028.

What exactly are 'sustainable' immigration levels?

Back to that question about "sustainable" immigration.

Kevin McQuillan, a research fellow at the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy, says it’s a concept that’s not easy to define.

As Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has made a “jarring cutback” to immigration through its policy changes, McQuillan reminds us that not everyone wants or benefits from lower immigration numbers.

Take universities and colleges, for example.

Last November, the University of Calgary told CBC News it was losing an estimated $34.7 million in 2025 due to the decline in international student enrolment.�

Many post-secondary institutions built new residences or expanded programs, in part, for the large influx of international students who pay higher tuition than domestic students, McQuillan said.

Now, those institutions are "feeling a pinch," he said.

“The idea of ‘sustainable,’ I think in principle is a good one, but to translate that into exact targets I think is difficult."

According to Worswick, “sustainable” is a fairly new term being used in immigration policy discourse to describe provincial and federal immigration targets.

“In the past, people would talk about absorptive capacity with respect to immigration,” he says.

An example of absorptive capacity is if Canada identified highly skilled immigrants who it thinks would likely find success in the labour market, the country may consider whether it can build new homes fast enough to house the new migrants, or if the health care system can be expanded quickly enough to absorb the additional load, Worswick explained.

A spokesperson for Lena Metlege Diab, the federal Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, says, “Our government and that of Alberta both agree on the need to restore sustainability to our immigration system and that’s exactly what Canada’s new government has been doing,” citing slowing population growth.

“We recently expanded the Provincial Nominee Program, giving provinces more control over the selection of immigrants. And, using existing powers, Alberta has already launched pathways for health-care workers, rural communities, law enforcement professionals, and entrepreneurs.”

LISTEN | Part one of a two-part documentary on Canada's political 180 on immigration: Front Burner 21:48 Canada's immigration 180: Part 1

What your 'yes' or 'no' vote could mean

At the heart of this question is a tug of war between federal and provincial control over immigration.

Voting "yes" to the first referendum question means supporting Alberta's pitch to exert more power over how many newcomers — and which kind — are welcome to the province.

For Worswick, the question signals that Alberta could be looking to develop a more independent economic immigration program, akin to Quebec.

That province has a special agreement with the federal government that asks skilled workers who want to become permanent residents to apply to the Quebec government first, allowing the province to set immigration targets.

But Tungohan said a "yes" vote could have enormous implications, creating a "chilling effect" that drives residents, and subsequently businesses, away from the province if they view Alberta's heightened immigration control as creating a "hostile" environment.

"It is going to turn our backs away from Alberta's long and storied history of being a place ... of settlement and immigrant innovation."

Already, the question has raised concerns among established immigrants in Alberta about whether they are welcome in the province they’ve called home for years.

WATCH | Alberta's Filipino community raising questions about its future ahead of referendum: Alberta’s Filipino community raising questions about its future ahead of referendum | Duration 1:53 The October 19th referendum has members of Edmonton’s Filipino community talking about their future in the province. As the CBC’s Tristan Mottershead reports, there’s growing concern from temporary residents.

Worswick said a “yes” vote could mean the public sentiment that has turned against newcomers could eventually turn again with a “stable, steady inflow” of immigrants and temporary residents.

But, he cautions that it largely depends on how the provincial government develops that policy if the referendum receives a majority.

In an online analysis of the referendum questions, the Alberta branch of the Canadian Bar Association notes that, "Giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities is legally problematic. All individuals (not only citizens) have equality rights under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms that prevent discrimination in hiring."

A “no” vote on the first referendum question means the voter would prefer to keep decision making on immigration primarily at the federal level, Worswick said.

“For example, if you're a resident of Alberta and you're not confident that the [provincial] governments that you see elected are going to do a good job of this, you might vote ‘no’ to say ‘I'm comfortable leaving this as a predominantly federal jurisdiction.’”

Ethel Tungohan, left, is an associate professor of politics at York University in Toronto and Canada Research Chair in Canadian migration policy, impacts and activism. Christopher Worswick, right, is a labour economist and professor at Carleton University. (Submitted by Ethel Tungohan, Christopher Worswick)

But he reminds voters that “the province deals with the problems” related to an increased population, not Ottawa.

“The province … should provide social housing and social assistance [and health care], and the federal government may or may not transfer funds,” Worswick said.

“A lot of these issues and housing all fall within either provincial or municipal levels. They're not really federal jurisdictions.”

World.title: Family wants killing of young engineer linked with case of kidnapped Canadian mining firm workers
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The family of Pablo Osorio Sánchez is calling on federal authorities in Mexico to link the killing of the 26-year-old engineer with the ongoing investigation into the January kidnapping of 10 Canadian mining firm workers.

Osorio Sánchez was kidnapped in the same town and around the same time that armed men seized the Vizsla Silver Corp. employees and contractors. His body was buried in the same clandestine graves where federal authorities located nine of the 10 kidnapped workers.

The family believes the facts around the Vizsla Silver kidnappings could also reveal the truth behind Osorio Sánchez's fate.

"We want answers, we need them to explain to us who kidnapped him, for what reason. Who were they? We have so many questions and so few answers," said Jaime López, Osorio Sánchez’s uncle, in a phone interview with CBC News from Florida.

Between 6 a.m. and 7 a.m. on Jan. 23, armed men, allegedly aligned with a Sinaloa cartel faction, stormed a gated compound in Concordia, Sinaloa, called La Clementina where Vizsla Silver housed its workers and parked some of its vehicles.

Around 7:30 that same morning, Osorio Sánchez walked from his residence in Concordia, a municipality roughly 50 kilometres east of the Pacific Coast city of Mazatlan, to a bus stop. He called his girlfriend while waiting for his regular weekday ride to his worksite at a highway tunnel several kilometres to the east.

During the phone conversation, his partner suddenly heard male voices. One said, "We can fix this." Then the line went dead. That was the last time she ever spoke to him, according to family testimony and filings from the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Inside the Clementina gated residential compound, where a number of vehicles with the Vizsla Silver Corp. logo are parked. The site, sealed by Sinaloa's state Attorney General's Office, is believed to be the place where 10 Vizsla Silver workers were kidnapped on Jan. 23, 2026. (Heriberto Luzanilla/CBC)

'Indicio C'

Federal authorities located the body of Osorio Sánchez, originally from Taxiaco, Oaxaca, about two weeks later. He was buried at a depth of two metres along with an unknown number of other bodies in one of at least two unmarked, clandestine graves dug into an open field in El Verde, a village about 19 km northwest of Concordia.

Authorities identified the spot where Osorio Sánchez was found as "fosa 2," or Grave 2, according to investigative records obtained by CBC News. They wrapped Osorio Sánchez's body in a blue surgical sheet and tagged his body bag with the label "Indicio C" to identify it among the other bodies found in the same area on Feb. 6.

Post-mortem examinations determined he died from a gunshot wound to the upper right side of the head and that his body suffered severe blunt-force trauma before his death. A suspected bullet wound was also found on his right jaw, with no exit point.

"We are destroyed, mentally, because this is a very big loss for us," said López.

Osorio Sánchez was the oldest of three brothers.

The El Verde gravesites also included the remains of nine of the 10 men kidnapped from the Vizsla Silver compound. Some of the other bodies were found with similar signs of blunt-force trauma with gunshot wounds to the head, according to information obtained by CBC News.

The whereabouts of the 10th kidnapped Vizsla Silver worker, F rancisco Antonio Esparza Yáñez, who was responsible for community relations, remains unknown.

Maurillo Santiago, a lead lawyer with the Centre for Human Rights and Legal Council for Indigenous Peoples in Oaxaca, said separate branches of the federal Attorney General’s Office are handling Osorio Sánchez’s case and the Vizsla Silver workers investigation.

Santiago, who is representing the family, said that investigators with the forced disappearances unit are managing Osorio Sánchez’s case, while the organized crime branch holds the Vizsla Silver file.

The Attorney General's Office did not respond to a CBC News request for comment.

'A gap that we can't cross'

Yetzy Santiago Lorenzo, a lawyer with the same human rights group that's also handling the case, said there are still outstanding questions around how the clandestine graves were found, who found them and who was buried alongside Osorio Sánchez.

She said it remains unclear whether it was federal and state authorities that found the graves in El Verde or civilian collectives that search for disappeared persons.

"There is a strange secrecy around this, because the moment the graves were found, federal authorities, the Attorney General’s office, took over and guarded the area," said Santiago Lorenzo.

"Why does the Attorney General’s Office separate Pablo’s investigation from the group? There is a space, a gap that we can’t cross yet."

Heavily armed Mexican troops patrol near an area where authorities say bodies and human remains were found near El Verde, Sinaloa, on Feb. 8, 2026. (Heriberto Luzanilla/CBC)

Osorio Sánchez and the Vizsla Silver workers were kidnapped and killed amid a more than two-year-long civil war within the Sinaloa cartel between La Chapiza, those still loyal to the sons of Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán Loera, and La Mayiza, those loyal to the son of Ismael "El Mayo" Zambado, who once co-led the Sinaloa cartel with El Chapo.

The civil war, which has left thousands of people dead and disappeared across the state, flared after one of El Chapo’s sons lured El Mayo to a July 2024 meeting on the outskirts of the Sinaloan capital of Culiacan to have him kidnapped and turned over to U.S. authorities.

Mexican federal authorities have said a cell linked to the La Chapiza faction was responsible for the kidnapping and killings of Vizsla Silver's workers.

In June, a local, La Chapiza-aligned boss named Gabriel Nicolás "El Gabito, El 80" Martínez Larios was arrested in connection with the Vizsla Silver kidnapping. This month, federal authorities announced the arrests of Angel Gabriel, known as "El Tronco," and Milton Yair, along with 11 other people, including two minors, who were part of the La Chapiza cell linked to the case.

Gabriel and Yair were reportedly members of a La Chapiza commando unit known as Los Menores.

In the middle of conflict territory

A July report from International Crisis Group on the civil war said hundreds of families fled the Concordia region in September 2024 as the conflict exploded and La Mayiza gunmen "dislodged the local strongman" affiliated with La Chapiza.

Vizsla Silver’s exploration operations are in the middle of this conflict territory. The Canadian mining firm is conducting exploration work across 35,000 hectares in a remote and mountainous area as part of its flagship Panuco Project, roughly 25 km east of Concordia’s urban centre.

"Dozens [of families] have since returned … Many services, however, are now controlled by [La Mayiza], including public transport," said the report.

Vizsla Silver's Panuco mining project headquarters in Sinaloa, Mexico. (Vizsla Silver)

The deaths, violence and chaos of the conflict in Sinaloa have likely played a role in the decision by federal authorities to treat Osorio Sánchez’s case differently from that of the Vizsla Silver workers, which received widespread coverage, said Mexico City lawyer Cesar Gutiérrez Priego, a specialist in national security and military affairs.

"That has created enormous legal uncertainty and problems. No matter how hard the federal government tries to show results, the reality is that Pablo’s case, for example, is just one more among many that keep piling up," he said.

"It isn’t a priority for the media or authorities. They simply haven’t placed the necessary emphasis on conducting the investigation as it should be done."

Gutiérrez Priego said the family’s lawyers should petition a federal judge to join the cases.

Santiago Lorenzo said that at the moment, they are focused on convincing the Attorney General’s Office to add the case to the one involving the Vizsla Silver workers before making any applications to the court.

The wait for answers weighs heavily on Osorio Sánchez’s family.

"I call on the Mexican authorities not to let this become normalized," said Lopez.

"There are many young people, students, who want to become engineers, too, and it would be sad if [their careers] ended in the same way."

World.title: Trump claims AI poses no real risk — but even some of his allies disagree
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Fresh warnings that artificial intelligence models could go rogue and wipe out the human race appear to have jolted some U.S. politicians into action, but not President Donald Trump.

In a flurry of posts to his Truth Social platform on Monday, Trump dismissed AI regulation as something that would drive the industry "into oblivion and bankruptcy" and claimed that the economic engine of AI "will not be stopped" while he is president.

"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," Trump declared in one post.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he said in another.

Trump's posts come in response to dire predictions about the technology's potential risks and mounting calls from executives and researchers to rein in the industry.

Last week, engineer Jacob Coxon thrust AI safety into the public spotlight by announcing his resignation from his job with Anthropic in a social media post that warned: " The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."

WATCH | Trump rejects calls for regulation: Anthropic CEO calls for AI development to slow down | Duration 2:48 Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that AI development needs to slow down for safety measures to catch up. U.S. President Donald Trump dismissed the risk of artificial intelligence when questioned by reporters.

While Trump is the most powerful voice in Washington opposing calls to rein in AI, he is far from the only one.

More than 260 bills have been introduced in Congress containing provisions to address the risks from AI since 2021, yet only two have become law, according to the Brennan Center's AI legislation tracker.

However, experts in AI policy see some encouraging signs in the past few days that the political momentum could now be shifting in favour of regulation.

'Full speed, no brakes'

Chris MacKenzie, vice-president of communications at Americans for Responsible Innovation, a non-profit advocacy group in Washington focused on AI safety, says one of the biggest obstacles to regulation has long been the amount of money stacked against it.

"We have a lot of money on the other side of this issue, a lot of money and lobbyists who do not want to see AI regulations," MacKenzie told CBC News.

"They want innovation at full speed, no brakes."

But as the public outcry grows for Congress to take action and the issue becomes a campaign talking point in the U.S. midterm elections, MacKenzie says he's confident there will be some movement.

Last December, Trump signed an order directing the Department of Justice and the Attorney General to challenge state-level AI regulations in court. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

"At the moment, what we see is a real window of opportunity where lawmakers and the public are mobilized around these issues and there's a clear desire to pass guardrails that will protect people from AI's risks," he said.

One event that helped fuel that desire came in late July, when OpenAI revealed that hundreds of its AI agents had gone rogue by independently breaking out of their secure testing environment and hacking into the servers of Hugging Face, an online platform of AI development tools.

Warnings about the risks have accelerated in the past week, kicked off by Coxon's post stating that AI "could kill us all." They include:

Thursday: Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, said it had banned some accounts linked to foreign governments and military actors for using its AI models to try to develop weapons.

Thursday: Former U.S. president Barack Obama told top Democrats to make AI safety policy a priority. "I f we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous," he said.

Saturday: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay urging a slower pace of AI development to manage the risks. His rivals Elon Musk, chief executive of X, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, supported his call.

Monday: Microsoft published its code of conduct to ensure human control of AI.

While plenty of Democrats lined up on the weekend to call for stricter AI regulation, even a few prominent Republicans expressed openness to tighten oversight. They included Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and the party's candidate for the Senate in Michigan, Mike Rogers, a former chairman of Intel.

"I believe we must slow down development of AI in order to allow the government and its partners to catch up and put stricter protocols and guardrails in place," Rogers posted on X.

WATCH | The risks of 'superintelligence': Superintelligence is 'an adversary,' says AI researcher | Duration 5:46 Concerns about the risks AI poses to humanity are growing, with some researchers calling for a slowdown in its development. AI researcher Connor Leahy says it's important to distinguish between AI and superintelligence, arguing that superintelligence is not a tool or a weapon, but 'an adversary.'

With major AI companies and an increasing number of Republicans agreeing that something needs to be done, Trump will likely need to compromise, says Nita Farahany, a Duke University professor who studies the legal and social implications of emerging technologies .

"I think it's going to be hard for the president to stay in the camp of 'No, let's go full speed ahead,'" Farahany told CBC News.

"I think you're going to see a shift, probably within the next 72 hours, out of the White House about what their tune is going to be on these issues."

Trump has long resisted AI regulation. Last December, he signed an order aimed at forcing states to drop their efforts at regulating the technology.

The top Republican in the U.S. House of Representatives, Speaker Mike Johnson, says Trump may meet with AI company executives at some point in the next two weeks, but he's making no promises about the outcome.

The meeting would be "a deliberate discussion about the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety, and what role, if any, the government has to play," Johnson told reporters on Capitol Hill on Monday.

One sign that regulating AI appeals across a wide range of the political spectrum is the eclectic list of people slated to attend the launch of the Pro-Human Assembly, a new coalition that says its mission is "charting a better path for AI."

Among the speakers at the event Tuesday in Washington: Steve Bannon, Trump's one-time chief of staff and a prominent MAGA voice, along with Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, a darling of the left.

World.title: N.S. families thought they buried their loved ones. Officials are now investigating
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The province and the Nova Scotia regulator of funeral directors are investigating after the new owners of an Annapolis Valley funeral home discovered the cremated remains of a “significant number” of people in storage, CBC News has learned.

It comes as several Nova Scotia families who used the services of Serenity Funeral Home say they were shocked and horrified to receive calls letting them know that ashes belonging to their dead loved ones had been found.

“I kind of started internally freaking out because I buried my mom in 2024,” said Kristina Sweeney.

“I don't even think the shock has worn off yet.… I thought I buried my mom, all of her. I put her in the ground by myself.”

Sweeney wasn't the only one contacted by East Coast Memorial, which recently purchased the buildings from Serenity Funeral Home. Serenity’s head office and crematorium were located in the small community of Coldbrook. The company also had other locations in the Annapolis Valley.

Michelle Carey and her sister Amanda Sabean used Serenity when they buried what they believed were the cremated remains of their father, Hendrik (Hank) Sabean, in the spring of 2018. On Sept. 8, Carey was informed by East Coast Memorial that her father’s full remains were found in storage.

“Having to, you know, bury him and to do this all over again. It's really hard,” said Carey.

The sisters are also left wondering whose remains they buried.

Hendrik (Hank) Sabean's family thought they buried his cremated remains next to his family in Weymouth, N.S., in 2018. But recently, they were told by the new owner of the funeral home that handled his arrangements that his full remains were found in storage. (Amanda Sabean)

“There’s a family out there that's missing remains of their family member,” said Sabean.

In an email, Andrew George, the owner of the new business East Coast Memorial, explained that his company discovered “a significant number of cremated remains that had been left in storage, some for many, many years.”

George said he and his staff are carefully reviewing the home’s information to “make every reasonable effort to locate and contact families so that these loved ones could be returned to their families or otherwise laid to rest appropriately.”

‘Dozens’ of other urns found, daughter told

Sweeney said when her mother, Elizabeth Pelton, died in 2023 at the age of 60, her body was cremated. Sweeney chose a green urn, which she received and buried.

This month, the employee of East Coast Memorial who returned what’s believed to be the rest of her mother’s ashes gave her a green urn with a different pattern. It had been identified with a sticky note label as her mother’s. Sweeney said the employee told her that there were “dozens” of other urns found.

Another family told CBC their loved one’s remains were delivered to them in a cardboard box.

When East Coast Memorial recently took possession of Serenity Funeral Home in Coldbrook, N.S., the new staff discovered a 'significant number' of cremated remains. The company has been calling families so they can retrieve them. (Angela MacIvor/CBC)

Sweeney wrote a post on Facebook about her experience and started receiving responses from other families. They recounted similar experiences, believing that they had received and buried their loved ones. Then they were contacted by East Coast Memorial years later suggesting otherwise.

“Every single person I've spoken to was under the impression that they had taken care of all the remains,” Sweeney said. “They were either buried or they took the urn home.”

George said his company is still assessing all the cases and doing its due diligence “as thoroughly as possible for each family,” and so he isn’t able to say exactly how many persons’ remains were found.

Former owner responds

When CBC reached Tony Facey, a former owner of Serenity Funeral Home for 12 years until December 2025, he confirmed there was a “whole stack” of cremated remains dating back as far as 25 years that had never been claimed by families. He said unclaimed remains is a wider issue all funeral homes are dealing with, and this has been an ongoing discussion at the regulatory board. Facey declined an interview.

The president of the Funeral Service Association of Nova Scotia, Kollin Weatherbee, said he’s never heard of a funeral home keeping decades of unclaimed remains.

“It is unusual that a funeral home would hold a portion of someone's ashes without the family knowing,” he said.

Weatherbee added that if a funeral home held ashes for a family, it would only be for a matter of weeks.

And in situations where a next of kin can’t be identified or reached, he said the public trustee usually gets involved within the first 12 days of a death.

Provincial inspectors visit

The province licenses and regulates funeral homes through Service Nova Scotia, while an arm’s-length board licenses and regulates funeral home directors.

The province learned of the stored ashes on Sept. 9 when it was contacted by that board and George, the owner of East Coast Memorial. It assigned two provincial inspectors to visit the crematorium the next day to learn more.

Adam Tipert, the chair of the Nova Scotia Board of Registration of Embalmers and Funeral Directors, told CBC in an email the board is taking the concerns “very seriously” and will collaborate with Service Nova Scotia in its investigation as more information emerges.

The province and the board also conducted an investigation at Serenity Funeral Home in 2018, when the location in Berwick mixed up the bodies of two women. A funeral director had his licence revoked.

That case eventually led to a change in the legislation surrounding funeral homes in 2025.

A provincial spokesperson said Serenity was routinely inspected in 2022, and some non-compliant administrative matters were resolved.

Following the sale to East Coast Memorial, Serenity is no longer licensed to operate funeral homes in Nova Scotia.

George said right now he is keeping focused on doing what is right for the families.

“We do not want to speculate about decisions or practices that occurred before our involvement,” he said, adding that his company will treat the remains with respect and dignity, as they were “received into our care when we acquired Serenity.”

George said his company is making plans for a community burial ceremony for any remains that can’t be reunited with a family, or if the families direct his company to do so.

Hendrik (Hank) Sabean was 67 when he died in 2018. He had specific wishes for his funeral arrangements, which included dealing with Serenity Funeral Home for the service and burial of his ashes. (Amanda Sabean)

Hank Sabean’s daughters still have many unanswered questions, especially since their father had been so clear about his own funeral arrangements and being laid to rest with his family.

“He had strong morals and values, and I know that he would think that this is so wrong that this could happen,” said Carey.

Kristina Sweeney said her mother would also be “really, really disgusted.”

“I felt like my mom and I had been violated,” she said. “I expect when someone passes away that, and I'm sure most people do, they're treated with dignity and respect.”
