Read across U.S. and Canadian outlets, court filings, agency releases, the Prime Minister’s Office and market pricing, and our own Washington, Ottawa and Toronto desks.

Canada Opens Its Shop Window

The first Canada Investment Summit began in Toronto on Monday 14 September, and its main programme runs today. Carney had set its tone the evening before it began.

At a Toronto welcome reception on Sunday 13 September, he said the world’s largest investors would come to “peer into our shop window”. He put their assets at over C$120 trillion (roughly US$86 trillion).

Reuters reported the remark on Monday morning, and that total is Carney’s own number. It measures attention rather than money committed.

Reuters named Larry Fink of BlackRock and Jon Gray of Blackstone among the investors invited. The Canadian Press reported that Stephen Harper will deliver closing remarks at the summit, citing a source not authorised to speak publicly.

TD Bank and Scotiabank published five-year commitments on Monday morning, C$150 billion (about US$108 billion) and more than C$100 billion (about US$72 billion). Both went out before the summit’s opening dinner, and neither release mentions it.

TD tied its commitment to its own economists’ report on a Canadian investment supercycle, not to the summit. Domestic money is cheaper to announce than foreign money.

The Prime Minister’s Office published a summit total at 9:25 a.m. Toronto time on Tuesday, nearly C$500 billion (about US$360 billion) of new investment. Its release says the agreements will catalyse that money into energy, critical minerals, new technologies and artificial intelligence.

The breakdown names a C$50 billion (about US$36 billion) Maple Fund from CPP Investments and Brookfield, and C$70 billion from BMO over ten years. PSP Investments adds C$25 billion (about US$18 billion) and Ontario Teachers’ C$10 billion by the end of 2027. Power Sustainable offers more than C$10 billion and Radical Ventures C$4 billion (about US$3 billion) for a new fund. Every institution on that list is Canadian.

Bell Canada and Saskatchewan announced a data centre expansion that the province valued at C$52 billion (about US$37 billion), with up to 500 permanent jobs. Such a project buys electricity before it buys software.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne gave investors committing C$1 billion (about US$721 million) or more priority access to binding rulings from the Canada Revenue Agency. Certainty costs a government less than money does.

Carney also introduced a Productivity Mega Deduction on Tuesday morning, letting businesses deduct eligible investments in full and at once. It widens the assets covered from roughly 15 per cent to more than 65 per cent. The Prime Minister’s Office says it cuts the tax rate on new business investment from about 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent. A deduction is the cheapest thing a government can offer.

Labour unions, Indigenous leaders and climate and housing advocates marched from Nathan Phillips Square to the opening dinner at the Art Gallery of Ontario. A shop window is also where people stand and object.

Wet’suwet’en Hereditary Chief Na’Moks disputed the framing of these projects as protection against American pressure. Consent is a cost that no prospectus lists.

A government source told Reuters that major deals could take twelve to eighteen months, and no aggregate total was published on Monday. A pledge is not yet a signature, and we say so plainly.

A country that must advertise itself has already learned something about its neighbours.

The Customer Canada Found Instead

Canadian exports to China rose 30.1 per cent in the first half of 2026, reaching C$21.74 billion (about US$15.7 billion). Bijan Ahmadi of the Canada China Business Council called it a record first half.

Imports from China fell 5.8 per cent to C$44.86 billion (about US$32 billion), narrowing the deficit by a quarter. Canada is selling more to the country it buys less from.

Energy exports rose 81.8 per cent and metal ores and minerals 29 per cent, together making 58.4 per cent of the total. The pivot is made of rock and oil.

Lobster exports fell 28 per cent over the same half year, and agricultural exports grew only 1.9 per cent. The gain is real and uneven.

The figures come from the Canada China Business Council and the University of Alberta’s China Institute. Statistics Canada’s full-year picture is not yet available.

A trade war teaches a country the names of its other buyers.

The Court Answers The Post Office

The Supreme Court refused on Monday 14 September to stay the nationwide injunction blocking the Postal Service’s new mail-ballot rule. Its order says the administration is unlikely to succeed on the merits.

Justice Samuel Alito, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, dissented and would have granted the stay. He wrote that the administration is likely to succeed on the merits of its appeal.

His reasons are that several plaintiff organisations likely lack standing and that the states’ claim is one courts rarely allow. He expressly took no view on a full review of the Postal Service’s powers.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh concurred, writing that applying the rule in this year’s elections would be arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. His reason was the calendar rather than the constitution.

Two injunctions stand, one from Judge Indira Talwani in Boston and one from Judge Carl Nichols in Washington. The order of 14 September addressed the Boston injunction, and no vote count has been reported.

This was an emergency order on likelihood of success and not a final ruling, so the case continues. What the Postal Service may do in later elections is unsettled.

A court can stop a rule without yet deciding whether the rule was lawful.

The Rate That Reached Five

The interest rate on the ten-year United States government bond touched 5.01 per cent on Monday. That rate is what Washington pays to borrow for a decade.

It was the first visit above 5 per cent since October 2023, and the Treasury’s own daily reading closed the day at 4.97 per cent. Three years is long enough for borrowing habits to settle.

The Federal Reserve’s rate-setting committee opened its two-day meeting today and announces its decision at 2 p.m. Washington time on 16 September. Nothing has been voted, and we treat the outcome as open.

The committee has held its target range at 3.50 to 3.75 per cent since July, under Chairman Kevin Warsh. A rise tomorrow would be his first.

Kiplinger reported CME FedWatch pricing at 93 per cent for a quarter-point rise on 14 September, against near 90 per cent on 11 September. Those are two readings of one measure on two days.

Brandon Zureick, senior managing director at Johnson Investment Counsel, said such a rise is widely anticipated. That is a forecast from a named source, not a decision.

American consumer prices rose 3.4 per cent in the year to August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on 11 September. Petrol rose 27.4 per cent and core prices 2.4 per cent.

Canadian prices rose 3.0 per cent in the year to August, Statistics Canada reported on 14 September, with petrol up 22.8 per cent. The Bank of Canada held its rate at 2.25 per cent on 2 September.

The Canadian dollar weakened to about 1.3929 per United States dollar on Monday, a twelve-day low. Two central banks moving apart show up first in a currency.

The price a government pays to borrow is the floor beneath every other price.

A Pipeline, A Strait And A Repeal

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said its East-West pipeline came under attack on the morning of Thursday 10 September, and shut it as a precaution. The line carries crude away from the Strait of Hormuz.

The Associated Press reported that Riyadh blamed drones from Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, and officials estimate repairs at three to five weeks. That is an estimate rather than a schedule.

Houthi forces seized the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish on Monday 14 September. They had taken the port of Mokha and Mayun island the week before.

Brent settled at US$105.68 a barrel on Monday 14 September, up US$1.07 on the day, and traded between US$105.10 and US$108.43 on Tuesday morning. Associated Press rewrites its markets copy through the day, so we carry the range.

On the same Monday the Environmental Protection Agency repealed the limits on greenhouse gases from power stations burning coal and gas. Administrator Lee Zeldin said the repeal would remove billions in costs for industry and “unleash” American energy.

The agency also proposes to rescind the remaining standards, and environmental groups have said they intend to go to court. Nothing about the repeal is settled until a judge says so.

Expensive energy makes governments generous towards the people who produce it.

The Builders Ask For A Brake

Dario Amodei of Anthropic published an essay on Saturday 12 September called “We Must Pace the Frontier”, urging a global slowdown in artificial intelligence work. Sam Altman of OpenAI agreed on X the same day, and Elon Musk posted that Dario is right.

David Sacks, who served as the White House’s artificial intelligence and crypto czar, has said top laboratories could be pursuing regulatory capture. Reuters reports his argument that such rules load smaller competitors with costly compliance and weaken competition. He reads the safety appeal as a business interest.

Semiconductor shares carried the dispute into Monday, with the VanEck Semiconductor exchange-traded fund down more than 4 per cent that day. Nvidia fell about 3.4 per cent.

Speaker Mike Johnson said on 13 September that developers rather than Congress carry responsibility for safety, and rejected a moratorium. Washington’s answer to the builders is that they should build.

Whether any company slows its work is not known, and none has published a timetable. An appeal is not yet an agreement.

When the builders of a machine ask for a brake, the question becomes who holds it.

One country spent the day selling itself to strangers. The other spent it being told what it may not do.

What This Means From Latin America

Diesel above US$6 a gallon since Thursday 10 September sets the freight cost that carries Brazilian soy and Chilean fruit northward. Food prices in this region follow that number after a delay of weeks.

A ten-year American borrowing rate near 5 per cent raises the price of dollar debt for every government and company in this hemisphere. Nobody in Brasília or Bogotá votes at the Federal Reserve.

Canada’s exports to China rose 30.1 per cent in the first half, the same substitution several Latin American exporters have already made. A tariff redirects a cargo rather than destroying it.

Canada’s government capital and incentives of about C$280 billion (US$202 billion) are expected to enable more than C$1 trillion of total investment. The queue for infrastructure money now has one more country in it.

What We Are Watching

Carney in Strasbourg and Liverpool — the Prime Minister’s Office sets the European visit at 15 to 17 September. It names an address to the European Parliament at President Roberta Metsola’s invitation, and a first meeting with the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham.

— the Prime Minister’s Office sets the European visit at 15 to 17 September. It names an address to the European Parliament at President Roberta Metsola’s invitation, and a first meeting with the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham. The Federal Reserve on 16 September — the decision lands at 2 p.m. Washington time, and the Fed’s own calendar attaches a Summary of Economic Projections to this meeting.

— the decision lands at 2 p.m. Washington time, and the Fed’s own calendar attaches a Summary of Economic Projections to this meeting. The main programme of the Canada Investment Summit — whether this week’s commitments become signed agreements. A government source told Reuters that major deals could take twelve to eighteen months.

— whether this week’s commitments become signed agreements. A government source told Reuters that major deals could take twelve to eighteen months. The Saudi East-West pipeline — officials estimate repairs at three to five weeks. Brent settled at US$105.68 a barrel on 14 September and traded between US$105.10 and US$108.43 on Tuesday morning.

— officials estimate repairs at three to five weeks. Brent settled at US$105.68 a barrel on 14 September and traded between US$105.10 and US$108.43 on Tuesday morning. The mail-ballot case on its merits — Monday’s order turned on likelihood of success rather than a final decision, and the case continues before the midterm elections on 3 November.

— Monday’s order turned on likelihood of success rather than a final decision, and the case continues before the midterm elections on 3 November. Quebec’s provincial election on 5 October — a Pallas Data poll taken on 12 September put the Parti Québécois at 27 per cent. The Coalition Avenir Québec and the Liberals stood at 23 per cent each, from a sample of 1,085 people.

Go Deeper. The web dossier carries the full deep dive on Canada’s search for foreign capital and three possible outcomes, a ten-dimension health check of the continent, the North American calendar and today’s verification notes.

More from the Rio Times Intelligence Desk on 15 September 2026: Africa · Asia · Europe. For how these stories developed, see the USA & Canada Intelligence Brief for 14 September and 13 September.

North American politics and trade policy and their bearing on this hemisphere run through our pillar coverage of The United States & Canada.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Canada Investment Summit, and has real money been committed?

It is Canada’s first national investment summit, held in Toronto on 14 and 15 September 2026. Its main programme runs today. Mark Carney has pledged to attract C$1 trillion (about US$721 billion) over five years. The Prime Minister’s Office says government capital and incentives of about C$280 billion (US$202 billion) are expected to enable that total. Reuters reported that the summit aims to match some 100 global investors with Canadian companies and officials. A prospectus seen by Reuters carries more than 160 projects. Money has been pledged, and most of it is Canadian. TD Bank published a C$150 billion (about US$108 billion) five-year commitment at 6 a.m. Toronto time on 14 September, before the summit’s opening dinner. Scotiabank published more than C$100 billion (about US$72 billion) an hour earlier. Bell Canada and Saskatchewan announced a data centre expansion the province valued at C$52 billion (about US$37 billion). The Prime Minister’s Office published a total on 15 September, nearly C$500 billion (about US$360 billion) of new investment. Every institution named in its breakdown is Canadian. A government source told Reuters that major deals could take twelve to eighteen months to materialise.

Has the Supreme Court decided the mail-ballot case?

No. On 14 September 2026 it refused to stay the nationwide injunction blocking the Postal Service’s new mail-ballot rule. The rule would require states to use envelopes carrying an election-mail logo, a machine-readable design and a barcode unique to each voter. It would also require states to upload basic voter information to a Postal Service portal. The court’s order says the administration is unlikely to succeed on the merits, and that the equities do not favour a stay. That is an emergency ruling on likelihood of success, not a final decision. Justice Samuel Alito, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, dissented and wrote that the administration is likely to succeed on the merits of its appeal. His reasons are standing and the narrowness of the claim, and he took no view on a full review. Justice Brett Kavanaugh concurred on the ground that applying the rule in this year’s elections would be arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. No vote count has been reported. The underlying case continues, and what the Postal Service may do in later elections is not yet known.

Is the Federal Reserve about to raise interest rates, and what would that change here?

Market pricing points that way, and the committee has not voted. The two-day meeting opened on 15 September and the decision lands at 2 p.m. Washington time on 16 September, with a Summary of Economic Projections attached. The target range has stood at 3.50 to 3.75 per cent since July, under Chairman Kevin Warsh. Kiplinger reported CME FedWatch pricing at 93 per cent for a quarter-point rise on 14 September, against near 90 per cent on 11 September; both are readings of the same measure on different days. Brandon Zureick of Johnson Investment Counsel expects a rise, which is a forecast and not an outcome. A higher American rate raises the cost of dollar borrowing across Latin America.

Why are oil and diesel prices rising again?

Two routes out of the Gulf are under pressure at once. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said the East-West pipeline, the line that carries crude away from the Strait of Hormuz, came under multiple attacks on the morning of Thursday 10 September. Its statement of 11 September announced a precautionary shutdown, and the Associated Press reported that Riyadh blamed drones from Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. The line had moved between 2.6 million and 4 million barrels a day since late August. Officials briefed on the damage estimate repairs at three to five weeks. Houthi forces seized the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish on 14 September, after taking the port of Mokha and Mayun island the week before. Brent settled at US$105.68 a barrel on Monday 14 September, up US$1.07 on the day, and traded between US$105.10 and US$108.43 on Tuesday morning. American diesel passed US$6 a gallon for the first time on Thursday 10 September, which sets freight costs across this hemisphere.

Sources: Prime Minister of Canada, Supreme Court of the United States, United States Department of the Treasury, Saudi Press Agency. Also Federal Reserve, Bureau of Labor Statistics, Statistics Canada, TD Bank Group, Scotiabank. And NPR, PBS NewsHour, The Spokesman-Review, CBC News, CTV News, BNN Bloomberg. Plus Reuters, The Associated Press, Kiplinger, Newsquawk, Yahoo Finance, TheStreet, Reason, Pallas Data. Reporting window 11–15 September 2026.

The full Africa Intelligence Dossier — the editor’s leader, the deep dive, the country health check and the people who matter — is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk. Open the dossier · The dossier archive

Lagos began selling a piece of its refinery on Monday, 14 September, and priced the future at 525 naira a share. Pretoria spent the same day counting what closing its own refineries cost.

Three capitals moved this Tuesday on one question: who should own the middle of the oil chain. The continent is buying back the part it once contracted out.

Read in English, French, Arabic, Portuguese and Swahili, across the continent’s largest outlets and our own Africa desk.

Nigeria: Lagos Sells A Share Of The Refinery

Dangote Petroleum Refinery opened its public share offer on Monday, 14 September, at 525 naira a share (about US$0.40). It is offering 4.1 billion ordinary shares.

The sale seeks about 2.15 trillion naira (about US$1.62 billion), or 3.3 per cent of the enlarged company. That prices the whole of it near US$49 billion.

Bloomberg reported in July that the refinery had raised US$2.5 billion privately, for a stake of up to 6 per cent. That placement priced the company near US$40 billion.

Aliko Dangote told the signing ceremony on 7 September that he wanted drivers, cooks and servants to hold stakes. He has named ten million shareholders as his target.

The offer closes on 13 October, the date Channels Television, Forbes Africa and allAfrica all carry. Ten shares cost about US$4.

The plant runs at 700,000 barrels a day and aims at 1.4 million, by 2028 in Forbes Africa’s account and 2029 in CNBC Africa’s. The shares list in Lagos in November.

The Nigeria Police Force circulated a security alert dated 13 September, which Nigerian outlets reported on Monday, 14 September. It names the Islamic State West Africa Province and armed elements moving from Katsina through Kaduna towards Plateau.

It lists places of worship, schools and National Youth Service Corps orientation camps, names no school, and gives no date. The force has not published the intelligence behind it.

The warning and the offer arrived on the same Monday. A country can sell its confidence and post its guards on one morning.

South Africa: The Bill For The Refineries That Closed

Business Day reported on 14 September that the South African Reserve Bank has costed the country’s lost refining capacity at 76 billion rand. That is about US$4.7 billion, over the four years to 2024.

The bank asked what the bill would have been had imported refined fuel held its 2010 to 2019 share. That share was about 25 per cent.

Konstantin Makrelov, the bank’s chief economist, approved the note, which also counts 5,400 direct and indirect jobs lost. Petroleum manufacturing output is down about a fifth since 2019.

Nearly half the country’s refining capacity shut in 2020, and two crude refineries remain: Sasol’s Natref and Astron Energy’s plant at Cape Town. Together they run about 208,000 barrels a day.

Neither the bank nor Business Day says how much of the gap the planned Sapref rehabilitation would close. A country that stops refining still pays for refining, in another currency.

Madagascar: The State Takes The Cargo Back

Radio France Internationale reported on 15 September that Antananarivo is moving fuel imports from four private distributors to a state buyer. The change ends about 25 years of private sourcing.

The buyer is State Procurement of Madagascar, created in 2019 to purchase rice, with capital of 100 million ariary (about €20,000). The law lets the distributors resume importing if it fails.

The Groupement pétrolier de Madagascar speaks for TotalEnergies, Vitol, Rubis Énergie and the Axian group. It calls the shift a nationalisation of the sector in all but name.

Parliament adopted law 021/2026 on 1 July, and the state requisitioned storage at Toamasina port on 4 August. The tanker Sunda 1 discharged about 67 million litres of diesel on 12 August.

The implementing decrees are not yet published, so how public and private importers share the port is not yet known. Antananarivo declared energy emergencies in April and again in July.

Three countries this week are arguing over the same link in one chain. Owning the barrel has never been the same as owning the refining of it.

Sudan: The Warehouses Empty At The End Of This Month

The International Organization for Migration said on 14 September that Sudan’s shelter, sanitation and relief supplies run out at the end of September. Its warehouses close in December without new money.

Amy Pope, the organisation’s director general, said the humanitarian system “could collapse within weeks”. The agency asks US$15 million to hold minimum capacity for twelve months.

Of 2.84 million people served since July 2023, more than a million came in 2024, 804,000 in 2025 and 330,000 this year. The line runs one way.

Carl Skau, the World Food Programme’s acting head, spoke to reporters on 14 September after an eight-day trip across Sudan. UN News reported the Sudan operation only about one-third funded.

He said: “Our main problem is funding”, and warned of significant cuts within weeks without more money. UN News puts 19.5 million Sudanese at crisis levels of hunger.

Neither agency has said which districts lose supply first. A warehouse with a date on it is a policy.

DR Congo: Two Governments, Two Tax Offices

The opposition coalition Article 64 marched in Kinshasa on Tuesday, 15 September, against a possible third term. It groups Martin Fayulu, Moïse Katumbi, Augustin Matata, Delly Sesanga and Jean-Marc Kabund.

Actualite.cd reported that the procession set off shortly after midday from the Échangeur de Limete, close to 5,000 strong. It moved down the boulevard Lumumba towards the boulevard Triomphal, opposite the Stade des Martyrs.

Jean-Marc Kabund and Delly Sesanga walked behind the militant lines in Limete, and police escorted the column. A second group gathered at the Moulaert roundabout in Bandalungwa, behind Dieudonné Bolengetenge and Francklin Tshamala.

At 12th Street the marchers met barriers put up by militants of the ruling UDPS, and the police fired tear gas. Police dispersed the Limete column there.

The coalition had told the city authorities on 11 September that it would sit in front of the Palais du Peuple, the parliament building. Israël Mutala, for the provincial government, said the route was corrected to respect the inviolability of parliament.

Lubumbashi’s mayor had reaffirmed a ban on public gatherings, and the governor of Tshopo barred the Kisangani march on Ebola grounds. Twelve coalition members were arrested in Kindu on 12 September.

Radio Okapi reported the march blocked at Matadi, not held at Gemena, and stopped at Kisangani by police. Police dispersed the Kananga march with tear gas, and detained people at Mbandaka and Uvira.

Police prevented the Lubumbashi march: Radio Okapi counted about twenty arrests, while the opposition’s Aubin Kasongo gave eight and reported several injured. No official count has been published.

The Constitutional Court validated the referendum law on 28 July with thirteen reservations, and a new constitution would reset the count of terms. Félix Tshisekedi’s second term ends at the close of 2028.

He signed an order on 13 September creating a committee for his national dialogue, which the opposition had refused. The Burkinabè daily Le Pays compares the manoeuvre to Joseph Kabila’s.

The New Humanitarian reported on 14 September that a 2024 United Nations experts’ report put M23’s coltan levies near US$10 million a year. Coltan is the ore that yields tantalum, a metal used in electronics.

The New Humanitarian also carries Twangiza Mining’s own claim that the rebels have looted gold worth about US$70 million. The company is Chinese and the mine is South Kivu’s biggest.

Zobel Behalal of the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime calls these arrangements “forms of criminal governance”. Josaphat Musamba of Ghent University holds that minerals are not the centre.

The rebels also charge for water, electricity, land titles and vehicle records, and both figures are claims rather than audited accounts. Two authorities tax the same citizens, and only one argues about term limits.

Kenya: Two Crowds, Two Arguments

Thousands gathered in Nairobi on Sunday, 13 September, behind Senator Edwin Sifuna and the Linda Mwananchi movement. Police deployed heavily around the church that opened the rally.

The movement’s name means “protect the citizen” in Swahili, and Sifuna is 44 and senator for Nairobi. He told the crowd: “Kenya is saying, Honorable Ruto, your time is up.”

The next day President William Ruto answered from Muhoroni, in Kisumu county, on a development tour of Nyanza. He called for competition over ideas rather than personalities.

“Kenyans will shock you, my friends,” he said, listing roads, housing, markets and schools. Both sides are already campaigning for August 2027.

Carine Kaneza Nantulya of Human Rights Watch said in a release of 11 September that the violence threatens a return to past rights abuses. No agency has published a verified count for this month.

Ruto and Sifuna spent the weekend addressing different crowds in different languages of grievance. A crowd is a poll that nobody has to certify.

Djibouti: One Signature In Washington

Djibouti signed the Artemis Accords at NASA headquarters in Washington on Monday, 14 September, the 72nd country to do so. Ambassador Mohamed Siad Douale signed for a country that already leases ground to foreign militaries.

The accords set shared principles for civil exploration of the Moon, and Djibouti is the eighth African country to join. Small states buy standing wherever standing is sold.

What This Means From Latin America

Mexico built the Olmeca refinery at Dos Bocas to cut petrol imports, and Brazil keeps refining inside Petrobras. Lagos, Pretoria and Antananarivo are arguing the same case.

A share priced near US$4 is the cheapest way any founder can widen who owns an asset. Dangote is asking small savers to fund what banks and states usually fund.

Coltan yields tantalum, and Brazil is among that metal’s larger producers, so Congo’s levies reach the same buyers. The aid budgets thinning in Sudan also fund Haiti.

What We Are Watching

Dangote’s retail take-up — whether small savers approach the ten million shareholders named as the target, before the offer closes on 13 October.

— whether small savers approach the ten million shareholders named as the target, before the offer closes on 13 October. The Lagos listing — whether the shares reach the Nigerian Exchange in November, and at what price against the 525 naira offer.

— whether the shares reach the Nigerian Exchange in November, and at what price against the 525 naira offer. Nigeria’s security alert — whether the police publish anything behind the message dated 13 September, which names a group but no date.

— whether the police publish anything behind the message dated 13 September, which names a group but no date. Pretoria’s answer — whether the Central Energy Fund’s Sapref rehabilitation moves, after the Reserve Bank put a number on the refining that closed.

— whether the Central Energy Fund’s Sapref rehabilitation moves, after the Reserve Bank put a number on the refining that closed. Madagascar’s decrees — whether the implementing decrees for law 021/2026 appear, and how they divide storage at Toamasina between the state buyer and the four distributors.

— whether the implementing decrees for law 021/2026 appear, and how they divide storage at Toamasina between the state buyer and the four distributors. Sudan’s end-of-month date — whether money arrives before the shelter and sanitation supplies run out, and which districts lose supply first.

— whether money arrives before the shelter and sanitation supplies run out, and which districts lose supply first. Kinshasa’s referendum — whether a date is set under the law the Constitutional Court validated on 28 July, after police dispersed Tuesday’s march.

— whether a date is set under the law the Constitutional Court validated on 28 July, after police dispersed Tuesday’s march. Eastern Congo’s levies — whether the United Nations experts revise the US$10 million a year their 2024 report attributed to M23’s coltan charges.

The Bigger Picture Africa exports crude and imports the fuel made from it, and three governments moved against that arrangement this week. Lagos sells shares, Antananarivo takes the cargo, Pretoria counts the cost. Refineries were built after independence, sold or shut when margins thinned, and are wanted again when import bills rise. The pattern is old, and it turns with the oil price. What none of the three has published is the running cost of owning the middle. Madagascar’s decrees are unwritten, and Pretoria’s rehabilitation has no costed timetable. For a reader with money or family in these places, the reading is short. A fuel price set at home answers to a different set of hands.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly is Dangote Petroleum Refinery selling, and at what price?

The company opened a public share offer on Monday, 14 September, at 525 naira a share, about US$0.40. It is offering 4.1 billion ordinary shares to raise about 2.15 trillion naira, about US$1.62 billion. Against existing capital of 120.13 billion shares, that is 3.3 per cent of the enlarged company, which the price values near US$49 billion. A private placement in July raised US$2.5 billion for a stake reported at up to 6 per cent, pricing the company near US$40 billion. The minimum purchase is ten shares, about US$4, and the shares are due to list in Lagos in November.

When does the Dangote offer close?

On 13 October. Channels Television gave that date on 9 September, as did Forbes Africa, and the allAfrica French press review followed on 14 September. It matches the timetable signed in Lagos on 7 September. An early Channels Television report of 7 September gave 9 October. The broadcaster’s own later reporting gives 13 October. The offer opened on 14 September and the shares are due to list in Lagos in November.

What did the South African Reserve Bank actually measure?

Business Day reported the note on 14 September. The bank asked what the oil import bill from 2021 to 2024 would have been had imported refined fuel held its earlier share. That share was about 25 per cent from 2010 to 2019, and the bill would have been 76 billion rand lower. That is about US$4.7 billion, and the note also counts 5,400 direct and indirect jobs lost. Konstantin Makrelov, the bank’s chief economist, approved it, and the note does not cost a rebuilt Sapref.

Why does Sudan’s aid pipeline have a date on it?

The International Organization for Migration said on 14 September that shelter, sanitation and emergency household supplies run out at the end of September. Its warehouses close in December without new funding. It asks US$15 million to hold minimum capacity for twelve months and US$42 million to reach up to one million people. UN News reported on 14 September that the World Food Programme is only about one-third funded in Sudan. Its acting head, Carl Skau, spoke to reporters that day after an eight-day trip across Sudan, and said funding was the agency’s main problem.

Sources: allAfrica, CNBC Africa, Channels Television, Forbes Africa, Business Day, Bloomberg, Tribune Online. Also Radio France Internationale, Capmad, UN News, Arab News, Darfur24. And TimesLIVE, The New Humanitarian, Radio Okapi, Actualite.cd, Journal de Kinshasa, Le Pays, The Star, Eyewitness News, Vanguard, NASA · 7-15 September 2026.

Asia woke on Tuesday to a row of appointments it did not choose and cannot easily move. The region’s mood now depends on other people’s diaries.

Beijing has attached a condition to a state visit, Tokyo is expected to make money dearer on Friday, and Jakarta changed its finance minister overnight. Each capital is being measured against a deadline it did not write.

Read in English, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, Bahasa Indonesia, Vietnamese, Thai and Tagalog, across the region’s largest outlets, each capital’s own press and our own Asia desk.

China And Taiwan: The Price Of A State Visit

Xi Jinping is due in Washington on 24 September, on an invitation President Donald Trump made during his May visit to Beijing. Beijing has now attached a condition to it.

The Taipei Times carried a Kyodo News report on 13 September that Beijing could scrap the visit if Washington approved new arms sales to Taiwan. No Chinese official has confirmed it, and Trump said on 13 September that he was not worried.

That report named no figure for those sales. Its only figure is about US$11 billion, the record package Washington announced in December 2025.

The sale Trump is weighing is a separate one, worth US$14 billion, on Bloomberg reporting carried by the Taipei Times on 15 September. Only one of the two is pending.

Two of the four MQ-9B SkyGuardian drones Taiwan ordered flew their first tests at Hualien Air Base early on Monday. An unnamed source told Focus Taiwan, and Taipei did not wait for Washington’s answer.

Taiwan’s Cabinet approved a 2027 budget on 20 August with defence at 3.01 per cent of national output. That is above NT$1 trillion, at NT$1.1225 trillion (about US$35 billion).

The trade truce between Washington and Beijing runs out on 10 November, seven weeks after the visit. A small country’s purchase order can move a large country’s calendar.

Indonesia: A Third Hand On The Budget

President Prabowo Subianto signed Presidential Decree No. 97/P on Monday, removing Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa as finance minister. Suahasil Nazara took the oath the same day.

Purbaya held the post for about a year, having replaced Sri Mulyani Indrawati on 8 September 2025. Nazara is the third finance minister since October 2024.

The Jakarta Composite Index fell as much as 2.6 per cent on Monday before closing at 6,534.69, almost flat. The rupiah weakened to 17,669 per US dollar.

Nazara told reporters his appointment was a continuation rather than a change, and promised a deficit below 3 per cent. He served as deputy finance minister before this.

Prabowo’s own approval has fallen from 81.2 per cent in November 2025 to 51.1 per cent in July 2026. Neither reading names its pollster in the reporting we read.

A president who changes his money manager twice in two years is explaining something to his own citizens. Continuity is easier to announce than to prove.

Thailand: The Chamber Accused Of Choosing Itself

Thailand’s Election Commission resolved on Monday to prosecute 77 people over the Senate election of June 2024. Twenty-six of them are sitting senators.

The 77 comprise those senators, 36 people eligible to vote in the Senate selection process and 15 others. The commission published none of their names, and must refer the case to the Supreme Court within 60 days.

All 21 Bhumjaithai politicians examined in the case, including Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, avoided criminal proceedings. The key witness, Ekkarat Changlao, withdrew his testimony.

Election Commission chairman Narong Klunwarin said the decision is not a finding of guilt, and the accused keep every right of defence. Senators are chosen by other candidates, not by voters.

The 200-member Senate appoints the heads of the Constitutional Court, the anti-corruption commission and the Election Commission itself. The body under accusation helps choose its own accuser.

Whether the Supreme Court accepts the case is the whole question, and nobody can answer it yet. Independence is hardest to prove when the same people do the appointing.

Japan: Tokyo Prepares To Make Money Dearer

A Reuters poll taken between 1 and 8 September found 66 of 68 economists expect the Bank of Japan to raise rates this week. The decision comes on 18 September.

The bank set the policy rate at 1.00 per cent on 16 June and held it there on 31 July, by eight votes to one. The poll points to 1.25 per cent, a forecast rather than a decision.

The yen traded at 154.81 to the US dollar on Tuesday, against 154.30 the day before. A weak currency is the strongest argument for moving.

The Nikkei 225 and the Kospi both closed lower on Tuesday, the Kospi for a fourth session running. Seoul’s market is not reading this week as calm.

Japan’s Digital Agency disclosed on Friday 11 September that about 246,000 records of personal data may have leaked from its shared government service. It had identified the intrusion on 9 July, more than two months earlier.

The agency traced the break-in to a flaw in a virtual private network device, and named neither its maker nor the attacker. Whether the data reached anyone outside is not established.

Tokyo is asking households to pay more for borrowed money days after admitting a silence. A state earns trust in one account and spends it in another.

South Korea: Thirty-Three Hours

Seoul’s bus drivers begin a full strike at 4 a.m. on Wednesday, Seoul time, after mediation broke down late on Tuesday. The argument is over a single number in a wage formula, the monthly hours divisor.

The union wants ordinary hourly pay calculated on 176 hours a month, and the operators propose 209. The gap is 33 hours, and the lower figure lifts every overtime rate.

The union cites a Supreme Court ruling from April, which a Seoul transport official says did not set 176 hours as the standard. The courts have not settled it.

Members voted 87.94 per cent in favour at 61 operators, covering 7,383 buses and about 18,600 staff. More than 3.79 million passengers use them each day.

President Lee Jae-myung holds a 90-minute news conference on Friday 18 September at Yeongbingwan in Seoul. He has not answered questions at length since the reshuffle.

Gallup Korea put his approval at 38 per cent last week, and Realmeter at 33.8 per cent on Monday. The two pollsters differ by more than four points.

A capital arguing about a divisor is arguing about who owns the arithmetic. Numbers become political the moment their definition is disputed.

The Electricity Behind The Machines

Vietnam has drawn several billion-dollar data centre commitments this year, and its operating capacity stood near 100 megawatts in late 2025. Shanghai had 1,070 and Singapore 740.

Building a megawatt in Vietnam costs US$5.7 million to US$8.7 million, against US$17.9 million in Singapore and US$19.2 million in Japan. Cheapness is the whole pitch.

Data centres take about 0.5 per cent of Vietnam’s electricity today, against 2 to 6 per cent in the United States. Officials warn of shortages as early as 2027.

In Thailand, Gulf Development chief executive Sarath Ratanavadi said proposed data centre power tariffs of 5 to 6 baht a unit are too high. That is about US$0.16 to US$0.19.

Malaysia recorded 9.25 million jobs in the second quarter, a record, while low-skilled posts fell 17 per cent over the year, on Department of Statistics Malaysia figures. New jobs numbered 31,550, down 1.2 per cent.

Three countries are bidding for the same buildings with three different shortages. A data centre is a promise about electricity first.

The Philippines: A Ship That Passed Its Inspection

The Philippine Coast Guard has searched every cabin and crew area of the MV June Aster (a passenger ferry), which burned off Coron in Palawan on Wednesday 9 September. A second sweep will follow.

Commodore Noemie Cayabyab, the coast guard spokesperson, put the confirmed death toll at 76, with 44 survivors and 12 people unaccounted for. About 65 per cent of the cargo hold has been reached.

Captain Roel Sarmiento presented himself on Monday at the operator’s Palawan office, five days after the fire. The coast guard confirmed that on Tuesday and has scheduled his questioning.

The coast guard sent the owner a demand letter requiring it to appoint a competent salvage contractor. The cause of the fire is not established.

Commodore Cayabyab said the ferry cleared an inspection in Manila and passed a Vessel Safety Enforcement Inspection in March, on the coast guard’s own records. The office that cleared the ship is the office now investigating it.

What This Means From Latin America

Latin America has watched an arms sale reshape a diplomatic calendar before. Conditions attached to visits are a currency of their own.

Brazil, Chile and Peru trade heavily with China and buy defence equipment from the United States. The Taiwan file is where those two habits meet.

Indonesia’s week carries a closer lesson, because a currency weakened while a share index recovered on the same announcement. Currency and equity investors were reading different sentences.

Higher Asian electricity costs and tighter Asian labour raise the price of goods arriving at Callao, Santos and Manzanillo. A power shortage in Vietnam eventually reaches a shelf in Lima.

What We Are Watching

The arms decision — whether Washington approves the US$14 billion sale before 24 September, and whether Xi travels if it does. Beijing has said nothing in public, so the warning rests on one Kyodo News report.

— whether Washington approves the US$14 billion sale before 24 September, and whether Xi travels if it does. Beijing has said nothing in public, so the warning rests on one Kyodo News report. The Bank of Japan on Friday — whether the bank moves to 1.25 per cent as 66 of 68 economists in the Reuters poll expect. Also what it says about October and December.

— whether the bank moves to 1.25 per cent as 66 of 68 economists in the Reuters poll expect. Also what it says about October and December. Seoul’s first buses on Wednesday — whether up to 1,500 free shuttle buses and 202 extra subway trips absorb more than 3.79 million daily passengers. The 176-hour question itself may end up back in the courts.

— whether up to 1,500 free shuttle buses and 202 extra subway trips absorb more than 3.79 million daily passengers. The 176-hour question itself may end up back in the courts. Thailand’s Supreme Court — whether it agrees to hear the Senate collusion case, and whether the Election Commission publishes the 77 names. A separate ruling on ballot barcodes is due on 28 September.

— whether it agrees to hear the Senate collusion case, and whether the Election Commission publishes the 77 names. A separate ruling on ballot barcodes is due on 28 September. Bangkok and Phnom Penh before a conciliation panel — Thailand told a five-member conciliation commission under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, sitting in Singapore, that Cambodia is playing the victim. About 27,000 square kilometres of seabed are in dispute, and the commission’s recommendations will not bind either side.

— Thailand told a five-member conciliation commission under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, sitting in Singapore, that Cambodia is playing the victim. About 27,000 square kilometres of seabed are in dispute, and the commission’s recommendations will not bind either side. Jakarta’s first budget test — whether Nazara holds the deficit below 3 per cent, and whether the rupiah stops at 17,669 per US dollar. It has lost 5.93 per cent this year.

— whether Nazara holds the deficit below 3 per cent, and whether the rupiah stops at 17,669 per US dollar. It has lost 5.93 per cent this year. What Captain Sarmiento tells investigators — whether his account explains the fire, and whether the last third of the cargo hold accounts for the 12 missing. The coast guard’s own records cleared the ferry in Manila and again in March.

The Bigger Picture Asia has spent forty years building institutions that promise predictability to outside money. This week several of them are being asked to prove it at once. A finance ministry changed hands overnight, an election commission accused 26 of its 200 senators, and a digital agency admitted a two-month silence. Each is a test of a promise rather than a crisis. The cycle behind this is older than the news. Every decade of fast Asian growth has ended with a round of institutional argument, in 1997, in 2008 and again after 2020. What follows those rounds is usually slower and duller than either the alarm or the boom suggested. Readers who remember that can watch a week like this one calmly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why would an arms sale to Taiwan cancel a meeting in Washington?

Beijing treats Taiwan as the most sensitive item in its relationship with the United States, and has answered past sales with sanctions on American defence firms. Xi Jinping is due in Washington on 24 September. The Taipei Times carried a Kyodo News report on 13 September that Beijing could scrap the trip over new arms sales. That report named no figure. Its only figure is a different package: about US$11 billion, announced in December 2025. The sale now in front of Trump is a separate one, worth US$14 billion on Bloomberg reporting of 15 September. No Chinese official has confirmed the warning, so the threat rests on reporting rather than on a statement.

Why did Indonesia change its finance minister, and does it matter for investors?

President Prabowo Subianto signed a decree on 14 September removing Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa and appointing Suahasil Nazara, who had been deputy finance minister. Purbaya had served about a year, and Nazara is the third holder of the post since October 2024. The share index fell as much as 2.6 per cent before closing almost flat at 6,534.69, while the rupiah weakened to 17,669 per US dollar. Nazara said his arrival was a continuation and promised a budget deficit below 3 per cent. No official reason for the removal has been published.

What is the Thai Senate case actually about?

Thailand’s Senate is not elected by voters. Candidates from twenty occupational sectors choose each other, and the 2024 round was the first since a military takeover a decade earlier. The Election Commission resolved on 14 September to prosecute 77 people for colluding in that process, among them 26 sitting senators. It has 60 days to refer the case to the Supreme Court, which then decides whether to hear it. Conviction carries up to ten years in prison for each offence and a fine of 200,000 baht, about US$6,200. The names have not been released.

What does any of this change for someone living in Latin America?

Three things, in plain terms. If the Bank of Japan makes borrowing dearer on 18 September, money borrowed cheaply in yen and invested elsewhere becomes more expensive to hold. Unwinding those positions can move emerging-market currencies, including the Brazilian real and the Mexican peso. If Asian electricity and labour costs keep rising, the imported goods on shelves in Lima, Bogota and Santiago cost more within a few months. And if the Washington visit falls through over Taiwan, the trade truce that expires on 10 November becomes harder to renew. That matters to every South American exporter selling into both markets.

And Korea JoongAng Daily, Seoul Economic Daily, The Japan Times and The Jakarta Post. Also Asia News Network, Bernama, Philstar and GMA News. And Daily Tribune and Kyodo News, with Bloomberg, Reuters and Associated Press reports carried by those papers. Also the Bank of Japan’s own policy statements and Japan’s Digital Agency release of 11 September. Reporting from 10 to 15 September 2026. Currency conversions are desk calculations against rates checked on 15 September 2026 and are approximate.

The full Europe Intelligence Dossier is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk. It carries the editor’s leader, the deep dive on Europe’s grey-zone week, the country health check and the people who matter. Open the dossier · All Europe dossiers

Europe woke on Tuesday to two attacks on its own ground that nobody has claimed: a drone over Lithuania, pipes on Dutch track. Neither country can yet name who did it.

Brussels is drafting a speech, The Hague is presenting a budget, and Athens has opened a prison gate for a convicted neo-Nazi. The continent is doing ordinary business under an unquiet sky.

Read across Dutch, Greek, Polish and Ukrainian outlets in their English editions, alongside European and American wire reporting, and our own Europe desk.

Pratkūnai: A First For Lithuania, Not For The Mission

Italian fighter jets flying NATO’s Baltic air policing mission destroyed a drone near Pratkūnai, in Kaunas county, at 1.19 a.m. Vilnius time. It is the first drone brought down in Lithuanian airspace.

Vilmantas Vitkauskas, who heads Lithuania’s crisis centre, told the broadcaster LRT that the drone most likely entered from Belarus. It stayed airborne for about thirty minutes.

Antanas Matutis, commander of the Lithuanian air force, said the recovered wreckage suggested the aircraft was likely carrying explosives. No investigator has confirmed the payload, the operator or the target.

President Gitanas Nausėda wrote that a drone entering Lithuanian airspace had been destroyed by NATO fighter jets. Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys called the alliance vigilant, committed and ready.

Mark Rutte, NATO’s secretary general, said on Monday that strikes close to alliance territory showed Vladimir Putin’s desperation and his wish to sow fear. Moscow had not commented by Tuesday afternoon.

The mission downed a drone over Estonia in May and one over Latvia on 14 August 2026. The interception was routine for the mission and new only for Vilnius.

Latvia’s armed forces said on 20 August 2026 that the drone downed there on 14 August was Ukrainian, and had entered from Belarus. Attribution in this airspace has already proved slower than interception.

Twenty Pipes Between Zwolle And Utrecht

Dutch track workers found pipes tied to railway lines at about twenty places, during an inspection that began at 5.30 a.m. Amsterdam time. ProRail said someone had placed the materials there deliberately.

The pipes measured roughly 1.5 to 2 metres and made the track circuits report empty sections as occupied, NL Times reported. Signals turned red, and trains stopped where no train was.

Police examined track near Deventer, Veenendaal, Brummen, Barneveld, Twello, Lunteren and Putten, and a train struck a pipe near Steenwijk. Nobody was hurt.

Services between Amersfoort and Zwolle, Utrecht and Arnhem, Arnhem and Zutphen, and Zwolle and Leeuwarden failed through the morning rush. The journey-planning app went down in the same hour.

Annet Bertram, the state secretary responsible, said she was deeply concerned and that thorough investigation was now crucial. No group has claimed the act, and the police name no suspect.

Bart Schuurman, a professor of terrorism studies, said those responsible could range from a state actor to a protest group. He described that range as speculation rather than a finding.

The morning fell on Prinsjesdag, the day the Dutch government presents its budget, and authorities have not said whether the two are connected. A country notices its railway on the morning it stops.

Gedser, And A Minute For Your Safety

A Russian frigate fired two flares at a Danish Fennec helicopter over international waters off Gedser on 14 September 2026. One flare passed close to the aircraft, and nobody was hurt.

The Danish Defence Command dated the episode to 14 September 2026, in a statement issued shortly after 11 p.m. Copenhagen time. Brussels Signal and the Copenhagen Post carry the same date.

Jeppe Bruus, the Danish defence minister, told the Ritzau agency the episode was serious and without precedent, and called the seamanship highly unprofessional. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the actions were meant to intimidate and divide.

Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen called the flares completely unacceptable and summoned Russia’s ambassador on Tuesday, with no date set for the meeting. Ambassador Vladimir Barbin said separately that Danish helicopters had repeatedly flown dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships.

Poland’s interior ministry has meanwhile paid 5.4 million zloty (about €1.3 million) for television segments teaching citizens how to act in an emergency. The ministry signed the contract on 4 September 2026.

The segments cover floods, power cuts, chemical contamination, evacuation and disinformation, and follow a security handbook sent to 17 million households. Denmark summons an ambassador, and Poland teaches a drill.

Both are answers to the same question, asked in different grammar. Preparation is what a country does when deterrence has stopped being certain.

The Hague Opens Its Books Without A Majority

Finance Minister Eelco Heinen carried the budget case to parliament at 3.30 p.m. Amsterdam time, the first budget of Rob Jetten’s minority cabinet. It arrived without an agreement to pass it.

The cabinet needs ten further votes in the lower house and sixteen in the senate, DutchNews reported. No opposition party has yet supplied them.

Ministers postponed €6.5 billion of welfare cuts by a year rather than cancel them, and raised €750 million from higher taxes on top earners. Jesse Klaver of Pro called the revised budget perhaps worse than the original.

Dutch inflation is running at 3.3 per cent, and the CPB, the government’s economic planning bureau, projects spending power falling 0.3 per cent next year. That is the bureau’s forecast, and forecasts of this kind have been wrong before.

RTL Nieuws reported its own panel on 15 September 2026, putting confidence in the cabinet at 16 per cent. That compares with 33 per cent in February 2026, and 29 per cent for Mr Jetten himself.

The farmers’ party holds eleven senate seats and has threatened to obstruct over nitrogen rules and asset taxes. A budget presented without a majority is a request rather than a plan.

Brussels Asks Others To Spend, And Itself To Stop

Ursula von der Leyen delivers her State of the Union address in Strasbourg on Wednesday 16 September 2026. The children’s online safety proposal is expected the next day.

A leaked draft seen by Euronews would bar under-fifteens from social media without a parent’s consent, with graduated rules running from age three upward. It reaches video games and companion chatbots as well.

The draft says technology companies bear the primary responsibility for making their products safe, and that parents rather than algorithms should raise Europe’s children. Ten member states are considering or advancing national legislation of their own, Euronews reported.

A confidential Council note, also seen by Euronews, records that most governments want the EU’s own administration cut in the 2028 to 2034 budget. Member states question the Commission’s proposed rise in staff numbers.

The Irish presidency is expected to table a compromise in early October, before the European Council meets on 15 and 16 October 2026. No figures for the reductions are public yet.

Defence, energy and Ukraine are the pressures governments name when they explain the squeeze. An institution asking Europe to spend more is being asked to spend less itself.

Athens: A Gate Opens At Domokos

Ilias Kasidiaris left Domokos prison at noon on Tuesday, after serving about six years of the thirteen-year sentence he received for directing Golden Dawn. An Athens appeal court convicted him in October 2020.

He told supporters he was returning to the front line, and that a strong national party stood with him. He called the present government the most corrupt since the dictatorship.

Greece’s supreme court barred him twice in 2023 from leading a party, finding its positions inconsistent with the free functioning of a democratic system. His lawyer says he may still stand on another party’s list.

Nikos Alivizatos, a constitutional scholar, argues that a 2023 law bars him while the imposed sentence runs, not merely while he is held. That reading is contested, and only the supreme court can settle it.

His lawyer says he is in contact with the Niki party and reaching toward other conservative voters. Whether any list will carry his name is not yet known.

Greece therefore has a released man, an unsettled disqualification and no ruling to point to. A sentence ends on a fixed day, a disqualification when a court says so.

The Euro Reads A Gas Bill

The euro traded at US$1.1537 on Tuesday, a one-month low, and Pound Sterling Live placed the cause in the gas price. Europe buys gas in dollars and earns in euros.

Dutch front-month gas traded at €82.80 per megawatt-hour (about US$95) on Tuesday, down 0.7 per cent, Tradingpedia reported. Pound Sterling Live put Monday’s move at €80 to €84.

European storage stood at 65.4 per cent full on 1 September 2026, more than sixteen points below the five-year average. That is the lowest reading for the date since the records began in 2011.

Anne-Sophie Corbeau of Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy said problems have repeatedly arrived together. A thin buffer turns every separate disruption into a shared one.

The European Central Bank’s deposit rate, the rate it pays banks on overnight deposits, reaches 2.50 per cent on Wednesday. The bank took that decision on 10 September 2026, against energy-driven inflation.

Brent crude settled at US$105.68 a barrel on Monday 14 September 2026, the last settlement before this edition closed. It traded between US$105.10 and US$108.43 on Tuesday morning.

Brent settled at US$101.21 on 9 September 2026, and the rise since then follows a Saudi pipeline shutdown. A currency that must buy its own heat cannot easily defend itself.

What This Means From Latin America

Brazil already has the law Brussels is preparing to propose, and in one respect it reaches further. Law 15,211 of 2025 links the accounts of users under sixteen to a legal guardian.

Its grace period ended on 17 March 2026, and Brazil’s data protection authority begins administrative sanctions in November 2026. Fines can reach ten per cent of a group’s Brazilian revenue.

A company that has already rebuilt its sign-up screens for São Paulo will find Europe’s draft familiar. The compliance cost was paid once, in the southern hemisphere first.

Europe’s gas bill weakens the euro, and exporters who invoice in euros earn fewer dollars for the same cargo. That is an energy price acting as a monetary one.

Dutch signalling failed because twenty lengths of cheap pipe confused a sensor, not because anyone entered a control room. Ports, railways and grids in Latin America run on the same logic.

For a reader in São Paulo or Lisbon the practical effects are a heating bill, a login screen and a delayed train. None of the three is decided where it is felt.

What We Are Watching

The wreckage at Pratkūnai — whether investigators confirm explosives on the drone destroyed on 15 September 2026, and whether Minsk or Moscow answers for it.

— whether investigators confirm explosives on the drone destroyed on 15 September 2026, and whether Minsk or Moscow answers for it. The Dutch investigation — whether the national police name a motive or a suspect for the pipes found at about twenty locations on Tuesday morning.

— whether the national police name a motive or a suspect for the pipes found at about twenty locations on Tuesday morning. Strasbourg on Wednesday — what Ursula von der Leyen says in her State of the Union address, and whether the children’s proposal appears on Thursday 17 September 2026 as the leak indicates.

— what Ursula von der Leyen says in her State of the Union address, and whether the children’s proposal appears on Thursday 17 September 2026 as the leak indicates. The Dutch arithmetic — whether Rob Jetten finds ten votes in the lower house and sixteen in the senate before the winter session closes.

— whether Rob Jetten finds ten votes in the lower house and sixteen in the senate before the winter session closes. Sweden’s last ballots — Bloomberg reported on 15 September 2026 that the final election result moves to Thursday, one day later than officials had planned.

— Bloomberg reported on 15 September 2026 that the final election result moves to Thursday, one day later than officials had planned. Greece’s supreme court — whether it rules on Ilias Kasidiaris’s eligibility before any candidate list is certified.

— whether it rules on Ilias Kasidiaris’s eligibility before any candidate list is certified. The storage curve — whether European gas stocks close the gap to the five-year average before the first sustained cold week.

The Bigger Picture Storage at 65.4 per cent on 1 September 2026 compares with 77.4 per cent a year earlier, and with a five-year average sixteen points higher. The records begin in 2011, and no first of September since then has been thinner. Anne-Sophie Corbeau of Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy warns that problems tend to arrive together. That is an observation about correlation, not a prediction of shortage. Lithuania used fighter jets to remove one drone, and ProRail needed a national inspection to find twenty pipes. The cost of defending is many times the cost of attacking. Cycles of this kind end when one side runs out of patience or the other runs out of cheap tools. Neither condition is visible this week. Each of Tuesday’s files is cheap to break and expensive to hold. A thin buffer, a cheap weapon and a minority budget all describe one tolerance.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened over Lithuania on 15 September 2026?

Italian jets flying NATO’s Baltic air policing mission destroyed a drone near Pratkūnai, in Kaunas county, early on Tuesday. Lithuania’s military called it the first in the country’s airspace, after earlier shootdowns over Estonia and Latvia.

What stopped Dutch trains on Tuesday morning?

Pipes tied to the track at about twenty places made signalling systems read empty sections as occupied. ProRail said they were placed deliberately, and no group has claimed responsibility.

What is not yet known about either incident?

No investigator has confirmed the drone’s payload, its operator or its target, and no government has claimed or denied it. Dutch police have named no suspect and no motive.

Why does a European gas price matter outside Europe?

Europe pays for imported gas in dollars, so a higher gas price pushes the euro down, and it sat at US$1.1537 on Tuesday. Exporters who invoice in euros then earn fewer dollars for the same cargo.
