World.title: Poland and other V4 countries will block EU climate policies that raise energy costs, warns Tusk
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that the Central European Visegrád Group (V4) would seek to block any European Union climate policies that push up energy prices. Speaking after a meeting with the leaders of the other V4 countries, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, Tusk said that they could not accept policies that further weakened competitiveness at a time when they were already facing high electricity costs. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Bratysława ⤵️ Polska i grupa #V4 nie pozwoli na żadne zmiany i na żadne propozycje instytucji europejskich, czy innych państw, które mogłyby wpłynąć na pogorszenie sytuacji energetycznej w naszych państwach. Ceny energii w tym regionie muszą spaść. pic.twitter.com/BFnRx8Clse — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 10, 2026 In recent months, Poland and some other member states have been pushing for a softening of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), a cap-and-trade scheme launched in 2005 that makes polluters pay for carbon emissions in sectors such as power generation and heavy industry. They have also secured a postponement of the introduction of ETS2, which will cover emissions from road transport and buildings. “Whether we are talking about ETS1, ETS2, or other proposals, anything that brings a risk of more expensive energy for us will be blocked by us,” said Tusk on Thursday at a press conference alongside the other V4 prime ministers, as well as Ireland’s Micheál Martin. “Poland and the V4 will not allow any changes or any proposals from European institutions or other countries that could worsen the energy situation in our countries,” he added. “Energy prices in this region, including in Poland, must fall.” Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Tusk argued that high energy prices pose a threat not only to Central European economies but also to the competitiveness of the EU as a whole. “We can forget about any dreams of competing with China or the United States if our energy prices remain as they are right now,” warned Tusk. Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico likewise said the V4 countries were united in their approach to the emissions trading system. “We will be very active, and we will also engage in discussions outside the meetings of the European Council and the Council of Europe to discuss what steps to take to bring down these energy prices,” he said. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš also expressed frustration with rising energy costs. “All of us in our industrial region pay a lot of money for emissions allowances. And what did the commission tell us in 2020? That the price of this allowance in 2030 will be €26.50. Right now, it’s €80,” he said. According to the Eurostat data, households in Poland paid €27.09 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh), including taxes and levies, for electricity in the second half of 2025. That was the 11th highest figure in the EU and below the figure of €28.96 across the bloc as a whole. However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in costs of living, Polish households faced the second-highest electricity prices in the EU, at 37.15 PPS per 100 kWh, behind only Romania (49.52 PPS) and the Czech Republic (39.16 PPS). The effects of ETS on electricity bills has moved to the centre of political debate this year after the main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from the system, saying it makes “Poles a cash machine for the EU’s absurd leftist climate policy”. The opposition-aligned conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, has also twice sought to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policies, including ETS, arguing they are too expensive. Both his efforts were rejected by the government’s majority in parliament. While the government has rejected the idea of withdrawing from ETS – which it says would result in large, ongoing fines being levied against Poland – it has pushed for reforms to the system. In July, the European Commission outlined proposals to soften ETS in response to pressure from countries such as Poland, allowing industries to continue emitting CO2 for longer while providing more financial support for investment in clean technologies. Yet there are also a number of other EU member states that argue against weakening ETS, saying it would penalise those who moved early to cut emissions. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Just before the European Commission unveiled its proposal in July, Poland’s climate minister, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, said she had assembled a coalition of 10 countries calling for ETS reform and a more realistic emissions-reduction path. They also want ETS funding mechanisms to account for national differences, including energy mixes and GDP per capita, to ensure a fairer transition for lower-income countries starting from a more challenging position. Poland, for example, has a historical reliance on coal, which it still uses to produce around half of its electricity, helping make it one of the EU’s biggest emitters. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. For more, read our full report: https://t.co/XjD9hfhabo pic.twitter.com/WklP7dYL78 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 2, 2026 However, the country has made significant progress in expanding renewables in recent years, particularly solar and onshore wind. In 2025, renewables accounted for just over 29% of Poland’s electricity generation, almost three times the share recorded a decade earlier. Further progress is expected this year, after Poland began to generate electricity from offshore wind farms for the first time. Under a national energy and climate plan approved by the current government in June, it plans by 2040 for Poland to generate 18-21% of power from offshore wind and 22-27% from onshore wind. A further 15-16% will come from nuclear, 14-18% from solar, 7-8% from gas and 0-5% from coal. Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish far-right leader Braun vandalises Ukrainian monument with hammer
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland dedicated to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two partisan formation that fought against the Soviet Union but was also responsible for massacring Poles. Braun declared that the monument, which was also recently vandalised by other unknown perpetrators, should be removed as it “insults the memory of victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles” and “glorifies Nazism”. The incident comes amid recent tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, and in particular the fact that the UPA continues to be honoured in Ukraine. Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️ Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ — Grzegorz Braun (@GrzegorzBraun_) September 10, 2026 The monument in question is located in the village of Liski, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and marks the burial site of 41 UPA soldiers killed while fighting against the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, in 1946, in the aftermath of World War Two. The area previously had a large ethnic-Ukrainian population. The memorial was vandalised last month, when it was sprayed with black paint and its arch was damaged. On Monday this week, further damage was discovered to the inscription on the monument. Police announced that they had launched an investigation into vandalism, property damage and ethnic hatred, but had not yet identified the perpetrators, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). On Wednesday evening, Braun published a video showing himself and another man using a hammer to repeatedly strike the front of the monument, causing visible damage to the stone, which contains the names of the killed UPA soldiers. They also appear to attempt to remove a separate plaque. During the video, Braun, who is a member of the European Parliament and finished fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, claimed that local residents are “afraid they would be set on fire” if they attempted to remove the memorial themselves. It is not clear when the video was recorded. Shortly after Braun published it, local police in Hrubieszów county, where the monument is located, issued a statement saying that officers were investigating damage to the monument. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka shared their statement and declared that “the perpetrators will not go unpunished”. Sprawcy zniszczenia pomnika w Białymstoku nie pozostaną bezkarni. Policjanci zabezpieczają dowody i przesłuchują świadków. https://t.co/7HCApuhPZ1 — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) September 10, 2026 Braun, who regularly carries out stunts intended to demonstrate his anti-Ukrainian, antisemitic and anti-LGBT views, and is already facing multiple legal cases over such incidents. He is currently on trial for attacking a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament using a fire extinguisher. Last month, he was charged with the crime of denying Nazi crimes for claiming that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake”. He was also charged with theft over incidents in which he tore down Ukrainian and European Union flags, and with vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition. If convicted, some of the crimes Braun is charged with carry potential years-long prison sentences. Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, which recently called for a “normalisation of relations with Russia”, enjoys support of around 8-9%, according to polling averages. That could make it a key player in deciding who can form a government after next year’s parliamentary elections. Figures from Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun's party celebrated Russia Day at the Russian embassy and presented a letter hailing Russia's development, blaming "globalists" for the Ukraine war and calling for normalisation of Polish-Russian relations https://t.co/SU3gEdVod0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2026 At the time of writing, there had been no response from Ukrainian authorities to Braun’s latest stunt. However, when the same monument was vandalised last month, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw issued a statement expressing its “deep indignation”. “Regardless of the difficult and tragic chapters of our shared history, burial and memorial sites should remain outside the realm of political disputes and be treated with respect,” they wrote. The embassy also expressed “particular concern that this incident occurs against the backdrop of a rising number of hostile acts toward Ukrainians in Poland, including reports of aggression and attacks on Ukrainian citizens” “Any attempts to shift historical disputes into the realm of vandalism, intimidation or hostility toward modern Ukraine and Ukrainians are dangerous and must be met with an appropriate legal response,” they added. Poland and Ukraine have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. His Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, responded by stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. Tensions have since cooled, and Ukraine has made moves to defuse the crisis. However, significant differences remain, in particular over memory of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the killing of around 100,000 Polish civilians. Poland regards the episode as a genocide. Ukraine strongly rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Recent months have also seen a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland, including a series of cases of verbal or physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported anti-Ukrainian hate crimes were up 30% in the first half of this year. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine responded to the dismantling of a UPA monument in Poland by introducing a ban on exhumations of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres on its territory. It is believed that tens of thousands still remain buried in unmarked mass graves. However, last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Kyiv allowed such exhumations to resume, and since then the remains of dozens of victims have been found, researched and reburied. Earlier this month, Poland also granted Ukraine permission to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. Following a crash between a train and a truck at a rail crossing that left one passenger dead and both drivers with serious injuries, Poland’s main train drivers’ union has announced a go-slow protest that will take place on Friday. They note that they have long been warning about a lack of sufficient safety measures at rail crossings, and say that a “red line has now been crossed”. In the wake of Wednesday’s tragedy, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has pledged that the government will introduce “very tough” new punishments for those who violate regulations at crossings. Poczułam takie jakby silne hamowanie, takie bardzo silne i nagle takie bujanie i do człowieka dociera, że zaraz się wykoleimy – mówiła pasażerka pociągu Intercity "Koziołek", jadącego z Lublina do Szczecina, który wykoleił się w miejscowości Sokolniki Suche w Mazowieckiem.… pic.twitter.com/enyjD2Wo6K — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 9, 2026 On Wednesday morning, a train travelling between the cities of Lublin and Szczecin partially derailed in the village of Sokolniki Suche in central Poland after colliding with a heavy goods vehicle that, initial findings suggest, had entered the tracks at a rail crossing despite warning lights flashing. The crossing had no barriers. The train was carrying at least 114 people, including three crew. One passenger in the first carriage, a 39-year-old woman, died in hospital from her injuries, prosecutors announced later on Wednesday. Four others, including the drivers of both the train and the truck, remain hospitalised in serious condition. Prosecutors say that, from the evidence collected so far, they will launch an investigation into the crime of unintentionally causing a rail disaster, which carries a prison sentence of six months to eight years. However, they have not yet been able to interview either driver due to their health conditions. On Thursday, the head of the Polish train drivers’ union, Leszek Miętek, announced that a protest would begin at midnight and last through the whole of Friday. “We are appealing to train drivers to travel at a safe speed of 20 km/h (12.4 mph) across every level crossing in Poland,” he said, adding that he had “received reports from across the country” that “there’s full support for this type of action”. Miętek noted that the Polish labour code allows employees to refrain from work if they believe it poses a threat to their life or health. While drivers would not go that far, they want to demonstrate in a bid to prompt “action from those responsible for safety.” He warned that train delays should be expected on Friday. Związek Zawodowy Maszynistów Kolejowych mówi "dość" i ogłasza ogólnokrajowy protest po tragicznej katastrofie w Sokolnikach Suchych. W piątek, 11 września, pociągi w całej Polsce będą zwalniać na przejazdach kolejowych do zaledwie 20 km/h. Więcej o tym: https://t.co/jj6jKm40X2 pic.twitter.com/ThqfLx3dEc — TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) September 10, 2026 The union chief said that Wednesday’s accident “was not a surprise to us, considering that statistically we have an accident at a railway crossing every two days”. However, “a red line has [now] been crossed”, he added, quoted by news website Interia. Miętek noted that, for over 18 months, the union has been running a campaign, titled “I Want To Live”, focused on safety. Just two days before the accident, it had issued a special appeal to drivers over “growing safety concerns on Polish railways”. “We have been doing everything we can in parliament and at the infrastructure ministry to make sure this problem is noticed,” added Miętek, who also welcomed the fact that, following Wednesday’s accident, Tusk has pledged to take action. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Katastrofa kolejowa w Sokolnikach miała miejsce na przejeździe kolejowym, dlatego natychmiast rozpoczniemy prace nad zaostrzeniem przepisów dla tych, którzy wjeżdżają na przejazdy kolejowe, mimo zapór i czerwonych światel. pic.twitter.com/BgaZQLEPbR — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 9, 2026 In those remarks, the prime minister lamented that the accident in Sokolniki Suche was “yet another case of such a catastrophe happening at a rail crossing”. “We must immediately begin urgent work on tightening regulations,” he continued. This would include “very tough” punishments “for those who, unfortunately, quite systematically drive onto railway crossings despite barriers and red lights”. Infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak later confirmed that they were working on “radical” measures to toughen penalties for those who violate the rules at rail crossings. He revealed that one proposal being considered is suspending for three months the licence of any driver who ignores red lights at rail crossings. However, critics noted that the ministry had already announced such plans in July 2025, and had failed to implement them since then. – Chcemy wprowadzić przepis, na podstawie którego każdy kierowca, który wjedzie na przejazd drogowo-kolejowy kiedy jest zapalone czerwone światło, straci prawo jazdy, zostanie mu ono zatrzymane na trzy miesiące. Chcemy także zmienić kodeks karny we współpracy z ministrem… pic.twitter.com/RhE8pcvlJ9 — Ministerstwo Infrastruktury (@MI_GOV_PL) September 9, 2026 The latest data from Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency, show that in 2024 Poland recorded the second-highest number of rail accidents, 220, among all member states, behind only Germany (366). However, 24% of Poland’s accidents took place at rail crossings, compared to 16% in Germany. In total, Poland had by far the highest number of deaths caused by accidents at rail crossings (45), ahead of Germany (26), France (20) and Hungary (18). When taking into account the size of countries’ rail networks, Poland had 4.3 rail deaths (from all causes, not just accidents at crossings) per thousand kilometres of track, which was the fifth-highest figure in the EU, behind Portugal (6.2), Hungary (5.8), Slovakia (5.7) and Lithuania (4.6). World.title: Prague Has the Most Unaffordable Rents for Minimum-Wage Earners in the EU
World.content:
Prague has the highest rent-to-minimum-wage ratio among EU capitals, with the average two-bedroom apartment costing 185% of the gross minimum wage.

Prague has become the European Union’s least affordable capital for minimum-wage earners looking to rent a home, according to a new analysis by the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC).



The average monthly rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the Czech capital reaches €1,710, compared with a gross monthly minimum wage of €924. This means rent alone amounts to 185% of the minimum wage.

Lisbon follows in second place, with rent accounting for 168% of the gross minimum wage. Budapest ranks third at 159%, followed by Bratislava at 158%.

Other capitals where average rent exceeds the gross minimum wage include Sofia (154%), Athens (153%), and Riga (151%).

The figures highlight the pressure facing minimum-wage earners in cities where housing costs have risen significantly faster than incomes.

How Prague Compares with Western Europe

Prague’s position is particularly striking when compared with several Western European capitals.

In Paris, average rent accounts for 138% of the gross minimum wage, while the figure stands at 125% in Madrid and 113% in Dublin.

At the other end of the ranking, Brussels is the most affordable capital for minimum-wage earners in the comparison. Average rent there represents 70% of the gross minimum wage. Berlin follows at 76%, while the figure is 85% in Nicosia and 87% in Luxembourg.

Housing Costs Across the EU

According to Eurostat’s latest figures cited in the analysis, housing and utility bills account for 23.6% of household spending across the European Union.

The ETUC has called for stronger collective bargaining, greater consideration of housing costs when setting minimum wages, and increased investment in social housing.

The organisation also noted that rents can be more affordable when measured against national minimum wages rather than those in capital cities. Among the 16 EU countries analysed, the share of the gross minimum wage required for rent ranged from 33% in Poland to 61% in Malta.

World.title: Prague 8 Pirates to Host English-Language Guide to Czech Local Elections
World.content:
EU citizens living in Prague 8 can learn how to vote in the upcoming municipal elections at an event on 17 September.

The Prague 8 branch of the Czech Pirate Party is inviting international residents to an English-language evening explaining how EU citizens can take part in Czech local elections.

The event, titled “Hey, You Can Vote Too!”, will take place on Thursday, 17 September, at 6 PM at Pauza Palmovka in Prague 8.



The evening will offer a practical introduction to the Czech voting system, an overview of the Prague 8 Pirates’ local programme, and an opportunity for international residents to share their views on life in the district.

Organisers say the event is intended to help EU citizens understand their voting rights and discuss what they would like to see improved in Prague 8.

Who Can Vote in Czech Local Elections?

Citizens of other EU Member States can vote in Czech municipal elections if they meet certain conditions.

Voters must:

Be at least 18 years old by the second day of the election.

Have permanent or registered temporary residence in the municipality.

Be entered in the supplement to the permanent electoral register.

EU citizens who are not already registered must apply by 7 October 2026 at 4 PM.

“Many people from other EU countries live in Prague 8, work here, raise their families here and use the same schools, parks, streets and public services as everyone else. Yet many still do not know that they can vote in local elections,” said Martin Štěrba, the Czech Pirate Party’s candidate for mayor of Prague 8.

“We want to explain how it works and hear directly from them what Prague 8 could do better.”

The Czech municipal elections will take place on 9 and 10 October 2026.

Voters in Prague 8 will elect representatives to both the Prague 8 Municipal District Council and the Prague City Assembly.

World.title: Nearly 40 Percent of Young Czechs Experience Financial Stress Every Month
World.content:
Money worries affect almost one in three Czech adults, but younger people are facing a greater burden.

A new survey found that 39 percent of people aged 18 to 26 experience financial anxiety at least once a month, with household income playing a major role in how people feel about their finances.



Financial concerns are common across the Czech Republic. According to a survey conducted by Ipsos for Home Credit, 28 percent of adults experience worries about money at least once a month. Another 35 percent report financial stress several times a year.

Young adults face the greatest pressure

People aged 18 to 26 are the most likely to experience regular financial stress. Nearly four in ten respondents in this age group said they worry about money at least once a month.

Home Credit attributed the pressure partly to the cost of housing and everyday expenses. For young adults trying to establish themselves financially, rising prices in recent years have made it harder to absorb unexpected costs.

An unplanned bill or other expense can therefore create a serious problem, particularly for those who have limited savings.

Household income makes a significant difference

The survey found a clear relationship between household income and financial anxiety.

Among households earning up to CZK 40,000 per month, 41 percent of respondents reported experiencing financial stress. The proportion decreases as household income rises.

People living in households with monthly incomes above CZK 70,000 reported the lowest levels of financial concern.

Age and education also appear to influence how people view their finances. Respondents aged 54 to 65 and university students reported lower levels of stress than some other groups. In both categories, 43 percent said they did not experience financial stress at all.

Financial stress may also affect physical health

The consequences of financial difficulties can extend beyond anxiety and everyday worries.

The material also refers to research published by the American Mayo Clinic in 2025. According to the research cited, long-term financial distress and food insecurity may be associated with poorer cardiovascular health and a higher risk of death.

The findings underline the potential connection between financial security and overall well-being. However, the Czech survey does not establish whether financial stress directly causes health problems.

The survey was conducted by Ipsos in June 2026 among 1,026 people.

World.title: Fresh from France: Meet Benjamin, the Founder of The French in Prague
World.content:
For the past 12 years, Benjamin has been building a life in Prague – and helping bring a taste of France to the Czech capital.

What began as a business supplying wine to hotels, restaurants and wine bars 10 years ago has gradually grown into The French, a food business focused on bringing French products directly to Prague.

The company started with an e-shop selling mainly wine, pâté, jam, honey and foie gras. But Benjamin soon realized there was something missing: fresh French produce.

“The idea, step by step, was that we were missing fresh products to be able to open a physical shop. That’s how, two years ago, we started importing fresh products.”

Today, The French operates two shops in Prague and imports a wide range of products directly from France, with a focus on freshness and quality while keeping prices accessible.

“It cannot be fresher than what we import.”

From Breakfast to Dinner

Fresh fruit and vegetables have become one of the shop’s main attractions. The products are imported weekly, with a truck leaving France every Tuesday carrying oysters, mussels, cheeses, fish, meat, fruits and vegetables.

“Two days ago it was in the sea and today it’s already in Prague, sitting in our fridge.”

The shop aims to cover the entire day, from breakfast to dinner. Customers can pick up croissants and pain au chocolat in the morning, fresh coffee, and a selection of French products for lunch and dinner.

Among the more distinctive products are French crème fraîche and salted butter. Benjamin points out that the natural colour of the dairy products can change during the year depending on what the cows eat. “If you have the same colour of butter or cream throughout the whole year, it’s because they are not eating grass.”

A New Home in Vinohrady

The company recently expanded with a larger shop in Vinohrady, giving customers access to a wider range of ultra-fresh products imported directly from France, as well as cosmetics from Provence.

The French also supplies restaurants and hotels across Prague with products including butter, cream, cheese, ham, sausages and olives. Much of the range comes directly from the Rungis International Market near Paris, one of the largest food markets in Europe.

The company also works with direct farmers, with some products clearly marked as coming from individual producers. “In Prague, you don’t have any shop that is grouping all of these categories of products.”

Customers can also order through The French’s e-shop at francouzske-speciality.cz and either have their purchases delivered or collect them from a shop.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The French.cz (@the_french_cz)

But Benjamin says the experience is intended to be more personal than a standard supermarket. “We are not a shop where people are just behind the cash desk. We have people going into the shop to explain what we have, recommend what to cook and what to pair.”

The shops also have a weekly tasting calendar, giving customers the chance to try different products and discover new flavours.

French Food for Everyone

Although many customers are French, The French is not specifically aimed at the French community.

The Vinohrady shop attracts a large number of expats, while the company’s Prague 4 location has a much higher proportion of Czech customers. Benjamin says the goal is to serve people living in the neighborhood regardless of nationality. “We are not targeting especially expats or especially French. We are trying to target everyone living in the area who like gastronomy.”

There are, however, some differences in what Czech and French customers look for. Stronger French cheeses, for example, can take some getting used to, while certain French cuts of meat differ from traditional Czech ones.

Some types of fish are also relatively unfamiliar. Red mullet, or rouget, is widely used in French cuisine and high-end restaurants but is less common in Czech kitchens.

Growing Across Prague

The French has ambitious plans for the coming years. After opening its Vinohrady location and another shop in Prague 4, the company is preparing to open another location in Prague 9 in January.

The long-term goal is to operate five or six shops across Prague, with Holešovice, Karlín and Dejvice among the areas being considered.

World.title: A Prague Institution: Indian Jewel Celebrates 30 Years of North Indian Flavours
World.content:
The family-run restaurant has been bringing authentic North Indian flavours and warm hospitality to Prague since 1996.

For 30 years, Indian Jewel has been serving authentic Indian cuisine in the heart of Prague. Established in 1996 by Sanjeev Wadehra, the family-owned restaurant is celebrating three decades in the Czech capital in 2026 — a milestone that makes it one of the longest-standing Indian restaurants in the country.



The restaurant’s story began with Sanjeev Wadehra, who brought recipes, cooking traditions and spice blends directly from India to Prague. Today, the kitchen continues to focus on authentic North Indian cuisine, with dishes prepared according to traditional recipes rather than adapted to passing culinary trends.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Indian Jewel Prague (@indianjewelprague)

To celebrate its 30th anniversary, Indian Jewel is offering Prague Morning readers a complimentary welcome drink or dessert. Simply mention Prague Morning when you visit.

Among the highlights are tandoor specialities, prepared in the traditional clay oven, alongside lamb, chicken and shrimp curries. The menu also offers a wide selection of vegetarian dishes, as well as biryanis, freshly baked naan and other Indian classics.

Popular choices include Butter Chicken, Chicken Tikka Masala and Lamb Rogan Josh, while the tandoor menu offers another way to explore the flavours of North India.

But food is only part of the restaurant’s story. Indian Jewel has built its reputation on consistent quality and warm, personal hospitality. Many members of the team have been with the restaurant for years, creating the family atmosphere that Sanjeev and his wife, Mohini, consider an important part of its success.

The restaurant moved to its current location at Rybná 9 in 2021, after many years at its previous home in the historic Týn Courtyard. Despite the change, the philosophy has remained the same: authentic food, attentive service and a welcoming atmosphere.

World.title: From Sri Lanka to Prague: How Tharusha Brought Coconut Culture to the City
World.content:
Tharusha De Silva, originally from Sri Lanka, has spent much of his life between different countries.

Today, he is bringing a taste closely associated with home to Prague through his beverage brand, The Coconut Culture which is also available at select cafés and restaurants across Prague.

We spoke to him about his journey to the Czech Republic, navigating life between cultures, and the story behind The Coconut Culture.



Journey to Prague

Prague was never part of a long-term plan for De Silva. He first came to the Czech Republic in 2016 to study mechanical engineering, after growing up in Sri Lanka and spending his teenage years in Dubai. By his own account, his decision to come here was almost entirely random.

“We had a counselling office that used to help us with university applications, and one day they changed the wallpaper to a map of Prague. I just went into the room, pointed at it and said, ‘Hey, what is that?’ They told me a little bit about Prague, and that’s how I got here.”

At first, Prague was simply where he planned to spend his university years. “I always thought that I would leave after university,” he says. But the longer he stayed, the less certain leaving became.

“It’s very difficult to give you a straight answer to what made me decide to stay. But I think the city has its way of keeping you.”

Freedom and opportunity were part of what made the city difficult to leave.

“You could really make something of yourself here if you really want to,” he says.

Eventually, staying stopped feeling like a temporary decision. “In a way, I found a part of home here. That was enough to make me stay.”

The Coconut Culture

King Coconut, a variety native to Sri Lanka, became the starting point for The Coconut Culture.

Unlike varieties grown primarily for their meat or oil, King Coconut has a more specific purpose. “The other coconuts have multiple uses. Some are used to get the desiccated coconut from the inside, to make milk out of it, to make coconut oil, even some kind of biofuel. But this variant, the King Coconut, has one use: it is to drink it.”

It is sweeter and lighter than regular coconut water, with a taste he compares to subtly sweet spring water.

For De Silva, however, the connection with King Coconut goes back to his childhood. He remembers his grandfather taking him and his sister out on his scooter. On the way back, they would stop beside a road running between paddy fields and have a King Coconut together.

Years later, that childhood ritual became part of the reason he wanted to introduce King Coconut to people who had never encountered it.

“I want to bring King Coconut out more, make more people be aware of it, and give it its place in the world.”

The name The Coconut Culture came later, during a conversation with a friend about Czech and Sri Lankan culture. De Silva remembers describing his background almost casually: “I come from the coconut culture.” The phrase stayed with him.

“I also want to thank Karim and Ghaith, who have been with me since day one. Together, we want to build something people can rely on not just as a product, but as a brand that does what it says,” added De Silva.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by @coconutculture.eu

Living Between Cultures

Having grown up in Sri Lanka, spent his teenage years in Dubai and lived in the Czech Republic since 2016, De Silva has spent much of his life between different cultures.

There are, of course, things he still misses about Sri Lanka.

“I come from an island, a very fairly simple life. I get to walk around without any shoes. We have the sea, we have the ocean. We have the sun, so many fruits, so many wild animals, forests, mountains.”

But perhaps the biggest difference is language and the sense of belonging that comes with it.

“The most important thing is I communicate in my own language back home. Here, I am the expat. I either communicate in English or with the little Czech I know.”

“Back home, it’s my language. I speak in my language, I’m more comfortable. I feel like I’m a fuller version of myself.”

Distance has also changed the way he sees the place he came from.

“The place that I will make home or call home in the future is just going to be a mix of the cultures that I’ve experienced. It’s going to be some of the things that I picked up from Dubai, some of the things I’ve picked up living in the Czech Republic or Europe, and then, of course, where I come from, my roots.”

Finding a Home in Prague

Prague, naturally, has become part of that mix. After years in the city, De Silva says one of the things he values most is the openness he finds here.

“I think here, Prague is one of the places where you could just walk out feeling or looking any way you want. And it’s very rare that anyone would tell you anything because people accept you as you are.”

Part of that openness, he says, also comes from the people who have made Prague their home from elsewhere.

“Prague has many, many expats and the city is filled with expats. Therefore, all of these expats bring different cultures into Prague.”

Beyond the bigger things that make Prague feel like home, it is also the everyday details that have become part of his life here.

“I would definitely miss the café culture. I love to sit in a café in the mornings, in the evenings, have coffee, read, do some work.”

A First Taste

The first real test came at the launch event, held before The Coconut Culture had even received its full stock. De Silva and his team brought in a small number of bottles specifically for the occasion and invited friends to try the drink.

“We had a launch event with some of our friends, and we got a lot of good feedback about the drink, especially about its taste, about the way it’s packed, about the branding that we’ve done.”

For the team, it was an early indication that the idea could work in Prague.

“This was maybe where we thought, okay, this is actually something that the people of the Czech Republic, all the expats and the locals, will enjoy.”

Beyond King Coconut

King Coconut is only the first of the discoveries De Silva hopes to bring to Europe. He describes The Coconut Culture as “an exploration company”, where “the fruit is the vehicle”.

The idea is to keep the range deliberately small, with the company eventually aiming for five to seven products.

“The Coconut Culture has a very simple vision: to find native fruits. We want to have between five to seven products, and be very specialized in them: find these native fruits that are specific to countries or communities. And we want to go there, we want to discover it, and we want to bring it to the European market and give it to the people here.”

For De Silva, however, the products are also a way of introducing the places they come from.

“We want to find these cultures, tell their story to the world here and, hopefully, respect, as we always try to, where it comes from and also respect the place that it’s being sold at.”

World.title: Czechia Considers One Million-Crown Reward for Second Child as Births Hit Record Low
World.content:
Prime Minister Andrej Babiš is considering a million-crown reward for families who have a second child, along with lifelong tax relief for parents of a third child.

The proposals are among several measures being discussed, including support for parents who are studying, childcare services and more affordable housing. Babiš said he would bring together the relevant ministers to discuss the issue.



The Czech Republic recorded just 77,600 live births in 2025, the lowest figure since statistical records began in 1785. Births fell in every region compared with the previous year.

The country’s total fertility rate also dropped to 1.28 children per woman, while the average age of women having their first child rose to 29.2 years.

Million-crown reward for a second child

Babiš said the government was examining several proposals to encourage families to have more children.

“One million crowns for a second child,” he said, describing a possible incentive for women who already have one child.

He also mentioned a lifelong tax break for a third child, support for studying parents, nurseries and children’s groups.

Babiš also criticized mortgage costs, questioning why Czech interest rates remain 1.5 percentage points above those in the eurozone. He has repeatedly criticized the Czech National Bank, while cheaper mortgages were among ANO’s key election promises.

Debate over assisted reproduction

Babiš also addressed a proposal from the Ministry of Health that would allow single women to undergo assisted reproduction without a male partner.

Responding to criticism from the Alliance for Family, he acknowledged the importance of fathers but pointed to divorce and child-support disputes.

“I know that. But what is the divorce rate here? Fathers leave families and then sometimes do not even pay child support,” he said.

Babiš added that he did not want to comment extensively on the issue because of possible accusations of having business interests in reproductive clinics.

“It’s nonsense. A woman can choose the clinic she wants. If she hates Babiš, then let her not go there. I don’t decide on that at all,” he said.

World.title: Czechia Ranks Fourth Among Russia’s “Enemies” in New Propaganda List
World.content:
Czechia has been ranked among Russia’s top five “enemy” countries in a new list published by Vzglyad, a Russian outlet widely regarded as a Kremlin propaganda mouthpiece.

Czechia has been ranked as the fourth-most “hostile” country toward Russia in a new ranking published by Vzglyad, scoring 65 out of a possible 100 points.



The list places Czechia alongside Romania, Poland, the United Kingdom and Canada, all of which received the same score.

Italy topped the ranking with 80 points, followed by Germany, Lithuania and Finland, which tied for second place with 75 points each. The United States, Latvia and France shared third place with 70 points apiece.

Japan makes the list for the first time

Most of the countries in the top ten appear regularly in the ranking. This time, however, Japan was included for the first time.

According to Vzglyad, Japan’s inclusion was prompted by Tokyo’s “firm protest” over Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Iturup.

Iturup is part of the southern Kuril Islands, which Japan claims as its “Northern Territories.” Russia considers the islands an integral part of its territory.

The territorial dispute dates back to the final days of World War II, when Soviet forces occupied Iturup and neighboring islands in 1945.

Czechia remains a regular presence

Czechia has consistently appeared among the top ten countries in the ranking.

The list was first published in November last year, when Czechia also placed fourth. In May, however, the country briefly dropped to the bottom of the ranking.

The index assigns countries a maximum of 100 points based on six criteria. According to Vzglyad editor Evgeny Pozdnyakov, the most important factor is military-political activity against Russia, which accounts for up to 30 points. Sanctions pressure contributes a further 20 points.

The ranking reflects the perspective of Russian state-aligned media and should not be interpreted as an official assessment of international relations or a measure of actual hostility between countries.

World.title: One more warm day until cold front splits Hungary in two
World.content:
Hungary is set for a dramatic weather divide this week as a wavy cold front crosses the country, bringing a sharp drop in temperatures to the west while summer-like warmth lingers in the east.

Wednesday will bring us one more warm day

According to a forecast video from the meteorologists at HungaroMet, the contrast will be particularly noticeable on Thursday, before another, even stronger cold front arrives early next week.

Wednesday will begin with a southerly airflow, bringing temporary warming to the Carpathian Basin. After patches of morning fog clear, mostly sunny conditions are expected, with afternoon temperatures reaching 23–28°C. Winds will strengthen in several areas, with particularly strong gusts possible around the Kisalföld region and Lake Fertő.

Cold front will divide the country

The weather will change considerably on Thursday as a cold front reaches Hungary and becomes temporarily stalled over the country. This will create a striking contrast between the western and eastern parts of the country.

Temperatures in western and north-western Hungary are expected to reach only 19–20°C, while the eastern Great Plain could still see highs of 28–30°C. Despite the unusually large regional difference, HungaroMet says the national average temperature will remain broadly in line with the seasonal norm.

The temperature divide will persist into Friday, while conditions become increasingly favourable for precipitation across a larger part of the country. Rain, showers and thunderstorms may develop in several areas, making Friday a more unsettled day.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Weekend offers temporary respite, but cold reclaims Hungary on Monday

By Saturday, the frontal system is expected to move eastwards away from Hungary. Some light rain may still occur across southern and eastern areas, but sunshine will dominate elsewhere. The temperature contrast will remain, with noticeably cooler conditions in Transdanubia while temperatures fall less sharply across the Great Plain.

Western areas may begin to warm gradually again during the weekend, but the improvement is unlikely to last. A new, fast-moving and more pronounced cold front is forecast to reach the region on Monday, bringing another 3–4°C drop in temperatures nationwide. The next front is not expected to produce particularly heavy precipitation, however, with only moderate rainfall effects currently anticipated.

World.title: Hungarian minority in Ukraine: Our reader writes from the scene – agreement signed, but where are the results?
World.content:
Hungary and Ukraine have recently reached an agreement in order to restore the rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine. The agreement defines basic rights in language, education, social and political, and cultural spheres. The Ukrainian side undertook to expand the range of rights of the Hungarian minority in settlements where ethnic Hungarians make up more than 10% of the population.

This article was written by our reader, P. M.

These are key known points from the agreement:

Names of streets, squares, and plates on buildings of local administrations must be translated into Hungarian

People may address local authorities using the Hungarian language, and local officials must speak it

Agitation for elections, voting rules, and ballot papers at local elections must be translated into Hungarian

Public events may be held in Hungarian. People are allowed to use Hungarian national symbols, but they can’t dominate Ukrainian ones

Educational facilities with Hungarian-speaking groups get the “school of national minority” status. Such schools must have a Hungarian-speaking principal and a vice principal. Students and teachers have a right to speak Hungarian in schools off-hours

Educational diplomas and certificates must be translated into Hungarian. Tasks of national exams (except Ukrainian language and History) must be translated too

The agreement was signed in June this year; however, Kyiv’s been slow to meet Budapest’s requirements, and, unfortunately, things are staying the same for the Hungarian minority in Ukraine now.

Who has the right to represent the Hungarian minority in Ukraine?

A bilateral group working on ensuring the rights of ethnic Hungarians was established after signing for rapid response to possible violations. From the Ukrainian side, we have non-governmental organisations and influencers. However, there is a nuance. There is a rising concern that Kyiv doesn’t fulfil the agreements responsibly.

Rumour has it that the group doesn’t consist of the largest organisations representing the Hungarian diaspora in Ukraine or organisations which are trusted not only by the local minority but also by Budapest, but consists of little-known regional organisations, which don’t even have any political representation in local authorities. For example, one of the participants of the group is Boris Vashkeba, a chairman of a small and rather young organisation called “Transcarpathian Society of Hungarians”.

It’s legitimate to ask about such organisations’ right to fully represent the interests of the community and about the appropriateness of their presence in important groups like this one.

Are the rights of the Hungarian minority a loophole for Ukraine’s EU accession?

There is also a certain point of view that Kyiv has agreed to this deal only in order to make Hungary stop interfering with negotiations on Ukraine’s EU accession. However, it didn’t work out. Only two (Fundamentals and External Relations) of the six negotiation clusters were opened. Budapest refused to approve screening results for the Internal Market and Competitiveness clusters on 1 September, for the third time since July.

The situation is pissing Ukrainian officials off, so they continue to blame Budapest for halting Ukraine’s EU integration. Despite this, Magyar states that Ukraine, like any other country, should have no privileges for EU accession and promises to open the other clusters only when all agreements are implemented, including the ones concerning ethnic Hungarians in Ukraine.

Fate of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine remains uncertain

After signing the agreement this summer, Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Orban claims that Ukraine’s accession process will automatically be halted if Ukraine fails to comply with the minority agreement. It’s reported that Ukraine undertook to implement education measures by the end of 2026, and social and political measures in 2027. It’s also reported that there would be an audit soon, which would determine if there was any work being done in this field.

Meanwhile, Magyar has recently said that Hungary doesn’t see enough progress made by Ukraine in complying with the agreement and once again has confirmed that the rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine are a very important problem for Hungary. That’s why Budapest voted against the EU’s initiative to stop granting temporary protection to military-age Ukrainian men.

Magyar explained that many people escaping from Ukraine to Hungary belong to Ukraine’s Hungarian minority, which his government tries to protect. Nevertheless, Kyiv keeps repeating that it’s illegal to cross the border for military-age men in Ukraine now.

World.title: FM Orbán files criminal complaint over former FM Szijjártó’s countless private jet travels
World.content:
Hungary’s Foreign Minister Anita Orbán has filed a criminal complaint over the use of private and military aircraft for official trips during the tenure of her predecessor, Péter Szijjártó.

Billions in additional costs alleged

Orbán said an internal review of the Foreign Ministry had uncovered serious irregularities and alleged that the routine use of chartered aircraft from 2022 onwards may have caused significant financial damage to the state. She says the ministry increasingly replaced scheduled commercial flights with private or military aircraft even though the number and nature of diplomatic engagements had not changed significantly.

She estimated that private flights between 2022 and 2026 cost around HUF 4 billion (currently more than EUR 10.9 million) more than travelling on scheduled services. This figure, she stressed, does not include the cost of military aircraft, meaning the total could be higher.

According to FM Orbán, they haven’t even considered cheaper options

Orbán also claimed that aircraft were chartered for relatively short journeys to cities including Bratislava, Vienna and Belgrade, where travelling by car or train would have taken only a few hours. She said investigators found no evidence that cheaper travel options had been systematically considered before individual journeys, even though these private flights should have not been considered as an opportunity, according to the policies of the ministry, writes ATV.

On that basis, Orbán said she believed the circumstances raised suspicions of mismanagement causing particularly significant financial damage and potentially involved responsibility among the ministry’s former senior leadership.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Fidesz calls complaint ‘frivolous’

The Fidesz parliamentary group rejected the allegations, calling the complaint frivolous and insisting that Szijjártó’s flights complied fully with the relevant government regulations. The party argued that the former foreign minister’s travel schedule was organised efficiently, claiming that Szijjártó frequently travelled overnight so that he could conduct meetings during the day.

It also said he returned home immediately after official programmes rather than unnecessarily extending his stays abroad. Fidesz further defended Szijjártó’s record as foreign minister, pointing to what it described as record levels of investment and job creation during the period.

Stay up-to-date: Hungarian Parliament elects five new constitutional judges

Szijjártó’s flights have long been controversial

The former foreign minister’s use of private aircraft has attracted media scrutiny for years. According to figures previously published by the Foreign Ministry, 53 private-jet journeys were made for Szijjártó over four years at a reported cost of HUF 4.87 billion (more than EUR 13.3), writes HVG.hu.

The issue has also been complicated by disputes over access to travel-cost information, with the government previously changing legislation concerning the disclosure of such data. The latest complaint is therefore likely to reignite a long-running political dispute over the cost and transparency of Szijjártó’s official travel. Any criminal responsibility, however, remains to be established.

World.title: Exotic South American animal spotted in Hungary’s mountains
World.content:
A trail runner had an extraordinary encounter in the Börzsöny hills after spotting and filming an exotic South American animal wandering through the forest.

Out-of-place exotic animal runs around in Hungary

Dániel Bárdos was running towards the Hárombarát Saddle on Sunday afternoon when he noticed an unusual animal moving through the woodland. He quickly took out his phone and recorded the creature, which appears to be a coati, also known as a red-nosed coati, a relative of the raccoon native to South America.

‘It wasn’t particularly interested in me’

Dániel said the animal was clearly aware of his presence but showed little fear. It continued sniffing and searching for food while moving in his direction, eventually prompting the runner to move away himself. He later shared the footage in the ‘Csak a Börzsöny!’ Facebook group, describing the encounter as an unexpected meeting with a South American mammal.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Is it the same coati seen last year?

The sighting has raised questions because a similar animal was reported in the Börzsöny area on 21 November 2025. At the time, speculation suggested that the coati could have escaped from the Törökmező Tourist Centre and Small Animal Park near Nagymaros. The park did not officially confirm this, however, writes KEMMA.hu.

Following the latest sighting, the park reportedly confirmed that all of its coatis were accounted for. It said it would nevertheless work with the local municipality to try to locate the creature and would be willing to take it in if it was found to be healthy.

The park’s owner believes the animal may instead have escaped from private ownership. Although the two sightings occurred in the same region less than a year apart, there is currently no evidence that they involved the same individual.

Hungary is full of exotic creatures: Hatvanpuszta zebra scandal deepens as details of illegal keeping, escaped animals, and carcasses dumped in a pig pit emerge

Keeping coatis is prohibited in Hungary

Norbert Riezing of the Duna–Ipoly National Park Directorate said that keeping coatis is prohibited in Hungary. The species was added to the European Union’s list of invasive alien species of Union concern in 2016, bringing strict restrictions on keeping, breeding, reproducing and trading the animals.

Certain people who legally owned coatis before the rules took effect on 3 August 2016 were allowed to keep them for the remainder of their natural lives, provided they prevented the animals from escaping or reproducing. For now, the origin of the coati filmed in the Börzsöny remains a mystery.

World.title: Hungarian police allegedly detained the 7th richest man of the country
World.content:
Police have reportedly detained billionaire property businessman Dániel Jellinek and Norbert Szivek, the former chief executive of Hungary’s Hungarian National Asset Management Inc. (MNV), in connection with a long-running investigation into alleged corruption surrounding state-owned Volán bus companies.

The two are linked to a long-running police investigation

Multiple Hungarian media outlets reported that the two men were taken from properties linked to them on Tuesday morning. However, police had not officially confirmed the detentions at the time of publication. Dániel Jellinek is currently the 7th richest Hungarian, while Norbert Szivek was the former head of the Hungarian National Asset Management Inc. (Magyar Nemzeti Vagyonkezelő, MNV).

Prime Minister Péter Magyar also referred to the reports on Facebook, saying police investigators had detained Jellinek, whom he described as one of Hungary’s wealthiest businessmen and a former business associate of István Tiborcz, son-in-law of former prime minister Viktor Orbán.

Investigation centres on allegedly overpriced buses

According to Telex, the reported detentions come days after Hungary’s National Investigation Bureau (NNI) announced that eight former executives had been made suspects in an investigation into allegedly overpriced purchases involving Volán companies.

According to the NNI, the investigation concerns transactions carried out between 2015 and 2018, which are suspected of causing around HUF 10 billion (EUR 27.4 million) in financial damage. Investigators say more than 600 used buses were purchased at inflated prices, while the acquisition of a Volán company’s headquarters in Kecskemét allegedly caused at least HUF 550 million (EUR 1.5 million) in losses.

The NNI is investigating suspected misappropriation causing particularly significant financial damage and money laundering involving particularly large sums. Police investigators say allegedly illicit funds were channelled through intermediary companies and fictitious loan agreements before being invested in property projects in Budapest, Balatonvilágos and Törökbálint.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Why Szivek is central to the case

Szivek headed MNV between 2015 and 2018, when the state asset manager exercised ownership rights over the Volán companies. According to police reports, the then leadership had knowledge of valuable state-owned properties that could generate significant profits if sold.

The authorities allege that money connected to the bus purchases and the Kecskemét property deal was transferred through intermediary companies and subsequently invested elsewhere. Szivek was among the eight people reportedly questioned as suspects last week. At that stage, investigators had not requested coercive measures against them.

Jellinek’s business connections

Jellinek, head of Indotek Group, is one of Hungary’s best-known property investors and has had extensive business dealings with companies linked to Tiborcz István, son-in-law of former prime minister Viktor Orbán.

Investigations by G7 cited by Hungarian media have examined financial transactions involving Jellinek-linked companies and businesses associated with Tiborcz. Jellinek has also been involved in major property deals, including the Gellért Hotel and a large Belgrade office complex. Jellinek was separately convicted of budget fraud in January 2025 in a case involving false invoices.

Stay up-to-date: Hungarian Parliament elects five new constitutional judges

Major escalation

The reported detention of Jellinek and Szivek would mark a major escalation in the Volán investigation, which has been under way for several years. The NNI has said the investigation is continuing, meaning further suspects could potentially be identified. Neither Jellinek nor Szivek has been convicted in connection with the Volán case, and the allegations against them remain subject to the ongoing criminal proceedings.

World.title: Hungarian Parliament elects five new constitutional judges
World.content:
Hungary’s parliament has elected five new members of the Constitutional Court in a secret ballot, replacing judges whose mandates have ended or are due to expire following recent constitutional changes.

New members join the court following constitutional changes and a major reshuffle

The new judges are Nóra Chronowski, a constitutional lawyer and university professor; András György Kovács, a Curia judge and administrative lawyer; Miklós Ligeti, criminal lawyer and legal director of Transparency International Hungary; Árpád Gábor Orosz, former head of the Curia’s Civil Law College; and Zsolt Szomora, a criminal law professor at the University of Szeged.

All five candidates, nominated by the Tisza majority, received 137 votes in favour and six against, with no abstentions. They subsequently took their oaths before parliament.

Why were five new judges needed?

The reshuffle followed the 17th amendment to Hungary’s Fundamental Law, which restored a compulsory retirement age of 70 for Constitutional Court judges. As a result, the mandates of Constitutional Court President Péter Polt, together with Mária Ádám Haszonicsné, Miklós Juhász and Zoltán Lomnici, ended on 1 September after all four reached the new age limit.

Parliament had 60 days to fill the vacancies. A fifth seat was also due to become vacant because Ágnes Czine, the court’s deputy president, will complete her 12-year mandate in November. Under the new rules, newly elected Constitutional Court judges will serve nine-year terms instead of 12. The reform also provides for the court’s president to be elected by the Constitutional Court judges themselves.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

What do the new judges stand for?

The nominees outlined their priorities during parliamentary hearings. Chronowski said she would see the annulment of legislation as evidence of successful constitutional review rather than failure. She highlighted the democratic rule of law, human dignity and the protection of minorities and vulnerable groups.

Kovács said the court should revive and further develop the constitutional jurisprudence established during Hungary’s democratic transition. Ligeti was particularly critical of the institution’s recent record, saying the Constitutional Court needed to be “rethought and rebuilt” and describing it as a “captured Constitutional Court”.

Orosz stressed that restoring public trust would require credible and independent judges, while Szomora advocated constitutional dialogue between the branches of government rather than treating institutional disagreements simply as conflicts.

Stay up-to-date: PM Magyar says former PM Orbán could face prison over threats against new asset recovery office staff

Fidesz-KDNP boycotts the election

Opposition Fidesz-KDNP alliance did not participate in the vote. Its MPs left the chamber beforehand, having described the procedure as illegitimate and a mockery of constitutionalism. The Mi Hazánk (Our Homeland) parliamentary group did participate and nominated five candidates of its own, but its nominees failed to receive backing from the relevant parliamentary committee.

The appointments mark a significant renewal of Hungary’s 15-member Constitutional Court, amid continuing political debate over judicial independence, the rule of law and the balance between state institutions.

Read also: Viktor Orbán’s great comeback or a sorry endgame at the Kötcse picnic?

World.title: Hungary has one year left of Russian gas – Could Putin turn the taps off sooner?
World.content:
Hungary may have little more than a year left of Russian gas under current European Union rules. But a recent diplomatic dispute with Moscow has raised a more immediate question: could Russia decide to cut supplies before the EU’s ban takes effect?

A diplomatic row has put Hungary’s energy dependence on Russia back in the spotlight

On 8 September, Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced that Budapest would expel ten employees of the Russian embassy, saying Hungarian authorities had found they had engaged in activities incompatible with their diplomatic status.

Moscow called the move unfriendly and promised a response, prompting speculation that retaliation could extend beyond diplomacy to oil or gas supplies. The following day, Russian gas deliveries to Hungary fell from the usual 22 million cubic metres to around 11 million. However, there was an important detail: the reduction was not ordered by Moscow. It was caused by planned Hungarian maintenance.

Gas flows were cut for scheduled maintenance

Hungary’s gas transmission operator FGSZ had already announced that capacity at the Kiskundorozsma 2 entry point from Serbia would be reduced by half between 9 and 12 September. Other maintenance work was also planned on the Hungarian-Croatian connection at Drávaszerdahely. Normal operations resumed on 12 September.

There was therefore no evidence that Moscow had retaliated by deliberately reducing gas supplies. Nevertheless, the timing highlighted how vulnerable Hungary could be to a genuine interruption.

Russian gas already has an expiry date

Under the EU’s REPowerEU framework, imports of Russian pipeline gas and LNG are due to be prohibited across the bloc by autumn 2027. This will also affect Hungary and Slovakia, the two EU countries that have continued to receive significant Russian pipeline gas.

The decisive moment is expected around 1 October 2027, or shortly afterwards when the gas storage season ends. That leaves roughly a year. The question is therefore not simply whether Russian gas will eventually disappear from Hungary, but whether Moscow has any reason to stop supplying it earlier.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Why Russia may keep the gas flowing

Hungarian energy-market experts generally believe Russia has little incentive to voluntarily abandon one of its last major European pipeline customers. The reason is primarily economic. With Russia’s wartime economy heavily focused on financing the war effort, giving up revenue from Hungarian gas sales would hardly be attractive.

According to Telex, Russia may also hope that European-Russian energy relations could eventually improve. Hungary and Slovakia remain among the last significant destinations for Russian pipeline gas in the EU. For Hungary, however, an abrupt interruption would still be painful.

Pipeline gas from Russia has been commercially attractive because the supplier effectively covers the transport cost to the delivery point. Alternative gas may be available at similar market prices, but transporting it to Hungary can add roughly 5–10 per cent to the cost.

Could Hungary replace Russian supplies?

The end of Russian gas would not mean Hungary simply runs out of energy. Gas currently reaches Hungary from Serbia, Romania, Croatia and Austria, with the Serbian route by far the most important. The southern connection carries Russian gas via the Balkan branch of TurkStream.

If Russian supplies disappeared, increased capacity from Romania and Croatia could help replace them, while Austrian imports could also contribute. The main challenge would be ensuring sufficient infrastructure and competitive prices rather than finding gas in absolute terms.

Could Russian gas be disguised?

One possible workaround could involve Turkey, which is becoming an increasingly important gas hub with supplies from several countries. However, turning Russian gas into “Turkish” gas is far from straightforward. The relevant TurkStream infrastructure does not simply connect Russia’s gas directly to Turkey’s domestic system in a way that would allow such a switch.

Additional infrastructure, including compressor capacity, would be required, while Russia and Turkey would also need to agree on how the resulting revenues were divided. Another possibility would be declaring Russian gas as originating elsewhere.

However, EU rules are expected to put considerable pressure on traders, who could face serious consequences if they falsely declared the origin of supplies. Gas is also harder to trace than oil because molecules from different sources can become mixed within interconnected networks.

Stay up-to-date: Russian gas deliveries to Hungary suddenly halved after diplomat expulsions: here’s the reason

The countdown is already under way

The latest diplomatic dispute may therefore be less important than the bigger trend: Hungary’s Russian gas relationship already has an expiry date. Industry sources suggest Budapest has increasingly accepted that Russian gas imports will end in autumn 2027, with no known major Hungarian initiative currently seeking to extend the EU timetable. Russia could still cut supplies earlier, but it may have little economic incentive to do so.

For Hungary, the loss of Russian gas would bring higher costs and logistical challenges, but it would not necessarily create a severe supply crisis. The real test over the next year will be whether Hungary can replace Russian gas without compromising energy security or paying a much higher price.
