World.title: After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019024/After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.content:
Hyrox has amended its official rulebooks after the winner of a recent Beijing event experienced bowel incontinence mid-race yet continued competing. The incident sparked widespread debate in China over sportsmanship and the organizer’s handling of potential hygiene risks.

On Monday, Hyrox updated its online rulebook to state that a race director may withdraw an athlete if their “blood, vomit, urine, or faeces pose a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers.”

The change comes in the wake of controversy surrounding the women’s solo elite race on Saturday, in which Australian athlete and Hyrox world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk finished first with a time of 1:01:23. Footage circulating online showed fecal matter staining Wietrzyk’s clothing and legs as she performed various exercises.

Hyrox has recently surged in popularity across China. Founded in Germany, the sport features eight 1-kilometer runs, each followed by strength training stations including sled pulls, rowing, and burpees. China’s first official race was held in Beijing in 2024 and drew 1,700 entries. Participants at this weekend’s Beijing event exceeded 11,000, with standard individual registration costing roughly 800 yuan ($125).

Competitors and social media users questioned organizers’ decision to let Wietrzyk continue racing. The Women’s Pro division won by Wietrzyk began at 2:40 p.m. Saturday, with other heats scheduled until 8:40 p.m. and another full day of competition Sunday.

“As someone who works in the public health sector, my biggest concern is that if she had a bacterial or viral infection, contamination like this could spread pathogens very quickly,” a Beijing-based athlete in her 20s, surnamed Wang, whose race began about an hour after Wietrzyk, told Sixth Tone.

Toilets were available at the venue, she noted, but using the bathroom counts toward an athlete’s total race time.

In a post made via its official account on microblogging platform Weibo Saturday night, Hyrox’s China division said organizers had “immediately” closed and disinfected affected areas and removed contaminated equipment. Wang said she had seen nothing “noticeably unusual” on the course.

Wietrzyk later posted an Instagram Story of herself receiving an intravenous infusion from what appeared to be a hospital. An accompanying caption read: “a win is a win.”

This drew further criticism from some Chinese social media users, who saw the remark as dismissive of concerns over other competitors’ health and safety.

Italian Hyrox pro-athlete Sara Gandola, who competed in the same race, told Sixth Tone that Wietrzyk should not be blamed for the incident.

Gandola said the responsibility of athletes is to perform at their highest level within the rules, while “it is the sport’s responsibility to set those rules and define what is acceptable.”

“If you disagree with the rules, debate the rules,” she said. “But attacking an athlete for doing exactly what elite athletes are supposed to do is completely backward.”

On Monday, Hyrox’s global headquarters issued a statement on Instagram, describing the incident as an “unforeseen situation” and adding that those who threatened its athletes would be permanently banned from future events.

However, Chinese social media users criticized their stance for not directly acknowledging failures in how it handled the incident at the time.

Later that day, Hyrox China admitted on Weibo that the incident exposed “shortcomings” in its competition rules and said it had proposed revisions to its global headquarters. The previous Hyrox rulebook imposes a two-minute penalty for littering, spitting, or blowing one’s nose onto the floor, but does not address fecal incontinence.

Hyrox China added that the venue’s carpets had been replaced and that the entire venue had been deep-cleaned overnight, pledging to disinfect both venues before future events and any shared equipment.

Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste also issued an apology via Instagram on Monday, admitting that “Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race.”

In a Sunday commentary, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said the incident highlighted a growing tension between the “rapid expansion” of commercial sporting events and “gaps in competition rules.”

Additional reporting: Xie Anran; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019025/The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.title: The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019025/The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.content:
A new Chinese dating app is betting that AI can do more than keep users chatting — it wagers it can see them married in three years or less.

If it fails, the team behind Liangpei — roughly “good match” in Chinese — promises to refund the user’s one-time fee of 2,000 yuan ($275). The guarantee comes as marriage rates fall in China, with only 6.76 million couples tying the knot in 2025, about half the number a decade earlier.

Launched this past July, Liangpei begins with a roughly 20-minute voice conversation with an AI matchmaker. Users answer 25 questions about their relationship history, marriage plans, and even whether they intend to buy property. The system then uses their answers to build a detailed profile, calculate compatibility scores, and recommend potential partners.

Once two people match, they can talk only until one decides to move on, a restriction the app’s developers say is intended to keep them focused on one relationship rather than constantly searching for alternatives.

“We want to get the users off the platform as soon as possible,” founder Zeng Xinxun told Sixth Tone.

Before launching Liangpei, the 32-year-old worked on AI search technology at Kimi, one of China’s best-known generative AI platforms. His 18-person team now uses similar technology to draw out information that basic dating-app tags such as age, occupation, and location cannot capture.

Approximately 91% of users who start Liangpei’s interview finish it, Zeng said, going on to create profiles averaging 516 Chinese characters, about four times as long as those on several major Chinese dating apps.

About one in 10 users has reached an exclusive one-on-one match, according to Zeng. Those conversations last more than 10 days on average and run to more than 200 messages.

“One-on-one allows both parties to invest more focus and effort into building a relationship,” Zeng said. “Even if it doesn’t work out, it’s a conclusion reached after genuine communication.”

So far, he said, Liangpei has more than 9,300 active users across 300 cities. Men account for 57% of users, and women 43%. The two largest age groups are 26 to 28 and 29 to 31.

China’s established dating and social platforms operate at a much larger scale. Tantan, one of the country’s oldest dating apps, had 10.7 million monthly active users in March 2025, while Soul draws large audiences with broader offerings that combine dating, social discovery, entertainment, and shared interests.

Liangpei also requires real-name registration, a marital status check, and live photo verification. The company has blocked 487 people found to be married, Zeng said. It also uses AI to watch for signs of fraud once conversations begin.

Wang, a Shanghai-based user who asked to be identified only by her surname for privacy reasons, has tried more than 10 dating apps. Liangpei was the first on which she was willing to answer so many questions.

“It has helped me understand myself better and clarified exactly what I’m looking for,” she said.

Within a week, Wang entered an exclusive one-on-one match. She said the format made online dating less exhausting and allowed her to focus on getting to know her counterpart. But with no other matches to turn to, the arrangement depended on that person keeping the conversation alive.

“Once matched, your slot is locked,” Wang said. “If the other person isn’t proactive, you’re left waiting with nowhere for the conversation to go.”

On Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, Liangpei has drawn sharply mixed reactions. Some users described it as a welcome option for people anxious about finding a spouse, while others questioned whether treating marriage as a fixed target made dating too rigid.

Free users can send only one “like” a day, according to posts reviewed by Sixth Tone. The app also prominently displays compatibility scores, which some users said made them more reluctant to start conversations.

Despite the compatibility score, several users admitted they still ended up judging potential partners by appearance.

Three-year itch

Six years ago, Zeng said he became frustrated trying to meet someone online — a period that lasted a year. He wrote a lengthy profile, but few people seemed to read it, and even fewer replied.

“Profiles were too bare to spark interest,” he said. Zeng eventually expanded his own to around 2,000 Chinese characters, then came across a woman whose profile was just as detailed.

“We quickly went from strangers to a close connection,” Zeng said. By the time they met in person, he thought the relationship might go somewhere.

They are now married. And Liangpei uses that same outcome as its measure of success.

His team had considered a first date or the start of a relationship instead. Marriage, Zeng said, was different: “It’s legally verifiable and undisputed.”

The three-year cutoff came after his team interviewed 150 couples obtaining marriage licenses at a civil affairs bureau in the southern city of Shenzhen. More than 70% said they had married within three years of meeting, Zeng said.

Liangpei has been operating for only a few months, so none of its users have yet to reach that deadline. For now, the company is reviewing the data it does have, including whether higher compatibility scores are associated with more likes, replies, and longer conversations.

“For example, among 1,500 users in Shenzhen, the AI can directly rank the top 10 people most likely to succeed with you,” Zeng said. “You don’t have to browse everyone — just start with the highest scores.”

To address relationship anxiety, Liangpei offers an “icebreaker” feature that suggests questions when a conversation stalls. An “AI wingman” can also analyze an exchange and offer advice.

But the “AI wingman” will not compose replies. Zeng said someone who struggles with online banter might still make a good partner in person, but AI should only carry early exchanges far enough for both people to find out.

Du Shichao, an assistant professor of sociology at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said Liangpei’s focus on marriage could appeal to people who already know what they are looking for. He also saw value in matching people using more than surface-level information.

“It may not address everyone’s pain points, but it can at least solve problems for some people and offer them more choice,” Du said.

But he was more cautious about AI taking on a larger role in relationships.

“This ‘enhancement’ can easily slide into ‘replacement,’” Du said. “When this kind of use is taken to an extreme, people need to be wary of ceding their capacity for emotional connection to technology.”

Whatever help an AI assistant can provide online, he said, people still have to learn about each other in person. “Ultimately, people must rediscover each other and themselves through real-world interaction.”

Du said technology may help with some of the difficulties individuals face in meeting and communicating with partners, but it cannot address the forces shaping marriage more broadly, including demographics, economic pressure, and family expectations.

“It may benefit some, but won’t significantly change China’s marriage patterns,” he said.

Zeng is making a more modest claim. “We don’t need to serve everyone,” he said. “We can’t help those with particularly poor prospects, or those with unrealistic expectations. If the people in between can find success in Liangpei, that’s good enough.”

Whether they do will become clear in 2029, when Liangpei’s first users reach the end of its three-year guarantee.

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019020/China Approves Obesity Drug for Severe Fatty Liver Disease
World.title: China Approves Obesity Drug for Severe Fatty Liver Disease
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019020/China Approves Obesity Drug for Severe Fatty Liver Disease
World.content:
China has approved the weight-loss drug Wegovy, a brand name for the medication semaglutide, to treat a severe form of fatty liver disease, making it the country’s first and only glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) drug approved for the condition.

The drug, approved Sept. 10 by the National Medical Products Administration, covers adults with moderate to advanced liver damage from metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) — the result of inflammation caused by excess fat — but no cirrhosis, or permanent scarring.

The move comes as obesity drugs become more widely available internationally and growing competition pushes drugmakers to differentiate products to treat a broader spectrum of diseases.

China has one of the world’s largest burdens of fatty liver disease, affecting about one in three adults and over 80% of people with obesity. An estimated 6.7% of Chinese adults have MASH, the disease’s more severe form, and may not qualify for GLP-1 drugs under previous weight-management indications.

The share of global liver cancer cases caused by MASH is forecast to rise from 8% to 11% by 2050, according to a report by the Lancet Commission on liver cancer published last year.

Effective drug options for fatty liver disease have long been limited, with treatment until now largely dependent on patients making lifestyle changes, Jia Jidong, director of the Liver Research Center at Beijing Friendship Hospital, told domestic media. He added that approval of the drug could help to raise public awareness of fatty liver disease, as the illness can be “silent and asymptomatic” in its earlier stages.

Semaglutide was originally developed to treat diabetes but has become widely used for weight management in recent years. It does so by mimicking the hormone GLP-1, released in response to eating, binding to the hormone’s receptors and suppressing appetite.

The medication is sold by Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk as Ozempic for diabetes and at a higher dose as Wegovy primarily for weight management. Wegovy was approved in China for weight management in June 2024.

The latest approval was based on a trial involving 1,197 MASH patients with moderate-to-advanced liver scarring. About two-thirds of patients who took semaglutide saw their MASH resolve, while slightly more than a third experienced reductions in liver scarring.

Other drugmakers are also exploring GLP-1 medications as potential treatments for fatty liver disease, with Chinese regulators fast-tracking approval for U.S. pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in January.

Chinese biotech firm Innovent Biologics has also reported fatty liver reduction with its drug mazdutide, which was approved in the country for weight management last year.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019019/A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.title: A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019019/A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.content:
Thanks to years of ecological restoration, endangered Oriental storks have been expanding their range around Gaoyou Lake in the eastern Jiangsu province. In recent months, dozens have descended on crab farmer Hu Dingsong’s ponds, bringing him online fame — and huge economic losses.

Hu first spotted two or three storks in April. After learning they were a nationally first-class protected species, he was delighted. “I even joked online that my pond had crabs to spare,” he said.

But the numbers quickly grew: over 20 by mid-May, to more than 40 by early June, to their present numbers of around 80. Hu estimates that the birds collectively eat roughly 2,400 crabs a day, costing him 30,000 to 40,000 yuan ($4,200-$5,600) daily. His agricultural insurance does not cover wildlife damage.

Forestry officials have also banned Hu from using firecrackers to drive the birds away, as they are a protected species. Netting such large ponds is also impractical, and offering the birds other food sources — such as fish — introduces disease risks, leaving him with little recourse.

Lu Changhu, a wildlife ecology professor at Nanjing Forestry University, said storks staying in the province during summer is not new. Once mainly winter visitors, more have begun staying around Gaoyou Lake and nearby wetlands as their population has grown. Some may skip migration when food is plentiful, he said.

Local officials have provided Hu with a drone to monitor the flock and are helping address his losses, but farmers currently lack official channels to pursue compensation for wildlife damage.

Hu is now urging authorities to work with farmers on solutions that protect both the birds and their livelihoods.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019013/Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.title: Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019013/Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.content:
A mobile game beloved by millions of Chinese users about a traveling frog is set to shut down after the game operator and the IP holder failed to reach a licensing agreement.

Announced Tuesday by its official account on microblogging platform Weibo, the game, Travel Frog: China Journey, will discontinue on Dec. 8.

“This time, the little frog is going on a long journey, with no set date of return,” the announcement read. “But that quiet companionship will always remain in our hearts.”

A video game insider told domestic media that the IP holder, Japanese gaming studio Hit-Point, sought harsher terms from domestic operator Lingxi Games, including stripping it of its right to collaborate with other companies and sell game-related merchandise. After multiple rounds of negotiations, the companies could not reach an agreement, though the insider disclosed that they are in a final round of talks.

Travel Frog, released in 2017, is an idle game, meaning gameplay progresses with little player input. Chinese users began downloading the Japanese version before tech giant Alibaba secured authorization to publish it exclusively in the Chinese mainland under its gaming division, Lingxi Games, a year later. By then, the original version was already popular, with iOS downloads in China alone exceeding 30 million.

At its peak, the game was more popular than the domestic, Tencent-produced game Honour of Kings, topping the domestic App Store free chart. Lingxi Games was acquired by the private equity firm Trustar Capital in August this year.

In Travel Frog: China Journey, the protagonist, a frog who lives alone in a cave, passes its days reading, writing in its diary, eating, and whittling wood. It also travels around China, such as to the Great Wall in Beijing and West Lake in the eastern city of Hangzhou. While on the road, it meets fellow animal travelers, brings back local specialties, and sends home postcards, which devoted users post on WeChat.

After learning that the game would be discontinued, a graduate student in Shanghai surnamed Fang spent a day trying to redownload it. She had played since her first year of university but hadn’t reinstalled the game after changing phones, not thinking it would shut down permanently.

“(I will have to) think of it as a child growing up and setting off on a new journey — a solo trip where the parents don’t need to worry anymore,” Fang said. “I really loved my frog … It felt like a real little baby.”

Another player, surnamed Wang, in the southern city of Guangzhou, first tried the game’s Japanese version in 2018. The frog’s ability to travel, rest, and meet friends whenever it wanted — moved her, as she said that adult life is all about KPIs, responsibilities, and pressure.

When she learned the game would be taken offline, Wang told Sixth Tone that she was devastated. “This isn’t just a game,” she said. “It’s a second life.”

Online, some called the move the “tears of an era,” a Chinese internet slang term referring to something that evokes a strong sense of nostalgia. Others lamented that their “youth is over,” or said they could not bear to delete the game, hoping it might one day be restored.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot from Travel Frog: China Journey. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.title: She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.content:
Chang Shana, one of China’s most treasured artists, is sitting on her living room sofa in Beijing, her eyes fixed on a TV documentary about Dunhuang, the northwestern oasis city where she spent much of her childhood. When a familiar face appears on screen, the 95-year-old breaks into a broad smile.

“That’s my father,” she says, pointing out Chang Shuhong, an accomplished painter best known for his research on the ancient Buddhist murals at the Mogao Grottoes.

Alzheimer’s disease, the most common cause of dementia, has robbed Chang Shana of most memories, yet her face still lights up the moment anyone mentions Dunhuang.

“Apart from Dunhuang, her family, and the caregivers who attend to her day and night, my mother has largely forgotten the people and things outside her immediate world,” says her son, Cui Donghui.

Gone are her memories of studying under world-renowned masters, of her mother walking out on the family, of helping design state gifts and landmark buildings like Beijing’s Great Hall of the People and the Cultural Palace of Nationalities, of losing her beloved husband, and of her tenure as the longest-serving president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, now Tsinghua University’s Academy of Arts and Design.

On a desk in her bedroom is “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” which compiles 328 color illustrations of cave murals and sculptures from various periods. “I drew this book. It’s all decorative motifs,” says Chang, standing up. After catching her breath, she points out another book: “This one, ‘Dunhuang! My Father’s Call,’ was written by my father, but I contributed many of the illustrations and written materials.”

Would she like to return to Dunhuang one day? “Yes,” she replies in a soft voice, without hesitation. Then, she slowly wanders back to the sofa to continue watching her documentary.

Life on the move

Chang Shana was born in Lyon, France, in 1931. Her father was among China’s first generation of French-trained artists, and both her parents went on to attend the prestigious Beaux-Arts de Paris school.

After being moved by a photobook about the Mogao Grottoes that he discovered in a secondhand book stall beside the Seine, Chang’s father returned to China alone in 1936 to head the fine arts department at the National Art School in Beiping, predecessor of Beijing’s Central Academy of Fine Arts.

However, as invading Japanese troops advanced toward Beijing, he was forced to flee, eventually moving with the academy to Nanjing in the eastern Jiangsu province — where he was joined by his wife, Chen Zhixiu, and daughter — and then to the southwestern city of Chongqing, which served as the nation’s wartime capital during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression. In 1943, the family relocated again to Dunhuang in the northwestern Gansu province, where Chang Shuhong was appointed director of the National Dunhuang Art Research Institute.

Chang Shana found it difficult adjusting to their austere life among the arid dunes. In her 2013 memoir, “Yellow Sands and Blue Sky,” the artist recalls that first winter night, eating cold noodles with only salt and vinegar, and her father promising, “Things will get better.”

Yet despite the lack of material comforts, she instantly found an abundance of inspiration at the Mogao Grottoes. On days without school, she would walk the dirt roads, past the shimmering poplars, and climb into the grottoes to copy the murals. “I loved going into the caves to draw. I was always eager to do it. My parents never had to tell me to go,” she wrote. She would also chat with the many visiting artists and scholars, laying a strong foundation for her artistic development.

Previously, students had typically copied the murals with tracing paper, which they secured to the walls with thumbtacks, leaving tiny holes. Chang Shuhong prohibited this practice to prevent further damage to the relics, meaning his daughter had to recreate the originals stroke by stroke through observation alone. Although laborious, it helped her develop extraordinary levels of precision.

But the desert took as much as it gave. Under the strain of his responsibilities, Chang Shuhong was often irritable, and his relationship with his wife became fractious. She eventually left him and moved back east in 1945.

Chang Shana was 14. She dropped out of school and stayed home to help with the housework and to knit sweaters for her 4-year-old brother.

That same year, the Nationalist government ordered the Dunhuang Art Research Institute to close. As funding dwindled and workers left, Chang Shuhong traveled extensively to enlist fresh support, eventually recruiting a group of teachers and students from art academies in Chongqing and Chengdu, capital of the neighboring Sichuan province.

With the institute’s future secured, he instructed his daughter to make copies of representative murals covering various Chinese dynasties. In her memoir, Chang recalls her work to recreate the figures of warriors from the Western Wei dynasty (535–556): “The lines followed my feelings; my brushwork was especially free and expressive.”

Finding faith

When Chang turned 17, a Canadian friend of the family sponsored her to study in the United States at what is today Tufts University’s School of the Museum of Fine Arts. There, she took classes in drawing, anatomy, art history, perspective, color, painting, and design.

Although confident in French, she initially struggled with some of the highly specialized English terminology. What baffled her most, though, was the painting course. With abstract expressionism on the rise, her professors required students to create work without recognizable forms or subjects. In a letter to her father, she wrote, “Perhaps I just don’t understand.”

According to her son, Chang’s diary entries from the early 1940s are filled with confusion and unease. She occupied her time with sketching and knitting, often questioning the meaning behind such pursuits. Yet her letters home in 1950 reveal “a completely different person,” he says.

In one, she wrote about “finally finding faith,” and expounded on her belief that art should be accessible and serve the people. In other letters, she displayed a weariness with life overseas. “Staying here, depending on others for everything, life feels so empty,” she wrote. “I have a perpetual sense that something is missing, like I owe a debt.”

Chang returned to China in December 1950 without completing her degree. She immediately began helping her father organize an exhibition of Dunhuang cultural relics in Beijing, featuring copies of murals she and several art researchers had made.

The following year, she was introduced to the influential architects Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin, who agreed to recommend her for a teaching assistant position at Tsinghua University’s School of Architecture. Under Lin’s guidance, she and two other students applied traditional cloisonné enamelwork techniques and motifs to everyday items such as table lamps, cigarette cases, and plates.

With a growing portfolio, Chang was commissioned to design themed gifts for the 1952 Asia and Pacific Rim Peace Conference, held in Beijing. She created a silk headscarf and large cloisonné plate with peace dove motifs, inspired by Dunhuang cave paintings from the Sui dynasty (581–618).

When China began reforming its university system in the early 1950s, she transferred to the Department of Applied Arts at the Central Academy of Fine Arts before ultimately joining the Central Academy of Arts and Design in 1956.

Gone too soon

Chang met her first husband while studying in the U.S. The couple married in China in 1953 but divorced after just a few years. The artist barely mentions this time in her memoir, not even naming him.

Her second husband, Cui Taishan, was a Japanese-language interpreter. They met while part of a Chinese cultural delegation to Japan in 1961 and were married two years later, spending 26 years together until Cui’s death in 1989.

The artist’s friend, Huang Xuanzi, recalls that Chang often talked to her late husband’s photo before she developed dementia. “She’d grumble at him for leaving her too soon, then turn to me and say, ‘Look at him, always smiling at me like that,’” she says, adding that Chang still sometimes recognizes him in photographs. “One day, she suddenly smiled and said to me, ‘Cui Taishan was very handsome.’”

Huang recalls a thick stack of flower studies Chang had painted when she was pregnant, each accompanied by a short poem handwritten by her husband. “They were never published, so almost no one outside the family knows about them,” she explains. “You can clearly feel the depth of their affection in those paintings and poems.”

In 1983, Chang was appointed president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, leaving her less time for family. Around the same time, Cui was diagnosed with diabetes and then liver cancer. Even during his final days, she was unable to stay with him full time, yet he would always reassure her, “You go ahead with your work. I’m fine.” He was just 62 when he died.

The artist struggled to cope with the combination of grief and work stress. “There were photos of her husband everywhere in the house,” says her sister-in-law, Wang Fulan. “She would always say, ‘He left us too soon. He was so young.’ She felt that she had devoted herself entirely to her work and left household matters to her husband, and that was what had worn him down.”

In later years, Chang told a friend: “I have done right by everyone and everything in my life. My father Chang Shuhong wanted me to carry on the cultural legacy of Dunhuang, and I spent my life doing so. Lin Huiyin mentored me to become a designer, and I devoted myself to that career. The only person I failed was my husband, Cui Taishan.”

Forever home

Shortly after losing her husband, Chang’s father was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. His condition remained largely stable until he took a serious fall at age 92. After that, his memory began deteriorating rapidly, and he passed away two years later in 1994.

Huang says Chang Shana was also healthy and mentally sharp until her early 90s. She might forget small things, but a little prompting was enough to bring her back.

During the pandemic, her son Cui Donghui couldn’t visit in person; he could see her only through the security camera installed at her home. When he checked late at night, he often saw her lying alone on the sofa watching television. When he was finally able to return, she opened the door, looked at him, and said, “Who are you?”

Leafing through his mother’s book, “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” he proudly remarks, “This is her life’s work. She systematically cataloged the motifs from different periods and defined their evolutionary progression. This foundational body of work is still essential today, whether for research or for the development of cultural products.”

All the detailed illustrations inside were completed during a special trip Chang took to the Mogao Grottoes in 1959 with two colleagues. For the artist, it was a joyous return to the place she once called home.

“We were young then,” she wrote in her memoir. “We rode horses and camels, climbed the Singing Sand Dunes barefoot, and had an absolutely wonderful time.”

At 95, the journey to Dunhuang is impossible. Yet smiling at that flickering TV screen, she is already back among the caves. The memories are gone, but the patterns remain.

This article, reported by Li Mei, edited by Peng Wei, originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019014/Pizza Bao, Spaghetti Stir-Fry: Chinese Students Hack Home Cooking Abroad
World.title: Pizza Bao, Spaghetti Stir-Fry: Chinese Students Hack Home Cooking Abroad
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019014/Pizza Bao, Spaghetti Stir-Fry: Chinese Students Hack Home Cooking Abroad
World.content:
Liu Zhenchao stands at a kitchen counter in Germany, filming himself making baozi, or Chinese steamed buns.

The 27-year-old student from Hefei, capital of China’s eastern Anhui province, chops onions and minces beef for the filling, then seasons it and mixes it by hand in a bowl.

But when it comes time to make the dough, he suddenly reaches for a cardboard box from a local supermarket.

Inside is a sheet of premade pizza dough.

“Both pizza dough and traditional baozi dough rely on yeast to ferment,” Liu told Sixth Tone, slicing the dough into neat rounds. “It allows the dough to expand, whether you steam it or bake it.”

Liu’s pizza dough baozi hack soon struck a chord with Chinese students abroad. Viewers called him a “genius,” marveling at a shortcut that eliminated the need to make dough from scratch and cut preparation time in half.

Like Liu, a growing number of Chinese students studying abroad are turning cooking videos into viral hits across Chinese social media. On Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, the hashtag “international students hunong cooking” — using the term “to do something halfheartedly” — has amassed 2.1 billion views.

The trend dates back to March this year, when a Chinese student in Italy posted a video on how to make gong jin bao dan, or crispy-fried eggs coated with a sweet-and-sour sauce. His recipe tutorial video went viral, garnering more than 2 million likes and triggering a wave of netizens to attempt the dish and share their results online.

Chinese students are the largest overseas student population in the world, with over 570,600 Chinese going abroad in 2025 alone, according to China’s Ministry of Education.

For these students, improvised dishes from back home made with whatever ingredients they can find have become a category of their own, jokingly dubbed the country’s “ninth cuisine” after its eight official regional cuisines.

Comfort food

Liu traces his love of cooking to his childhood, when he spent hours watching cooking programs on TV.

When he arrived in Germany in October 2020 to pursue a master’s in engineering economics, it was only natural that he began cooking his own meals to cut costs; a meal at the school cafeteria cost 6 euros on average, but cooking at home kept his expenses below 5 euros, he said.

The choice was not only about saving money. Liu grew up with dishes known for their rich sauces, bold flavors, and vibrant colors.

The novelty of Western foods quickly wore off after he arrived. “The longer I stayed abroad, the more I found myself craving the familiar tastes of home,” Liu said. “Common Chinese dishes like stir-fried shredded potatoes with green peppers just suit my taste better than cheese and steak.”

Recreating those same flavors, however, was not easy. With many key ingredients unavailable in German supermarkets, he learned to improvise, replacing familiar ingredients from home with local ones. In one recipe, he uses Italian spaghetti in place of Chinese noodles, stir-frying it with green peppers and pork.

For Liu, cooking also had to fit around the intense pressure of studying. During exam periods, he would study from around 9 a.m. until midnight, so cooking had to be quick and simple, while also tasty and authentic.

“Good food is important to me,” Liu said. “During exam periods, when the pressure is already so high, if the food doesn’t turn out well, I feel like I have nothing to look forward to that day.”

When he launched his Douyin account in 2024, he initially wanted just to capture his everyday life abroad. But as he shared more of his life overseas, cooking gradually took center stage.

“I found that cooking is what resonates most with viewers online,” Liu said. He has since attracted more than 780,000 followers.

“Such content also has a particularly powerful sensory appeal,” Hu Zhiwen, a critical food studies scholar with a Ph.D. from the University of Georgia, told Sixth Tone. Images of cooking can trigger memories of smell, taste, and texture, which resonate strongly with audiences, he said.

Food has also become a way for Liu to connect with his contemporaries abroad. He often invites local friends over to try his cooking, including the baozi he made with store-bought pizza dough.

“They found it magical because store-bought pizza dough is something they’ve seen all their lives, yet no one had thought to use it this way,” Liu said. “Some even tried making them at home.”

The food sometimes gives his friends ideas for innovating foods from their own cultures, too. His Italian friends, for example, compared Chinese dumplings to their own filled pastas.

Cooking can offer overseas students a path to independence, emotional comfort, and cross-cultural connection, Hu, the food scholar, noted. “When you are in a new environment, there is a natural desire to seek out things that make life feel more familiar.”

In China, where food is deeply woven into everyday life and regional cuisines offer enormous variety, cooking can be more than a practical necessity, Hu added.

“Chinese students will be particularly drawn to cooking when they move to places where the food culture is markedly different from what they grew up with,” he said.

For Chen Wan’er, cooking abroad was a different kind of challenge. She had barely cooked before leaving China, but after a month in the UK, she was making almost all of her meals herself — and not only for the economic benefits.

In a new country, seven hours away from her family and friends and with no close connections, cooking gave her days meaning and shape. Even when a dish didn’t turn out perfectly, she enjoyed the satisfaction of making something from scratch.

Chen began filming her cooking and posting it on China’s lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, but unlike Liu, she maintains a small audience of roughly 1,000 followers. Initially, she saw the account as a way to give her parents a window into her new life abroad, letting them glimpse her daily routine and easing their worries about how she was doing.

Her parents were surprised when they saw a video she posted of herself making mian geda tang, a northern Chinese homestyle dish of small pieces of dough cooked in soup. Chen grew up in the eastern Chinese city of Wenzhou, where noodles were not part of her family’s cooking tradition and flour was rarely bought. Now, living alone in Britain, she taught herself to make a dish she had never cooked before.

Away from home, Chen has discovered that she actually enjoys cooking without worrying about getting everything right. At home, she was often hesitant to cook with her mother nearby, reminding her not to make a mess.

“Here, I can just let myself go with no one watching over me. The fact that I can feed myself is already good enough,” Chen said. “I don’t have to worry about whether the kitchen is messy.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Screenshots from Liu's cooking videos on Xiaohongshu.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019007/Top-Ranked Chinese Netflix Series Divides Viewers at Home
World.title: Top-Ranked Chinese Netflix Series Divides Viewers at Home
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019007/Top-Ranked Chinese Netflix Series Divides Viewers at Home
World.content:
Chinese romantic drama “The Early Spring,” an adaptation of a 2021 web novel, has become the highest-ranked Chinese series on streaming giant Netflix’s weekly non-English TV chart. However, the show has divided domestic viewers over whether it romanticizes an unhealthy power imbalance between its protagonists: a male boss and his female subordinate.

The TV series, which premiered Aug. 26 on both Netflix and Chinese streaming platform Youku, follows the workplace romance between demanding advertising agency corporate executive Luan “Luke” Nian, played by Jing Boran, and 22-year-old newcomer Shang “Flora” Zhitao, played by Sun Qian.

After a drunken encounter, the two begin a secret relationship. Over time, Shang advances in her career, while Luan’s harsh and arrogant demeanor softens.

“The Early Spring” ranked No. 2 on Netflix’s global weekly chart for non-English TV series from Aug. 24 to 30, garnering 2.4 million views. The series also made Netflix’s weekly Top 10 in 22 markets, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brazil, and ranked No. 1 in Thailand and Vietnam.

In China, the series recorded 547 million views and topped domestic entertainment data platform Maoyan’s weekly popularity ranking on Sept. 7.

Many domestic social media users praised the chemistry and sexual tension between the two leads — developed with the help of an intimacy coordinator, a role still relatively uncommon in Chinese television, according to the show’s producers.

Liu, a viewer in her 30s who works in the arts in Shanghai, said that the show’s appeal lies in its escapism via a “straightforward” romance.

“It’s simply: I like you, so I like you,” Liu told Sixth Tone, in reference to the show’s driving sentiment. “Physical attraction is unavoidable.” Unlike many Chinese romance dramas that typically withhold physical intimacy between their leads, she added, “The Early Spring” brings Luan and Shang together almost immediately.

Liu also praised the 24-episode TV adaptation for bringing more warmth to its relationships. She said that compared with the original work, published under the pen name Guniang Bieku on the literature platform Jinjiang, the TV series more clearly establishes Luan and Shang as two people in love rather than primarily a sexual relationship. It also fleshes out Shang’s friendships, giving her a stronger support network.

Critics, however, have questioned whether Luan exploits his workplace authority to pursue Shang, pointing to scenes where he belittles her professional abilities. For example, when he suspects she is considering another job, he describes her as “cheap” and “obedient.”

Xu Xin, a 29-year-old media professional based in Beijing, said she agreed with much of the criticism, particularly over the couple’s first sexual encounter. “Imagine this happening in real life: a young woman fresh out of college gets drunk, and her sober male supervisor takes her home and has sex with her. That’s problematic,” she told Sixth Tone. “Even if they are attracted to each other, did it have to happen that night, when she was drunk?”

“It feels like a female fantasy,” she added. “In male-oriented fantasies, the protagonist turns his life around by becoming rich or powerful. Here, the fantasy is that a woman starts invisible, works her way up and becomes ‘better’ — and then the man comes back for her.”

For her, the series also reflects how messy real relationships can be. “People aren’t always rational, nor can they always live up to their own feminist ideals.”

The power-dynamic debate has extended to the web novel the series is based on. In it, after Shang quits her job and starts her own business, she initially decides to hire only men. The TV adaptation omits this plotline, which some had previously criticized as “discriminatory.”

Two prominent female influencers — Zhan Qingyun and Pang Ying, who are known for discussing gender equality issues in China — have also faced criticism after promoting the show.

In a Sept. 6 video posted on domestic lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, the two discussed the show, arguing that a good relationship “does not require two people to be perfect from the beginning” but can involve “two imperfect people growing together.” The video was later taken down.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A still from “The Early Spring.” From Douban)

World.title: Basilan vice governor’s son takes 4th District seat in BARMM Parliament
World.content:
JOINING THE RACE. Jay Hataman Salliman files his certificate of candidacy for the position of 4th District representative of Basilan to the Bangsamoro Parliament on May 5, 2026.

Jimael Salam Datumanong Salliman, better known as Jay Hataman Salliman, is also a lawyer and former Basilan provincial board member

MANILA, Philippines – Another Hataman is assured of a high-ranking seat representing Basilan province, this time as the province’s 4th District representative to the Bangsamoro Parliament.

Jimael Salam Datumanong Salliman, better known as Jay Hataman Salliman, is the son of Vice Governor Jim Hataman Salliman. Salliman topped the Basilan 4th District representative race during the 2026 Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) parliamentary elections on Monday, September 14.

The 29-year-old lawyer and former Basilan provincial board member obtained 41,675 or 81.51% of the votes. This is based on Basilan’s certificates of canvass from the Commission on Elections’ website.

He ran under the Bangsamoro Federalist Party alongside his relative Abrar Hataman, who won his bid for representative in Basilan’s 3rd District.

Salliman won by a landslide over four other candidates.

Coming in second is Alzad Sattar, who chairs the Bangsamoro Peoples Party and is a former member of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament. He got 8,364 or 16.36% of the votes.

Next is Bangsamoro Party candidate Monar Ibno, who placed third with 562 or 1.1% of the votes.

Moro Islamic Liberation Front Joint Action Group leader Omar Gapor Muallam came in fourth place, with 424 or 0.83% of the votes. He ran under the MILF’s political party, the United Justice Bangsamoro Party.

In last place is Bangsamoro Empowerment and Social Transformation Party candidate and Lantawan resident Pendatun Mohamad, with 101 or 0.2% of the votes.

As the winning candidate for Basilan 4th District representative, Hataman will serve a special five-year transition term from October 30, 2026 to June 30, 2031. He will be one of the 32 district representatives making up 40% of the 80-seat Bangsamoro Parliament.

Basilan was the last province to transmit its certificates of canvassing after pre-shaded ballots were found in Maluso town on Monday. This prompted the Commission on Elections to place the town under its control and delayed the start of voting there to Tuesday, September 15.

The 32,000 registered voters in the municipality make up half of the 67,000 from the 4th District. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sara Duterte declared businesses but not value of stocks | The wRap
World.content:
Here are today’s headlines – the latest news in the Philippines and around the world:

The prosecution in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial seeks to establish… she did not declare the value of her new business stocks despite being listed in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth or SALN through the years.

Mastura: 3 biggest BARMM parties should form coalition

World.title: Remembering Eggie Apostol, purveyor of truth, independence
World.content:
'Eugenia Apostol’s passing marks the end of an era, but her legacy endures in every journalist who continues to defend truth, independence, and the people’s right to know,' the UP College of Mass Communication writes

MANILA, Philippines – As the Filipino journalism community mourns the passing of Eugenia “Eggie” Apostol, the late veteran’s peers are choosing to remember her for her fierce stance on truth and the freedom to do powerful reportage.

Apostol, a renowned publisher and veteran journalist, founded the Philippine Daily Inquirer in 1985, just a few months shy of the 1986 People Power Revolution. She was well-known in the world of the “mosquito press” — newspapers and media outlets that were vocal about their criticism toward Ferdinand E. Marcos and his dictatorship.

According to Marixi Prieto, the former chair of the Philippine Daily Inquirer’s board of directors, Apostol had always been known to stand up for reporters, editors, and their work when it came to doing hard-hitting reportage. “Those moments captured so much of who she was — strong, principled, courageous, and unwavering in what she believed was right.”

“Eggie was a woman of extraordinary strength and courage, someone I had the privilege of knowing. She built the Inquirer on a foundation of truth and independence and fiercely protected those values through the years,” Prieto said in her statement.

Apostol, who died at 100, was the first-ever awardee of the Gawad Plaridel, the highest honor the University of the Philippines confers to media practitioners who strive to make a difference in their line of work and contribute to shaping the Philippine media landscape.

“Eugenia Apostol’s passing marks the end of an era, but her legacy endures in every journalist who continues to defend truth, independence, and the people’s right to know. She is survived by her family, colleagues, and generations of media practitioners who carry forward her vision of fearless journalism,” the UP College of Mass Communication said in its statement.

She was the publisher of Mr. & Ms. Special Edition, a weekly tabloid that would carry reports against the Marcos administration.

“MR. & MS. became our Facebook or our social media when it was not there yet, so the Filipino people will know the TRUTH about our country and more about our aspirations for our people and our country,” wrote the August Twenty-One Movement, a civil rights group established after the assassination of former president Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr.

In 1999, Apostol would then go on to establish Pinoy Times, another tabloid that would publish exposés about then-president Joseph “Erap” Estrada’s administration.

“I join the many mourning the passing of Eggy Apostol who came into the lives of people like me through Mr. & Ms. And then the Inquirer. She very kindly asked me to join her venture, the Pinoy Times where I wrote a column in Filipino. When the country needed fighting journalism, she was there,” historian and veteran writer Manolo Quezon shared.

Historian Xiao Chua, meanwhile, lauded Apostol for her work at Mr. & Ms. Special Edition, PDI, and the Pinoy Times Special Edition, and her overall dedication to press freedom and democracy.

“Nagpakita ng tapang at malayang pamamahayag bilang saligan ng kapayapaan at demokrasya. Paalam po (She showed that courage and freedom of the press are the foundation of peace and democracy. Farewell),” Chua said about Apostol in a Facebook tribute.

Hailing from Sorsogon, Apostol received the Ramon Magsaysay Award for Journalism, Literature and Creative Communication Arts in 2006.

In 1948, she completed her journalism degree at the University of Santo Tomas, where she graduated magna cum laude. She was also the editor of the women’s sections of The Manila Times and The Manila Chronicle. – Rappler.com

World.title: DOJ subpoenas Robin Padilla over Bato dela Rosa escape
World.content:
SENATOR. Senator-judge Robin Padilla questions National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 22, 2026.

The senator is directed to appear before state prosecutors on September 25 and October 9 at the Department of Justice headquarters

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Justice (DOJ) has issued a subpoena to Senator Robin Padilla over an obstruction of justice complaint filed against him for his alleged role in Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa‘s escape from the Senate.

“The Department confirms that subpoenas were served on Sen. Robinhood Padilla and Lt. Col. Jean Alla Yasin Robles at around 2:30 pm today at the Senate, in connection with the pending complaint against them for alleged violation of PD 1829 (Obstruction of Justice),” DOJ spokesperson Raphael Martinez said.

Play Video

Based on the subpoena, Padilla was directed to appear before state prosecutors on September 25 and October 9 at the DOJ headquarters in Ermita, Manila.

Rappler reached out to Padilla for comment, but he has yet to respond as of this writing. He seemingly alluded to the subpoena in an earlier Facebook post.

“A subpoena has arrived,” his post read.

Dela Rosa escape

In May, the DOJ’s National Prosecution Service confirmed that the police had referred an obstruction of justice complaint against Padilla and other individuals for allegedly “facilitating” Dela Rosa’s escape from the Senate.

It can be recalled that Dela Rosa initially went into hiding to evade an International Criminal Court warrant over his alleged crimes against humanity in connection with former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs and the Davao Death Squad killings.

He reappeared on May 11 to back Senator Alan Peter Cayetano’s bid for Senate presidency and sought refuge inside the Senate. However, he left the premises on May 14, hours after a shooting incident inside the Senate, and has remained out of public view.

Padilla was named a person of interest by the National Bureau of Investigation on May 15 after it was revealed that Dela Rosa had left the Senate compound with him at around 2:30 am on May 14.

On May 22, the lawmaker said his ally had merely asked him for a ride and that Dela Rosa got off somewhere in Makati City, where a vehicle was already waiting for the former Philippine National Police chief. – Rappler.com

World.title: Poa: Defense has ‘strategy’ to address questions on Duterte SALNs
World.content:
ARRAIGNED. Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City RTC on September 11, 2026, to attend arraignment proceedings for her grave threats case.

The defense questions whether Ombudsman records division OIC Karen Batu was in a position to testify on alleged irregularities in Duterte's SALNs

MANILA, Philippines– The defense counsel of Vice President Sara Duterte questioned on Tuesday, September 15, the competence of an official of the Office of the Ombudsman to testify on alleged irregularities in the Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs) of the country’s second-highest official.

On Day 25 of the impeachment trial, defense lawyer Justin Nicol Gular underscored that Ombudsman records division officer-in-charge (OIC) Karen Batu has no personal knowledge of the contents of Duterte’s SALNs including her personal properties, liabilities, net worths, and disclosures of business interests and financial connections.

Batu also has no personal knowledge whether or not there were irregularities, unusual entries, or errors in Duterte’s records, he added.

“In testifying in today’s trial, you cannot conclude whether the Vice President has or does not have ill-gotten wealth,” said Gular.

The prosecution swiftly objected, saying “it was clear from the very start that the witness was only testifying based on the [Ombudsman’s] records.”

“We’ve been fair with the witness in our direct [examination] only asking her to that,” private prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim Alih said.

Duterte’s financial records were scrutinized during the trial, with prosecutors presenting her SALNs from 2007 to 2025. The defense initially objected to the presentation, explaining that she was not an impeachable officer prior to 2022. Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero, however, allowed the presentation, citing the need to establish a baseline.

“The Chair would like to remind counsel for the respondent of the ruling of the Chair with respect to the issuance of the subpoenas covering the period 2007 up to 2025, that pursuant to OMB, Office of the Ombudsman vs. Bernardo GR No. 181598 dated March 2013, there is a necessity to establish the baseline, not for the prosecution but equally for the respondent, in order to find out what is the base figure for the computation of the SALN during her term,” Escudero said.

Defense spokesperson Michael Poa, in a press briefing, said Batu was not the proper witness to interpret the SALNs, adding she was called to testify to identify Duterte’s SALNs that were in the custody of the Ombudsman. He also said the defense will present a strategy, during their presentation of evidence, to address questions on the SALNs.

“We have our strategy on that matter, actually. Because obviously, I will not, without disclosing the specifics, I will also not deny na siyempre, napag-isipan na ng depensa kung paano natin gagawin yan at ipapaliwanag ang mga bagay-bagay,” Poa said.

(We have our strategy on that matter, actually. Because obviously, I will not, without disclosing the specifics, I will also not deny that we have already formulated ways on how we will explain the SALNs.)

“Meron naman kaming mga naisip na paraan at estratehiya… Asahan niyo na lang po at abangan niyo na lang po ‘pag kami naman ang nag-present ng ebidensya kung sakaling may mga kailangan ipaliwanag doon sa mga nakalagay,” he added.

(We thought of ways and strategies. We will show that to the public during our turn to present evidence.)

Amici curiae

In a related development, the Senate impeachment court is now preparing for the presentation of the amici curiae, or “friends of the court” on Wednesday, September 16.

The impeachment court has tapped four retired Supreme Court (SC) justices to provide guidance on the resolution of the voting threshold for Duterte’s trial. They are: retired Chief Justices Artemio V. Panganiban, Reynato S. Puno, Hilario G. Davide Jr., and retired Associate Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna.

Panganiban, Puno, and Azcuna will physically attend the presentation while Davide will submit an advisory to be read before the court.

RELATED STORY: ‘Amici curiae’: Where do invited ex-justices stand on conviction threshold debate?

Each senator-judges will be provided five minutes to pose a question to the retired SC justices. Following their presentation, an oral argument between the defense and prosecution panels on the matter will be held on September 23, with each side given 15 minutes to present its position.

Senator-judges are expected to cast their votes on the voting threshold issue on the same day. – Rappler.com

World.title: Poland seeks new defense deals with Philippines
World.content:
Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Wladyslaw Bartoszewsk says Poland is investing nearly $50 billion for its defense industry and could sell military hardware abroad, including to the Philippines

MANILA, Philippines – Poland is seeking new defense partnerships with the Philippines, a senior foreign ministry official said on Tuesday, September 15, after completing the delivery of Black Hawk helicopters to Manila last month.

Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Wladyslaw Bartoszewski, who was in Manila for annual political consultations with the Philippines, said Poland is investing nearly $50 billion for its defense industry and could sell military hardware abroad, including to the Philippines.

Bartoszewski said Poland could sell both reconnaissance and fighting drones, radar equipment, anti-aircraft missiles and armored personnel carriers. A Philippine military delegation recently visited Poland to look into equipment that Manila can buy, he said.

The Philippines acquired 32 S-70i Black Hawk helicopters from Polish Sikorsky subsidiary PZL Mielec in a deal worth P32 billion ($509.60 million) in 2022. The delivery of the last seven helicopters was completed last month, the Philippine military said.

Bartoszewski said separately talks were ongoing between Ukraine and Poland for the transfer of Warsaw’s MiG-29 fighter jets in exchange for drone technology from Kyiv.

Bartoszewski said the two sides are discussing whether to refurbish the jets before transferring them to Ukraine as well as the kind of technology Warsaw gets in return.

Poland has been one of Ukraine’s strongest backers since Russia began its full-scale invasion in 2022, providing military aid and serving as a ​key logistics hub for Western assistance.

– Rappler.com

($1 = P62.7940)

(Reporting by Mikhail Flores; Editing by Martin Petty)

World.title: Tokayev Calls for New Chapter in Kazakhstan–South Korea Ties, Signs $19 Billion in Deals
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and South Korea signed commercial agreements worth $19 billion during President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state visit to Seoul on Sept. 15, with both sides seeking to expand cooperation in investment, industry, urban development and cultural and humanitarian ties, Akorda reported.

“Our goal is the comprehensive development of bilateral relations,” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said during talks with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.

Speaking about the outcome of his visit, Tokayev highly assessed the current state and prospects of cooperation between the two countries.

“As for bilateral relations, during this visit, commercial agreements worth $19 billion were signed. We are satisfied with our work with Korean investors and are ready to continue working with them. There are good plans for the construction of hotels, an oil refinery and urban development. Particular attention is paid to strengthening cultural and humanitarian ties,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev also highlighted the high level of coordination between Astana and Seoul on the international stage, noting that the two countries share common positions on global sustainable development and security.

“Our states share common positions on issues of global sustainable development and security,” Tokayev said.

Lee reaffirmed South Korea’s commitment to further deepening bilateral cooperation, pointing to the growing alignment of the two countries’ foreign policy priorities.

“The Republic of Korea and Kazakhstan are broadening the scope of their external cooperation and pursuing pragmatic diplomacy focused on national interests and tangible results. Kazakhstan is an important partner for us in the area of economic security. The country is not only rich in energy and natural resources, but also has significant potential in promising high-tech industries,” Lee said.

He added that South Korea was ready to support the modernization of Kazakhstan’s industrial sector by leveraging its advanced industrial and digital technologies.

“Amid an increasingly unpredictable international environment, our two countries should strengthen cooperation by bringing together our respective strengths and capabilities and actively creating new opportunities for mutually beneficial growth,” Lee said.

President Tokayev expressed gratitude to Lee for the invitation to visit South Korea, describing the country as a strategic partner of Kazakhstan. He noted the longstanding ties of friendship and mutual understanding between the two peoples, as well as close cultural and humanitarian links, stressing that there are no contradictions or disagreements between Kazakhstan and South Korea.

He said the two countries are pursuing ambitious projects across a range of sectors and highlighted the importance of the Kazakhstan-Korea business forum held in Seoul with the participation of representatives of the two countries’ business communities. Among the projects discussed was the further development of Alatau City, which Tokayev described as an important initiative for Kazakhstan.

“The provisions concerning the status of this city have been incorporated into the Constitution. Korean companies will be provided with all legal guarantees. More than 120,000 ethnic Koreans live in Kazakhstan. All conditions have been created for them, and they are active members of our society,” Tokayev said.

He also highlighted the historical significance of General Hong Beom-do, a Korean independence movement figure whose remains were returned from Kazakhstan to South Korea in 2021. Tokayev said he was well acquainted with Hong Beom-do’s history and described him as a hero and patriot. He noted that preserving the general’s memory and returning his remains to South Korea demonstrated mutual understanding between the two countries.

“It is remarkable that even after more than a hundred years, the Korean people have not forgotten their general. Bowing to his memory, we returned his remains to his homeland, thereby fulfilling our civic duty,” Tokayev said.

Lee warmly welcomed Tokayev and emphasized the importance of his visit to Seoul. He thanked Kazakhstan for the decision to return Hong Beom-do’s remains and expressed appreciation for the way ethnic Koreans were received in Kazakhstan.

“We are grateful for your decision to return the remains of General Hong Beom-do, who played a special role in the history of Korea and in protecting the Korean people during difficult times. Korean citizens were warmly welcomed in Kazakhstan at the time. We are grateful to you and the Kazakh people for this,” Lee said.

The two presidents said they were ready to cooperate long-term and provide comprehensive mutual support when needed. Following the talks, the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the strategic partnership between Kazakhstan and South Korea and giving it new practical substance.

Earlier, Tokayev met with South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong-sook, congratulated her on her recent appointment, and wished her success in the post. Tokayev said Kazakhstan-South Korea relations are developing steadily within the framework of their strategic partnership, with numerous mutually beneficial initiatives being implemented. South Korea is among Kazakhstan’s top 10 trade and investment partners, while more than 1,000 joint ventures with Korean capital operate in Kazakhstan.

“However, there are still many important tasks ahead of us. Therefore, I am confident that, working together as one team, we will successfully implement all the plans we have outlined,” Tokayev said.

President Tokayev said Kazakhstan had created favorable conditions for business and investment, including for small and medium-sized enterprises alongside major Korean corporations. He noted the role of the Intergovernmental Commission on Trade, Economic and Scientific-Technical Cooperation and the Business Council, as well as the bilateral legal framework supporting cooperation.

Tokayev thanked Han Seong-sook for taking part in the roundtable of Kazakh and Korean business representatives and expressed confidence that the agreements signed during the event would contribute to expanding bilateral ties.

He also said his upcoming talks with Lee were intended to open a new chapter in the history of Kazakhstan-South Korea relations.

Tokayev outlined several priorities for further government cooperation, including a target to double bilateral trade turnover.

“It is important not only to increase volumes, but also to qualitatively change the structure of trade and expand the range of goods with high added value. Therefore, I consider it highly relevant to develop a Comprehensive Program for Trade, Economic and Investment Cooperation between Kazakhstan and Korea for 2027-2030,” the President said.

He also proposed preparing a separate roadmap for industrial cooperation, incorporating the most promising localization projects and initiatives to export products to third-country markets.

Tokayev reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s commitment to comprehensive strengthening of its partnership with South Korea.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans $60 Million Tokenization Pilot for Alatau City Projects
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to tokenize up to $60 million in real estate and logistics projects by the end of 2026, launching its first major test of digital assets as a new source of financing for the economy, National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov said at a Sept. 15 government meeting.

The plans include up to $50 million for the Iconic Tower complex and $10 million for the Birlik logistics center in Alatau City in the Almaty Region. Both are expected to be issued through the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange’s digital infrastructure.

Kazakhstan also plans to link its nationwide regulatory framework with the separate regimes of the Astana International Financial Centre and Alatau City, creating what officials describe as a single digital asset market.

Under that model, authorities are considering a regional payments and settlement hub with Binance. Suleiemenov said the project would involve establishing a Binance legal entity in Kazakhstan and obtaining a top-tier payment organization license, potentially allowing the hub to serve clients across the Commonwealth of Independent States, Eastern Europe and Asia, Suleimenov said.

The projects are part of a 65-measure plan approved by the government on Sept. 15 to expand Kazakhstan’s regulated digital asset market.

Kazakhstan plans to tokenize major infrastructure projects, real estate and commodity assets to attract investment. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov instructed the National Bank to compile a priority list of assets for tokenization and establish rules intended to protect investors.

“The digital assets sector is a completely new area of Kazakhstan’s economy. The basic conditions for the development of the digital assets market have already been established. We are now in the process of forming a comprehensive ecosystem,” Bektenov said.

“We have major infrastructure projects, real estate, commodities and other assets. Tokenization can be used to attract additional financing for these projects,” he added.

The government seeks to attract investment and bring more cryptocurrency activity into the regulated economy under the new plan. It also calls for expanding the use of the digital tenge, exploring digital instruments for cross-border payments and developing a more tightly regulated cryptocurrency-mining industry.

The National Bank expects the initial pool of tokenized assets to include government securities, corporate bonds, real estate, infrastructure projects and mineral deposits. Suleimenov called on the Finance Ministry, Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund, Baiterek Holding, KASE and the Central Securities Depository to prepare the first large-scale issuances.

What is tokenization

Tokenization records rights to an asset on a digital ledger. It can divide assets such as real estate, infrastructure or corporate debt into smaller digital units that investors can buy and trade. Supporters say the technology could accelerate transactions, reduce administrative costs and make investments previously dominated by large institutions accessible to a wider range of investors.

Larry Fink and Rob Goldstein of BlackRock have compared tokenization’s current development to that of the internet in 1996, noting that the technology could advance more quickly than many expect. They do not expect it to replace conventional finance soon, but envision the two systems gradually converging.

They portrayed that transition as a bridge being built from two sides: traditional financial institutions on one side and stablecoin issuers, fintech companies and blockchain networks on the other.

Global trends

The World Economic Forum describes 2026 as a “defining moment for digital assets.” It said clearer regulation, wider institutional adoption and greater interoperability are moving blockchain beyond experimentation and into the infrastructure supporting digital financial markets.

Tokenized real-world assets remain a small part of the global digital asset market. Boston Consulting Group estimates that around $30 billion in such assets are publicly visible, compared with roughly $3 trillion in cryptocurrencies and $300 billion in stablecoins. Under the firm’s more expansive scenarios, tokenized assets could represent nearly 16% of global investable assets by 2035, although the outcome would vary considerably by asset class.

According to Suleimenov, the digital assets market now has approximately 750 million users worldwide. Stablecoin transaction volume reached $50 trillion in 2025, while the market for tokenized assets expanded 12-fold over the past three years.

“Three major trends have emerged globally. The first is a shift from prohibition and observation toward licensing, supervision and common international standards. The second is the integration of digital assets with banks, payment infrastructure and capital markets. The third is a move toward practical applications,” Suleimenov explained.

Digital assets are increasingly used for cross-border payments, custody services and the tokenization of real and financial assets.

“Kazakhstan’s objective is to create a competitive, regulated market, with transactions, liquidity and capital concentrated within the country,” he added.

Steady progress

Suleimenov said Kazakhstan began building a regulated digital asset market in 2022. Then, it allowed cryptocurrency exchanges licensed by the Astana International Financial Centre to work with local banks. The parliament followed with a digital assets law in 2023.

By the end of 2025, AIFC-based providers had processed $10.6 billion in transactions and attracted approximately 215,000 users, according to figures cited by Suleimenov. The framework, however, remained limited to the financial center and did not cover the wider domestic market.

The National Bank expanded its approach in July 2025 by launching a regulatory sandbox where companies could test digital asset products under its supervision.

“The sandbox now includes 34 projects across 14 areas. Among them are stablecoins, tokenization, cryptocurrency exchanges, custody and services connecting cryptocurrencies with conventional currencies,” Suleimenov said.

Legislation that took effect on May 1 extended regulation nationwide and formally recognized digital financial assets, including stablecoins and tokenized real and financial assets. It also introduced licensing requirements for tokenization platforms, cryptocurrency exchanges and exchange services. Suleimenov described it as Central Asia’s first comprehensive nationwide regulatory framework for digital assets.

A presidential decree in July expanded the effort by seeking to establish a fully-fledged digital assets industry, encouraging the transition of digital asset transactions to the country’s regulated ecosystem and launching the tokenization of the economy and diversifying sources of financing for the economy.

Key figures

The National Bank has authorized the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange to operate platforms for issuing and trading digital assets. Its digital platform has recorded 34,000 transactions worth 20.5 billion tenge (US45.9 million) in an exchange-traded fund linked to bitcoin futures.

Three newly introduced cryptoasset ETFs have generated 650 transactions worth one billion tenge (US$2.2 million), according to Suleimenov.

Three licensed cryptocurrency exchange operators have also processed around two billion tenge (US$4.5 million) during their first two months of operation, while five more companies are seeking licenses.

Yerkegali Yedenbayev, chief authorization and fintech officer at AIFC’s Astana Financial Services Authority, said Kazakhstan’s citizens are estimated to hold around one million cryptocurrency wallets worldwide, suggesting that much of their trading still takes place through foreign platforms.

He said the center’s regulated digital asset providers currently serve nearly 270,000 clients, up from 53,000 in 2023.

“Today, there are 35 providers operating in the AIFC that offer services in the digital assets sector. Among them are 11 digital asset exchanges, including Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, and Bybit, the fourth-largest crypto exchange. In addition, there are 16 investment service providers and eight payment organizations, including three stablecoin issuers,” Yedenbayev said.

“While the volume of transactions in the licensed market reached $320 million in 2023, this figure reached $10.5 billion by the end of last year. In the first half of this year, the volume of transactions reached $5.5 billion. Thus, in a short period of time, the regulated market has grown more than 30-fold,” he said.

Digital tenge

The newly adopted plan also calls for wider use of the digital tenge, the central bank’s digital currency. Unlike cryptocurrencies, it is issued by the National Bank.

Bektenov instructed the Finance Ministry and the National Bank to examine its use in government procurement, corporate transactions and programmable contracts, which could automate payments when predetermined conditions are met.

“Unlike cryptocurrencies, the digital tenge is a centralized digital currency issued by the National Bank and is therefore legal tender. Its use should improve the efficiency of public spending and support the development of digital financial services. Digital contracts could help automate payments in government procurement and corporate transactions,” he said.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, Binur Zhalenov, deputy governor of the National Bank of Kazakhstan (NBK), said the digital tenge has the potential to transform how money moves. Most of the real-world use cases of digital tenge will be related to government spending, including public procurement and social spending.

What needs to be done

Suleimenov said the plan’s success would depend on competitive tax rules, more targeted compliance controls by banks and a sufficient supply of high-quality assets for tokenization. He said concerns involving an individual transaction or customer should not result in banks freezing all accounts held by a licensed digital asset provider.

The concern echoes findings reported earlier. Ainur Zhanturina, founder of RISE Research, said limited access to banking services was the principal barrier identified in the organization’s survey and interviews with Kazakhstan’s digital asset companies.

“Many banks are unwilling to work with companies in this sector, viewing them as higher-risk clients, which complicates transfers and account management,” Zhanturina said.

Сryptocurrency mining

While the digital tenge and tokenization are intended to expand Kazakhstan’s financial infrastructure, the plan also addresses a more established and energy-intensive part of the digital asset industry: cryptocurrency mining.

Kazakhstan has 76 licensed cryptocurrency miners and five accredited mining pools, with around 470,000 pieces of mining equipment registered with the government, said Vice Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Gizzat Baitursynov.
