World.title: Middle Corridor likely to boost trade between Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan - CPR
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. The potential of the Middle Corridor could help accelerate and expand trade between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan, Mirshohid Aslanov, head of Uzbekistan’s Center for Progressive Reforms (CPR), said while speaking at the presentation of the “Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan Business Barometer” initiative, Trend's correspondent reports.

According to him, logistics will be one of the key areas of the joint “Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan Business Barometer,” which the CPR is developing in collaboration with the CASPIA think tank. “We will examine, in particular, logistics as well as the potential of the Middle Corridor,” Aslanov said.

He noted that the development of this route could be of particular importance for expanding trade ties between Central Asia and the South Caucasus.

According to Aslanov, completing certain logistics and customs procedures can currently take weeks, which creates additional costs for businesses. “For businesses, every day is money,” he emphasized.

Aslanov believes that transit times can be significantly reduced through the digitization of procedures, the advance exchange of data, and the mutual recognition of documents.

In particular, he proposed creating a system that would allow the necessary procedures to be completed even before the cargo arrives, as well as the advance identification of reliable exporters. “All these procedures can be completed before the goods arrive here,” Aslanov said.

According to him, such a system should include permits, certificates, and other information necessary for the movement of cargo between the two countries.

M. Aslanov also noted that more efficient logistics should become part of a broader ecosystem to support small and medium-sized businesses, which are often insufficiently informed about opportunities to export to the markets of Azerbaijan and other countries in the region.

He emphasized that combining Uzbekistan’s industrial potential with Azerbaijan’s logistical capabilities could, in the long term, create conditions not only for the growth of bilateral trade but also for the entry of joint products into the markets of other countries.

World.title: EU’s move away from Russian gas opens door for new suppliers – IEA
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. The European Union’s decision to stop importing Russian natural gas will create additional opportunities in the European market for non-Russian suppliers, particularly in Central and Eastern Europe, where Russian pipeline gas continues to account for a significant share of supplies.

This is stated in information published on the website of the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Meanwhile, it is noted that, according to EU legislation adopted in December 2025, imports of Russian LNG under short-term contracts will be prohibited starting at the end of April 2026, and imports of Russian pipeline gas will be prohibited starting in mid-June: “EU countries must completely halt imports of Russian LNG by January 1, 2027, and the remaining supplies of Russian pipeline gas no later than November 1, 2027.”

According to the agency, the implementation of these measures is expected to result in a reduction in Russian pipeline gas and LNG supplies to the EU by approximately 33 billion cubic meters per year between 2025 and 2028.

The IEA estimates that part of the reduction in supplies could be offset by lower demand for gas resulting from improved energy efficiency and further electrification: “At the same time, the space freed up in the market could be filled by non-Russian suppliers.”

“Since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022, Europe’s gas market has changed significantly. The share of Russian natural gas in EU demand has fallen from nearly 40% in 2021 to about 10% in 2025.

Against this backdrop, the share of LNG in EU demand rose from less than 20% to nearly 45%.

Between 2021 and 2025, imports of Russian pipeline gas fell by nearly 90%, or 120 billion cubic meters.

However, the diversification process has been uneven. Northwestern Europe and Italy have effectively stopped importing Russian pipeline gas, while a number of countries in Central and Eastern Europe continue to depend on Russian supplies.

“At the same time, imports of Russian LNG into the EU increased by more than 40%, or 6 billion cubic meters, between 2021 and 2025. The bulk of this growth occurred in Northwestern and Southwestern Europe,” the IEA reports.

Furthermore, it is emphasized that from 2021 through 2023, annual gas demand in Central and Eastern Europe fell by more than 20% amid record-high prices, which led to a decline in industrial gas consumption: “In 2023–2025, demand partially recovered, increasing by approximately 10%.

“Unlike in Western Europe, natural gas demand in Central and Eastern Europe is expected to continue growing in the medium term as the region further phases out coal-fired power generation.

Historically, the region has been heavily dependent on Russian pipeline gas. In 2021, it accounted for about 60% of primary gas supplies to the region.

“Although imports of Russian pipeline gas have declined from 55 billion cubic meters in 2021 to just over 15 billion cubic meters in 2025, they still cover about 20% of the region’s gas demand,” the agency reports.

In addition, it is noted that further diversification in Central and Eastern Europe is taking place against the backdrop of a significant expansion in global LNG production capacity.

The IEA emphasizes that disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz amid the war in the Middle East have led to a significant reduction in gas supplies to the global market: “From March through July 2026, LNG exports from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates fell by 43 billion cubic meters on an annualized basis.”

“However, the impact of this decline on the global market was partially offset by growth in LNG production in other regions.

From March through July, LNG production outside the Persian Gulf increased by nearly 16%, or more than 30 billion cubic meters on a year-over-year basis. This offset about 70% of the decline in LNG supplies from Persian Gulf countries.

This growth was driven primarily by increased production from new LNG projects in North America and Africa, as well as by greater availability of gas for LNG production among existing producers in Africa and Asia.

According to current project plans, more than 350 billion cubic meters of new annual LNG export capacity is expected to come online worldwide by the early 2030s. The United States and Qatar are expected to account for more than 70% of this increase.

“An increase in LNG supply will ease market tensions and exert downward pressure on gas prices in the medium term,” the IEA reports.

According to the agency, further adaptation of gas infrastructure will be required to replace the remaining supplies of Russian pipeline gas to Central and Eastern Europe.

"This primarily involves the ability to transport large volumes of non-Russian LNG from import terminals to the region’s domestic markets. However, the growth in LNG import capacity has slowed in recent years due to constraints in transporting regasified gas from coastal terminals to demand centers located within the region, as well as limited interregional pipeline connections.

Since late 2021, LNG import capacity in Central and Eastern Europe has increased by approximately 15 billion cubic meters per year, reaching nearly 35 billion cubic meters by the end of 2025. This corresponds to more than 40% of the region’s natural gas demand.

In particular, the capacity of the Świnoujście LNG terminal in Poland was expanded, and in January 2023, the Inkoo LNG regasification terminal, serving the gas markets of Estonia and Finland, began operations.

In Southeast Europe, the Alexandroupolis LNG terminal in Greece began operations in October 2024. Its capacity is 6 billion cubic meters per year.

The Croatian Krk LNG terminal was also expanded and reached a capacity of 3.4 billion cubic meters per year in November 2025.

“Central and Eastern Europe can also utilize expanded regasification capacity in Germany and Italy through existing regional gas interconnections,” the IEA reports.

According to the IEA, cross-border gas pipeline connections between countries in Central and Eastern Europe have also improved significantly since 2022: “This has enabled an increase in regional gas flows and indirect LNG supplies to landlocked countries.”

Among such projects, the agency highlights the gas interconnector between Poland and Slovakia, the Greece-Bulgaria interconnector, and the modernization of the Hungary-Slovakia and Hungary-Romania interconnectors.

According to the agency, it is also necessary to expand the existing capacity of gas pipelines that transport gas from south to north: “This will allow for more efficient distribution of regasified LNG throughout the region.”

"Gas transmission system operators are working on the Vertical Gas Corridor project. It is intended to increase gas transmission capacity from south to north via the former Trans-Balkan Gas Pipeline system, which will enable the delivery of regasified LNG from Greece to Moldova and Ukraine.

According to the IEA, this pipeline system could provide approximately 10 billion cubic meters of annual capacity and help ensure gas supplies to Ukraine.

The IEA notes that infrastructure alone will not be sufficient to strengthen the region’s gas supply security: “As the shift away from Russian pipeline gas progresses, more flexible procurement strategies will also be needed, including contract diversification and additional purchases on the global spot gas market.”

Moreover, it is emphasized that, starting in 2022, European buyers have signed contracts to import more than 45 billion cubic meters of LNG per year: “Buyers from Central and Eastern Europe accounted for less than one-fifth of these volumes. At the same time, based on existing contracts, buyers from Central and Eastern Europe have secured approximately 5 billion cubic meters of LNG per year through 2028. This corresponds to about 5% of the region’s current gas demand.”

It is noted that if new contracts are not concluded, the region’s dependence on the global spot market, which is becoming more liquid but is also subject to volatility, will increase significantly.

The IEA notes that a diversified supply portfolio, including long-term LNG contracts, can enhance the security of gas supplies and provide greater certainty regarding future deliveries.

“Contracts with the option to change the destination can also provide European buyers with additional commercial opportunities without creating a long-term commitment to specific supplies,” the agency reports.

According to the IEA, this will be crucial for ensuring relative price stability and security of supply as Central and Eastern Europe phase out Russian pipeline gas after more than five decades of dependence.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Switzerland explore new horizons for trade and investment (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. The development of the Azerbaijani-Swiss economic dialogue, as well as issues related to expanding trade and investment ties, were discussed.

This was reported by the Ministry of Economy of Azerbaijan.

Meanwhile, it is reported that a Swiss-Azerbaijani Business Forum was held as part of Economy Minister Mikayil Jabbarov’s working visit to the Swiss Confederation.

“The event was attended by government officials from both countries, as well as representatives of companies operating in sectors such as energy, transportation and logistics, construction, mechanical engineering, metallurgy, the food industry, tourism, healthcare, telecommunications, consulting, finance, the chemical and pharmaceutical industries, and other sectors.

Speaking at the forum, Minister of Economy Mikayil Jabbarov discussed the dynamics of Azerbaijani-Swiss economic cooperation, noting that trade and mutual investment are the main pillars of bilateral economic ties. The minister highlighted Azerbaijan’s favorable business and investment environment, its strategic geographic location, transportation and logistics capabilities, and its growing role within the Middle Corridor. He noted that the country’s free economic and industrial zones, as well as its potential in green energy, create new opportunities for cooperation for investors, including Swiss companies.

According to reports, the importance of the Second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum, which will be held on September 25–26 of this year in Baku under the guidance of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, was emphasized in terms of establishing new partnerships and attracting investment:

“Speaking at the event, a representative of the Swiss Federal Council’s Committee on Trade Agreements, Andrea Rauber Saxer, Head of the Office for Bilateral Economic Relations at the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs, noted the importance of developing the Azerbaijani-Swiss economic dialogue, expanding trade and investment ties, and intensifying direct contacts between business communities.”

“During the forum, participants discussed global trends in the Fourth Industrial Revolution, innovation ecosystems, and investment promotion; heard presentations from Azerbaijani and Swiss companies; and exchanged views on investment priorities, opportunities for entering global markets, and models of cooperation,” the statement said.

World.title: Azerbaijan, ADB explore new opportunities in transport cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. Representatives of Azerbaijan and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) held a meeting to discuss cooperation in the transportation sector.

This was announced by Rashad Nabiyev, Azerbaijan’s Minister of Digital Development and Transportation, on his “X” account.

“We held a meeting with members of the Board of Directors of the Asian Development Bank.

At the meeting, we discussed the current state and prospects for cooperation between Azerbaijan and the Asian Development Bank, as well as opportunities to expand cooperation toward the modernization, digitalization, and decarbonization of railway, metro, and transportation infrastructure in general.

We also exchanged views on potential financing opportunities in air and maritime transport, as well as in the aerospace industry,” the post reads.

According to the Azerbaijani Ministry of Finance, since Azerbaijan joined the Asian Development Bank (ADB), a total of $5.6 billion has been allocated to finance 160 projects as part of the country’s cooperation with the bank. The partnership between Azerbaijan and the ADB covers the areas of transportation, energy, water supply, and private sector development. In recent years, the main priorities have been strengthening regional transport connectivity, developing the Middle Corridor, and promoting clean energy.

The ADB plans to further deepen integration in the transportation, trade, and energy sectors along the Middle Corridor. In particular, the bank is working on a strategy to transform the CAREC 2 corridor, which corresponds to the Middle Corridor, into an integrated economic corridor aimed at modernizing border crossings, digitizing trade, and developing logistics infrastructure.

The Asian Development Bank (ADB), in collaboration with the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), is supporting the development of a feasibility study for the “Green Energy Corridor” project, which calls for the transmission of clean electricity from Central Asia to Azerbaijan, and then to Europe via an undersea power cable beneath the Caspian Sea.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan and World Bank discuss progress on Kambarata HPP-1
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. Kyrgyzstan and the World Bank have discussed the implementation of the Kambarata HPP-1 project.

This was announced in a statement published by the Ministry of Finance of Kyrgyzstan, following the meeting between the Minister, Ruslan Suynaliev, and World Bank Regional Director for Central Asia, Najy Benhassine.

"The participants exchanged views on the implementation of the Kambarata HPP-1 project, budget support and additional financing under the IDA-21 program," the Ministry said.

According to the Ministry, in the course of the meeting, the minister highly appreciated the World Bank's support in advancing the Kambarata HPP-1 project.

Furthermore, the sides discussed strengthening cooperation under the AgriConnect initiative, aimed at developing agriculture in Kyrgyzstan.

Particular attention was also paid to the international CPIA and Business Ready assessments.

The sides discussed further advancement of reforms aimed at improving public administration, public financial management and the business environment.

Following the meeting, the parties confirmed their readiness to further strengthen the strategic partnership between the Kyrgyz Republic and the World Bank, expand cooperation on the implementation of new major projects and contribute to the country's sustainable development.

Meanwhile, cooperation between Kyrgyzstan and the World Bank covers a broad range of development priorities, including economic growth, infrastructure, social protection, human capital, energy, water resources and climate resilience. The World Bank has continued to support reforms and development initiatives aimed at strengthening the country's economic foundations and improving the quality and accessibility of public services.

Further cooperation is expected to focus on mobilizing financing and technical expertise for projects aligned with Kyrgyzstan's development priorities, while supporting sustainable economic growth and strengthening the resilience of the country's infrastructure and social sectors.

World.title: Nick Reiner will not face death penalty over parents' killings, prosecutors say
World.content:
The Los Angeles County District Attorney has announced his office will not to seek the death penalty against Nick Reiner, the son of Hollywood filmmaker Rob Reiner, who has pleaded not guilty to murdering his parents in their home in December.

District Attorney Nathan Hochman told reporters outside a downtown Los Angeles courthouse that prosecutors took into account the wishes of the surviving Reiner family members in reaching their decision.

The announcement came shortly before Nick Reiner, 33, was scheduled to appear for a pre-trial hearing where the judge is expected to set a preliminary trial date and consider various pleadings in the case.

Rob Reiner and his wife, photographer Michele Reiner, were found stabbed to death in their home in Los Angeles’ Brentwood neighbourhood.

Nick Reiner, the younger of their two sons, was arrested later that day and charged with first-degree murder.

The maximum penalty prosecutors said they would now seek against him is life in prison without parole.

Last month, Nick Reiner was indicted over his parents's murder.

Rob Reiner, second left, and his wife Michele, left, and children Jake, center, Romy, and Nick in 2014. (AP: Evan Agostini/Invision)

The indictment added the allegation that Nick Reiner was lying in wait before attacking his parents.

The grand jury, which had been meeting in secret, returned the indictment on July 20.

It was unsealed on August 12 when Nick Reiner entered a not guilty plea.

At the time, it was noted he would be eligible for the death penalty if prosecutors chose to pursue it.

The high-profile murders left Hollywood shocked and led the eldest son of Rob and Michele, Jake, to later state that the aftermath as being like a "living nightmare".

Reuters

World.title: China tightens travel restrictions on its own citizens amid AI race with US
World.content:
China has imposed sweeping travel restrictions on its citizens, including exit bans on those deemed to endanger the country's "industrial or technological security".

The new border control rules took effect in China on Tuesday as part of a broader overhaul of border regulations, reflecting in part a heightened government concern about the export of technology at a time of growing competition with the US in artificial intelligence and other emerging areas.

The opening clause of the regulation says it was drawn up to "safeguard national sovereignty, security and development interests", according to China's State Council.

A citizen deemed to be engaging in illegal or criminal activity overseas which endangers national security could be prohibited from leaving China again for six months to three years, from the date of their return.

Experts say the new regulations indicate a heightened sense of security control from the Government. (AP: Mark Schiefelbein)

Similarly, a citizen who violates technology export or import regulations could be banned from leaving if the action endangers industrial or technological security, the regulation says.

Included in the fine print, a provision that could ban foreigners from entering for one to five years if they provide false information in a visa application or at the port of entry.

The regulations also seek to prevent citizens from being deceived into travelling abroad and then forced to participate in illegal gambling or online and phone scam operations, a persistent problem in recent years.

The new regulations were announced in July, and came into effect on Tuesday. (Reuters: Carlos Garcia Rawlins/File)

The Cyberspace Administration of China, which monitors online discussions, sought to assuage concerns that the new rules would make travel more difficult.

The measures target people involved in illegal cross-border activities, not ordinary citizens with legitimate reasons to travel abroad, the agency said in an online post last week.

Experts sound the alarm

Analysts have warned that the travel rules give China a "wide remit".

Chong Ja Ian from the National University of Singapore told AFP security and criminal activities "can be vaguely defined and easily adjusted".

"The outside world will only know how it applies that remit after there are cases of implementation," he said.

Mr Ja pointed to reports of exit bans on foreign nationals, including the recent case of US citizen Min Zin.

The US government said the political analyst was taken into Chinese custody in Yunnan province on June 3 and was held improperly.

China refuted the accusations in August, saying Min Zin was suspected of violating Chinese law.

"The case of Min Zin is a reminder that the range of people (that China) could restrict from exiting could be quite wide, and potentially arbitrary," Mr Ja said.

China's new strategy near Taiwan Australia raises concerns about China's latest activities near Taiwan "directly to Chinese officials" as tensions simmer in the region.

Dylan Loh, an associate professor at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told AFP the travel restrictions "send a message" that China will take action to prevent "leaks in security or national interest-sensitive areas".

A note released by Trivium, a consultancy firm specialising in Chinese policy trends said the new regulations “are another indication of just how serious China is about preventing the transfer of key tech and technical knowledge,”

Global tech competition

China and the United States have been locked in a tech race, with both sides accusing the other in recent months of stealing the capabilities of locally developed artificial intelligence models.

Earlier in the year China blocked tech company Meta from acquiring artificial intelligence startup Manus.

The deal aroused government concern from the Chinese government about the transfer of advanced technology, despite Manus being a Singaporean company with Chinese roots.

AP / AFP

World.title: The US has admitted deploying weapons in space and China is sounding the alarm
World.content:
The US has confirmed it has stationed arms in orbit around the Earth, in a move China warns could turn space into a "battlefield".

The revelation by Washington confirmed an open secret but the timing of the announcement risked exacerbating tensions with Beijing and the risk of a weapons race in space.

The announcement marked a new stage in the major powers' rush for military space capabilities, driven by rapid technological advancements but lacking a comprehensive legal framework.

Here's what we know about the US's latest move and what it could mean for the future.

US Space Force was established during Donald Trump's first presidency in 2019. (Reuters)

What are the US's capabilities?

The US statement did not provide concrete details about what weapons are deployed in space and how many.

"Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain — employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities," the statement said.

"These capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes," it added.

Non-kinetic means could include lasers to blind satellites, or even electromagnetic or cyber jamming of their data links.

Why does the US want weapons in space?

For Washington, both Russia and China — its two main geopolitical rivals — pose potential threats to US interests in space.

China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy," according to the US Space Force.

Russia, meanwhile, "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts", it said.

The US Space Force's deployment will likely provoke other countries to follow suit, experts warn. (Reuters: Mike Blake)

The militarisation of space is as old as the space race itself.

As soon as the USSR's Sputnik was launched into orbit as the first probe in space in 1957, Washington and Moscow began exploring ways to both arm and destroy satellites.

India in March 2019 said it had destroyed a low-orbiting satellite, following in the footsteps of Russia, China and the US, in a missile test that proved the nation was among the world's most advanced space powers.

How has China reacted?

China's foreign ministry has already expressed its opposition to the move, warning against the "weaponisation of outer space, turning it into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there".

"The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," a US Space Force spokesperson said in a statement that did not provide specifics on the weapons.

China is among the countries with its own space ambitions. (China Daily via REUTERS)

Song Zhongping, an independent military commentator based in Hong Kong and former Chinese army instructor, told AFP the announcement was "no surprise at all" as the fact that the US possesses such weapons "has long been an open secret".

"The only difference is that the US used to keep it ambiguous, whereas now it has gone public, which shows that Washington is no longer trying to hide it," he added.

"China will not stand by and do nothing," he warned, noting Beijing already has its own space station in orbit.

"Whether China deploys weapons in space will depend entirely on whether the United States moves in that direction," he said.

The Wall Street Journal said Beijing supplied Iran with satellite imagery that enabled Tehran to precisely target military facilities and kill US service members in Jordan in July, a claim China has denied.

Russia, meanwhile, called for space to be kept "free of any weapons".

Can weapons in outer space be regulated?

The biggest worry was once about nuclear weapons in space, but the superpowers and other countries signed the Outer Space Treaty in 1967, banning weapons of mass destruction in orbit.

Since then, Russia, the United States, China and India have explored ways to fight in space outside of that treaty, including by targeting rivals' satellites, which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

"There is a regulatory vacuum because Article 4 of the 1967 treaty only forbids weapons of mass destruction and nuclear weapons in orbit," said space law expert Laetitia Cesari.

She said the topic would likely be on the agenda at the next UN disarmament meeting in November.

"Moscow and Beijing have been wanting to work for about twenty years on a treaty to prevent the placement of weapons in space," while "Western states are trying instead to work on the notion of responsible behaviour," Ms Cesari said.

The US announcement "will likely give impetus to the restrictive approach that Moscow and Beijing are pushing for," she said.

AFP

World.title: 'Complete failure': UK baby killer inquiry findings handed down
World.content:
British nurse Lucy Letby was able to murder seven babies because of a "complete failure" to protect babies at the hospital at which she worked, and some of the deaths could have been avoided, the chair of an inquiry has said.

Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall criticised senior staff for not acting sooner, blaming dysfunctional management at the Countess of Chester Hospital, in northern England, and a basic lack of understanding of safeguarding, when she handed down her findings on Tuesday, local time.

Letby, 36, was convicted in 2023 of murdering seven newborns and attempting to murder six others, making her Britain's most prolific serial child killer of modern times. She was later convicted of another attempted murder charge.

Prosecutors said Letby attacked the newborns by giving them an overdose of insulin, injecting them with air or force-feeding them milk between June 2015 and June 2016, in a case that shocked Britain and drew worldwide attention.

But Letby, who was sentenced to life without parole and maintains she is innocent, has also been the subject of a growing campaign, backed by some medical experts and specialists, which has publicly questioned her convictions.

This public inquiry was set up to examine the events at the hospital and the UK health system's handling of them, not Letby's conviction.

Ms Thirlwall, who previously criticised "noise" around the case, did not address Letby's guilt or innocence in her report, dealing with the Countess of Chester Hospital's response and whether suspicions should have been raised earlier.

She also emphasised the impact on those whose children were harmed, saying: "The families must not be collateral damage in the public argument about whether or not Letby is guilty."

Lady Justice Thirlwall made 17 recommendations on Tuesday. (Pool: Peter Byrne via Reuters)

The contents of her report, though, will be pored over by those who assert Letby's innocence, around two dozen of whom gathered outside Liverpool Town Hall on Tuesday.

It will also be examined by the Criminal Cases Review Commission, an independent body that reviews potential miscarriages of justice and is considering an application from Letby's legal team.

"This inquiry has proceeded on the wrong premise and it follows that this has inevitably affected the report as a whole," Letby's lawyer, Mark McDonald, said in a statement.

"Once there was suspicion that Letby may be causing harm deliberately, safeguarding steps should have been taken," Ms Thirlwall said as she delivered her final report.

" No one seems to have thought that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm," she added. "Suspicion is enough. "

She made a series of recommendations to improve neonatal services in the state-run National Health Service, calling on the government to tackle the "long-standing underfunding of hospital services for babies and children".

Thirlwall also suggested a series of measures to protect patients, including fitting cots and incubators with cameras, stronger insulin storage safeguards and an NHS protocol for when staff are suspected to have deliberately harmed a patient.

Inside the Lucy Letby trial Neonatal nurse Lucy Letby's job was to care for some of Chester's sickest babies. She's now been found guilty of their murder.

Richard Scorer, a lawyer at Slater and Gordon who represents three families, said Thirlwall's recommendations should be implemented without delay. "Far too often public inquiry recommendations are left to gather dust," he said.

Ms Thirlwall's report was particularly critical of senior executives and nursing leaders at the Countess of Chester Hospital, saying at least two of Letby's murders could have been prevented if action was taken sooner.

Three senior hospital managers were arrested last year on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter and remain under investigation, Cheshire Police said, with one of the three also suspected of perverting the course of justice.

Evidence submitted by the force in support of further charges relating to Letby's time working at the Countess of Chester Hospital and Liverpool Women's Hospital was, however, deemed to be insufficient by prosecutors last year.

Speaking in the House of Commons after the findings were delivered, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said "the suffering endured by these babies and their families is impossible to comprehend".

"On behalf of the government, and the health service, I am profoundly sorry for the failures set out so clearly in this report. For the harm, distress and unthinkable loss for their families, and for the failures to keep their babies safe," she said, adding it "must be a turning point" for Britain's public health service.

Ms Cooper said the UK government would consider the report and provide a comprehensive response later.

Reuters

World.title: Russia and Ukraine trade energy strikes, as NATO downs drone in Lithuania
World.content:
Russia has hit petrol stations in Kyiv and Ukraine has struck a Russian oil refinery, as the warring sides carried on with strikes on each other's energy targets despite an announcement by US President Donald Trump that they had agreed to stop.

Moscow launched 200 drones at Ukraine's capital and other cities in overnight attacks on Tuesday, local time, killing two people.

In addition to petrol stations in Kyiv, Russia struck energy and port infrastructure in other regions, Ukrainian officials said.

Meanwhile, Ukraine hit a Russian oil refinery in Syzran in Russia's Samara region on the Volga River, and also drone production facilities in the Taganrog and Oryol regions, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

Russia is exploiting Ukraine's shortage of interceptors by launching ballistic missiles at major cities. (Reuters: Gleb Garanich)

The Samara governor said an industrial facility was hit there without identifying it. The Taganrog governor said a warehouse of e-commerce firm Ozon was struck there.

"Russia continues to attack our energy sector, regular logistics and critical infrastructure. And our responses to them for this are tangible," Mr Zelenskyy said on the Telegram app.

Mr Trump said on Monday, local time, that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure, which he said was the main factor in a global fuel shortage that has driven diesel prices in the United States to record highs.

Donald Trump is trying to limit the damage to global energy supplies as Iran and its proxies pressure key shipping routes. (Reuters: Cathal McNaughton)

Mr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to halt such strikes, but required credible guarantees from its partners that Russia would also stop.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Mr Trump's suggestion was a "very good idea", but that it would take more to bring down global fuel prices.

"It is necessary to ensure safe commercial shipping and navigation here, including for oil tankers," Mr Peskov said, adding that Russia would stay in touch with the US about Mr Trump's proposal.

NATO shoots down drone over Lithuanian airspace

The renewed strikes between the two sides came as a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone in Lithuanian airspace that "most probably" came from Russia, Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said.

The drone entered Lithuanian airspace from Russian ally Belarus after midnight and was shot down near the southern village of Pratkunai not far from the city of Kaunas, the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said.

"Last night, again, the Italian pilots have intervened and they have shot down a threat that most probably came from Russia", Mr Crosetto told reporters at Siauliai Air Base, where Italian fighters are based as part of the NATO Baltic Air Defence mission.

"The presence of Italian aircraft here is the clear demonstration of the value of the Atlantic alliance for Italy and what it means to be an ally", he said after meeting crews with Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas.

Debris of what, according to the Lithuanian national crisis management centre, was a drone shot down by a NATO fighter jet. (Lithuanian Army via Reuters)

Russia did not immediately comment on the incident.

Mr Kaunas told reporters that the drone had probably not carried explosives, and the debris of the drone would be examined.

"Then we will be able to say clearly, whether this is a Russian drone and it's possibly a provocation, or whether it is another country's drone", he said.

Ukrainian drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace in the Baltic region in recent months. Kyiv says they were steered off course by Russian signal jamming.

Denmark's foreign minister said the flares came within metres of the helicopters. (Supplied: Defence Command Denmark)

Meanwhile, Russia has accused Danish military helicopters of making dangerous manoeuvres near its warships in the Baltic Sea and handed an official note to Copenhagen complaining about such incidents, according Russia's ambassador to Denmark, Russia's RIA state news agency reports.

Denmark's Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters no warning or radio contact was made before a Russian frigate fired the flares.

At the same time, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Tuesday that the spread of the Ukraine-Russia war to the Black Sea and threatening the safety of Turkish citizens was unacceptable, adding that attacks in vessels in the region were harming navigational safety.

Speaking at a press conference alongside his counterpart in Azerbaijan's Baku, Mr Fidan said Türkiye had intensified its efforts to find a solution to the war through an agreement, without elaborating.

Russian forces hit a cargo ship and a ferry carrying military supplies in Ukraine's port of Chornomorsk, the Russian defence ministry said on Tuesday.

Reuters

World.title: 'Disgusting': Leaders condemn alleged Islamophobic attack on bus
World.content:
The Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia has condemned alleged verbal abuse hurled at a 13-year-old girl, who was called an "immigrant mutt" and a "terrorist" on a Sydney bus last week.

The 50-year-old man, who was charged on Tuesday, appeared in videos of the incident obtained by the ABC allegedly telling another girl, "I can't wait until they kill all of you".

His comments appeared to be directed to Muslim women on the bus last Thursday.

According to the 13-year-old, Janna, the incident began when she stood up for another girl in a hijab who the man was allegedly taking photos of without her knowledge.

NSW Police said he was arrested at a Greenacre home about 2:20pm on Tuesday.

Loading...

He was taken to Bankstown Police Station and charged with stalking and intimidation intending fear or physical harm.

Australia's special envoy, Aftab Malik, said the alleged abuse was not unheard of.

"Unfortunately, the Islamophobia victim pool is getting younger, according to the Islamophobia Register Australia," he said.

"Islamophobia does not require spectacular violence to cause serious harm to people.

"The spread of hateful stereotypes, the normalisation of online abuse, the offline threats, and physical attacks to individuals and institutions, all degrade Muslim Australians."

'Everyone has the right to feel safe when travelling'

Mr Malik said he invited Transport for NSW (TfNSW) to work directly with his office to take active steps to ensure the safety of Muslim school children wearing the hijab.

TfNSW said it was aware of the incident which was reported by the bus driver after the fact.

A spokesperson for the department said it was serious about improving safety across the network.

"We welcome engagement with the Office of the Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia and are willing to meet to discuss any concerns raised," they said.

"Everyone has the right to feel safe when travelling on the public transport network, and Transport for NSW works closely with operators, police and community stakeholders to support customer safety and respond to incidents when they occur."

Premier Chris Minns says Muslim women and children deserve to feel safe while using public transport. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

NSW Premier Chris Minns said he was deeply concerned by the increase in Islamophobia.

"Muslim women and girls have every right to wear a hijab, catch a bus, go to school, or walk down the street without being abused or intimidated," he said.

"What happened to this young girl was disgusting, and she should never have had to defend her right to belong in her own country.

"Everyone, no matter your background or religion, deserves to feel safe and respected in New South Wales."

Shadow Minister for Multiculturalism Mark Coure described the incident as "deeply distressing".

"There is no place for Islamophobia in our community. Racism and religious hatred have no place in our society," he said.

'We have a right'

There has been a 612 per cent jump in reported Islamophobic attacks across Australia in the last three years, according to Islamophobia Register Australia.

The figure is based on an increase of average weekly reported incidents, which has risen from 2.5 reports per week to 18.

The organisation has a backlog of 400 cases like Janna's.

Janna said she was subjected to Islamophobic abuse last week. (ABC News)

Executive director Aishah Ali said government funding had dried up.

"We're going to be relying on community fundraising to actually stay operational," she said.

"We've increased our volunteer team, but it's unsustainable for the breadth and the severity of the work to being encapsulated in a volunteer capacity, and nor should it be, because we have a right to equal safety, protection, remedy and recourse."

The register received some funding from Multicultural NSW for youth education initiatives, which Ms Ali said did not cover their core operational work.

The department has also delivered $15 million to support safety and security at places of worship, including mosques, since February 2023.

'It's their choice'

Janna's mother Roula said some politicians were to blame for the unprecedented levels of Islamophobia.

"I think some of the politicians have … a lot to do with this," she said.

"They have views about Islam, that we're oppressed … us women, but we're not.

"The biggest example is me not being a hijabi, and my daughter is. And it's a choice."

Sydney student Janna with her mother Roula (right). (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

Roula said the government should support what women want to wear.

"It's their choice. You want to walk out naked or want to walk out dressed up, your choice," she said.

The man charged over the incident was refused bail to appear before Bankstown Local Court on Wednesday.

World.title: Impact of colonisation on First Nations people far greater than previous estimates, research finds
World.content:
Australia's Indigenous population was up to seven times larger before colonisation than previously estimated, but was devastated following the arrival of Europeans, new research reveals.

Researchers from across Australia say their findings paint a more accurate picture of the impact of colonisation on First Nations people, updating previous population estimates calculated using anthropological information gathered in the 1930s.

In a research paper published on Tuesday evening, the researchers estimated Australia's median pre-colonial Indigenous population was 2.22 million people — significantly higher than previous estimates of between 250,000 and 1 million people.

Find Deep Time stories of ancient Australia near you Ancient First Nations stories are all around us — if you know where to look.

But according to the new research, an estimated 2.06 million First Nations Australians were likely to have died from diseases, massacres and mortality associated with displacement and other colonial-related disturbances to Indigenous ways of life over the late 18th and 19th centuries.

Just over 70 years after the First Fleet landed in Australia in 1788, only seven per cent of Australia's pre-colonial population was estimated to have survived.

The researchers used computer modelling and reviewed ethnographic observations and archaeological and genetic reconstructions to calculate the revised estimates.

"These research findings challenge us to rethink the scale of what happened after 1788," University of Technology Sydney professor and Eualayai/Gamillaroi woman Larissa Behrendt said.

" We are not talking about a marginal consequence of colonisation, but a demographic catastrophe at the heart of the Australian story. "

Lethal disease, frontier violence decimated Indigenous population

Report co-author and Flinders University global ecology professor Corey Bradshaw said he found it "unsurprising" that it had taken until now to form a more accurate picture of Australia's pre-colonial Indigenous population, given historical biases and racism towards First Nations people.

He said previous studies underestimated the impact of lethal diseases and frontier and structural violence on the population.

Professor Bradshaw said smallpox alone could have killed up to 220,000 First Nations people along the country's east coast within the first 10 years of colonisation.

Professor Corey Bradshaw said previous research had underestimated the impact of lethal diseases on Indigenous peoples after colonisation. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

He said while some massacres were recorded in databases, the information represented "only the tip of the iceberg".

"Probably most of the frontier violence was done under the cover of night, so to speak," he said.

" We expect that the recorded massacres are probably out by an order of magnitude of what was actually happening. "

Research important to truth-telling and reconciliation

Australia's First Nations population has grown since the 1950s, with latest census data showing in 2021, it was at about 37 per cent of the estimated median pre-colonial size.

Researchers estimate that achieving parity with the 1788 pre-colonial population would not be reached until 2047, if current growth trends continue.

In their paper, the researchers wrote that estimating the size of Australia's Indigenous population before colonisation was "invaluable to truth-telling and reconciliation".

"Removing 93 per cent of the (Indigenous) population in 70 years, it can't be interpreted in any other way but disastrous," Professor Bradshaw said.

"On the flip side, these Indigenous cultures survived and these people, despite all that horrendous treatment and dispossession and death, managed to perpetuate their languages, their culture, their managing of country and that is worth celebrating."

World.title: Western Renewables Link passes planning hurdle as cost review ordered
World.content:
Victoria's premier has ordered a cost review of a controversial $1.5 billion transmission line project, the same day the planning minister approved a major planning hurdle.

Ben Carroll ordered the immediate and independent cost assessment of the Western Renewables Link (WRL) today, after Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny announced the approval of the project's environment effects statement (EES) overnight.

Mr Carroll said in a statement the review aimed to reduce building costs, and there would be no compulsory acquisition of property while it was underway.

"I respect the public's money. This project was planned almost 10 years ago and Victorian consumers deserve updated, transparent costings," Mr Carroll said.

The proposed route for the Western Renewables Link. (Supplied: Jeremy Harper)

The proposed 190-kilometre transmission line would run between Bulgana, near Ararat in the state's west, and Sydenham in Melbourne's north-west, to connect renewable energy projects in western Victoria to the energy grid.

In the EES, Ms Kilkenny found the project would likely have a significant impact on the environment, namely on "visual amenity" and "landscape values".

But, overall, she found the possible community benefit meant it could proceed and environmental damage could be managed.

The project has caused significant, enduring unrest for many landholders who live in its corridor.

The premier did not indicate whether Labor was reconsidering its commitment to the project when announcing the cost review.

More approvals required

Mr Carroll said in a statement the EES was not a final approval, and the project still required state and Commonwealth agency approvals and the green light from parliament.

Ben Carroll has ordered an immediate review into the cost of the WRL. (ABC News)

However, AusNet, the company responsible for the WRL, can use the assessment as leverage to gain other approvals.

According to AusNet, those secondary requirements may include a permit to remove protected flora under the Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act 1988, a permit to relocate wildlife under the Wildlife Act 1975 and a permit to work within or over waterways under the Water Act 1989.

Mr Carroll said in a statement the EES would be completed by the end of the year and its findings would be made public.

Shadow Energy Minister David Davis condemned the government for approving the EES two and a half months before the November election.

David Davis is critical of the government's energy rollout. (ABC News: Richard Sydenham)

"The opposition wrote to the government and said not to grant or provide approvals at this point under the cover of the pre-election period," Mr Davis said.

"The government has sat on this document, it seems, since July and now released it late in the piece in the lead-up to the state election.

"We say the government should not make steps that bind future governments."

Mr Carroll told ABC he was unavailable for an interview.

The future of the WRL is uncertain if Labor loses the November election.

The Coalition has promised it would pause and reconsider the future of WRL if it was elected.

One Nation has said it would cancel the project entirely.

The latest costing for the project is $1.5 billion, more than three times the initial figure given in 2019.

The project has also suffered timeline blowouts. The latest estimate from AusNet said the project would be completed by 2029.

Project 'does not have social licence'

Ripon's Labor incumbent Martha Haylett, the state member for the local government areas where the WRL and a second proposed transmission line called VNI West are set to be built, said in a statement she was glad Mr Carroll had listened to her objections.

Farmers rally at the Marnoo recreation reserve in support of One Nation and against VNI West. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

"It has been 1365 days since I spoke about our community's opposition to the Western Renewables Link in my first speech in Parliament," Ms Haylett said in the statement.

"I have raised my objections to this project with three successive Premiers …

"I've said from day one that this project does not have social licence in our community, and that has not changed."

Fifth-generation beef, sheep and potato farmer Gerald Conroy said the EES identified the same issues he and his neighbours in Ballan had been raising for six years.

He said he disagreed with the government's stance that environmental impacts could be appropriately managed.

Gerald Conroy farms in the project corridor at Ballan. (ABC News: Coco Veldkamp)

Mr Conroy said the project had divided his community, and he would no longer vote for Labor.

"[I'm] very disappointed in the government. They think they can mitigate these issues by giving more money to the community," he said.

Victorian Farmers Federation (VFF) president Ryan Milgate welcomed the cost review and said the government should reconsider the state's transmission rollout more broadly.

Ryan Milgate says the government needs to apply greater scrutiny to all energy projects. (ABC News: Sean Warren)

"Farmers have been saying for years that the WRL needs greater scrutiny. The government has now acknowledged that," Mr Milgate said.

He said the same questions needed to be asked of VNI West and other renewable energy projects.

"What will these projects cost, and are there better alternatives that don't decimate productive farmland and regional communities?" Mr Milgate said.

Generous jobs forecast

An AusNet spokesperson for the WRL said the project was required to support Victoria's transition from coal-fired power stations.

They said WRL would help power 1 million homes and would carry more than 3,000 megawatts of electricity through 500 kilovolt lines.

The WRL spokesperson said it also aimed to deliver lasting benefits to regional communities along the proposed project route.

"If approved, WRL is estimated to generate around 700 full time construction jobs, with more expected at the height of construction," the spokesperson said.

"A further 1,100 jobs are forecast to be created as a result of building the transmission line.

"This includes $15 million in funding made available during the project's development phase in response to community feedback calling for earlier benefits, including a $4 million Local Grants Fund, which recently received almost 200 applications for locally-led projects."

The councils set to host the transmission lines were contacted for comment.

World.title: WA’s wildflower season was the ‘best in recent memory’. Here’s why
World.content:
NationalWABiodiversity WA’s wildflower season was the ‘best in recent memory’. Here’s why Holly Thompson September 16, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Western Australia’s Mid West has recorded the best wildflower season in almost two decades, with early winter rains contributing to ideal conditions for seeds that had been lying dormant for years to finally sprout. In the Shire of Murchison, more than 800 kilometres north of Perth, flowers blanketed the region across August and into September. The CSIRO Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory in WA’s Mid West wildflower region. CSIRO/ Red Empire Media At the CSIRO’s Radio-astronomy Observatory, the variety has impressed long-time Murchison local Andrew Whitmarsh – also the CSIRO’s land manager for the observatory site. The flowers this year have bloomed right up against the radio telescopes that peer into the far reaches of space.



The season also began early this season, triggered by generous downpours starting with Cyclone Mitchell back in February. Whitmarsh said the soil’s “seed bank” had come alive, with the early season rains allowing many seeds that were dormant for years through drier conditions to germinate. “Different species like different conditions, but this year has been a free-for-all with so many varieties blooming at the same time,” he said. “I don’t think I’ve seen a display this good since 2008.” The CSIRO’s observatory land management team work closely with WA biodiversity experts to monitor and document the species at the observatory.



Over the last decade, the observatory’s presence has necessitated a change in land use for the site, from pastoral lease to radio astronomy only, which included adapting water management and land care activities. Calandrinia Mirabilis. CSIRO/ Red Empire Media “We take samples and help monitor populations, gathering information to support biodiversity work in Western Australia,” Whitmarsh said. “We’ve helped trace new populations of protected wildflowers, resulting in one already being reduced from a priority 1 to a priority 3 protected species last year.” That species is the Calandrinia Mirabilis, listed as priority 1 until 2025, when the flower’s classification was dropped after additional populations were documented at the observatory site.



At the beginning of the 2026 season, Bush Heritage senior ecologist Michelle Hall said this year’s wildflowers were putting on a “spectacular show”. Related Article Biodiversity In WA’s ochre-red Mid West, a cyclone’s deluge fuels carpets of wildflowers “There aren’t many places in the world where you can see this kind of thing,” she said. “The Mid West is particularly known for these amazing carpets of flowers. It’s an extreme arid environment that occasionally gets cyclones coming through. That’s what caused this big display.” As the wildflower season comes towards its end across the Mid West, the CSIRO team already has their eyes on the future.



“We plan to increase our water flow management activity across the site, minimising the movement of water where it wouldn’t naturally go through reducing road-side windrows and constructing pond banks,” Whitmarsh said. While he said he doesn’t expect to see another wildflower season like this one again next year, it is likely there will be growing displays as the land changes with its new use. “We’re seeing extra plant variety and growth in the areas where the soil has been disturbed near the telescopes, as well as slow-growing tree species like Mulgas growing and surviving in new spaces across the site,” he said.

World.title: High seas and low fuel: Energy-efficient ship launches in Fremantle
World.content:
NationalWAShipping High seas and low fuel: Energy-efficient ship launches in Fremantle Michael Philipps September 16, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As Western Australians prepare for more shocks at the petrol station with the price of fuel set to increase once again due to the ongoing war in the Middle East, Klaveness Combination Carriers chief executive Engebret Dahm understands the situation in the Strait of Hormuz better than most. One of the company’s ships was trapped in the Middle East Gulf since the start of the conflict in February this year, before finally safely exiting the area late in June. The MV Baltazar was officially named at a ceremony in Fremantle port this week. KCC was a frequent visitor to the region, delivering WA alumina to the area on a regular basis, where the export was one of the company’s major markets until the war began. “Our company is probably the biggest shipper of alumina to the Middle East,” Dahm said.



“Unfortunately, at the moment, it’s not working as it should because we can’t take the ships through the Strait of Hormuz.” With fresh concerns growing over the price of oil due to the conflict, KCC has launched a brand-new vessel that aims to use wind technology that the company believes will not just reduce emissions, but also improve fuel efficiency on its voyages between China and Australia. Equipped with the first wind-assisted propulsion system in KCC’s fleet and a range of advanced energy efficiency technologies, MV Baltazar was officially launched at Fremantle Port this week, with WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti given the honour as the ship’s “Lady Sponsor” at its naming ceremony. As part of the ceremony, a portrait of the state’s deputy premier is on show in the ship’s mess and she is considered a permanent, although honorary, member of the crew. According to the company, due to the ship’s trading area, size and advanced energy efficiency measures including suction sails, MV Baltazar has the lowest carbon footprint of any vessel in these trades.



The company is currently working with several WA-based importers and exporters, including Alcoa, South32, Fenix Resources, Wesfarmers and CSBP, in addition to shipping some grain for CBH. Dahm said Fremantle was chosen as the place for the ship’s launch due to the number of customers and clients that were able to be in attendance, while also honouring the connection the company has with the state’s local ports. KCC chief executive Engebret Dahm with MV Baltazar captain at the launch of the ship. Michael Philipps In Western Australia, the ship delivers caustic soda and fertiliser products to clients at Bunbury, Kwinana, Fremantle and Geraldton ports. It then exports iron ore, alumina and grains among its dry goods. South32 and the shipping company have jointly developed a mechanism called the carbon adjustment factor to link freight paid to the carbon emission performance of KCC’s vessels relative to an agreed baseline.



The deal results in KCC being paid a higher rate if greenhouse gas freight emissions are below the baseline or a lower rate if emissions exceed the baseline. Dahm said companies like South32 are focusing on reducing the carbon footprint of the supply chain, and believes KCC’s new ship technology will be able to deliver for the client. However, he stressed that the ship is about to undergo its maiden voyage which will give KCC a better understanding of how the technology will improve energy efficiency and reduce emissions. “We think the wind is probably one of the more promising types (of fuel efficiency measures),” he said. “If you add up all the different initiatives, you probably come up to between 12 and 13 per cent reduction, depending on how they impact each other.”



Dahm said the vessel is also prepared for future retrofitting to enable the use of zero or near-zero emission fuels. “If you take the wind, the potential, the shaft generator, you’re probably talking about $8 or $9 million,” he said. “We have an estimate to make the ships one of the most energy-efficient ships in the world.”

World.title: Tree canopy vs junior footy: Freo community clashes over plan to chop 26 trees
World.content:
NationalWALocal council Tree canopy vs junior footy: Freo community clashes over plan to chop 26 trees Indigo Lemay-Conway September 16, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fremantle residents have had their say on the two dozen trees earmarked for removal to make way for a playing field expansion in Beaconsfield – and they didn’t hold back. About 300 residents crammed into the Fremantle Town Hall for a special electors’ meeting on Tuesday night with two opposing goals in mind: halt all tree removals across the port city, or rip the trees out to make another oval as originally planned. Locals were outraged when they learned last month that 26 trees were earmarked to get the chop at Hilton Park, one of Fremantle’s largest recreation and sporting open spaces. The popular playing fields are in the midst of a major redevelopment, and the trees, some of which included Norfolk Pines, would have to be removed to make way for a junior football oval.



‘Not an either-or choice’ Mark Woodcock’s motion to halt all mature tree removals in the City was passed - but only narrowly. The motion will be discussed by council next week. Indigo Lemay-Conway A petition signed by almost 600 electors triggered the special council meeting, where they called on the council to pause the removal of the trees, and also consider their tree retention policy as a whole. The proposed motion by resident Mark Woodcock asked the council to “immediately halt all clearing and mature tree removals across the City of Fremantle, specifically including the destruction of mature trees at Hilton Reserve”. It also requests a mandate that “any future infrastructure, sports, or masterplan developments must be redesigned to prioritise 100 per cent retention of mature urban canopy.”



Hilton Park is approximately 19 hectares and is framed by Carrington Street, Lefroy Road, Shepherd Street and Jeffery Street. Despite plans for the park’s redevelopment being cleared by council in 2024, residents claimed the extent of the tree removal was not quantified until signs went up in the northern portion of the playing fields. Footy club warns of project delay The masterplan for the park sets out a staged approach for the works over 10 years and includes a new community hub, shared soccer facilities, southern cricket and community building, a basketball court, skate park, additional recreation spaces and more trees and shade. To create a new junior oval, the council endorsed the removal of the 26 trees and claimed to have undertaken community consultation where “seventy per cent of respondents supported the concept”.



The plan would also see 61 new native trees – more than double the number of trees removed – planted in the park. Work was due to begin in August to remove asbestos from the site of what was once a BMX track in the park, followed by the removal of the trees, but both were paused until after the electors’ meeting. The town hall was split, with tree canopy advocates and parents of children who play for the Fremantle City Dockers Junior Football Club – one of the groups who would best benefit from the new oval. At least 35 people spoke at the meeting, with many playing tit-for-tat on how many generations they’ve lived in the area for (the highest was 135 years). Three additional motions were submitted to the meeting in relation to the tree removal at Hilton Park.



Woodcock said he made his original motion “just to call attention to what was going on”. “[I wanted] to send a very clear message to council that I feel the vast majority of Fremantle wants to protect the tree canopy,” he said. Fremantle Town Hall was jam packed with electors ready to debate the removal of 26 trees at Hilton Park. Indigo Lemay-Conway “It’s not either or a choice between trees and sports. We don’t have to choose one or the other. We should have both. “Voting tonight does not cancel the sports upgrade. It simply pauses the destructive works that council will take to the tree canopy, and this will allow a review or alternative layouts and engage in a genuine co-design with the community.”



On the opposing side, Fremantle City JFC president Connor Magee said if the motion was successful, it could jeopardise the junior AFL oval that is “so desperately needed” by the club. “It also jeopardises the improvements to the cricket facilities, pump tracks, park accessibility, walking trails, and much more,” he said. “It has been part of our plan for a number of years. We cannot afford to go back to the drawing board now.” ‘No one in here knows what’s going on’ When it came time for the vote on Woodcock’s motion, electors only narrowly voted in favour of it. But before they could get to the other motions, half of the room quickly emptied, with the majority of supporters of the master plan leaving.



What ensued was bureaucratic chaos as the electors shouted that they weren’t aware the following motions would be considered as amendments to Woodcock’s initial motion, instead voting under the assumption they would be individual motions. Related Article Opinion

Environmental protection ‘Perth needs regreening’: Why West Australians should care about our dwindling tree canopy Brendan Foster Contributor “No one in here knows what is going on,” one elector shouted. “I do not believe this was clear. I think this is really unfair, and I’m very frustrated and disappointed,” another elector said, to a room of applause. After a tense few minutes of back and forth, the city’s chief executive, Glen Dougall, gave the approval for each amendment to be considered as new motions.



“It’s a special meeting that’s been asked for a specific purpose. So it’s not like an annual general meeting, so you have to stay on topic,” Dougall said. “At Fremantle, we allow it to bend a little, but we need to keep it at least proximate to the intent of the meeting. The reason 583 people signed that petition was to talk about tree canopy and that’s what we’re trying to stick to.” Dougall said they decided to allow each motion to be voted on individually because “there’s a lot of people who just wanted to vote on it”. “At the end of the day, we’re here to listen to what people have to say. So, they put the motion up, and they voted on it and the council will talk about it next week. Andrew Burton was one of the three electors who put up an additional motion and was under the impression it would be voted on in that manner.



Related Article Updated

Local government City of Perth faces yet another inquiry – this one, with teeth “It’s a very poor process. It doesn’t help the community. It doesn’t help your transparency and democracy, and it doesn’t help show that you’re making evidence-based decisions that give the best solution,” he said of the mismanagement of the meeting. “I hope that we can proceed in a non-polarised way so that we can really just drive for a good solution for everybody. Because at the moment, I don’t see anybody winning.” With half the room gone, each item was voted for and passed and will be discussed by council members at next week’s ordinary council meeting.

World.title: ‘Not the people I interviewed’: Trump lashes Supreme Court after election ruling
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS politics ‘Not the people I interviewed’: Trump lashes Supreme Court after election ruling Michael Koziol September 16, 2026 — 2:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump has launched an extraordinary attack on the US Supreme Court, complaining that the justices he appointed in his first term had failed him, after the court rejected his attempt to curb mail-in voting at the upcoming midterm elections. The conservative-majority bench on Monday (US time) struck down the Trump administration’s bid to require states to submit lists of voters’ names and addresses to the US Postal Service to receive mail-in ballots. Usually, the USPS – an independent agency of the federal government – plays no such role. US President Donald Trump speaking to reporters on Air Force One on Sunday. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson In a one-paragraph emergency ruling, the justices denied the administration’s request to stay a lower court’s decision, saying the government was “unlikely to succeed on the merits of its legal challenge”. Two conservative justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, dissented. It was the third time the Supreme Court torpedoed one of Trump’s signature policy commitments, after ruling his so-called reciprocal tariffs were illegal, and striking down an executive order to end birthright citizenship.



A furious Trump labelled it a “horrible, highly political, ruling” that would damage Republicans and reward the Democrats, whom he baselessly accuses of cheating using mail-in ballots. “The Supreme Court has really let our Country down!” he wrote on Tuesday (US time). “Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America.” Members of the US Supreme Court in 2022: Front row: from left, Sonia Sotomayor, Clarence Thomas, Chief Justice John Roberts, Samuel Alito, and Elena Kagan. Back row, from left, Amy Coney Barrett, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Ketanji Brown Jackson. AP In a lengthy post on Truth Social that reflected on all three judgments against him, the president effectively accused the three conservative justices he appointed to the bench – Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett – of betraying him. “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” he said on Truth Social.



“They are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won’t be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal. “It is a Court that will go down as having rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country’s history.” Trump added that it was “not easy” for him to criticise the court so severely, but he felt he had to. Related Article US midterm elections ‘Trump got the headlines he wanted’: Inside the Republican midterm convention The president’s diatribe contradicted several of his own previous statements. For example, in February, he had lavished praise upon Kavanaugh after the justice dissented in Trump’s favour on the tariff decision. In the past, he claimed that the court’s tariff ruling would not cost the US Treasury anything because the tariffs would be reapplied in a different, lawful way. Now, he says the court has cost the country “trillions”.



Monday’s decision means mail-in voting should proceed as normal ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Time was a key factor in the court case and the decision, with some states already sending out ballots to voters. Kavanaugh, who joined the majority decision to preserve mail-in voting, said in an additional statement that he believed there was a “fair prospect” the Trump administration could succeed on the merits. Related Article Exclusive

US midterm elections No need for midterm election emergency, says Trump’s ‘transparency’ aide “But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections,” he wrote. “For that reason, I concur in the denial of the application for stay.” It remains to be seen what, if anything, Trump can do before the election to curb mail-in voting. His attempts to get Congress to pass the SAVE Act have not succeeded to date, with several Republicans refusing to vote for it.



Meanwhile, some MAGA diehards, including former Trump strategist Steve Bannon, have been calling for the president to call a “national security emergency” ahead of the election that could not be challenged in court. Australia’s Matt Renshaw scored a maiden one-day international century while Nathan Ellis took five wickets to guide their side to a 59-run win over hosts Zimbabwe on Tuesday (local time) in the first clash of their three-match series.

Australia chose to bat first, and the surprise decision from captain Mitchell Marsh was vindicated as they scored 294-8 in their 50 overs, setting Zimbabwe an imposing target at Harare Sports Club.

Australia’s batsman Matt Renshaw celebrates his century during the first ODI against Zimbabwe. AP Photo/Wonder Mashura

In reply, Zimbabwe were dismissed for 235 in 45.1 overs, showing good fight but always behind the required run rate.

Renshaw, who last scored an international ton in a Test against Pakistan in 2017, made 109 and featured in key partnerships after Cooper Connolly survived a few let-offs before being bowled by Zimbabwe captain Sikandar Raza for 51.

World.title: Gambling company let more than 150 problem gamblers stay on platform
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesOnline gambling Gambling company let more than 150 problem gamblers stay on platform Elias Visontay September 16, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dabble, a social media-linked betting platform, has been slapped with more than $1 million in penalties after it breached self-exclusion laws, kept the accounts of more than 150 problem gamblers open and sent marketing material to them more than 800 times. The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) on Wednesday announced its investigation into the wagering platform – that allows users to copy bets from friends, former sports stars or other personalities – found a range of breaches of national self-exclusion laws known as BetStop. Dabble was fined more than $1 million for breaching self-exclusion laws. iStock The ACMA said Dabble, for which betting giant Tabcorp paid $33 million for a 20 per cent stake in 2022, failed to close 157 wagering accounts after the account holders registered with BetStop. The betting platform founded by former PointsBet and CrownBet executive Tom Rundle in 2020 and known for its sponsorship of the National Basketball League and Supercars Championship, also sent 165 self-excluded people a total of 839 electronic messages as either SMS, emails or app push notifications, the ACMA found.



Related Article Exclusive
