World.title: WA’s wildflower season was the ‘best in recent memory’. Here’s why
World.content:
NationalWABiodiversity WA’s wildflower season was the ‘best in recent memory’. Here’s why Holly Thompson September 16, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Western Australia’s Mid West has recorded the best wildflower season in almost two decades, with early winter rains contributing to ideal conditions for seeds that had been lying dormant for years to finally sprout. In the Shire of Murchison, more than 800 kilometres north of Perth, flowers blanketed the region across August and into September. The CSIRO Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory in WA’s Mid West wildflower region. CSIRO/ Red Empire Media At the CSIRO’s Radio-astronomy Observatory, the variety has impressed long-time Murchison local Andrew Whitmarsh – also the CSIRO’s land manager for the observatory site. The flowers this year have bloomed right up against the radio telescopes that peer into the far reaches of space.



The season also began early this season, triggered by generous downpours starting with Cyclone Mitchell back in February. Whitmarsh said the soil’s “seed bank” had come alive, with the early season rains allowing many seeds that were dormant for years through drier conditions to germinate. “Different species like different conditions, but this year has been a free-for-all with so many varieties blooming at the same time,” he said. “I don’t think I’ve seen a display this good since 2008.” The CSIRO’s observatory land management team work closely with WA biodiversity experts to monitor and document the species at the observatory.



Over the last decade, the observatory’s presence has necessitated a change in land use for the site, from pastoral lease to radio astronomy only, which included adapting water management and land care activities. Calandrinia Mirabilis. CSIRO/ Red Empire Media “We take samples and help monitor populations, gathering information to support biodiversity work in Western Australia,” Whitmarsh said. “We’ve helped trace new populations of protected wildflowers, resulting in one already being reduced from a priority 1 to a priority 3 protected species last year.” That species is the Calandrinia Mirabilis, listed as priority 1 until 2025, when the flower’s classification was dropped after additional populations were documented at the observatory site.



At the beginning of the 2026 season, Bush Heritage senior ecologist Michelle Hall said this year’s wildflowers were putting on a “spectacular show”. Related Article Biodiversity In WA’s ochre-red Mid West, a cyclone’s deluge fuels carpets of wildflowers “There aren’t many places in the world where you can see this kind of thing,” she said. “The Mid West is particularly known for these amazing carpets of flowers. It’s an extreme arid environment that occasionally gets cyclones coming through. That’s what caused this big display.” As the wildflower season comes towards its end across the Mid West, the CSIRO team already has their eyes on the future.



“We plan to increase our water flow management activity across the site, minimising the movement of water where it wouldn’t naturally go through reducing road-side windrows and constructing pond banks,” Whitmarsh said. While he said he doesn’t expect to see another wildflower season like this one again next year, it is likely there will be growing displays as the land changes with its new use. “We’re seeing extra plant variety and growth in the areas where the soil has been disturbed near the telescopes, as well as slow-growing tree species like Mulgas growing and surviving in new spaces across the site,” he said.

World.title: High seas and low fuel: Energy-efficient ship launches in Fremantle
World.content:
NationalWAShipping High seas and low fuel: Energy-efficient ship launches in Fremantle Michael Philipps September 16, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As Western Australians prepare for more shocks at the petrol station with the price of fuel set to increase once again due to the ongoing war in the Middle East, Klaveness Combination Carriers chief executive Engebret Dahm understands the situation in the Strait of Hormuz better than most. One of the company’s ships was trapped in the Middle East Gulf since the start of the conflict in February this year, before finally safely exiting the area late in June. The MV Baltazar was officially named at a ceremony in Fremantle port this week. KCC was a frequent visitor to the region, delivering WA alumina to the area on a regular basis, where the export was one of the company’s major markets until the war began. “Our company is probably the biggest shipper of alumina to the Middle East,” Dahm said.



“Unfortunately, at the moment, it’s not working as it should because we can’t take the ships through the Strait of Hormuz.” With fresh concerns growing over the price of oil due to the conflict, KCC has launched a brand-new vessel that aims to use wind technology that the company believes will not just reduce emissions, but also improve fuel efficiency on its voyages between China and Australia. Equipped with the first wind-assisted propulsion system in KCC’s fleet and a range of advanced energy efficiency technologies, MV Baltazar was officially launched at Fremantle Port this week, with WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti given the honour as the ship’s “Lady Sponsor” at its naming ceremony. As part of the ceremony, a portrait of the state’s deputy premier is on show in the ship’s mess and she is considered a permanent, although honorary, member of the crew. According to the company, due to the ship’s trading area, size and advanced energy efficiency measures including suction sails, MV Baltazar has the lowest carbon footprint of any vessel in these trades.



The company is currently working with several WA-based importers and exporters, including Alcoa, South32, Fenix Resources, Wesfarmers and CSBP, in addition to shipping some grain for CBH. Dahm said Fremantle was chosen as the place for the ship’s launch due to the number of customers and clients that were able to be in attendance, while also honouring the connection the company has with the state’s local ports. KCC chief executive Engebret Dahm with MV Baltazar captain at the launch of the ship. Michael Philipps In Western Australia, the ship delivers caustic soda and fertiliser products to clients at Bunbury, Kwinana, Fremantle and Geraldton ports. It then exports iron ore, alumina and grains among its dry goods. South32 and the shipping company have jointly developed a mechanism called the carbon adjustment factor to link freight paid to the carbon emission performance of KCC’s vessels relative to an agreed baseline.



The deal results in KCC being paid a higher rate if greenhouse gas freight emissions are below the baseline or a lower rate if emissions exceed the baseline. Dahm said companies like South32 are focusing on reducing the carbon footprint of the supply chain, and believes KCC’s new ship technology will be able to deliver for the client. However, he stressed that the ship is about to undergo its maiden voyage which will give KCC a better understanding of how the technology will improve energy efficiency and reduce emissions. “We think the wind is probably one of the more promising types (of fuel efficiency measures),” he said. “If you add up all the different initiatives, you probably come up to between 12 and 13 per cent reduction, depending on how they impact each other.”



Dahm said the vessel is also prepared for future retrofitting to enable the use of zero or near-zero emission fuels. “If you take the wind, the potential, the shaft generator, you’re probably talking about $8 or $9 million,” he said. “We have an estimate to make the ships one of the most energy-efficient ships in the world.”

World.title: Tree canopy vs junior footy: Freo community clashes over plan to chop 26 trees
World.content:
NationalWALocal council Tree canopy vs junior footy: Freo community clashes over plan to chop 26 trees Indigo Lemay-Conway September 16, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fremantle residents have had their say on the two dozen trees earmarked for removal to make way for a playing field expansion in Beaconsfield – and they didn’t hold back. About 300 residents crammed into the Fremantle Town Hall for a special electors’ meeting on Tuesday night with two opposing goals in mind: halt all tree removals across the port city, or rip the trees out to make another oval as originally planned. Locals were outraged when they learned last month that 26 trees were earmarked to get the chop at Hilton Park, one of Fremantle’s largest recreation and sporting open spaces. The popular playing fields are in the midst of a major redevelopment, and the trees, some of which included Norfolk Pines, would have to be removed to make way for a junior football oval.



‘Not an either-or choice’ Mark Woodcock’s motion to halt all mature tree removals in the City was passed - but only narrowly. The motion will be discussed by council next week. Indigo Lemay-Conway A petition signed by almost 600 electors triggered the special council meeting, where they called on the council to pause the removal of the trees, and also consider their tree retention policy as a whole. The proposed motion by resident Mark Woodcock asked the council to “immediately halt all clearing and mature tree removals across the City of Fremantle, specifically including the destruction of mature trees at Hilton Reserve”. It also requests a mandate that “any future infrastructure, sports, or masterplan developments must be redesigned to prioritise 100 per cent retention of mature urban canopy.”



Hilton Park is approximately 19 hectares and is framed by Carrington Street, Lefroy Road, Shepherd Street and Jeffery Street. Despite plans for the park’s redevelopment being cleared by council in 2024, residents claimed the extent of the tree removal was not quantified until signs went up in the northern portion of the playing fields. Footy club warns of project delay The masterplan for the park sets out a staged approach for the works over 10 years and includes a new community hub, shared soccer facilities, southern cricket and community building, a basketball court, skate park, additional recreation spaces and more trees and shade. To create a new junior oval, the council endorsed the removal of the 26 trees and claimed to have undertaken community consultation where “seventy per cent of respondents supported the concept”.



The plan would also see 61 new native trees – more than double the number of trees removed – planted in the park. Work was due to begin in August to remove asbestos from the site of what was once a BMX track in the park, followed by the removal of the trees, but both were paused until after the electors’ meeting. The town hall was split, with tree canopy advocates and parents of children who play for the Fremantle City Dockers Junior Football Club – one of the groups who would best benefit from the new oval. At least 35 people spoke at the meeting, with many playing tit-for-tat on how many generations they’ve lived in the area for (the highest was 135 years). Three additional motions were submitted to the meeting in relation to the tree removal at Hilton Park.



Woodcock said he made his original motion “just to call attention to what was going on”. “[I wanted] to send a very clear message to council that I feel the vast majority of Fremantle wants to protect the tree canopy,” he said. Fremantle Town Hall was jam packed with electors ready to debate the removal of 26 trees at Hilton Park. Indigo Lemay-Conway “It’s not either or a choice between trees and sports. We don’t have to choose one or the other. We should have both. “Voting tonight does not cancel the sports upgrade. It simply pauses the destructive works that council will take to the tree canopy, and this will allow a review or alternative layouts and engage in a genuine co-design with the community.”



On the opposing side, Fremantle City JFC president Connor Magee said if the motion was successful, it could jeopardise the junior AFL oval that is “so desperately needed” by the club. “It also jeopardises the improvements to the cricket facilities, pump tracks, park accessibility, walking trails, and much more,” he said. “It has been part of our plan for a number of years. We cannot afford to go back to the drawing board now.” ‘No one in here knows what’s going on’ When it came time for the vote on Woodcock’s motion, electors only narrowly voted in favour of it. But before they could get to the other motions, half of the room quickly emptied, with the majority of supporters of the master plan leaving.



What ensued was bureaucratic chaos as the electors shouted that they weren’t aware the following motions would be considered as amendments to Woodcock’s initial motion, instead voting under the assumption they would be individual motions. Related Article Opinion

Environmental protection ‘Perth needs regreening’: Why West Australians should care about our dwindling tree canopy Brendan Foster Contributor “No one in here knows what is going on,” one elector shouted. “I do not believe this was clear. I think this is really unfair, and I’m very frustrated and disappointed,” another elector said, to a room of applause. After a tense few minutes of back and forth, the city’s chief executive, Glen Dougall, gave the approval for each amendment to be considered as new motions.



“It’s a special meeting that’s been asked for a specific purpose. So it’s not like an annual general meeting, so you have to stay on topic,” Dougall said. “At Fremantle, we allow it to bend a little, but we need to keep it at least proximate to the intent of the meeting. The reason 583 people signed that petition was to talk about tree canopy and that’s what we’re trying to stick to.” Dougall said they decided to allow each motion to be voted on individually because “there’s a lot of people who just wanted to vote on it”. “At the end of the day, we’re here to listen to what people have to say. So, they put the motion up, and they voted on it and the council will talk about it next week. Andrew Burton was one of the three electors who put up an additional motion and was under the impression it would be voted on in that manner.



Related Article Updated

Local government City of Perth faces yet another inquiry – this one, with teeth “It’s a very poor process. It doesn’t help the community. It doesn’t help your transparency and democracy, and it doesn’t help show that you’re making evidence-based decisions that give the best solution,” he said of the mismanagement of the meeting. “I hope that we can proceed in a non-polarised way so that we can really just drive for a good solution for everybody. Because at the moment, I don’t see anybody winning.” With half the room gone, each item was voted for and passed and will be discussed by council members at next week’s ordinary council meeting.

World.title: ‘Not the people I interviewed’: Trump lashes Supreme Court after election ruling
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS politics ‘Not the people I interviewed’: Trump lashes Supreme Court after election ruling Michael Koziol September 16, 2026 — 2:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump has launched an extraordinary attack on the US Supreme Court, complaining that the justices he appointed in his first term had failed him, after the court rejected his attempt to curb mail-in voting at the upcoming midterm elections. The conservative-majority bench on Monday (US time) struck down the Trump administration’s bid to require states to submit lists of voters’ names and addresses to the US Postal Service to receive mail-in ballots. Usually, the USPS – an independent agency of the federal government – plays no such role. US President Donald Trump speaking to reporters on Air Force One on Sunday. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson In a one-paragraph emergency ruling, the justices denied the administration’s request to stay a lower court’s decision, saying the government was “unlikely to succeed on the merits of its legal challenge”. Two conservative justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, dissented. It was the third time the Supreme Court torpedoed one of Trump’s signature policy commitments, after ruling his so-called reciprocal tariffs were illegal, and striking down an executive order to end birthright citizenship.



A furious Trump labelled it a “horrible, highly political, ruling” that would damage Republicans and reward the Democrats, whom he baselessly accuses of cheating using mail-in ballots. “The Supreme Court has really let our Country down!” he wrote on Tuesday (US time). “Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America.” Members of the US Supreme Court in 2022: Front row: from left, Sonia Sotomayor, Clarence Thomas, Chief Justice John Roberts, Samuel Alito, and Elena Kagan. Back row, from left, Amy Coney Barrett, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Ketanji Brown Jackson. AP In a lengthy post on Truth Social that reflected on all three judgments against him, the president effectively accused the three conservative justices he appointed to the bench – Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett – of betraying him. “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” he said on Truth Social.



“They are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won’t be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal. “It is a Court that will go down as having rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country’s history.” Trump added that it was “not easy” for him to criticise the court so severely, but he felt he had to. Related Article US midterm elections ‘Trump got the headlines he wanted’: Inside the Republican midterm convention The president’s diatribe contradicted several of his own previous statements. For example, in February, he had lavished praise upon Kavanaugh after the justice dissented in Trump’s favour on the tariff decision. In the past, he claimed that the court’s tariff ruling would not cost the US Treasury anything because the tariffs would be reapplied in a different, lawful way. Now, he says the court has cost the country “trillions”.



Monday’s decision means mail-in voting should proceed as normal ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Time was a key factor in the court case and the decision, with some states already sending out ballots to voters. Kavanaugh, who joined the majority decision to preserve mail-in voting, said in an additional statement that he believed there was a “fair prospect” the Trump administration could succeed on the merits. Related Article Exclusive

US midterm elections No need for midterm election emergency, says Trump’s ‘transparency’ aide “But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections,” he wrote. “For that reason, I concur in the denial of the application for stay.” It remains to be seen what, if anything, Trump can do before the election to curb mail-in voting. His attempts to get Congress to pass the SAVE Act have not succeeded to date, with several Republicans refusing to vote for it.



Meanwhile, some MAGA diehards, including former Trump strategist Steve Bannon, have been calling for the president to call a “national security emergency” ahead of the election that could not be challenged in court. World.title: Judicial review sought over fast-track for Auckland seaside village redevelopment
World.content:
A group of Devonport locals are taking legal action against the government after a multi-storey development in their suburb was referred to the fast-track process.

Developer Peninsula Capital wants to transform the seaside village on Auckland's North Shore, with residential apartments and a 50-room hotel.

But at a community meeting in July, Devonport Heritage Society members said the up to eight-storey or 27-metre-high buildings would overpower the suburb's heritage main street and block views of the Takarunga Maunga.

Transport Minister Chris Bishop referred the proposal to the fast-track approvals process in August.

Devonport Heritage Society chair Margot McRae said they applied for a judicial review of the minister's decision at the High Court in Wellington this week.

"The society's decision to issue proceedings follows a groundswell of anger in Devonport about the proposed building heights and the fact that Peninsula Capital have side-stepped local consultation by going through fast-track.

"We haven't taken this step lightly, and we have a big task ahead. But we felt we had to do this to protect this unique and beautiful place."

An artist's impression of plans for 'Devonport Lanes' at the centre of the issue. Peninsula Capital

By law, some groups must be consulted on fast-tracked projects, including relevant local authorities and iwi groups, and owners of neighbouring land.

But there would not be an opportunity for the Heritage Society or the general public to submit feedback on Peninsula Capital's plans as part of the fast-track process.

McCrae said the fast-tracking had become a "rubber-stamp exercise".

"Once these applications are on fast-track, it seems difficult to decline them, and this has led to some irrational outcomes.

"So we are taking this on behalf of not only Devonport but for all the communities around New Zealand who are outraged about how these out-of-sequence housing developments are being pushed through. It's all speed and no care. By taking legal action, perhaps it will lead to better decision-making."

A community meeting in July to oppose the project. RNZ / Jessica Hopkins

The group argued the developer should instead go through Auckland Council's resource consent process.

She said the group had hired Alan Webb KC to represent them in court, and they expected the legal fight would cost them upwards of $70,000.

"We'll be trying to raise money from our community and from the rest of the country to do this.

"We're asking our community and anyone who loves Devonport to put money in."

Bishop's office said it would not be appropriate for him to comment while the matter was before the courts.

Peninsula Capital managing director Mark Hiddleston said it would be inappropriate to comment as "this is a matter between Devonport Heritage and the Government".

World.title: Wellington Hospital closes off part of corridor for extra beds
World.content:
Wellington Hospital's emergency department has closed off part of a corridor this week to accommodate extra beds as patient numbers remain high.

Health NZ acting interim group director of operations for Capital, Coast and Hutt Valley Robert Blaikie said: "At times when there is high occupancy [in ED], steps are taken to temporarily increase capacity by placing up to four beds in a corridor outside the ED observation unit for stable patients awaiting admission or discharge."

That was the case on Wednesday morning.

"A nurse is assigned to this area for monitoring," he said. "To minimise disruption and create privacy for these patients, access to the corridor is temporarily restricted."

This winter had brought a significant increase in presentations to emergency departments across the country, he said.

This flu season, a particularly contagious strain of influenza, coupled with already high occupancy rates in hospitals, was contributing to high levels of stress across the health system nationwide.

Alongside steps to temporarily increase capacity, Blaikie said Health NZ was prioritising acute care, increasing temporary capacity in wards, freeing up more inpatient beds by frequently reviewing ward patients to assess if they were ready for discharge, and using additional community support, such as early supported discharge.

It was also ensuring suitable ED patients were being seen in alternate primary care places, outside of EDs.

Blaikie said it reinforced the importance of work underway to relocate and expand the ED and increase capacity in acute services.

World.title: Getting youth to the polls - a perennial problem
World.content:
Changes to enrolment rules may mean potential voters are left without a voice.

Getting youth to the polls - a perennial problem The Detail Download MP3 21m

Why are young people not enrolling to vote?

For the past five elections, the numbers of eligible voters aged 18-24 has been dropping and this year is no exception.

As of the end of August, just 57.4 percent of 18 to 24-year-olds were enrolled, down nearly three percent from 2023 and five percent from the previous election.

Associate Professor of Politics at Victoria University of Wellington Dr Lara Greaves says there are theories why young people are not enrolling but they can not be certain.

"There's something in society that's not quite going right, and young people are the ones who are picking up on it."

Dr Greaves says a declining trust in politics, experts and government institutions is an issue and there needs to be more effort from groups such as political parties to connect with young people.

"That could mean doing politics a little differently right? That could mean citizens assemblies or some other type of what they call 'deliberative democracy', which is actually talking to people and recording their views in some way and having that be part of the policy process or input.

"So there are other ways you can go about politics but the system has been pretty reluctant to change and change the status quo," Greaves tells The Detail.

There are also concerns changes to the enrolment rules will see potential young voters turned away from the polls.

Voters must now be enrolled before 25 October, the day before advance voting begins.

Dr Greaves says last election, 48 percent of Māori aged 18 and 19 enrolled during the two-week lead up to polling day.

"That's my big concern this election. You can't just show up and enrol and vote and that could be what some of that 43 percent are waiting for."

One initiative motivating young Māori across the motu to get to the polling booth is 'The Landline' campaign.

Ngā iwi o Taranaki have come together to create the online campaign to "entertain, educate and encourage Māori to enrol and vote".

'The Landline' campaign was created to entertain, educate and encourage Māori to enrol and vote, says Anaru Marshall. Supplied

Ngāti Maru Pouwhakahaere and chief executive Anaru Marshall says getting Māori enrolled and out voting is important this election - pointing to the last local body elections as an example of what happens when you do not.

"There was a referendum around the Māori ward seats on district councils. Here in Taranaki we lost our Māori ward seats from the three district councils - New Plymouth, Stratford and South Taranaki...

"So, part of the reason is we need to become enrolled and have representation ... we felt the seats weren't necessarily voted out, it's just that Māori didn't turn up and vote them in," Marshall tells The Detail.

Based around the symbol of the kūmara vine, Marshall says the campaign hopes to encourage "Māori to pick up that kōrero and reach out to each other, ensure that they enrol and cast their vote at the end of the year".

The campaign features well known Māori faces like musician Stan Walker, Māori AI founder Dan Te Whenua Walker, comedian Joe Daymond and Māori lawyer Riana Te Ngahue.

Marshall says one thing that became apparent when asking rangatahi questions about why they weren't enrolled was that they "aren't aware of the electoral system".

"That's simply because they're just not engaged in it, they're not engaging in it and that's a risk...

"And some of the feedback was they felt their vote wouldn't count, politics is nasty, and it just won't make any change, there won't be any difference. So, that was a lot of the impetus for launching this campaign."

Dr Greaves says getting people to understand how our everyday lives are affected by decisions made in parliament is important and their vote does make a difference.

"So, if you have a hundred thousand people that go 'oh my vote doesn't make a difference', that's a hundred thousand votes right? That's an election changing amount of votes that could change the outcome of New Zealand's history right?"

Check out how to listen to and follow The Detail here.

World.title: Is it time to check your streaming subscriptions?
World.content:
Could I run out of money in retirement and other questions experts wish you'd ask No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

Do you really need all the TV streaming services you're paying for?

Westpac says it has noticed an increase in the amount people are paying for streaming services, and the number of services they are subscribing to.

The bank said the median amount being spent by its customers on streaming was $34 a month. But about 10 percent of customers who were paying for TV subscriptions were spending more than $80 a month on them.

Managing director of product, sustainability and marketing Sarah Hearn said it could be a good time to review entertainment spending.

"Some people may want to keep all their services, but we know other people may have just lost track of how many subscriptions they're currently paying for.

"Our data shows around 15 percent of our customers who are paying for TV subscriptions currently have three or more subscriptions - up from 9 percent on the same timeframe last year - so it's worth taking the time to look at what you're signed up for."

The Westpac data includes subscriptions such as Netflix or Disney+, as well as Sky TV.

"We know the cost of living is something that's been a concern for many people this year and some people may have already been looking to cut back on their spending," Hearn said.

She said another 7 percent of customers were spending at least $100 a month.

The Westpac data showed TV subscription spend over the winter months was up 5 percent this year compared to last year.

Younger customers spent slightly less than older customers - those aged 18-29 typically spent $26 per month, compared to $34 per month for those in the 30-to-49 and 50-plus age groups.

Head of everyday banking product Simon Macdonald said daylight saving beginning was a good time to do a spring clean on spending.

"Subscriptions can be a bit of a classic (leak as the spend just rolls over from month to month."

World.title: Westport's new real-time flood forecasting system to help plan for evacuations
World.content:
A new real-time flood forecasting system will help Westport Civil Defence to plan possible evacuations a day or more in advance.

Developed by Earth Sciences New Zealand and West Coast Regional Council, the system is the first of its kind in the country.

It combines tides, river flows and weather forecasts to predict where floodwaters might go during severe weather, the probability of that flooding happening, and how deep the water could get.

The system, which can produce flood projections 48 hours in advance, could then be passed on to emergency management staff to plan how to respond before flooding arrived.

Regional council hydrology manager Samwell Warren said traditionally, flood warnings tended to be reactive.

"Five years ago, a river alarm would go off to say a river level was rising and then that would create a chain of action."

At that time, emergency management staff would have about six hours' notice to plan evacuations.

Now, if damaging flooding looked likely, then older people and other vulnerable residents could be evacuated early and other residents could be put on stand-by.

That was important in a place like Westport, he said.

"Evacuation routes can get cut off for all sorts of things, landslides through the Buller Gorge, river flooding, bridges being overtopped, that sort of thing."

Westport has flooded repeatedly over its history, escalating in recent years.

The low-lying West Coast town is hemmed in by the ocean and the Buller River, along with the Orowaiti River, which can rise dramatically when the Buller floods.

Westport suffered damaging floods in 2021 and 2022. ESNZ / Stuart Mackay

ESNZ hydrological forecasting scientist Céline Cattoën-Gilbert, who led the project, said that made any severe weather event "high stakes" for Westport.

"It can find itself in the middle of two riverbeds when [the Orowaiti] gets activated, and it can be quite dangerous if it keeps rising because it becomes effectively an island."

Twin floods in 2021 and 2022 left more than 100 Westport homes uninhabitable, and damaged farms and infrastructure.

Late last year, AA Insurance informed Buller District Council it would not offer new policies there until the town's flood exposure dropped below the company's maximum exposure level.

Buller District Council has endorsed a plan that could eventually see the town gradually relocated to higher ground away from the Buller River, by opening up lower-risk land for development.

In the meantime, the regional council has begun work on its 'Resilient Westport' project, which includes building 17 kilometres of stopbanks.

The flood forecasting system - which is now fully operational and automatically updates every six hours - was a crucial part of the town's overall flood management plan, Samwell Warren said.

"If the model is showing us something 48 hours out that we're concerned about, that kicks off our flood impact risk specialist team."

Earth Sciences New Zealand hydrological forecasting scientist Dr Céline Cattoën-Gilbert leads a workshop with West Coast regional council staff and locals about the new flood inundation forecasting system. Supplied / ESNZ

The projections would refine and improve the closer a severe weather event got.

"One of the really smart things the model does is that it feeds in flow information and river level information that we have at a number of our sites," he said.

"If it's forecasting something is going to happen at one of those locations and then what our monitoring equipment is picking up is different, it adapts its forecast based on that."

There were still limitations, he said.

"Given that it's driven by a forecast, rainfall can arrive somewhere differently in the catchment or at a different time, sometimes it lasts longer, and as a result, flood outcome can change," he said.

"So we keep a very close eye on local conditions and changes to things like river channels, what our rain gauge network is showing us relative to what's been forecast, to start building that confidence in what the model is telling us between that 48-hour and 24-hour window."

As a long-term goal, ESNZ was keen to develop real-time flood forecasting for other parts of the country, such as Tairāwhiti, Cattoën-Gilbert said.

"Westport was a great proof of concept that we could do this," she said.

"Aotearoa has one in seven people living in a floodplain... There's things we can do and these systems help us."

West Coast Regional Council chief executive Darryl Lew said work on Westport's physical flood protection scheme was developing through consenting, design, public and land access negotiations.

Community consultation was underway, with significant construction planned from January next year.

The council had also been engaging with the Insurance Council, Lew said.

World.title: Tom Phillips report: The missed opportunities to find the children
World.content:
Less than three months after disappearing with his children for the first time, Tom Phillips did it again. A public inquiry into the handling of the case has found Police and Oranga Tamariki missed opportunities to protect the children and bring them home sooner. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood looks into what the report reveals about the second disappearance.

Eighteen days after Tom Phillips left his ute on the Kiritehere beach, disappearing with his children and making headlines throughout the country, he and his children suddenly reappeared.

He initially refused to speak to police, but the following day he gave them a statement. He said the disappearance was merely a spontaneous camping trip, and "not a deliberate act to take the kids away and avoid the Family Court proceedings".

He also said it was the "first time [he] had taken the kids camping like that".

As for why he had decided to return, the father-of-three said he "had a little supplies left… but couldn't [have] stayed for too much longer", and would not tell police where he had taken the children.

Less than three months later he took his children again. This time he spent 1358 days in the bush, the saga ending with Phillips dying following a shootout with police after they were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of 8 September 2025.

Following his death, the Government announced an inquiry into the handling of the Phillips case by authorities and whether all "practicable steps" were taken to ensure the safety and welfare of the Phillips children as well as whether the agencies responded appropriately and in a timely way to locate the children once they had disappeared.

The final report of the inquiry, by Honourable Justice Simon Moore KC, was released on Tuesday.

The report says the harm Phillips caused in isolating the children as well as concerns from the maternal whānau were "minimised or overlooked by agencies for significant periods".

It also says that while agencies worked well together at times a more consistent and collaborative interagency approach "could have prevented the children's disappearance and brought them back sooner".

As for his explanation about his first disappearance, the report says it "sits uncomfortably with the known facts".

"It is incapable of belief for a variety of reasons. The plain inference to be drawn from all of the known facts is that Tom Phillips went into the bush with his children with the intention of not being found."

It says Marokopa was an area Phillips knew very well.

"In some ways it was his backyard"

The sighting of Tom Phillips by a woman who had him in her car in May 2023. Supplied / NZ Police

Operation Marokopa

After Tom Phillips and his children were first reported missing in September 2021, police launched an extensive multi-agency search and rescue investigation dubbed Operation Marokopa.

Moore KC's report said as part of the investigation police built an "extensive and comprehensive profile" of Phillips by speaking to family, friends and searching the properties he and the children had been living in.

Police understood he had significant mental health issues and there were concerns regarding his alcohol use and "conspiracy views".

A person close to Tom Phillips said they were worried that, if cornered, he would turn "violent".

Another person close to him told police he had a dislike of government agencies, "meaning anyone that might try and remove his children from him".

A neighbour reported he had said "f [Covid-19] gets any worse I'm going to the bush". He had also been seen going into Ōtorohanga to purchase alcohol wearing "a full face army-style gas mask".

Moore KC's report said that police did not appear to accept his claims that the first disappearance was simply an impromptu camping trip.

"They appeared to see it for what it was; a father prepared to put his children at risk, and likely to have staged his own death and that of his children by accidental drowning, to defeat the Family Court's processes and deny their mother access."

Police contacted Oranga Tamariki to make a report of concern on 30 September 2021.

Oranga Tamariki's record of the first phone call noted police as saying Phillips had not said anything to police about what happened while he was away with the children.

"There are concerns that Thomas has the potential to do this again and questions as to why his ute was stuck in the sand under the tideline. There are questions around Thomas's mental state."

The report also recorded that police had "no immediate concerns for the childrens (sic) safety".

On 1 October, police developed a "safety plan" to be followed by Phillips which said he would not leave the family farm, would have another family member present at all times, and that police were to be advised of any plans to leave the farm.

A day later police visited him and noted "there were no indications or comments from Tom that he would go bush again with the kids".

Tom Phillips. Supplied

On 5 October, Phillips was charged with making a false report to police, and two days later a police staffer completed a report assessing his suitability to hold a firearms licence.

The report mentioned Phillips' "bizarre" behaviour, including mentions of doomsday prepping, telling family members he would "just take the kids and disappear" from authorities.

Police recommended temporary suspension of his licence on the basis he was not a fit and proper person. They issued the notice on 8 October, but it was not served on him for nearly two months.

Also on 5 October, a social worker and social work supervisor visited the children at the Marokopa home of his parents. Phillips told the social worker he "had no idea" a search and rescue operation was underway, and said he had been wanting to go camping for a while.

He said the trip was "spontaneous but somewhat planned", and that he "would never harm his children nor did he intend to".

Following the visit, Oranga Tamariki (OT) recorded that the family "presented well".

"Tom did not present out of the usual, there were no obvious signs of drug use or mental health. Family was co-operative… Tom appeared to be upset when discussing the court process, but relieved that his family would support him and the children if the children needed to be placed elsewhere."

Phillips' first appearance on his charges was adjourned to January 2022 as a result of Covid-19 restrictions.

OT head Amanda Malu at the Tom Phillips Inquiry release. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The second disappearance

The report says when Phillips took the children for a second time in December 2021, police led the efforts to try and locate them.

The report said some officers who spoke as part of the inquiry said they were worried for the children from the moment they were taken again.

"The then-district commander told the inquiry of his sense of 'foreboding' on learning that Tom Phillips had disappeared into the bush again with the children.

"In fact, such was his level of concern that he wondered whether Tom Phillips had caused himself and the children harm."

However, the report says the "dominant view" of the police on the ground was that there were no immediate concerns for the children's safety.

A senior officer originally assigned to the matter told the inquiry about the thought process.

"The information that I had and the assurance that I sought… from staff that were working on the [first disappearance investigation] was that the kids being away for the first period, there was no major concerns with them being in the bush…. So, I made the assessment at that point given that it had been a short period of time that there was no risk to their health and safety at that point."

Moore KC said this assessment was reflected by police in the following months in internal notes, including one from January 2022 which said "there is no evidence to indicate that the children are at any risk if Phillips has gone bush with them again".

"Given the lack of evidence indicating any concern for the welfare of the children, the need to act or direct resources into locating/arresting Phillips from a risk perspective is low"

The then-area commander told the inquiry that he felt the most effective response was to "softly bring him out" via the use of local staff who knew the rural community they lived and worked in.

The report quotes the area commander as saying it was a deliberate strategy not to "scare Tom because this is a guy that doesn't like the limelight".

Moore KC said the strategy was to "work softly within the community to get him and his children back".

"The sense was that Tom Phillips was likely fearful of the ramifications of a second disappearance and that escalating public interest might be counterproductive to a safe and voluntary return."

In January and early February there were two key sightings which confirmed Phillips was in the broader Marokopa area.

This included Phillips visiting his parents' home alone on 9 February about 12.30am.

The following day, about 3.30pm, police drove to the Te Kūiti Police Station to report the visit.

"His parents told police that the children were not with Tom Phillips when he visited. They said that their son did not disclose the whereabouts of the children but assured them they were safe."

Phillips asked his parents for cash, and he took a significant amount of food.

"He told them he was concerned about the charges against him, and about the children's mother having access to the children."

Minister for Social Development Louise Upston at the Tom Phillips Inquiry release RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Operation Curly

In April 2022, police reassessed their approach and formalised the investigation, Operation Curly.

Moore KC said during Operation Curly police "never gave up on trying to find Tom Phillips and the children", with about 1080 "taskings", such as reported sightings or offending attributed to him generated and followed up.

"They followed up on most reported sightings, even where the likelihood of obtaining a useful lead might have seemed tenuous. They tried to generate leads through media campaigns, area canvasses and, later, the offer of an $80,000 reward for information.

"They examined phone records, bank accounts and social media in an effort to identify any signs of activity. They actively investigated persons of interest who might have some knowledge of the whereabouts of Tom Phillips or who might be assisting him in one way or another."

Moore KC's report divided Operation Curly into four phases. He said that in May 2022, the area commander emailed the district commander and assistant commissioners that "all enquiries have been completed and have not yielded a result".

"Police hold no current intelligence that can be acted on or can enable a deployment of resources."

It was then decided to appoint a "highly experienced" Detective Senior Sergeant as day-to-day officer in charge.

In January, 2023, 13 months into the second disappearance the then-police commissioner made a request for the investigation team to reconsider the possibility of offering a reward.

An application for approval was submitted to the assistant commissioner.

However, the assistant commissioner repeated earlier concerns around "creating a precedent", Moore KC said.

"Currently the only offence committed by Mr Phillips is breach of a parenting order and failing to appear on charges relating to wasting police time post their initial disappearance.

"It is the lack of a serious offence that is causing concern and could potentially create an unruly precedent. This is also an investigative hindrance in terms of specialist investigative capability.

"To date the reward is not supported by either [the district commander] or [the assistant commissioner]."

They also noted the absence of Oranga Tamariki and their views as to the children's welfare.

"At this stage I agree with the decision in regard to the breach of a parenting order however if a Place of Safety warrant or OT has specific concerns then these may need to be factored into the considerations."

Moore KC said the inquiry had seen no evidence that this was put to OT. He said senior police staff "maintained an interest" in the progress of the investigation.

"Through the officer in charge and area and district commanders, requests were made for assistance from specialist police units and NZDF. However, the inquiry notes something of a pattern of these not being followed through in a timely way."

Richard Chambers at yesterday's media conference. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The internal review

In October 2022, the area commander arranged for a police officer from outside the investigation team to review the investigation to date. Then, in March 2023, he asked a detective sergeant from Hamilton who had not been part of the investigation to undertake a more thorough review.

"The March 2023 review noted that the investigation had effectively stalled, relying as it had been, on new sightings reported to police or information provided, largely by the children's mother.

"It noted there were reputational issues for police through the investigation not advancing in the way the public believed it should. It identified that the investigation had been hampered by being carried out largely by uniform staff, with no single person having the necessary 'ownership'."

It also said relevant information was "also being split over different locations within various police databases," Moore KC said.

The review also identified leads that could be followed up from information already gathered, and noted concerns over Phillips' mental health and the children.

"The children are young and vulnerable due to their ages. Some of the information obtained about Thomas Phillips reveals he is an alcoholic. Taking the children in order to hide them from their mother is not in the best interests of the children. As time passes without any sighting of the children, concern for their welfare mounts. In my view Police are obligated to commit more resource to finding the children, hopefully safe and well...

"The paramount consideration is the safety and welfare of the missing children. In order to finalise this investigation and to achieve the safe return of the children it will be necessary to commit the resources needed to locate them."

From May 2023, the investigation was moved to the Major Crimes Unit at District Headquarters.

One of the the family's campsites. NZ Police / Supplied

The May 2023 sighting

Then, on 28 May 2023, a resident living on the main road out to Marokopa called police on the 105 line and reported a possible sighting of Phillips and his children.

The resident, referred to in the report as Rhonda, said that about 90 minutes earlier a man had knocked on her door and asked for a jump start for his car which he claimed was stuck on a forestry road.

She described him as Caucasian, in his late 30s to early 40s. She said he was wearing a black hat, black/grey shirt, black jeans, and work boots.

She said that he smelled strongly and like someone who had not had a shower in a very long time.

Rhonda and her mother-in-law drove the man along Te Anga Rd to a forestry road, where the man's car was parked. Rhonda took a note of the man's number plate, and said she saw a girl by the car as well as other children inside the car.

She expressed her concern about the man and the children because they seemed to be stuck in the middle of nowhere on a forestry road. Her and her mother-in-law suspected it was Phillips.

Following the report, police dispatched a unit about half an hour after receiving the call, but that unit was diverted to a family harm incident shortly after at a different address on Te Anga Rd. The report noted family harm incidents were usually given priority.

Not long after that, the unit advised no further action was required from police.

There was a brief follow up after this, by an "astute senior constable" but what followed was a "series of unfortunate mis-steps and circumstances" that together "conspired to compound the delay in police properly appreciating and investigating the significance" of the sighting.

There is no evidence that the first unit tasked with the report visited the woman's home or attempted to visit the location of the sighting. Police have not been able to explain to the inquiry why the report was designated as requiring no further action, Moore KC said.

The inquiry found police inaction on the day led to avoidable delays.

It said police should have recognised the sighting was credible, and investigated "more thoroughly and in a more timely way," and had there been no delay, "there might have been a real prospect of locating the children".

Phillips warned police 'would not take him alive'

In July and August 2023, detectives from the new investigation team went to the Phillips family farm to introduce themselves.

During one of the visits, police discussed Phillips' visit to the property in February 2022. Phillips' father said that during that visit Tom had warned that the police would not take him alive.

"The officer in charge at the time told the inquiry that this information materially changed the police assessment of the risk Tom Phillips posed.

"It also materially informed what actions were available to them. From that point on, police undertook no searches without Armed Offenders Squad or Special Tactics Group involvement."

In August, Phillips was also seen by his family on CCTV at his parents' farm, and the following day he was seen at Bunnings in Hamilton and on Kawhia Rd.

This led to him being identified as the offender in an armed robbery in Te Kūiti which happened several months earlier.

"There then followed a surge of activity in the Police investigation," Moore KC said.

Then in October 2024, Phillips and the children were photographed by pig hunters on open farmland near Marokopa.

Moore said NZ Police and the New Zealand Defence Force developed a "comprehensive strategy" using trail cameras and road cameras to narrow down the area the group was operating in. These cameras picked up three further sightings of the group over the next six months.

"While the use of cameras and the drone was successful in narrowing the location of the group and gathering intelligence about their habits, police were becoming increasingly concerned about what might happen if they were involved in a violent confrontation with Tom Phillips.

"Their greatest anxiety centred around avoiding any risk of harm to the children, police or the public."

On July 28 2025, a meeting was held between members of the investigation team, police district management, Technical Operations Group and Special Tactics Group to discuss the next stage of Operation Curly.

Moore KC referred to the minutes of that meeting which said the focus was on "identifying Phillips' resupply location to support STG in safely rescuing the children and arresting Phillips".

The following month there were several burglaries in the area which police believed were committed by Phillips.

Then on 8 September, Phillips died following a shootout with police after they were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of the morning in Piopio.

The 'ripple effect'

In his findings, Moore KC said police had "limited options" to impose constraints on Phillips to "mitigate the risk of a second disappearance".

However, he said that police and Oranga Tamariki did not communicate again from 1 October 2021 until after the second disappearance in December 2021.

He also said police's report of concern to Oranga Tamariki was "commendable", but police should have ensured all information was provided and "critical discussions were ongoing".

In relation to Police action after the second disappearance, he said Police should have identified the serious risk to the welfare of the children from the time they were taken, and they should have developed a proactive investigation strategy at the outset.

"During the first two months, police missed specific opportunities to gather more information about where the children might be."

Operation Curly also should have involved more CIB staffing from the beginning and a review of progress and future options, should have occurred much sooner.

"In the inquiry's view this delay is likely a result of the initial and erroneous assessment that there were no concerns about the children...

"After April 2022, investigation efforts were stepped up incrementally, but slowly, from that starting point. This failed to recognise the seriousness of the risk to the children, and, as time went on, the ongoing harm from being alienated from their mother, siblings and wider families escalated."

He also said the police should have taken some steps "much earlier".

Moore KC said in his report that for the family of the children the four years "represented a long and harrowing ordeal".

"Every day that the children were missing added to a catalogue of fear and worry borne by the children's mother and older sisters. At times they wondered whether they were even alive."

He said Phillips' family also spoke of the "significant toll", and added that the "ripple effect" caused by the uncertainty also spread to those involved in trying to find them.

World.title: Christchurch police close to arresting psychiatric patient before murder - inquest
World.content:
Christchurch police were close to arresting a psychiatric patient for attacking a nurse shortly before he murdered a woman while on community leave from Hillmorton Hospital, an inquest has heard.

Laisa Waka Tunidau was stabbed to death by Zakariye Mohamed Hussein outside her Sockburn home on 25 June 2022.

Hussein was jailed for life with a non-parole period of 13 years in November that year.

He had previously been jailed for more than six years for kidnapping, stabbing and intimidating people across Christchurch in March 2012.

At the time of Waka Tunidau's death, Hussein was allowed to leave Hillmorton on unescorted community leave but failed to return when required.

On Tuesday, the inquest heard a nurse had complained that Hussein had tried to stab her in the neck with a shank in December 2021 but she was able to fend him off.

Before the attack Hussein was said to have been brooding over being declined leave.

Waka Tunidau family lawyer Nikki Pender put to another nurse giving evidence that it had been a serious attack.

"It was potentially a very, very serious assault wasn't it? If she had been taken unawares and he had stabbed her in the neck, it could have been fatal couldn't it? It was that level of severity," Pender said.

The nurse agreed, saying she was aware of the incident and a complaint being made to police.

The inquest heard that police emailed Hillmorton Hospital staff in February 2022 to say they were intending to arrest and charge Hussein and were seeking assistance to ensure it was not too disruptive.

Police then took a further statement from a staff member on 14 June and told them that police were about to arrest Hussein.

Pender said the process took some time, partly because police were under the impression that Hussein was in a secure unit and would not be released into the community.

The nurse who reported the attack said one of the reasons she laid the complaint was because she was concerned that Hussein might be released, Pender said.

The inquest heard that Hussein made a hot cup of coffee and threw it at nurse in 2018.

He was still serving the sentence for his 2012 crimes, so was transferred back to prison.

On the day of Waka Tunidau's murder Hussein was irritable and unhappy about staples being removed from a magazine, telling the nurse who took them out that they were "cruel, not kind".

Another nurse who was working in the unit on 25 June said that it was important to recognise that forensic health care staff were working with patients not prisoners.

"So people being able to go into the community as safely as possible was always something that in pyschiatric nursing was really important because when people aren't in their community it impacts their mental health further," the nurse said.

"For Mr Hussein at that time was there was a significant recognition that being institutionalised and contained within the environment negatively impacted his mental state."

When Hussein was feeling upset or not at a "complete calm baseline", giving him leave to go for a walk or to McDonald's was useful, the nurse said.

The nurse agreed that leave was used therapeutically at times when Hussein was agitated and upset.

Another nurse told the inquest that the unit was under "super stress" at the time of Waka Tunidau's murder.

He said there had been a lot change in systems and staff at the unit, the team was "ragged" and many people had not worked there for long.

Less experienced staff sometimes took on special patients, which was a particularly hard job and a "bit of a nightmare", and was the case at the time of Waka Tunidau's death, the nurse said.

"You've got stressed nurses, some burnt out, some of the time I am too, and everybody is trying to do their best but there are holes in the system," he said.

On Monday, the inquest heard Hussein had left the hospital on 35 occasions and returned without incident between being granted leave in late April 2022 and the day of Waka Tunidau's murder.

Her family has questioned how he was ever assessed as safe enough to leave the hospital on his own.

World.title: 'I understand how that sounds': Police push back on Tom Phillips finding
World.content:
Inquiry into handling of the Tom Phillips says harm overlooked by agencies Checkpoint Download MP3 12m

While Oranga Tamariki is admitting fault and failure in the Tom Phillips case, police are pushing back on the finding that it could have been prevented or ended earlier.

Police Deputy Commissioner Jill Rogers told Checkpoint host Lisa Owen she remains proud of what police investigators did to recover the children.

Phillips died in a shootout with police a year ago, nearly four years after disappearing from Marokopa with his children.

Government ministers apologised after the release of the damning report into the handling of the case on Tuesday afternoon.

Multiple instances of missed opportunities were found, including police failing to begin a search after the disappearance and again after the discovery of Phillips' ute, failing to pass on details about Phillips' alcohol use and concerns about his safety with firearms, and Oranga Tamariki dismissing concerns raised by the children's mother and failing to inform the Family Court of those or the police investigation.

Agencies working together, the inquiry found, could have prevented the children's disappearance and brought them back sooner.

Rogers said the report highlighted "occasions when we didn't get things right, but I will point out that it also highlighted just how complex this investigation was".

She acknowledged that did not excuse police failings in the case, calling the report a "learning document and a lessons identifying document", but pushed back on the idea the children's disappearance could have been prevented or ended early as the report claimed.

"We don't know that there would have been different outcomes. We had an extremely determined father there. He had nothing to lose, and so every activity that we did was couched in the full awareness of the risk that he posed," she said.

"We've publicly said that we accept the recommendations. But we are also aware the report acknowledges the effort and the diligence of those investigators and what they did over those four years.

"The outcomes, we just don't know what, and when it would have ended."

She said police regretted not following up a sighting of Phillips in May 2023, saying that had been a "golden opportunity" to narrow down the area he was in, but "it was never as simple as just going into the bush to get him out".

"It was picked up at a later stage by another officer ... it was too late but we don't know that that changed the outcome or the timing of when we recovered the children."

Authorities could have prevented Tom Phillips disappearing with kids Checkpoint Download MP3 14m

The discovery of Phillips' abandoned ute had been "assumed that that was another staged effort by Tom Phillips to divert us away from his activities".

Owen: "There's a few assumptions going on here, Jill."

Rogers: "There are, and I understand how that sounds when you add them all together. But what I would say is the report also highlights over the four years the extensive work that shows that despite some delays, the activities that the investigative team did do didn't bring up any of the results that people thought or assumed would come from a normal investigation."

Rogers acknowledged it was "stark reading" to see the magnitude of failings but said "this was a complex, unique, and never-anticipated event".

She said that did not justify the mistakes made, and there was "such a degree of sadness amongst those investigators".

Rogers: "Did we get some things wrong? Yes. Did we miss some opportunities? Yes. Were we slow to react to some things? Yes. But would it have changed the outcome? No.

Owen: "How do you know it wouldn't have changed the outcome ... you can't know that."

Rogers: "Yeah, our mission was always to recover the children. That was always our priority, and you know I remain proud of what those investigators did in recovering the children."

Amanda Malu. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Oranga Tamariki chief executive Amanda Malu told RNZ they had "failed the children and the mother and older sisters".

"We did not listen and pay anywhere near as much attention as we should have to what the mother and sisters were telling us, and we didn't speak with our police colleagues anywhere in anywhere near enough detail," she said.

"This is one instance, and it had awful consequences for these children, and I'm deeply sorry about that. I do know that we have made a number of changes since ... that really addresses any concerns around implicit bias and ensures that we are taking the views of all family members into account."

Malu, who was appointed to head Oranga Tamariki in December, said there was still work to do there, "and that's why I am here".

"I understand the concerns, and it simply isn't good enough ... I am seeking some further answers."

She said she had not been chief executive when an affidavit from an older sister of the children was ignored by the social worker who received it.

"I can't speak to why they were ignored. I can tell you though that you know I I am absolutely blown away by their perseverance and the courage that they showed.

"It's not acceptable. We've been down this road before, and I'm not prepared to go down it again. I think we need to step up our game as government departments."
